classical.verse: unnumbered prose at the very end of the chapter, printed page 570 of Bhishagratna volume 1
classical.establishes: That Sushruta carves an explicit exception out of the rule he has just stated: the evening meal may be taken even on undigested daytime food without counting as adhyashana, while the same conduct overnight does count and is answered by fasting the next day. The texts are therefore not uniform on the central timing rule, and the exception is argued from a diurnal physiological claim (the heart unfolded in waking, constricted in sleep) that is internal to the system.
classical.quote: With the dawn of day a man wakes from sleep, and his heart unfolds like a lotus flower, and so remains till sleep folds up his eyelids. Hence, the root principles of the body continue non-humid during the state of waking. Accordingly, a man may partake of a meal at night, even if the food eaten in the day continues till then undigested, without the fear of committing the physical sin of Adhyashanam (super-eating). But the reverse is the case in respect of a similar conduct in the night when man has recourse to sleep and his heart remains constricted in a state of unconsciousness, and the root principles of his body become loose and charged with humidity. Hence, it is beneficial to fast on the following day in the event of the food taken overnight being found to be not properly digested.

modern.title: Similar weight loss with low-energy food combining or balanced diets.
modern.journal: Int J Obes Relat Metab Disord
modern.establishes: Golay and colleagues, International Journal of Obesity 24(4):492-496. Randomised controlled trial, 54 obese inpatients, 6 weeks, energy-matched at 1100 kcal/day: a 'food combining' (dissociated) diet produced no greater weight loss (6.2 kg) than a balanced diet (7.5 kg) and no additional fat loss.
modern.quality: A real randomised controlled trial with a controlled inpatient setting, which is unusually strong for this question. Limitations: small, short, surrogate endpoints, and it tests the Western Hay-style food-combining scheme rather than the specific Ayurvedic samyoga pairs. It is nonetheless the only randomised evidence located bearing on the general claim that keeping foods apart matters independently of their composition, and it is null.

modern.title: Association Between Eating Speed and Metabolic Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
modern.establishes: Yuan and colleagues, Frontiers in Nutrition. Systematic review and meta-analysis, 29 studies, 465,155 subjects: faster eating was associated with metabolic syndrome (OR 1.54), central obesity (OR 1.54), raised blood pressure, low HDL, raised triglycerides and raised fasting glucose. This is directionally consistent with Charaka's 'do not eat too fast' rule.
modern.quality: Large, but the pooled designs are overwhelmingly cross-sectional with self-reported eating speed, concentrated in Japan, China and Korea, with high heterogeneity and only a single randomised trial included. Observational and cannot establish causation; fast eating plausibly marks other behaviours. It supports one of the twelve rules as an association, not as a validated intervention, and says nothing about the other eleven.

modern.title: Time-restricted eating with calorie restriction on weight loss and cardiometabolic risk: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
modern.establishes: Sun and colleagues, European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. Meta-analysis of 8 randomised trials, 579 participants: time-restricted eating combined with calorie restriction reduced body weight, fat mass and waist circumference, but conferred no significant additional benefit over calorie restriction alone on blood pressure, glucose or lipids.
modern.quality: A properly conducted meta-analysis of randomised trials, but small total sample and short durations. Relevant here as the nearest modern analogue of the rule 'eat only after the previous meal is digested': it suggests that restricting the eating window has little effect beyond the energy restriction it produces. It is a comparator, not a test of the Ayurvedic rule, which is symptom-keyed rather than clock-keyed.

modern.title: Viruddha Ahara: A critical view.
modern.establishes: Sabnis, Ayu 33(3):332-336, 'Viruddha Ahara: A critical view'. The most-cited indexed paper on the topic. It restates the classical categories and proposes biochemical analogies.
modern.quality: A NARRATIVE REVIEW. It reports no original experiments, no systematic search and no evidence appraisal. It is the textbook example of the pattern this project was set up to flag: classical doctrine restated in modern vocabulary, a mechanism gestured at, no data. It should be cited as evidence of what the field says, never as evidence that viruddha ahara causes disease.

modern.establishes: 'Insights into food incompatibilities: Ayurveda and modern perspectives', Journal of Drug Research in Ayurvedic Sciences 9(Suppl 1):S30-S36. A review searching PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, MEDLINE and the AYUSH and NAMASTE portals from 2000 to 2024, which reports that empirical validation of viruddha ahara is largely absent and that the biochemical mechanisms of combinations such as fish with milk or heated honey remain unexplored.
modern.quality: A review rather than primary research, and published in a supplement of a journal with limited indexing. Recorded because it is the most recent attempt at a comprehensive search and because its own conclusion is the honest one: after searching Ayurvedic and biomedical databases together, the authors find the evidence base essentially empty. Its value here is as a negative finding, not as support.

modern.establishes: Shapla and colleagues, BMC Chemistry, on 5-hydroxymethylfurfural levels in honey and other foods and effects on bees and human health. Establishes that HMF forms in honey on heating and rises steeply with temperature, and reviews reported mutagenic, genotoxic and cytotoxic effects alongside reported beneficial ones.
modern.quality: An analytical-chemistry review, not a clinical study. It is included because it is the only retrievable empirical thread touching the classical prohibition on heated honey, and it must be reported carefully: HMF formation on heating is a real and measured phenomenon, but whether HMF at dietary concentrations causes human harm is contested in the source itself, and HMF is present in many ordinary heated foods including bread and dried fruit. This is a partial parallel, not a vindication of 'heated honey induces death'.

modern.title: Association between eating rate and obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
modern.establishes: Ohkuma and colleagues, International Journal of Obesity. Systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 published epidemiological studies searching MEDLINE, EMBASE and CINAHL: mean BMI difference between people who ate quickly and people who ate slowly 1.78 kg/m2 (95% CI 1.53 to 2.04), pooled odds ratio for obesity in quick eaters 2.15 (95% CI 1.84 to 2.51). The authors note significant heterogeneity.
modern.quality: A second, independent meta-analysis of the eating-rate association, with a different study set and a different outcome from the Yuan 2021 entry, which is why it is worth carrying separately: the association replicates across reviews. But interventional studies were excluded by design, so the pooled evidence is observational, eating rate is self-reported in the pooled studies, and the review establishes association only. It is NOT a test of ahara vidhi vidhana. It tests one separable behaviour that the classical rule set also recommends, which is a different claim, and it says nothing about the other eleven rules or about Charaka's stated reason for this one.

modern.title: A structured literature review on the role of mindfulness, mindful eating and intuitive eating in changing eating behaviours: effectiveness and associated potential mechanisms.
modern.establishes: Warren, Smith and Ashwell, Nutrition Research Reviews. Structured literature review of 68 publications on mindfulness, mindful eating and intuitive eating: 23 interventions in overweight or obese populations, 29 in normal-weight populations, 16 observational studies. The reviewers report that mindfulness-based approaches appear most effective for binge eating, emotional eating and eating in response to external cues, that there is a lack of compelling evidence for their effectiveness in weight management, and that the evidence for intuitive eating is limited to date.
modern.quality: A structured but not systematic review, broad in scope by the authors' own statement, pooling heterogeneous interventions and measurement tools. Recorded because it is the paper that would have to carry any claim about Charaka's 'eat with attention concentrated on the act', and because its own conclusion is mixed rather than supportive: the effects are on disordered eating patterns, not on the outcomes the classical rule is about. Like the eating-rate reviews it tests a separable modern construct, mindful eating, which is not the same object as tanmana bhunjita inside a doshic rationale. It cannot be cited as validation of the classical rule.

records.title: Ama and its formation
records.summary: Ama is the Ayurvedic name for the product of failed digestion: material that has been taken in but not properly transformed, and which is held to become a cause of disease rather than a source of nourishment. The classical mechanism is straightforward in outline. When agni is weakened by fasting, overeating, incompatible or heavy food, mistimed therapy, illness, seasonal mismatch or suppression of natural urges, food is not digested, and the undigested residue is said to turn sour and to act like a poison. Charaka describes this material combining with each of the doshas to produce their characteristic diseases, entering urine, stool and the tissues, and in acute form producing the conditions visuchika and alasaka, which he says physicians call ama-visha, the poison of undigested food, because the symptoms resemble poisoning. Later texts, principally Vagbhata, reify ama into a general morbid substance that blocks the channels and adheres to doshas to make them sama, with a standard ten-sign checklist (heaviness, lassitude, loss of appetite, coated tongue, malaise and so on) distinguishing sama from nirama states. Ama has no stated composition, location outside the gut in the earliest sources, or means of detection other than that symptom list.
records.evidenceState: Ama has no operational definition that anyone outside the tradition could apply, and no validated biological correlate. Every ama measurement located in the peer-reviewed literature is a symptom checklist assembled from the same classical verses that define the concept, which makes validation circular: the instrument agrees with the doctrine because it was built from it. Three studies located here attempt to break that circle, and none succeeded cleanly. The Ama Assessment Instrument correlated with ESR at r=0.287 at baseline, falling to 0.160 by the third follow-up, and with DAS-28 at r=0.231 at baseline (PMID 36822147), weak enough that the authors reframed the weakness as evidence of independence, and a later group abandoned those comparators entirely (PMID 42497784). The stronger correlation with CDAI (r=0.645) in that later study is the best result located but comes from 38 RA patients and against a composite that is itself largely subjective, so it may reflect general illness severity; that same group's proposal to merge the Ama-score and CDAI into one composite is difficult to reconcile with the score measuring something CDAI does not, which is the gatherer's reading of the proposal and not a position either author states. The only attempt located at an observer-independent measure, tongue-coating photography scored by five clinicians, failed its pre-specified analysis outright (PMID 42142499) and survives only through post-hoc regional subgroups. A fourth study is sometimes read as relevant and is not an attempt on the circularity: the untargeted metabolomics of RA patients on Ayurvedic treatment (PMID 38972279) neither defines nor scores ama, so it cannot test an ama measure. It is recorded above because it is the one open-ended biochemical method located in this area, and it produced no ama-specific signature. The mechanistic correlates named in Ayurvedic writing are not addressable from that writing alone. Free radicals were proposed in 1999 (PMID 22556911) with no data. Gut dysbiosis is proposed in narrative review (PMID 33281390), which argues from the classical diet rules for amavata to published effects of individual foods without measuring ama or microbiota in anyone. Endotoxin and intestinal permeability are invoked by analogy to a primary literature that the Ayurvedic sources do not cite and that does not mention ama: the metabolic-endotoxemia work, which is a mouse study (PMID 17456850), and the zonulin barrier-function review (PMID 21248165). Those two are recorded above so that the analogy is at least checkable. No study located in the searches recorded under gatheringNotes measures endotoxin, permeability, dysbiosis or an oxidative marker against any ama assessment, and the searches that were run are named there so the limits of that statement are visible. The concept also carries an unresolved internal problem that the modern literature located here does not engage: Charaka's ama, as rendered by his public-domain translator, is largely literal undigested food and undigested rasa in the gut, whereas the systemic circulating toxin of modern Ayurvedic writing owes more to Vagbhata and to twentieth-century reinterpretation. A second problem, whether ama names anything beyond the consequences of weak agni, is recorded under notKnown rather than asserted here, because no source located poses it. What this record supports is narrow. Ama is the traditional name for a symptom cluster of heaviness, lassitude, anorexia, coated tongue and impaired digestion; that cluster can be scored by a single examiner using a checklist derived from the classical signs; whether two examiners scoring the same patient would agree is not known, which is notKnown item 4; and nothing located here establishes ama as a distinct substance or process rather than a name for the cluster. The record makes no claim that the concept is clinically usable or that the cluster tracks any distinct underlying process, because it holds no evidence that would support either.

contested.question: What is ama? A product of failed digestion, or the doshas themselves?
positions: Undigested or improperly formed rasa retained in the amashaya because agni is weak. This is Ashtanga Hridaya Su.13/25 and the standard modern teaching.

Greatly increased doshas that mix with one another and thereby become toxic, on the analogy of poison arising in stored kodrava grain. Vagbhata gives this at Su.13/26 as an alternative immediately after the first definition, so the tradition records the disagreement without resolving it.

In Charaka the term is used more loosely still, for literally undigested food passed by a vitiated grahani (Ci.15/55-56) and for ama-rasa spreading through the body (Ci.15/74). No single referent is fixed.

contested.question: Is ama a localized gut phenomenon or a systemic circulating entity?
positions: Charaka's clearest statements are gut-localized: food not digested in the stomach, food adhering to the pakvashaya, undigested matter discharged in stool.
Charaka also states that the poison enters urine, stool and the dhatus, and that ama-rasa may spread over the whole body requiring fasting and pachana, which supports a systemic reading.

Modern Ayurvedic writing treats ama as unambiguously systemic, blocking srotas anywhere in the body. This is the reading that underwrites all the ama-in-rheumatoid-arthritis research, and it is a stronger claim than the earliest source clearly supports.

contested.question: Does the Ama score measure ama, or does it measure disease activity?
positions: Pandey and colleagues (PMID 36822147) argue the instrument is an independent disease-status marker precisely because it correlates only weakly with ESR and DAS-28.
Wagh and colleagues (PMID 42497784) found it correlates strongly with CDAI (r=0.645) and propose merging the Ama-score and CDAI into a single composite measure.
Wagh and Raut (PMID 38056374) note it has never been tested in any non-rheumatic ama-dominant disease, so its specificity to ama rather than to inflammatory illness is unknown.

contested.question: Is coated tongue a valid sign of ama?
positions: It is the sign most relied on in clinical practice and is treated as the canonical external marker of ama.

The only quantitative test of this located here (PMID 42142499) found no significant correlation between whole-tongue coating index and Ama score in its pre-specified analysis; only a posterior-middle sextant subgroup correlated.

Tongue coating is independently determined by oral microbial biofilm, hygiene, smoking, hyposalivation and medication, none of which was controlled in that study, so even the positive subgroup finding has an obvious alternative explanation.

contested.question: Is ama-visha a distinct toxic entity or a descriptive label?
positions: Charaka Vi.2 states plainly that physicians call it the poison of undigested food because its symptoms resemble poisoning, which is an explicitly analogical naming.
Much modern writing treats ama-visha as a claim about actual toxicity, and builds endotoxin and free-radical analogies on it. The classical text does not make that claim.

notKnown: What ama is, in any material sense. No composition, no chemical class, no proposed molecule has been isolated or measured. Candidates named in reviews (free radicals, endotoxin/LPS, advanced glycation end products, undigested macromolecules, dysbiotic metabolites) have not been tested against any ama assessment in the literature located here.
Whether anything measurable actually accumulates in a person judged sama and clears in one judged nirama. No before/after biochemical study of ama-pachana treatment has been located.

What srotorodha, channel obstruction, corresponds to. This is the load-bearing step converting a digestive failure into systemic disease, and nothing located specifies it. That absence is now a searched one rather than an assumed one, which is what the revision was asked to establish: a PubMed search on 2026-10-06 for 'srotorodha' returned no records at all, and a search for 'srotas' returned 21, whose titles are conceptual appraisals of particular srotas (for example PMID 23723638, a critical appraisal of doshavaha srotas, and PMID 22131705 on herbs acting on mutravaha srotas) and disease-specific case reports; none reports a measurement of channel obstruction. The search did not cover transliteration variants, Sanskrit-language sources, the AYUSH Research Portal or DHARA, or the many Ayurvedic journals that PubMed does not index, so this remains the result of a bounded search and not an established absence. No one has been identified as having attempted to specify the step.

Whether ama assessment is reproducible between examiners. No interrater reliability figure for an ama score was located in the PubMed searches recorded under gatheringNotes; the only agreement statistic found (0.73-0.76) was for tongue-photograph coating scores, not for ama itself. This gap is load-bearing: the record's description of ama as a scorable symptom cluster assumes only that one examiner can apply the checklist, and says nothing about two.

The prevalence and distribution of ama scores in healthy populations. One study included 20 healthy volunteers (PMID 42497784) and found their scores indistinguishable from treated RA patients in remission, which is a single small data point and the only normative information located.

Whether ama scores respond to non-Ayurvedic treatment. If a DMARD-induced remission lowers the ama score as much as ama-directed therapy does, the score is tracking inflammation rather than ama; the remission group in PMID 42497784 was on treatment but the question was not framed or tested. The one blinded trial located in the paradigm ama disease, individualized classical Ayurveda against methotrexate and their combination (PMID 21617554), found no statistically significant difference between arms on DAS28-CRP and ACR response, but it recorded no ama score at all, so it does not answer this question either. It does show that the trial design the question needs is achievable.

Whether the sama/nirama sequencing rule, that ama must be digested before nourishing or oleating therapy, actually improves outcomes. This is one of the most consequential practical rules in Ayurveda and no comparative trial of the sequencing itself has been located.

Whether the classical acute ama disorders map onto anything modern. The two public-domain translators are the source of the modern equations, and they do not agree. Kaviratna's Charaka renders Visuchika as cholera and Alasaka as Tympanites in his running text (Lesson XIX, printed p. 217) and repeats both in his own footnotes at Vimanasthana 2 (printed p. 466, each marked '- T.'). Bhishagratna's Sushruta also renders Visuchika as 'cholera' (Sutrasthana XXI, 'Sthana-Samshrayam', printed p. 207), but the occurrences of Alasaka located in his translation render it 'flatulence' (Sutrasthana XLII, printed p. 387) or leave it untranslated, so the alasaka-tympanitis equation should be attributed to Kaviratna alone. No examination of either equation was located in the searches recorded here, and both are probably artefacts of early-twentieth-century translation practice.

Whether ama is one thing. The concept is applied to acute food poisoning, chronic dyspepsia, coated tongue, rheumatoid inflammation and general malaise; nothing establishes that these share a mechanism rather than a vocabulary.

Whether ama is a category distinct from agnimandya at all, that is, whether the concept does any work beyond naming the consequences of weak agni. The question can be put from the record's own quoted material: Charaka's list of the signs of indigestion at Ci.15/44-45 already contains 'disgust for food' and 'lassitude of the limbs', which are aruchi and alasya among the ten sama-dosha signs by which ama is identified at Ashtanga Hridaya Su.13/23-24, and a third of those ten, apakti, is impaired digestion itself, so a checklist built from those signs cannot separate ama from weak agni. No source located in this gathering, classical or modern, poses the question, so it is recorded here as unaddressed rather than as a dispute between positions. Nothing in this record answers it.

What a test of the endotoxin, intestinal-permeability or dysbiosis correlates would consist of. The primary literature these analogies borrow from (PMID 17456850, in mice; PMID 21248165, a review) does not mention ama, and the Ayurvedic writing that invokes them (for example PMID 33281390) measures neither ama nor any marker. The minimum the claim would require is a marker measured in the same patients who are scored sama and nirama, and no study doing that was located.

components.gloss: Weakening of the digestive fire, the stated precondition. Charaka lists the causes: fasting, indigestible food, overeating, incompatible combinations, unassimilable, heavy, cold, excessively dry or spoiled food, errors in purgation, emesis and oleation, debility from disease, mismatch of place, time and season, and suppression of natural urges.
The improperly formed first product of digestion. Vagbhata's definition makes ama specifically the rasa dhatu left unformed and retained in the amashaya.
The souring or fermenting of retained undigested material. Charaka: food that is not digested 'causes acidity and even becomes poison'.

The acute toxic form, named because its presentation mimics poisoning. In Charaka this arises from incompatible food, eating on top of an undigested meal, or overloading, and is stated to be incurable because the indicated treatments are mutually contradictory.

A dosha to which ama has adhered, held to behave differently from the same dosha in its pure (nirama) state and to require ama-directed treatment first. The sama/nirama distinction governs the sequencing of therapy.
Obstruction of the bodily channels by ama, offered as the mechanism by which a gut-level failure produces systemic disease. It is the least specified step in the whole chain.

The clinical checklist for ama: channel obstruction, loss of strength, heaviness, torpor of vata, lethargy, impaired digestion, excessive salivation, retention of wastes, anorexia and exhaustion (Ashtanga Hridaya Su.13/23-24). Coated tongue is the sign most used in practice.
The therapeutic response: fasting or lightening, then drugs that digest ama without stimulating appetite, before any nourishing or oleating treatment is given.

The paradigm ama disease, in which ama and vata together lodge in the joints. Described in Madhava Nidana ch. 25 and used in nearly all modern ama research as the clinical model, usually equated with rheumatoid arthritis.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's Lesson XV, verses 41-43 (cited in the modern vulgate as roughly 15/42-44)
classical.establishes: The complete classical etiology of ama in one passage: the list of agni-impairing causes, the failure of digestion, souring, and the transition to a poison-like state. This is the primary formation verse.
classical.quote: From abstention from all food, from eating food that is indigestible, from eating to excess, from eating food consisting of inharmonious ingredients, from eating food that is not assimilable, or is heavy, or cold, or excessively dry (unoily), or vitiated, from errors in the administration of purgatives, emetics, and oils, from affliction (i.e., weakness, emaciation, &c.,) by diseases, from absence of harmony in respect of place (habitat), time (age), and season, from suppression of the urgings (of nature), the (digestive) fire is vitiated. The vitiated fire cannot digest food that is even light. The food, again, that is not digested, causes acidity and even becomes poison.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's Lesson XV, aphorisms 44-45 (this symptom list is printed immediately above the number 44-45, which also covers the 'terrible poison' sentence quoted in the following entry)
classical.establishes: Charaka's own list of the signs of indigestion, that is, of agnimandya with food still undigested. It is quoted here because it overlaps the later sama-dosha checklist by which ama is identified: 'disgust for food' is aruchi, 'lassitude of the limbs' is alasya, and the checklist's apakti is impaired digestion itself. That overlap is the textual reason the question of whether ama is a category distinct from agnimandya can be asked at all; the record does not answer it and records it under notKnown.
classical.quote: The following are the symptoms of indigestion (of the food taken): flatulence of the stomach, langour of the body, headache, swoons, vertigo, pains in the back and the waist, yawns, lassitude of the limbs, thirst, fever, vomiting, dysentery (white flux), disgust for food, and absence of transformation into healthy stools.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's Lesson XV, verses 44-48
classical.establishes: The dosha-combination doctrine (what later becomes sama vata, sama pitta, sama kapha) and the claim that ama distributes into excreta and into the dhatus, which is the classical warrant for treating ama as a systemic and not merely a gastric problem.
classical.quote: The food in the stomach that is not digested is a terrible poison. Combining with excited bile, this undigested food, which becomes poison, produces burning of the skin, thirst, diseases of the mouth, sour bile, and other ailments born of (excited bile). Combining with (excited) phlegm, it produces phthisis, inflammation of the Schneiderian membrane, gonorrhoea, and other diseases born of (excited phlegm). Combining with the (excited) wind, it produces diverse diseases that are born of the (excited) wind. When it goes into the urine, that poison causes diseases of the urine. When it goes into the stools, it causes diseases of the abdomen. When combined with 'Rasa' and the rest, it produces diverse diseases born of 'Rasa' and the rest.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's Lesson XV, verses 55-56
classical.establishes: The anatomical seat and the one place where Kaviratna's translation glosses the term 'Ama' explicitly. Note that here ama is literally undigested food passed in the stool, not an abstract toxin.
classical.quote: The duct called 'Grahani' is the seat of the digestive fire, and because it takes the food that is eaten, therefore is it called 'Grahani' (taker). It is placed above the (region of the) navel. According to the strength (or weakness) of the (digestive) fire, it becomes extended or contracted. It holds the food in its undigested state. After digestion, it lets out the digested food through its lower opening. When the digestive fire is weak, the 'Grahani' becomes vitiated. It then discharges only undigested food (called Ama).

classical.verse: Kaviratna's Lesson XV, aphorism 74 (corrected in the 2026-10-06 revision from '74-75'; the quoted material ends with his aphorism 74, and his 75, on correcting the amashaya, is not quoted)
classical.establishes: The treatment logic and, importantly, the term ama-rasa spreading through the body: the point at which Charaka's gut-level ama becomes a circulating entity. Also fixes the classical distinction between deepana and pachana drugs.
classical.quote: If undigested food adheres to the 'Pakkasaya', it should be expelled by such drugs as are called 'Dipana'. When the 'ama Rasa' (i.e., the undigested juice of the food taken) spreads over the whole body, fasting and the administration of 'Pachana' (i.e., drugs which assist in digesting undigested food, without increasing the appetite) are prescribable.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorisms 17-18 (corrected in the 2026-10-06 revision from '17-19'; the quoted material ends with his 18, and his 19 continues the alasaka description and is not quoted). Cited in the modern vulgate as roughly Vi.2/10-11.
classical.establishes: The two named acute ama disorders and their mechanisms. The cholera and tympanitis equations attached to this passage are the translator's voice, not Charaka's, and belong to Kaviratna alone: he footnotes his aphorism 17 with "'Visuchika' is identified with the modern cholera. Its chief symptoms, as here declared, are vomiting and purging. - T." and his aphorism 18 with "The disease called Alasaka has been identified with Tympanitis. - T." (both printed p. 466), and he puts the same equations in his running text at Lesson XIX, printed p. 217: "Diseases of the Ama or stomach are of two kinds. They are 1. Alasaka or Tympanites, and 2. Visuchi or Visuchika, i. e., Cholera." These are early and unreliable equations worth flagging as the translator's own.
classical.quote: Physicians say that the diseases born of undigested food are of two kinds. These are Visuchika and Alasaka. Of these, that disorder born of undigested food should be known as Visuchika which has an upward and downward tendency of the kind already referred to. We shall now explain what is meant by Alasaka. Of one that is weak, of a weak digestive fire, and of excess of phlegm, that suppresses the urgings of wind, urine, and stools, and that takes food that is solid, heavy, beyond measure, unmoist, cold and dry, such food and drink, oppressed by wind, and having its outlets of escape closed up by phlegm, become exceedingly compressed, and in consequence of their movelessness, lose the power of escaping out (of the system).

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorism 20 (cited in the modern vulgate as Vi.2/12)
classical.establishes: The ama-visha concept in Charaka's own terms, and crucially its basis: the naming is explicitly by resemblance of symptoms to poisoning, not by any claim about the substance itself. This is the single most important verse for reading ama honestly.
classical.quote: Again, of one that takes such food as is compounded of hostile ingredients, or that takes food after a previous stuffing of the stomach with food, or that takes food anew before the food taken previously has been digested, the (excited) faults are spoken of by physicians as 'the poison of undigested food,' in consequence of their symptoms being similar to those of poison. When such has been the case, it becomes incurable, in consequence of the rapidity of its action and the hostile character of the treatment (that is deducible from the ordinances).

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorism 16 (cited in the modern vulgate as Vi.2/9)
classical.establishes: That the classical model already treats psychological state, inactivity and sleep loss as sufficient to cause indigestion independent of the food itself. Often cited as the earliest gut-brain statement in the corpus, though the text makes no mechanistic claim.
classical.quote: Even food that is prescribable and that is taken according to proper measure is not digested in consequence of anxiety, grief, fear, wrath, misery, (the inactivity of continuous) lying down, and wakefulness.

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no Sanskrit verse numbers in this passage, only his chapter and section headings; the passage is on printed p. 207 of Vol. I (Sutrasthanam), the page carrying the running head '208 THE SUSHRUTA SAMHITA. [Chap. XXI.' immediately after it. No vulgate verse number is asserted.
classical.establishes: Added in the 2026-10-06 revision to make the record's claim about colonial-era disease equations addressable in Sushruta as well as Charaka. Bhishagratna renders Visuchika as 'cholera' in his running text, so the visuchika-cholera equation is shared by both public-domain translators. He does not share the other half: the occurrences of Alasaka located in his translation render it 'flatulence' (Sutrasthana XLII, printed p. 387: 'Largely and exclusively partaken of, it brings on cough, dyspnoea, flatulence (Alasaka), vomiting...') or leave it untranslated in a list, so the alasaka-tympanitis equation is Kaviratna's alone.
classical.quote: These humours, confined in the abdomen, give rise to Gulma (abdominal glands) tumours, internal abscesses (Vidradhi), abdominal dropsy, impaired digestion in the bowels, constipation (Anaha), cholera (Visuchika) and dysentery.
classical.translator: Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (Vol. I, 1907), public domain

classical.establishes: Vagbhata's definition, which is the one modern textbooks use: through weakness of agni the first dhatu (rasa) is not properly formed, remains vitiated and is retained in the amashaya, and this is called ama. This narrows Charaka's looser 'undigested food' into a specific claim about the first tissue.

The competing classical account, given by Vagbhata himself in the next verse: that ama is produced when greatly increased doshas mix with one another, on the analogy of poison arising in stored kodrava grain. That Vagbhata records two accounts side by side is the clearest evidence that the tradition did not settle what ama is.

The ten signs of sama dosha that constitute the operational definition of ama in clinical practice: srotorodha (channel obstruction), balabhramsha (loss of strength), gaurava (heaviness), anilamudhata (torpor of vata), alasya (lethargy), apakti (impaired digestion), nishtheeva (excess salivation), malasanga (retention of wastes), aruchi (anorexia) and klama (exhaustion), with their opposites defining nirama.

The standard samprapti of amavata: mandagni produced by unctuous, cold, heavy and sluggish food, formation of ama, and the concurrent movement of ama and vata into the trika and the joints producing stiffness. This is the source of the disease model used by essentially all modern ama research.

modern.title: Development and validation of an ama instrument for assessing the disease activity on the basis of constitutional features in Amavata (Rheumatoid Arthritis).
modern.establishes: Development and clinical testing of a ten-item Ama Assessment Instrument in 79 patients with rheumatoid arthritis. Correlation with ESR was 0.287 at baseline falling to 0.160 by the third follow-up, and with DAS-28 was 0.231 at baseline. The authors nonetheless argue the score is an independent disease-status marker.
modern.quality: Empirical and the most-cited ama instrument study located here, but the headline numbers do not support the headline claim. Correlations of 0.16-0.29 are weak, and the authors' interpretation, that weak correlation with established measures shows the instrument captures something they miss, is equally consistent with it capturing noise or general malaise. Items are drawn from the same classical checklist used to diagnose ama, so textual validation is circular by construction.

modern.title: Aam assessment instrument for disease activity in Aamavata: Scope and challenges.
modern.establishes: A published commentary on the above instrument, calling for joint counts to be added, warning about the limitations of patient-reported outcome measures, and noting that the instrument has not been validated for any non-rheumatic ama-dominant disease.
modern.quality: Commentary, not data. Valuable as an in-field acknowledgement that the leading ama instrument is not yet reliable, specific or reproducible, and that ama-specific features have not been adequately developed.

modern.title: Systemic Ama assessment and Clinical Disease Activity in patients with Amavata (Rheumatoid arthritis).
modern.establishes: Ama-score compared against the Clinical Disease Activity Index in treatment-naive RA (n=13), RA in remission (n=25) and healthy volunteers (n=20). Spearman r between Ama-score and CDAI was 0.645. The paper states explicitly that the Ama-score did not correlate well with DAS or ESR, which is why CDAI was substituted. Ama-scores in the remission group did not differ from healthy volunteers.
modern.quality: Small empirical study, and honest about the failure that motivated it. The 0.645 correlation is the strongest number located in the ama literature, but CDAI is itself built largely from patient and physician global assessments and tender/swollen joint counts, so a symptom checklist correlating with it may be measuring illness severity rather than ama. Group A n=13 is very small. The comparison against healthy volunteers is the only genuine discriminant-validity element located anywhere in this literature.

modern.title: Tongue coating, severity of Ama, and disease activity in patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis: A pilot study.
modern.establishes: Pilot study of tongue coating as a proxy for ama in 22 RA patients, scored from smartphone photographs by five clinicians using the Winkel Tongue Coating Index. The pre-specified correlations failed: WTCI against CDAI r = -0.084 (p=0.71) and WTCI against Ama-score r = -0.161 (p=0.47). Only a post-hoc regional analysis of the posterior-middle sextant reached significance (r=0.479 against Ama-score, r=0.439 against CDAI). Inter-rater agreement was 0.73-0.76.
modern.quality: Empirical and unusually transparent about a negative primary result, which deserves credit. But n=22, the positive findings are post-hoc subgroup analyses of tongue regions, and the abstract's claim of a 'positive association' rests on those rather than on the pre-specified test. Tongue coating is also a known microbial biofilm phenomenon with its own determinants (oral hygiene, smoking, saliva flow, medication), none of which were controlled. This is the closest thing to an objective ama measurement located here, and it did not work as specified.

modern.title: A clinical study on the role of ama in relation to Grahani Roga and its management by Kalingadi Ghanavati and Tryushnadi Ghrita.
modern.establishes: Three-arm clinical study in 66 patients with grahani roga, assessing the role of ama and treating with Kalingadi Ghanavati, Tryushnadi Ghrita or both, with the combination reported as superior.
modern.quality: Open-label, no placebo arm, outcomes scored on rogabala/dehabala/agnibala/chetasabala, all investigator-rated ordinal scales derived from classical categories. No objective endpoint, no biomarker of ama, no blinding. Illustrates the standard design of this literature.

modern.title: Possible Correlates of Free Radicals and Free Radical Mediated Disorders in Ayurveda with Special Referance to Bhutagni Vyapara and Ama at molecular Level.
modern.establishes: An explicit proposal that ama, arising from disordered bhutagni function, corresponds to free radicals and free-radical-mediated damage.
modern.quality: Narrative and speculative. No data of any kind. It is the archetype of the genre described in this project's reconnaissance: it restates classical doctrine in modern vocabulary, asserts a correlate, calls for research, and stops. Cited here precisely because it is the most-invoked 'modern correlate' of ama and no test of it was located.

modern.title: Clinical metabolomics investigation of rheumatoid arthritis patients receiving ayurvedic whole system intervention.
modern.establishes: Clinical metabolomics of rheumatoid arthritis patients receiving a whole-system Ayurvedic intervention, the closest thing located to an untargeted search for metabolic signatures in an ama-model disease.
modern.quality: Exploratory metabolomics in a small uncontrolled cohort. It does not define ama, does not measure an ama score, and cannot attribute any metabolite shift to ama rather than to the intervention, the disease course or diet change. It is therefore not an attempt to test an ama measure and is not counted as one in evidenceState. Relevant as the only study located in this area using an open biochemical method rather than a symptom checklist, and it produced no ama biomarker.

modern.title: Double-blind, randomized, controlled, pilot study comparing classic ayurvedic medicine, methotrexate, and their combination in rheumatoid arthritis.
modern.establishes: Double-blind, randomized, double-dummy pilot trial comparing individualized classical Ayurvedic treatment, methotrexate, and their combination in 43 seropositive RA patients over 36 weeks (MTX plus Ayurvedic placebo n=14, Ayurveda plus MTX placebo n=12, Ayurveda plus MTX n=17). From the abstract: 'There were no statistically significant differences among the 3 groups on the efficacy measures,' with ACR20 of 86% for MTX, 100% for Ayurveda and 82% for the combination, and DAS28-CRP change of -2.4, -1.7 and -2.4. The authors conclude that 'all 3 treatments were approximately equivalent in efficacy, within the limits of a pilot study.'
modern.quality: Added in the 2026-10-06 revision; its absence was a real gap, since it is the one blinded, placebo-controlled randomized trial located in the paradigm ama disease while three open-label investigator-scored studies were included. Its value here is methodological rather than evidential about ama: it demonstrates that classical individualized Ayurvedic treatment can be blinded and double-dummied, and it found no separation between arms at n=43, which is a pilot and underpowered for equivalence. It recorded no ama score and does not use the concept as an outcome, so it cannot settle notKnown item 6, which asks whether an ama score falls under non-Ayurvedic treatment. An erratum (J Clin Rheumatol 2011 Oct) and a published comment (J Clin Rheumatol 2013;19(4):227) are attached to the record in PubMed and were not retrieved.

modern.title: Therapeutic influence of some dietary articles on gut microbiota in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis (Amavata) - A review.
modern.establishes: Narrative review arguing that the classical pathya (dietary rules) for amavata act on the gut microbiota of RA patients. From the abstract: 'Amavata is a chronic immune-inflammatory systemic disorder caused by the formation of Ama and its association with Vata at Kaphasthana (joints) and can be simulated with rheumatoid arthritis (RA)... Increased inflammatory status in RA is suggestive of gut dysbiosis involving gut microbiota (GM),' concluding that 'Pathya Ahara mentioned for Amavata have a direct link with GM of RA patients.'
modern.quality: Added in the 2026-10-06 revision so that the record's claim about dysbiosis-as-ama is attached to an actual source rather than invoked in the abstract. It is a review of texts and of other people's pharmacology papers: it measures no patient, scores no ama, and assays no microbiota. The 'direct link' in its conclusion is an argument by assembly, from classical diet lists to published anti-inflammatory effects of individual foods, with the ama step never measured. It is evidence of what the field asserts, not evidence for the assertion.

modern.title: Metabolic endotoxemia initiates obesity and insulin resistance.
modern.establishes: The primary source of the metabolic-endotoxemia hypothesis, in mice. From the abstract: 'we have identified bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) as a triggering factor... a 4-week high-fat diet chronically increased plasma LPS concentration two to three times, a threshold that we have defined as metabolic endotoxemia,' and continuous LPS infusion for 4 weeks reproduced weight gain, raised fasted glycemia and insulinemia, adipose inflammation and hepatic insulin resistance, while CD14 mutant mice 'resisted most of the LPS and high-fat diet-induced features of metabolic diseases.'
modern.quality: Added in the 2026-10-06 revision. Cited for one purpose only: the record previously named endotoxin as a proposed correlate of ama without citing the literature that would have to be engaged, which made the claim unfalsifiable. This is a mouse study in diabetes and obesity. It does not mention ama, Ayurveda, or any symptom checklist, and nothing in it supports or refutes the ama analogy. Its presence here makes the analogy addressable, not supported.

modern.title: Zonulin and its regulation of intestinal barrier function: the biological door to inflammation, autoimmunity, and cancer.
modern.establishes: The standard review of the intestinal-permeability mechanism that the 'leaky gut' version of the ama analogy draws on. From the abstract: 'Zonulin is the only physiological modulator of intercellular tight junctions described so far that is involved in trafficking of macromolecules and, therefore, in tolerance/immune response balance. When the finely tuned zonulin pathway is deregulated in genetically susceptible individuals, both intestinal and extraintestinal autoimmune, inflammatory, and neoplastic disorders can occur.'
modern.quality: Added in the 2026-10-06 revision for the same reason as PMID 17456850: the record invoked intestinal permeability without citing it. A single-author physiology review, not primary data, and the zonulin pathway's identity and assay specificity have themselves been disputed in the barrier-function literature, which this record has not surveyed. It makes no reference to ama. Cited to make the analogy checkable.

records.title: Asatmyendriyartha-samyoga (unwholesome contact of the senses with their objects)
records.summary: Asatmyendriyartha-samyoga is the third of Charaka's three general causes of disease: pathological contact between a sense organ and its object. The scheme is formal in the sense that the same small set of failure modes is applied to each of the five senses in turn. The sense-by-sense verses enumerate four modes, excessive contact (atiyoga), absent contact (ayoga), deficient or sparing contact (hinayoga) and perverse contact (mithyayoga), where perverse means contact with objects that are hostile, repulsive, frightening or out of season. The summary verse then counts three rather than four, and this record does not resolve that discrepancy: it is recorded under contested and under notKnown rather than smoothed over by merging ayoga and hinayoga. Charaka works the modes through sense by sense: sounds too loud or too faint or terrifying, touch withheld or excessive or untimely, sights too bright or too minute or seen in darkness, tastes taken in excess or wholly abstained from or combined against habit, smells too keen or too faint or putrid. The diseases arising this way are given a name of their own, aindriyaka. The concept defines a harmful exposure as one that does not suit the particular organism, satmya being habituated suitability, which makes the judgement individual rather than absolute.
records.evidenceState: This concept rests on classical exegesis. The classical base, stated precisely rather than by a citation count, is three loci in Charaka: the general statement at Sutra Sthana 8/10 in Kaviratna's numbering, the three-causes elaboration at Sutra Sthana 11/37 in standard numbering, and one continuous block at Sharira Sthana 1/125-136 in Kaviratna's numbering (1/118-129 standard). Twelve of the fourteen entries in the classical array resolve into those three loci, two of the twelve are Kaviratna's own translator's notes rather than text, one further entry is a bare pointer to standard-numbering locations and one is explicitly marked unsourced. The locus audit is set out in gatheringNotes. Earlier wording called this the thinnest of the four concepts in the cluster without saying thin in what, which was fair criticism. What is thin is not the Charaka attestation, which is a sustained and consecutive treatment, but two other things. Independent classical attestation outside Charaka: no public-domain translation of Ashtanga Hridaya or Ashtanga Sangraha was located, no Sushruta parallel was retrieved for this record, and nothing outside Charaka is quoted here. And the modern evidence base. The dedicated modern literature retrieved in this pass consists of narrative and conceptual reviews, mostly in non-indexed Ayurvedic journals and two in PubMed-indexed ones, which restate the Charaka verses and then assert, without measurement, that modern exposures such as headphones, screens, noise and bright light are instances of the category. Nothing retrieved here defines atiyoga, ayoga, hinayoga or mithyayoga in measurable terms for any sense; no threshold was found proposed, let alone validated; no inter-rater reliability study was located; no cohort followed under this framing was identified. There is a real and substantial modern literature on sensory exposures and health, covering noise-induced hearing loss, unsafe listening, screen time and myopia, light at night and circadian disruption, and sensory deprivation, and some of its findings are broadly congruent with the classical intuition that both excess and deprivation can harm. That congruence should be stated carefully, and the record states the caveat in the same breath as the adjacency. The mapping is this record's translation and not one the classical text makes. Those results were generated independently, with quantified exposures and comparison groups, and they neither derive from nor test the Ayurvedic scheme. The mapping is also lopsided: the retrieved epidemiology is almost entirely about excess, whereas Charaka's category covers deficient and absent and perverse contact just as much as excessive contact, so the adjacency covers at most one of the four modes and leaves ayoga, hinayoga and mithyayoga without a comparator. The one genuinely distinctive element of the classical account, mithyayoga defined by the hostile, repulsive or frightening character of the stimulus rather than by its intensity, is also the element with the least modern purchase, since it makes the harmfulness of an exposure depend on its affective meaning to a particular organism. Charaka's own translator noted in the 1890s that the scheme counts three modes after enumerating four, that the definition of asatmya is merely verbal, and that the first and third causes are scarcely exclusive of each other. No answer to those criticisms was retrieved in this pass.

contested.question: Are there three modes of faulty contact or four?
positions: Sharira 1.134 and the summary formulations state three.
The sense-by-sense verses enumerate four: atiyoga, ayoga, hinayoga and mithyayoga.
Kaviratna's note takes the view that hinayoga has simply been dropped from the count; other traditions merge ayoga and hinayoga into one. The texts do not resolve it.

contested.question: Is asatmya absolute or individual?
positions: The definition given, that which does not accord with the organism, plus the okasatmya discussion in the taste verses, makes it strictly individual and habituation-dependent.
The enumerated lists (loud sounds, dark objects, putrid smells) read as absolute and universal.
If it is individual, the category cannot generate population-level prescriptions; if absolute, the okasatmya clause is redundant. Commentators use both readings depending on context.

contested.question: Is this cause genuinely distinct from prajnaparadha?
positions: The classical scheme treats them as distinct members of a triad.
Kaviratna objected in his note to Sharira 1.135 that the first and the third 'are scarcely exclusive of each other', since choosing to over-expose a sense is itself an act of faulty judgement.
Some modern authors subordinate sensory misuse to prajnaparadha entirely, which collapses the triad into two causes.

Sutra Sthana 11/37 applies the same three modes, excess and absence and injudicious contact, uniformly to sense objects, to acts and to time. On that reading the triad is one scheme applied to three domains rather than three independent causes, which makes the exclusivity question a question about the scheme and not about this category alone. This is a reading of the verse quoted in the classical array, offered as a position and not as a resolution.

contested.question: What does mithyayoga actually pick out?
positions: A physical reading: stimuli that are physically damaging or out of the organ's operating range.
An affective reading, which the verses support more directly: stimuli that are frightening, repulsive or hostile, that is, harmful by meaning rather than by energy.
A seasonal reading, given the recurrent anartava clause about out-of-season scents and untimely heat and cold, which folds mithyayoga back into kala.

notKnown: What quantity of any sense exposure counts as atiyoga. No threshold was found proposed for any sense in the classical or the modern material retrieved here.
Whether two trained examiners would agree on whether a given patient's exposure history constitutes ayoga, atiyoga or mithyayoga. No reliability study was retrieved in this pass.
Whether the claimed route from faulty sense contact to dosha provocation to disease can be observed, or whether the dosha step is inferred purely from the outcome.
Whether the affective criterion for mithyayoga (dreadful, repulsive, uncongenial stimuli) predicts anything beyond what ordinary stress and adversity measures already capture.

Whether the classical claim of harm from sensory deprivation (ayoga) holds for the senses other than vision, where it is best documented, and whether the classical account of it is more than a plausible guess. No deprivation literature for hearing, smell or taste was searched for this record, so the record carries no comparator for the ayoga and hinayoga modes at all.
Whether the category adds predictive value over quantified exposure assessment for the specific exposures where both could be applied, such as noise or screen time.
Why hinayoga is enumerated and then not counted, and whether the omission is scribal, commentarial or substantive. Kaviratna's note raises it; no commentarial resolution was located for this record.
How the individual-relative definition of asatmya is meant to be determined in a new patient before any harm has occurred.

Whether Ashtanga Hridaya and Ashtanga Sangraha in fact carry this threefold cause with the same four modes. The record previously asserted this. No edition of either text was consulted for this record and no public-domain English translation was located, so the claim is now carried in the classical array marked unsourced and the gap is stated here instead.

Whether Sushruta has a parallel to this category. No Sushruta passage was retrieved for this record, so no judgement is offered either way. Bhishagratna's translation is public domain and quotable, so this is a gap that a later pass can close rather than a permanent limit.

Whether the clinical construct of sensory overload, as used in autism and sensory processing research, is a genuine adjacent literature for atiyoga or merely a verbal resemblance. That literature was deliberately not reached for in this pass: the construct measures a person's response rather than an exposure dose, which is a different object from atiyoga, and asserting the adjacency without retrieving and reading it would repeat the error this revision is correcting.

What a search wider than the one recorded in the modern array would return. Diacritic transliterations, hyphenated and space-separated variants, Devanagari, the AYUSH Research Portal, DHARA and Google Scholar were not searched, so the record's statement about indexing is a statement about four transliterations in two databases on one date and nothing more.

Whether Kaviratna's aphorism numbering offset holds outside the passage checked. The plus-seven offset was verified for Sharira 1/125-136 by matching the sense-by-sense content against carakasamhitaonline's standard numbering. It is not asserted for any other sthana or chapter, and in Sutra Sthana 11 Kaviratna's numbering does not appear to map onto the standard numbering by a constant offset at all, since he splits into separate aphorisms what the standard edition carries as one.

components.gloss: Excessive contact: too much of an otherwise suitable sense object
Absence of contact: total deprivation of the sense object
Deficient or sparing contact. Listed in the sense-by-sense verses but dropped from the summary count of three, which Kaviratna flags as an inconsistency
Perverse contact: objects that are hostile, repulsive, terrifying, out of season, or contrary to what the organism is habituated to
Ear and sound: loud and harsh, or none at all, or very low; perverse contact is with rough, dreadful, uncongenial or danger-signalling sound
Skin and touch: total abstention, excess, or partial indulgence; perverse contact includes untimely oleation and untimely heat or cold
Eye and form: very brilliant or very minute objects, or never exercising the eye; perverse contact is with hateful, terrible, distant or dark objects
Tongue and taste: excess of any taste, total abstention, or tastes taken against okasatmya (habituated suitability)
Nose and smell: very mild or very keen scents, or total abstention; perverse contact is with putrid, poisonous, repulsive or out-of-season scents
Habituated suitability. Asatmya is defined negatively as that which does not accord with the organism, which makes the whole category individual-relative

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson VIII (Indriyopakramaniya), verse 10 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 10 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The general statement of the three modes of faulty sense contact, and that the immediate injury is to perception itself, with disease as a consequence rather than the first effect. Verified in the Kaviratna OCR: the chapter header reads 'LESSON VIII. We shall now explain the lesson on the Analysis of the Senses', and the aphorism number 10 is printed after the aphorism, as Kaviratna does throughout. No standard-numbering equivalent is asserted for this locus because none was retrieved.
classical.quote: In consequence again of the excessive correlation, the absence of (judicious) correlation, and the impropriety of correlation, of the senses with their respective objects, the senses including the mind, falling away from their normal condition, become hurtful to the perceptions of which they are the respective sources or channels. In consequence again of a judicious correlation of the senses with their objects, they preserve their normal condition, and maintain in their normal condition the perceptions or knowledge respectively derived through them.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson XI (Tistraishaniya), the three-causes passage; standard numbering Sutra 11/37
classical.verse: 37 (standard numbering per carakasamhitaonline.com); no Kaviratna aphorism number asserted, see numberingProblem
classical.establishes: A second and textually independent Charaka locus for the same scheme, outside the Sharira 1 block. It matters for two reasons. First, it shows the sense-by-sense working out is not confined to one passage. Second, it applies the same three modes uniformly to sense objects, to acts and to time, which bears directly on whether this cause is distinct from prajnaparadha and parinama or is one scheme applied to three domains.
classical.quote: There are three causes of disease. They are excess of correlation, absence of correlation, and injudicious correlation in respect of perceptible Objects, of Acts, and of Time. A continuous gaze at objects of great power is an instance of excessive correlation. A total abstention from exercising the eye is absence or want of correlation. Injudicious correlation arises where the eye is directed to objects that are very minute, that are in close adjacence, that are very remote, that provoke anger or terror or amazement or aversion, that are repulsive, and that are exceedingly ugly. [...] Excess of correlation as regards objects of hearing arises from constantly exposing the ear to the stunning report of thunder or beat of drum or loud cries. To totally abstain from hearing (by shutting up the ears) is absence of correlation. Injudicious correlation arises from hearing harsh sounds, or words expressive of the death or destruction of persons and objects that are liked, or sounds produced by the sudden clash or impact of hard substances, or those expressive of censure and dire reproof.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verse 125 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 125 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The atiyoga, ayoga and hinayoga forms for hearing, stated as damage to the sense organ itself.
classical.quote: In consequence of hearing sounds that are very loud and harsh, in consequence, again, of hearing no sound at all or of hearing sounds that are very low, the sense of hearing becomes destroyed.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verse 126 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 126 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: That mithyayoga is defined by the affective and semantic character of the stimulus, not by its physical intensity. This is the point at which the category stops being about exposure dose.
classical.quote: The contact of the ear with sounds that are rough, exceedingly dreadful, uncongenial, disagreeable, and indicative of danger, is regarded as false correlation.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verses 127-128 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 127-128 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The atiyoga, ayoga, hinayoga and mithyayoga forms for touch. Added in revision: the record's components section already asserted the touch content, including untimely oleation and untimely heat and cold, with no quoted citation behind it.
classical.quote: Total abstention from touch, excessive indulgence in touch, and partial indulgence in it, impair the sense of touch, as has been said in the abstract of touchable objects. Contact with winds raised by evil spirits and those proceeding from poisonous substances, and contact with oily substances and heat and cold that are all untimely, are called false Correlation of touch.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verses 129-131 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 129-131 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The sense-by-sense working out for vision and taste, and the explicit appeal to okasatmya (habituated suitability) as the standard for taste.
classical.quote: In consequence of beholding objects that are possessed of great effulgence, or objects that are very minute, or of never exercising the eye at all for vision, the power of vision becomes destroyed. The sight of objects that are hateful, or terrible, or repulsive, or of objects at a great distance and seen with straining eyes, or of objects that are of a dark hue, is regarded as false correlation in respect of vision. Excessive indulgence in any of the tastes, or a total abstention from all the tastes, or indulgence, while taking things that are from habit suitable to the physical organism, in tastes that do not at all agree with them, or a very sparing indulgence in tastes, impairs the organ of taste.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verses 132-133 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 132-133 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The atiyoga, hinayoga and mithyayoga forms for smell, including the anartava (out-of-season) clause that the contested section treats as pulling mithyayoga back towards kala. Added in revision: the components section already asserted this content with no quoted citation behind it.
classical.quote: Indulgence in scents that are very mild or very keen, or a total abstention from all scents, is destructive of the organ of scent. The contact of scent with the organ of scents, emitted by putrified objects or objects that are poisonous, or of scents that are disagreeable or repulsive, or of scents that do not belong to the season, is regarded as false correlation in respect of the power of scent.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verse 134 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 134 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The link from faulty sense contact to dosha provocation, and the circular definition of asatmya as that which does not accord with the organism.
classical.quote: Even this are the three kinds of contact with the senses of objects not in accordance with them. Each is provocative of the faults (viz., wind, bile, and phlegm). That should be known as Unaccordant which does not accord with the human organism.

classical.text: Kaviratna's translator's note to Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verse 134
classical.verse: note to 134
classical.establishes: A documented internal inconsistency in the classical scheme (four modes enumerated, three counted) and a contemporaneous translator's objection that the definition of asatmya is merely verbal. This is a primary-source criticism, not a modern one.
classical.quote: It will be seen, however, that with regard to every one of the senses, four and not three kinds of samyoga or yoga have been spoken of, viz., Atiyoga, Ayoga, Hinayoga, and Mithyayoga. The first implies excess of contact; the second, a total absence of contact; the third, sparing or partial contact, and the fourth, contact with objects that are hostile. In speaking, however, of only three kinds of contact, in verse 134, it would seem that the third (or Hinayoga) has been left out of consideration. The definition of asatmya as something that sahatmyatam na yati is a mere verbal one.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verse 135 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 135 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: That diseases from this cause form a named class, aindriyaka, parallel to the prajnaparadha-derived and time-derived classes.
classical.quote: The diseases which spring from the false, the excessive, and the partial correlation of sounds and the rest (with the corresponding organs of sense), should be known by the learned by the name of diseases appertaining to the senses.

classical.text: Kaviratna's translator's note to Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verse 135
classical.verse: note to 135
classical.establishes: The source of the exclusivity objection that the contested section attributes to Kaviratna. Added in revision because contested question 3 quoted this note without the record carrying the note as an addressed citation. It is a translator's objection from the 1890s, not a classical doctrine, and is labelled as such.
classical.quote: It will be seen that diseases, according to their causes, are divided into three classes: 1. those due to impairment or destruction of the understanding, memory, etc., or, as it is otherwise called, 'Prajnaparadha', i.e., faults of judgment; 2. those which fall within 'Kalasamprapti', i.e., the influence of time; and 3. the improper correlation of objects with the senses by which they are apprehended. The first and the third, it would seem, are scarcely exclusive of each other. Some of the diseases, again, which fall under the second class, may be due to the same causes, which bring about those of the first and the third classes. Altogether, the classification does not seem to be scientific.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verse 136 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 136 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The closing statement of the etiology: samyak yoga, judicious correlation, is the single cause of health, and the text concedes it is extremely hard to attain.
classical.quote: Even these are regarded as the causes of all sensations which are productive of misery. As regards happiness, it is said that there is only one cause, viz., harmonious correlation. It is extremely difficult of attainment.

classical.text: Charak Samhita New Edition (carakasamhitaonline.com) cites the threefold general cause at Sutra 11/43, Sutra 20/5, Sutra 28/7 and Nidana 1/3
classical.establishes: Standard-numbering locations where asatmyendriyartha-samyoga appears alongside prajnaparadha and parinama. This is a pointer, not a quoted locus, and is not counted as one in the locus audit in gatheringNotes. A dedicated page for this term was sought at carakasamhitaonline and returned HTTP 404, which is itself worth recording.

classical.text: UNSOURCED: a claim carried over from gathering that Ashtanga Hridaya and Ashtanga Sangraha reproduce the same threefold cause with the same four modes of yoga
classical.establishes: Nothing, as it stands. No edition of either text was consulted, no chapter and verse was located and nothing is quoted, so under this project's no-quote-no-citation rule this entry is not a classical reference and must not be counted as one or published as one. It is kept here, marked unsourced, rather than deleted, so that the claim is visible as an unverified one and can be checked or dropped at audit. The corresponding gap is stated in notKnown.

modern.establishes: The searches actually run, with their strings, databases, dates and counts. Run 2026-10-06 against the NCBI E-utilities esearch endpoint. db=pubmed: 'asatmyendriyartha' 0 records; 'asatmendriyartha' 0; 'asatmya' 0; 'indriyartha' 1 record (PMID 23723664), unrelated to this etiological category. db=pmc, which searches full text rather than title, abstract and MeSH: 'asatmyendriyartha' 3 records (PMC3331430, PMC3336277, PMC3336657); 'asatmendriyartha' 2 (PMC11831738, PMC6521746); 'asatmya' 16; 'indriyartha' 7. Five of the compound hits were retrieved and read in full.
modern.quality: This entry replaces an earlier flat assertion that the term 'does not appear in PubMed at all', which the critic was right to flag and which these searches falsify. The accurate statement is narrower and has two halves. The compound is absent from the fields PubMed itself indexes: a db=pubmed search returns nothing for any of the four transliterations tried, and the 1981 Ancient Science of Life paper that discusses the category at length has a PubMed abstract that does not contain the word. The compound is present in the full text of PubMed-indexed journals, which only a PMC search reaches. The five records read in full (PMC3331430, PMC3336277, PMC3336657, PMC6521746, PMC11831738) use the compound as a label in an introduction or a discussion; none defines it operationally, measures it, or treats it as a variable. Three of those five are now cited individually below. This is a bounded search: four transliterations, two databases, one date. Diacritic forms, hyphenated and space-separated variants, Devanagari, AYUSH Research Portal, DHARA and Google Scholar were not searched, so this record makes no claim about what a wider search would return.

modern.establishes: Compiles the classical material on asatmyendriyartha-samyoga and restates it.
modern.quality: Conceptual review in a non-indexed Ayurvedic journal. No data, no method section, no outcome. Representative of the whole available literature on this term.

modern.establishes: Argues that asatmyendriyartha-samyoga is a major cause of contemporary lifestyle disorders.
modern.quality: Narrative review in a non-indexed multidisciplinary journal. The claim is asserted, not tested. No exposure measurement, no comparison group.

modern.establishes: Applies the category to headphone use as an instance of atiyoga of hearing.
modern.quality: Conceptual paper in a non-indexed journal. Interesting as an illustration of how the framework is applied to modern exposures, but it generates no audiometric or any other data.

modern.title: The association between screen time exposure and myopia in children and adolescents: a meta-analysis.
modern.establishes: Meta-analysis reporting an association between screen time exposure and myopia in children and adolescents.
modern.quality: Real empirical meta-analysis of observational studies, with the usual limitations of that design (confounding by outdoor time, heterogeneous exposure measurement, publication bias). Included strictly as an outside comparator: it shows that a specific sense-exposure to disease link is measurable when the exposure is defined and quantified. It was not designed around the Ayurvedic scheme, does not test it, and does not validate it.

modern.title: Association of physical activity, sedentary behaviour, sleep and myopia in children and adolescents: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis.
modern.establishes: Dose-response meta-analysis of physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep in relation to myopia.
modern.quality: Empirical systematic review with dose-response modelling. Cited as a comparator to make the contrast concrete: the modern literature that does study sensory exposure quantifies dose and models a response curve, whereas the classical scheme offers only ordinal categories of too much, too little and wrong, with no thresholds.

modern.title: The psychosomatic disorders and their management in ayurveda.
modern.establishes: That the category has been read, in a PubMed-indexed journal, as a classification of stress factors, with the perception itself (asatmya indriya buddhi) as the step that disturbs the manasa doshas and then the sharira doshas.
modern.quality: Theoretical paper, 1981, no data, no method, no outcome. Quoted here for two purposes and no others. It is direct evidence for the corrected search statement above, since it is the clearest case of the compound sitting in PMC full text while being absent from the PubMed abstract of the same record. And the word 'excellent' in the quote is the author's appraisal, carried here as the author's and not endorsed. Transliteration in the quote is the paper's own, including 'that this an excellent', which is as printed.
modern.quote: Ayurveda describes three categories of etiological factors viz. 1. Asatmyendriyartha Samyoga, 2. Prajnaparadha, 3. Parinama. A critical examination of the nature of these three categories of aetiological factors would indicate that this an excellent classification of stress factors which are responsible for stress and psychosomatic diseases.

modern.title: Lifestyle - A Common Denominator for the Onset and Management of Migraine Headache: Complementing Traditional Approaches with Scientific Evidence.
modern.establishes: That the application of the category to specific modern sensory exposures is made in a PubMed-indexed journal and not only in non-indexed Ayurvedic ones.
modern.quality: Narrative review. The sentence quoted is an assertion referenced to a classical textbook; the paper measures no exposure and reports no migraine outcome against one. Cited for the fact that the claim is made in indexed literature, not as evidence that the claim is true. 'starring' is as printed and presumably 'staring'.
modern.quote: Asatmendriyartha samyoga (improper stimulation of sense organs) is considered an important factor for trigger of diseases as Ayurveda considers the sense organs to be the route to the brain. Constant glare, starring, bright light, loud noise, certain types of smell could trigger migraine.

modern.title: Prevalence and global estimates of unsafe listening practices in adolescents and young adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
modern.establishes: Pooled prevalence of exposure to unsafe listening from personal listening devices of 23.81 percent (95 percent CI 18.99 to 29.42) across 33 studies and 19,046 individuals aged 12-34, with a modelled 48.20 percent for loud entertainment venues and a global estimate of 0.67 to 1.35 billion young people potentially at risk of hearing loss.
modern.quality: Systematic review and meta-analysis, searched 2000-2021. An outside comparator, included because the record already carries a non-indexed Ayurvedic paper applying atiyoga of hearing to headphone use, and the comparison is the point: this review defines the exposure by intensity threshold and duration and reports a prevalence with an interval, which is what the classical ordinal categories do not do. It was not designed around the Ayurvedic scheme, does not test it and does not validate it. The adjacency between 'unsafe listening' and atiyoga is this record's translation, not Charaka's.

modern.title: Occupational noise-induced hearing loss in China: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
modern.establishes: In 71,865 workers exposed to a mean 98.6 dB(A) for a mean 9.9 years, prevalence of occupational noise-induced hearing loss of 21.3 percent, with noise level, exposure duration and age each carrying their own odds ratios (reported as 5.63, 1.75 and 1.35 for high-frequency loss) and complex noise worse than Gaussian noise at OR 1.95.
modern.quality: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies, with the confounding and heterogeneity limitations of that design and a single-country evidence base. An outside comparator only. It is the dose-response half of the noise adjacency, where the BMJ Global Health review is the exposure-prevalence half. Again: the mapping of this literature onto atiyoga of shabda is this record's translation and not a claim the classical text makes.

records.title: Chikitsa Sutra (principles governing treatment choice)
records.summary: Chikitsa sutra is the classical Ayurvedic label for the set of rules a physician is supposed to apply when deciding what to do for a given patient, as distinct from the list of drugs used. The core claims are that disease is a disturbance of equilibrium among the bodily constituents, that treatment is whatever restores that equilibrium, that treatment succeeds only through the joint adequacy of four participants (physician, drug, attendant, patient), and that the same substance is medicine or poison depending on dose, timing, route, the patient's strength and the state of the doshas. Underneath these sits the samanya-vishesha rule (Ca.Su.1.44-45), that like increases like and unlike decreases it, which is what makes 'treat with the opposite' a rule rather than a slogan.
