An auditor must read the surrounding printed aphorism numbers, not count matches.

records.title: Dhatu Formation and the Three Models of Tissue Nutrition
records.summary: Ayurvedic physiology holds that food, once digested by jatharagni, yields a nutrient essence (ahara rasa) that is progressively converted into seven bodily tissues (dhatu) in a fixed order: rasa, rakta, mamsa, medas, asthi, majja, shukra. Each conversion is said to be driven by a tissue-specific fire (dhatvagni) and to yield two fractions, a usable portion (prasada) and a waste portion (kitta). Both samhitas assert the sequence, the fire-driven conversion and the prasada and kitta split, and Charaka also names the secondary tissue and the waste product belonging to each stage; neither names a mechanism. How many fires there are, and whether agni is anything other than pitta, is disputed inside the tradition rather than settled by it. The three named nutrition models (kshira-dadhi, kedari-kulya, khale-kapota) do not occur in the mula texts of either samhita as translated by Kaviratna or Bhishagratna; the secondary literature attributes the terminology to the medieval commentators, and no commentary passage for any of the three has been retrieved for this record. Kshira-dadhi (milk-to-curd) reads the sequence as complete serial transformation; kedari-kulya (field-and-irrigation-channel) reads it as a nutrient stream distributed through channels to tissues in order; khale-kapota (threshing-floor-and-pigeons) reads it as each tissue drawing selectively from a common pool. On how long the cycle takes, the texts give figures that are not directly comparable and neither is offered as an observation: Charaka reports, as the view of 'some', six days and nights for one dhatu to become the next, while Sushruta gives 3,015 kalas for each stage and a month for the whole chain, with a month defined in the same chapter as 18,090 kalas. The familiar 'five days per dhatu' is not a statement of either text. It is Bhishagratna's own conversion, printed in his brackets as 'according to our modern computation', and it holds only if the month is taken as thirty days.
records.evidenceState: This concept rests on classical exegesis. The seven-tissue sequence and the prasada and kitta split are stated plainly in both Charaka and Sushruta, and the upadhatu and mala of each stage are stated in Charaka, so the doctrine is well attested as doctrine. What it lacks is measurement. Nothing retrieved for this record reports a rate at which any tissue is converted into any other, identifies a dhatvagni with an enzyme, organelle or pathway, or describes an experiment that could discriminate between kshira-dadhi, kedari-kulya and khale-kapota; the three models make no differing predictions that any retrieved author has stated in testable form. The searches behind those statements are bounded and named: PubMed esearch on 2026-10-06 for 'dhatu poshana' returned 55 records and all 55 titles were screened; 'dhatvagni' returned 2; 'khale kapota' returned 1 (PMID 32855015); 'kedari kulya' returned 0. Four search strings on one date is not a systematic review and will not support a claim that no such study exists anywhere. Within that set, four of the five references carried here are non-empirical, three narrative or conceptual reviews and one hypothesis paper. The fifth, PMID 24250128, is a randomised placebo-controlled trial of 46 patients whose rationale runs through rakta-dhatvagni, but its endpoints are haematological and the dhatvagni premise is assumed rather than measured, so it does not test the doctrine either. On the commentarial side the three nyayas are not scriptural: searches for kedari, kulya, kapota, khale and dadhi across the full retrieved text of both public-domain translations return only unrelated hits, drug names, pigeon flesh, snake species and colour terms, and none in a tissue-nutrition context, so the nyaya names are absent from the mula texts in these translations and the terminology is attributed by the secondary literature to the medieval commentators. A caution about that secondary literature: papers on these models routinely assert correspondences to absorption, circulation and cellular metabolism, and PMID 26664231 is carried here as a named example, proposing dhatu siddhanta as a probable predecessor of stem cell therapy. Those are restatements of classical doctrine in modern vocabulary, not findings. The honest summary is that dhatu formation is a coherent and internally detailed physiological narrative, disputed at its own foundation on the question of how many fires drive it, with no independent empirical support and no validated modern correlate in the literature retrieved here.

contested.question: How long does the full transformation from rasa to shukra take, and do the two texts actually disagree?
positions: Charaka Chikitsasthana 15.21 (Kaviratna's 20) reports, as the opinion of 'some', six days and nights for the transformation of ONE dhatu into the next. The figure is per step, and the disciple's objections follow immediately, so it is presented as a held view rather than as settled doctrine.
Sushruta Sutrasthana 14 gives 3,015 kalas for each stage and a month for the whole chain, and the same chapter defines a month as 18,090 kalas, which is six times 3,015.

The familiar 'five days per dhatu' is not in either text. It is Bhishagratna's bracketed conversion, marked in his own translation as 'according to our modern computation'. It follows arithmetically from 3,015 of 18,090 kalas if a month is taken as thirty days, but the text states no absolute length for a kala and performs no such conversion.

The record previously set Charaka's six days against Sushruta's one month and called them conflicting. That comparison was between a per-step figure and a whole-chain figure. Compared per step the two come out at six days against five, which is a narrower disagreement than the record claimed; compared over the chain, six days a step would run to about thirty-six days. Whether that is a real disagreement, two different quantities, or two measurement conventions is not resolved by either text.
Later and secondary literature circulates other figures, commonly 'about a month' or 'six days', without resolving the question. No text offers an observation supporting any number.

contested.question: Is agni a single principle identical with pitta, and how many dhatvagnis are there?
positions: Charaka Chikitsasthana 15.13-15.14 numbers the fires as five, elemental; two aphorisms later, at 15.16, it speaks of seven, tissue-level, without explaining the change. Kaviratna's own footnote at that place concedes the difficulty in as many words: 'This sudden mention of seven fires after having numbered them as five, requires explanation.' The reason he then supplies is his, not the text's.
Bhishagratna's Introduction reports Sushruta as holding 'that the Pittam is the only fire present in the system', which if taken strictly leaves no dhatvagni as a separate agent at all.

The same passage reports that 'Agnivesha and certain sections of the Ayurvedic Acharyayas hold that there are five Anjali-fuls of Agni in the human organism', a quantity rather than a count of fires, and Bhishagratna reconciles it with pitta only by his own device.
Arunadatta, commenting on the Ashtanga Hridaya and reported in the same passage, 'holds that there are as many Dhatvagnis as the constituents of the body', which abandons the number seven.

PMID 22131747 records the thirteen-fold scheme, one jatharagni with five bhutagni and seven dhatvagni, as the standard modern presentation, and also documents that the identity of agni with pitta is itself disputed inside the tradition.

All of the above except the Charaka aphorisms reach this record through a translator's Introduction or a modern review. No commentary text stating any of these positions has been retrieved, so the positions are reported, not sourced to the commentators themselves.

contested.question: Are the three nyayas competing explanations or complementary aspects of one process?
positions: The dominant modern reading (PMID 32855015) treats them as complementary: kshira-dadhi describes transformation, kedari-kulya describes transport, khale-kapota describes selective uptake.

A stricter reading treats kshira-dadhi as literal serial conversion, in which case it is incompatible with khale-kapota's parallel selective uptake from a shared pool, since they cannot both describe the same instant.
Some authors treat the nyayas as pedagogical analogies rather than mechanistic claims at all, in which case the question of compatibility does not arise.

contested.question: Is nutrient supply to tissues sequential or simultaneous?
positions: Serial reading: rasa must become rakta before rakta can become mamsa, implying a delay proportional to position in the chain.

Charaka Chikitsasthana 15.36 (Kaviratna's 35) states that rasa is diffused through every part of the body simultaneously by vyana vayu, which is the textual basis for a simultaneous model and for the explanation of immediate drug effects.

contested.question: Is ojas an eighth dhatu produced at the end of the chain?
positions: Bhishagratna's explanatory footnote to Sushruta Sutrasthana 14 records that 'certain authorities hold albumen (protoplasmic matter) to be the eighth or the culminating principle of the body', produced from the thin fraction of shukra. This is in his footnote and not in the text he is translating, it names no authority, and 'albumen' and 'protoplasmic matter' are his renderings; it is reported here as a translator's note, which is all it is.
The standard enumeration in both samhitas stops at seven dhatus and treats ojas as the essence (sara) of all of them rather than as a further member of the sequence.

contested.question: Does the three-fold resolution of each stage belong to the texts, to Dalhana, or to the translator?
positions: The secondary literature attributes to Dalhana the analysis in which each stage resolves into a sthula or excreted fraction, a condensed fraction that maintains the tissue, and a sukshma fraction that becomes the next tissue.
The only retrieved statement of it is Bhishagratna's own footnote at Sutrasthana 14, which runs the three-factor resolution through every stage from rasa to shukra but names no commentator.

Charaka Chikitsasthana 15.16-15.19 states a two-fold resolution, prasada and kitta, and separately names the upadhatu of each stage. Whether the three-fold scheme is a commentator's refinement of that or a later reorganisation of it is not settled by anything this record has retrieved.

notKnown: No measured rate of conversion of any dhatu into any other was found. The searches behind that statement are bounded and named: PubMed esearch on 2026-10-06 for 'dhatu poshana' (55 records, all titles screened), 'dhatvagni' (2 records), 'khale kapota' (1 record) and 'kedari kulya' (0 records). None of the screened records reports such a measurement. This does not establish that no such study exists outside those four search strings.

No enzyme, transporter, organelle or metabolic pathway has been identified with any of the seven dhatvagnis in the literature retrieved here; the correspondences offered in the review articles cited are analogies, not assays.
No experiment has been designed, among the sources retrieved, that would distinguish kedari-kulya from khale-kapota, and no author in them states what observation would falsify either.

The earliest datable source of the three nyaya names is not established. The names are absent from the mula texts as translated by Kaviratna and Bhishagratna; secondary literature points variously to Dalhana, to Chakrapanidatta and to the Bhavaprakasha Purva Khanda, and no commentary or nighantu passage naming any of them has been retrieved, so none of those attributions is carried as a citation here.

Meulenbeld's A History of Indian Medical Literature is the reference that would settle which commentator originates which nyaya, and it was not consulted. The attribution question above stays open for that reason and not because the question is unanswerable.

The thirteen-agni enumeration, one jatharagni with five bhutagni and seven dhatvagni, is carried here only from the mula-text aphorisms that state its three parts separately (Charaka Chikitsasthana 15.13-15.14, 15.16 and 15.39) and from PMID 22131747. The enumeration is widely attributed to Chakrapanidatta commenting on Charaka Chikitsasthana 15, and no text of that commentary has been retrieved, so the attribution is not asserted and no verse is cited for it.
Whether 'rasa' denotes plasma, chyle, lymph, interstitial fluid, or a composite of these is not settled, and the choice changes every downstream correspondence.

The upadhatu and mala correspondences are now cited to mula text (Charaka Chikitsasthana 15.17-15.19) but they are stated there, not explained: the text gives no reason why bone should yield hair or rasa yield phlegm, and nothing retrieved here examines the question.

One of those correspondences is textually unsettled in the translation this record quotes. Kaviratna divides the last pair as marrow yielding an oily substance and skin yielding the eye secretions, while secondary renderings of the same aphorism assign the oily eye and skin secretion to majja. No standard Sanskrit edition was retrieved to adjudicate, so the record quotes Kaviratna as printed and relies on neither division.

Sushruta's kala is defined in this chapter only as one part in 18,090 of a month. No independent definition of its absolute length was found, so 'five days per dhatu' holds only on the assumption that the month in question is thirty days.
It is not known whether Charaka's reported six days a step and Sushruta's 3,015 kalas a stage reflect two different processes, two measurement conventions, or simple disagreement.

Vagbhata's compressed restatement of tissue increase and decrease at Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 11 is not covered here. No public-domain English translation of the Ashtanga Hridaya was located, and this project does not quote in-copyright translations, so nothing from Vagbhata is quoted or cited in this record even though the chapter is a real locus for the material.

Fetal dhatu formation is out of this record's scope. Charaka Sharirasthana and Sushruta Sharirasthana 4, which Bhishagratna's own contents page describes as treating 'the development of Factors in the womb as well as the Factors which contribute to the growths of its different bodily organs and principles', were not worked through. The one prenatal passage cited here (Sushruta Sharirasthana 3, section 17) is included for the transudation mechanism only and the record makes no claim to cover embryonic tissue formation.

Dwarakanath's Digestion and Metabolism in Ayurveda (1967), the standard monograph on exactly this subject, was not consulted; it is in copyright and no retrievable copy was found. This record therefore does not represent the scholarship on dhatu formation, only the sources it could retrieve and quote.

No biological correlate of the dhatu chain was found. The nearest body of work in this field, the Ayurgenomics literature, addresses prakriti, that is constitutional classification, rather than tissue nutrition, and no study was retrieved that tests any step of dhatu poshana against a measurement. That literature is not cited here because it would be cited for a question it does not ask.

components.gloss: The nutrient essence extracted from digested food; the input to the whole tissue chain.
The central digestive fire in the gut, held to be the root on which all other fires depend.
Five elemental fires; each is said to digest the corresponding elemental fraction of food (earthy, watery, fiery, airy, ethereal).

Seven tissue-level fires, one per dhatu, that 'cook' the incoming nutrient into that tissue. The seven-fold count is what Charaka Chikitsasthana 15.16 states, but how many such fires there are, and whether any fire exists in the body distinct from pitta, is disputed: Bhishagratna's Introduction has Sushruta holding pitta to be the only fire and Arunadatta holding that there are as many dhatvagnis as there are body constituents. See the contested entry on dhatvagni.
The two products of each tissue-level cooking: the usable refined portion and the waste portion (e.g. kapha from rasa, pitta from rakta, sweat from medas).
Rasa (plasma/chyle), rakta (blood), mamsa (flesh), medas (fat), asthi (bone), majja (marrow), shukra (reproductive tissue).
'Milk-into-curd' analogy: the law of transformation. Each dhatu is wholly converted into the next, so nourishment is strictly serial.
'Field-and-irrigation-channel' analogy: the law of transmission. A common nutrient stream is carried through channels (srotas) and fills each tissue-field in turn.
'Threshing-floor-and-pigeons' analogy: the law of selection. Each tissue draws what it specifically needs from a shared nutrient pool, at its own rate and distance.
A fourth model, of simultaneous nourishment, invoked to explain immediate whole-body effects; it corresponds to the classical statement that rasa is diffused everywhere at once by vyana vayu.

Secondary tissues and the excretory by-product of each stage. Charaka Chikitsasthana 15.17-15.19 names them: milk and menstrual blood from rasa, vessels from rakta, fat and the six skins from mamsa, tendons and muscles from medas; and phlegm from rasa, bile from rakta, the body filths from mamsa, sweat from medas, hair from asthi. The assignment of the oily eye and skin secretion is where Kaviratna's English and the standard reading diverge; see notKnown.

classical.verse: 14-15 as printed by Kaviratna; standard (Trikamji) 15.15-15.16
classical.establishes: The seven-fire model and the prasada/kitta split, and the canonical serial order of tissue derivation, stated in a lawfully quotable public-domain English translation.
classical.quote: They who sustain the body, viz., the 'dhatus' (i. e., 'Rasa' or juice, blood, flesh, adeps, marrow, bones, and vital seed), are cooked by their seven respective fires. This process of cooking which they undergo is of two kinds in consequence of the 'Kitta' (refuse) and the 'Prasada' (pure substance) which results from it. From 'Rasa' (juice) arises blood; from blood is flesh; from flesh is adeps; from adeps is bone; from bone is marrow; from marrow is vital seed: from the vital seed arises the foetus.

classical.verse: 20 as printed by Kaviratna; standard (Trikamji) 15.21
classical.establishes: That Charaka reports a transformation period as the opinion of 'some' rather than as settled doctrine, and that the figure given is six days and nights for ONE dhatu becoming the next, not for the whole chain. The disciple's objections follow immediately, which is why the record treats it as a reported opinion.
classical.quote: Some are of opinion that the transformation (of one 'dhatu' into another) takes place in six days and nights. Of food and the 'dhatus' this transformation goes on eternally like (the motion of) a wheel.

classical.verse: 12-13 as printed by Kaviratna; standard (Trikamji) 15.13-15.14
classical.establishes: The bhutagni (five elemental fires) layer, and the like-nourishes-like principle operating at the elemental level beneath tissue formation.
classical.quote: Since the five heats, viz., that appertaining to earth, that to water, that to fire, that to air, and that to ether, digest earth and the other properties, respectively, numbering five, of the food eaten, Therefore, the material properties in the body (that is, those that relate to the five material substances already named) are nourished, respectively, by their correlative elements. The earthy properties (in food) nourish the earthy elements in the body. The rest nourish the rest, in detail.

classical.verse: 16-18 as printed by Kaviratna; standard (Trikamji) 15.17-15.19
classical.establishes: The mula-text source for the secondary tissues (upadhatu) and the waste product (mala) belonging to each stage: milk and menstrual blood from rasa, vessels from rakta, fat and skin from mamsa, tendons and muscles from medas; and phlegm from rasa, bile from rakta, body filths from mamsa, sweat from medas, hair from asthi. This was the record's largest acknowledged gap and it is mula text, not commentary.
classical.quote: As regards women, from 'Rasa' are both milk and blood ; from blood are ducts large and small ; from flesh is fat or adeps and six varieties of skin ; and from adeps is the origin of the tendons and muscles. The above are the transformations of 'Prasada.' That which is called the 'Kitta' (refuse) of the food taken, consists of stools and urine ; the 'Kitta' of 'Rasa' is phlegm ; that of blood is bile ; that of flesh are the filths of the body, including the secretions (from the nose, the ears, &c.) ; while swea[t] forms the 'Kitta' of adeps. The 'Kitta' of bones is hair (of the head and the body) ; that of marrow is the oily-substance in the body ; that of the skin is the secretions flowing from the eyes. From digestion (of the food eaten) thus arise, it is said, both 'Prasada' and 'Kitta' of the 'Dhatus.'

classical.verse: footnote to Kaviratna's 15 (standard 15.16); no verse number of its own
classical.establishes: That the move from five fires to seven inside the same passage is a difficulty the text does not itself resolve, and that Kaviratna had to supply a reason for it. This is the only retrieved contemporary statement of the problem at this locus.
classical.quote: This sudden mention of seven fires after having numbered them as [f]ive, requires explanation. The fact [is], as there are seven 'dhatus', and as those seven derive nourishment from the food eaten, there must be seven fires to cook the food into seven substances, food itself containing seven elements corresponding with or capable of nourishing the seven 'dhatus'. - T.

classical.verse: 35 as printed by Kaviratna; standard (Trikamji) 15.36
classical.establishes: The simultaneous-distribution statement in the mula text, which is the textual basis for the later eka-kala dhatu poshana model and which sits in tension with a strictly serial reading.
classical.quote: The 'dhatu' called 'Rasa' (that is, the juicy matter into which food is first converted) is continuously diffused through every part of the body simultaneously, by the life-breath called 'Vyana' whose function it is to diffuse.

classical.verse: 38 as printed by Kaviratna; standard (Trikamji) 15.39
classical.establishes: The subordination of the seven dhatvagnis and five bhutagnis to jatharagni, which is the doctrinal link between digestion and all downstream tissue formation. Taken with the two aphorisms above it, this is the mula-text basis for the structure later counted as thirteen fires: one that cooks the food, five elemental, seven tissue-level.
classical.quote: That heat which cooks (digests) the food eaten is the prince of all heats whose function is cooking. Indeed, all the other heats have the food-cooking heat for their root. Their increase or decrease depends on its increase or decrease.

classical.verse: none. Bhishagratna prints no Sanskrit verse numbers in this chapter; it is continuous prose, at his p. 109
classical.establishes: Sushruta's timing figures as the text gives them: 3,015 kalas for each stage, and the whole chain completed in a month.
classical.quote: The Rasa is successively transformed into each of the six remaining fundamental principles of the body, and continues in the shape of each for the period of three thousand and fifteen kalas [five days according to our modern computation]. Thus the Rasa is converted into semen, or into the menstrual blood (ovum) in women, in the course of a month.

classical.verse: none; Bhishagratna's marginal heading reads 'Authoritative verse on its computation', at his p. 110
classical.establishes: The text's own definition of the month in kalas, which is what makes the 3,015-kala figure add up to a month over six stages and what Bhishagratna's five-day conversion rests on. It also shows that the kala here is defined only as a fraction of a month, not in any independent unit.
classical.quote: In the present work, as well as in other works of recognised authority, a month is calculated to consist of eighteen thousand and ninety Kalas.

classical.verse: none; prose, at his p. 108
classical.establishes: The irrigation image in the mula text on which the later kedari-kulya analogy is built, and the text's own admission that the operating cause is not understood.
classical.quote: The Rasa or the lymph chyle, thus flowing out of the heart, constantly soothes, maintains, and irrigates by transudation the body, and further contributes to its growth, and supports life owing to the dynamical effects of causes which lie beyond the ken of human understanding.

classical.verse: none; under Bhishagratna's heading 'Metrical texts', at his p. 108
classical.establishes: Sushruta's statement of the same seven-tissue order as Charaka, independently.
classical.quote: The chyle produces blood. From blood is formed flesh. From flesh originates fat which gives rise to bones. From bones originate marrow, which, in its turn, germinates semen.

classical.verse: Sushruta Samhita, Sutrasthana 14 (Shonita-Varnaniya); Bhishagratna's asterisked footnote at the foot of vol. 1 pp. 109-110 (NOT 109-111). Numbering: Bhishagratna's own printed page numbers in volume 1 of his translation, read off the running heads of the archive.org scan (englishtranslati01susruoft, pagination identical to the cited b24758619_0001). No verse number is involved; the page range is the whole address.
classical.establishes: The only statement this record has actually retrieved of the three-fold resolution of each stage into an excreted, a condensed and a subtile fraction, which is the analysis the secondary literature attributes to Dalhana, together with the eighth-principle view of ojas.
classical.quote: Subsequently it enters into the bodily principle of Rasa, becomes matured by the native heat of the latter, and is resolved into three factors, or in other words, its excreted matter is transformed into phlegm, its thick or condensed portion is transformed into and assimilated in the matured Rasa of the body, whereas its subtile essence is metamorphosed into blood. [... the same three-factor resolution is then run through blood, flesh, fat, bone and marrow ...] The semen again, in its nascent stage, enters into the organic principle of that name and there matured under its native heat is resolved into two factors, viz. thick and thin. The thick portion is assimilated into the organic principle of semen, the thin one being metamorphosed into (albumen). Semen, like gold a thousand times purified, casts off no dregs. Hence certain authorities hold albumen (protoplasmic matter) to be the eighth or the culminating principle of the body.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section 17 (his own section number; he prints no Sanskrit verse numbers)
classical.establishes: The prenatal nutrition model (percolation and transudation, later glossed as upasneha and upasweda), which modern reviews cite as the Ayurvedic counterpart of histotrophic then haemotrophic nutrition.
classical.quote: The umbilical chord (Nadi) of the foetus is found to be attached to the cavity of the vein or artery of its maternal part through which the essence of lymph-chyle (Rasa) produced from the assimilated food of the mother, enters into its organism and fastens its growth and development, (a fact which may be understood from the analogy of percolation or transudation of blood). Immediately after the completion of the process of fecundation, the vessels (Dhamani) of its maternal body which carry the lymph-chyle (Rasa) and run laterally and longitudinally in all directions through it, tend to foster the foetus with their own transudation all through its continuance in the womb.

classical.text: Sushruta Samhita, Bhishagratna's Introduction (his own dissertation, not the Samhita)
classical.chapter: section headed 'Agni and Dhatvagnis', his pp. xlviii-xlix
classical.verse: none; the Introduction is unnumbered prose
classical.establishes: That the dhatvagni doctrine the whole record treats as its causal engine is disputed at its foundation, in a public-domain source: whether any fire exists in the body other than pitta, whether the measure of agni in the body is five anjalis, and how many dhatvagnis there are, with Sushruta, Agnivesha and Arunadatta ranged against each other. This is the material behind the new contested entry on dhatvagni.
classical.quote: Sushruta raises the question whether there is any kind of fire in the human organism other than the Pittam ; or are they identical ? Sushruta holds that the Pittam is the only fire present in the system, in as much as all acts from the digestion of food to the disintegration of tissues are performed with the help of the Pittam, which includes within its signification what is connoted by Anabolism and Katabolism of Western Physiologists. But Agnivesha and certain sections of the Ayurvedic Acharyayas hold that there are five Anjali-fuls of Agni in the human organism. This discrepancy is best explained away by including one Yava measure of Agni (enzymes, ferment) in the five Anjali-measures of Pittam. The A[y]urvedic Physiology recognises the exist[e]nce of another kind of Agni, which is called Dhatvagni (protoplasm) and which it cl[a]ssifies into seven different kinds, Arunadatta, the celebrated commentator of the Ashtangahridayam, holds that there are as many Dhatvagnis as the constituents of the body.
classical.translator: Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907), Vol. I Sutrasthanam

modern.title: Explication on tissue nutrition in prenatal and postnatal life: An Ayurveda perspective.
modern.establishes: Sets out all three nyayas plus eka-kala dhatu poshana as a single framework and maps them onto prenatal histotrophic and haemotrophic nutrition and postnatal enteral nutrition. A PubMed search for 'khale kapota' run on 2026-10-06 returns exactly one record, this one, so within that bounded search it is the only indexed paper that treats the khale-kapota model at all; that is a statement about one search string on one date, not about the literature as a whole.
modern.quality: Narrative review with no data, no systematic search and no stated methodology. It presents the correspondences (upasneha and upasweda as histotrophic nutrition, garbhanabhinadi as the umbilical cord) as interpretive readings, and the mapping is asserted rather than tested. Useful as a map of the doctrine; it is not evidence that the doctrine is true.

modern.title: Physiological aspects of Agni.
modern.establishes: A conceptual account of agni as the transformative agent, including the thirteen-fold scheme of one jatharagni, five bhutagni and seven dhatvagni that underlies dhatu formation, and the internal debate over whether agni is identical with pitta.
modern.quality: Conceptual and textual paper in Ayu, not an empirical study. No measurements, no subjects. Its value here is that it documents that the agni and pitta identity is itself disputed inside the tradition, which matters because dhatvagni is the causal engine the dhatu-formation model depends on.

modern.title: Clinical efficacy of panchakola on raktakshaya.
modern.establishes: The one primary clinical study surfaced by this record's searches in which dhatvagni is the stated causal premise. Its abstract reasons: 'Because of Jatharagnimandya, Rakta Dhatvagni gets disturbed and leads to Raktakshaya.' 46 patients with raktakshaya were randomised to a Panchakola tablet or a rice-powder placebo for six weeks, with haematological endpoints.
modern.quality: Randomised and placebo-controlled, which is more than any other reference here, but it does not test the doctrine. The endpoints are haemoglobin, serum iron, total iron-binding capacity, ferritin and blood indices; dhatvagni impairment appears only in the rationale and is never measured. A drug effect on anaemia is compatible with any mechanism, so this trial is evidence about Panchakola and not evidence for or against dhatvagni as the engine of tissue formation. Single centre, n=46, reported in Ayu.

modern.title: Concepts of Dhatu Siddhanta (theory of tissues formation and differentiation) and Rasayana; probable predecessor of stem cell therapy.
modern.establishes: A named instance of the pattern this record's evidenceState describes, offered so that the warning is not a general statement with no example behind it: a review proposing dhatu siddhanta, the theory of tissue formation and differentiation, as a 'probable predecessor of stem cell therapy'.
modern.quality: Narrative review with no data and no stated search. The authors' own framing is prospective rather than evidential: 'This review may be helpful to open the door of future research area in the field of reverse scientific approach of Ayurveda in the context of Dhatu Siddhanta ... and theory of stem cell.' The stem-cell correspondence is proposed, not tested. Cited only as an example of asserted correspondence, and it supports no claim about dhatu formation.

modern.title: Can cholesterol and its products serve as biomarkers for ojas?
modern.establishes: Relevant to dhatu formation only indirectly: it links specific dhatus to cholesterol-derived steroid hormones, continuing a 1995 proposal. It is the nearest thing in the retrieved literature to a proposed biochemical substrate for the dhatu chain.
modern.quality: Hypothesis paper. The authors describe their own output as 'candidate biomarkers' and 'indirect' proof. No experiment, no cohort, no assay was performed. It should not be read as establishing any dhatu-to-molecule correspondence.

records.title: Dinacharya: the classical rationale for a daily regimen
records.summary: Dinacharya is the classical Ayurvedic prescription of a fixed daily sequence of self-care acts, covering oral care including tooth cleaning and tongue scraping, application of oil to head, ears, body and feet, collyrium, medicated smoke and snuff, bathing, exercise in measure, dress, and a code of conduct. The rationale the retrieved classical passages actually give for the regimen is twofold and modest. Charaka grounds it in the stated purpose of the discipline, which is protection of the health of the healthy rather than treatment of the sick, in okasatmya or the habituation that makes a practice tolerable, and in the claim that the practices of the good secure health and self-restraint together. Separately, in his chapter on seasonal regimen rather than in his daily-regimen chapter, Sushruta states a parallel between the parts of a day and night and the seasons of the year, and says the doshas accumulate, aggravate and subside within a day as they do across a year. No passage retrieved for this record derives the daily acts from that parallel, and the two sit in different chapters of Sushruta. The classical chapters present the regimen as an enumerated list of acts with attributed benefits; they do not present it as a tested intervention, and no test of it as one was located in the searches this record rests on.
records.evidenceState: Dinacharya as presented in this record rests on classical exegesis. The classical rationale actually retrieved is of two kinds: a stated purpose and a habituation principle in Charaka (the aim of the discipline is protection of the health of the healthy; okasatmya makes a practice tolerable; observing the practices of the good secures health and self-restraint together), and, in a separate chapter on seasonal regimen, Sushruta's parallel between the parts of the day and the seasons of the year with the doshas cycling within the day. That parallel has not been operationalised into a measurable prediction in anything this record consulted, and no passage retrieved here derives any daily act from it. On the modern side this record's base is narrow and should not be read as speaking for the regimen: it is three oral-hygiene references and one abhyanga pilot, covering three of seventeen enumerated limbs, with the per-limb breakdown and the bounds of the search set out in modernCoverage. Within that base: oil pulling has a systematic review of randomised trials finding a probable small benefit at very low certainty and inferior performance to chlorhexidine; tongue scraping had a Cochrane review resting on 40 participants which has since been withdrawn; abhyanga has one uncontrolled 20-person pilot. No trial of dinacharya as a composite regimen, and nothing testing the ordering of the acts, the timing rules, the doshic rationale, or the claim that the package prevents disease, was located in the searches described in modernCoverage.searchBound; because that search was bounded as described, this record cannot and does not assert that no such study exists. A reader should treat dinacharya as a coherent and internally argued traditional hygiene and self-care protocol whose individual components range from plausibly useful on general grounds (oral hygiene, moderate exercise, regular bathing, regular sleep) to uncovered by anything in this record, and whose distinctive claims, that the ordering and timing matter and that the practice prevents disease through doshic regulation, are not evaluated by any source cited here.

contested.question: Is the 'dosha clock' of the day, kapha in the morning, pitta at midday, vata in the evening, and so on, a classical doctrine?

positions.view: Sushruta's seasonal-regimen chapter gives a five-part mapping of the day onto seasons (morning as spring, noon as summer, evening as rains, midnight as autumn, pre-dawn as hemanta), which yields a different and more complex schedule than the three-part clock.
positions.source: Sushruta Samhita, Sutrasthana 6, Bhishagratna vol. I pp. 50-51, unnumbered prose. Quoted in full in this record's classical section.

positions.view: The popular modern three-part clock, widely taught as classical, appears to be a later schematisation. No classical verse stating it in the modern three-part form was retrieved during this work, in either the Charaka, Sushruta or Ashtanga Hridaya material read here; it may exist in Ashtanga Hridaya elsewhere, in Bhavaprakasha, or in commentarial literature, but that was not checked.
positions.source: none. This is a negative result from a bounded search, not an established absence. See notKnown.

contested.question: When should one rise?

positions.view: Charaka's Sutrasthana 5, which enumerates the daily acts, gives no waking hour at all, and neither does Sutrasthana 8, which enumerates them again alongside the conduct code.
positions.source: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 5 and Sutrasthana 8, Kaviratna. Both chapters were read in full for this record.

positions.view: The brahma-muhurta rule, rising in the last watch of the night, is stated in the opening verse of Ashtanga Hridaya's daily-regimen chapter: brāhme muhūrta uttiṣṭhet svastho rakṣārtham āyuṣaḥ. The attribution is now verified against the Sanskrit rather than reported from secondary literature.
positions.source: Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 2.1, Sanskrit, GRETIL e-text. Retrieved and read during this revision.

positions.view: The same rule is also widely attributed to later texts such as Bhavaprakasha. That attribution remains unverified in this record.
positions.source: none retrieved. See notKnown.

contested.question: Is abhyanga appropriate for everyone daily?

positions.view: Charaka Sutrasthana 5 recommends daily oiling of skin, head, ears and feet without listing exclusions in the passage retrieved, and argues for it from the vata-touch-skin chain.
positions.source: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 5, Kaviratna's printed aphorisms 77-79, quoted in this record.

positions.view: Sushruta makes anointment conditional on habit, temperament, climate, season and doshic preponderance, and then explicitly prohibits it in undigested (ama) states, acute fever, indigestion, immediately after emetics, purgatives or a nirudha basti, and in diseases of repletion (santarpana), stating that anointing in fever and indigestion makes the disease difficult or impossible to cure.
positions.source: Sushruta Samhita, Chikitsasthana 24, Bhishagratna's numbered sections 21 and 22-24, quoted in this record.

positions.view: Ashtanga Hridaya prescribes daily abhyanga and in the next verse excludes it for those affected by kapha, those who have just undergone purification, and those with undigested food (a-jīrṇin).
positions.source: Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 2.8-2.9, Sanskrit, GRETIL e-text. Reported at the level of lexical identification; no English translation is offered.

contested.question: Is daily vigorous exercise prescribed or restricted?

positions.view: Both texts do both, and the apparent disagreement between them was an artefact of a short quotation in the earlier version of this record. Sushruta says exercise 'should be taken every day' and lists extensive benefits, and in the same numbered section caps it at 'the half extent of his capacity (Valardha), as otherwise it may prove fatal', and in the next section lists the diseases that follow from excess and the states in which it is forbidden.
positions.source: Sushruta Samhita, Chikitsasthana 24, Bhishagratna's numbered sections 25 and 26-27, quoted in this record.

positions.view: Charaka likewise prescribes exercise and limits it: 'One should have recourse to it in due measure', with the harms of excess enumerated and a general rule against excess in exercise, laughter, talking, walking, sexual congress and night-keeping.
positions.source: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 7, Kaviratna's printed aphorisms 29-32, quoted in this record.

positions.view: What remains genuinely different is emphasis and wording, not the presence or absence of a limit. Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 2.10-2.11 also pairs the benefits of vyayama with exclusions and a half-capacity rule.
positions.source: Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 2.10-2.11, Sanskrit, GRETIL e-text, read but not quoted in this record.

notKnown: Whether performing dinacharya as a package changes any clinical outcome. No trial of the composite regimen was located in the searches described in modernCoverage.searchBound.
Which components, if any, carry whatever effect exists. No dismantling or factorial study was located in that search.
What dose or duration would be required. The texts prescribe daily practice indefinitely; no study of adherence or dose-response was located in that search.
Whether the day-as-year doshic mapping generates any measurable physiological prediction that could be tested or refuted.

Whether any classical text derives the daily regimen from Sushruta's day-as-year parallel. The parallel is stated in Sushruta's seasonal-regimen chapter (Sutrasthana 6) and his daily-regimen material is in Chikitsasthana 24; nothing read for this record links them, and the commentarial literature (Dalhana on Sushruta, Chakrapani on Charaka, Arunadatta and Hemadri on Ashtanga Hridaya) was not consulted on this point. The parallel should not be presented as the regimen's rationale on the strength of what is here.
Whether the claimed benefits of oil applied to head, ears and feet exceed those of any emollient or of touch alone. No active-comparator trial was located in that search.

Adverse events. Oil pulling and nasal oil instillation carry aspiration and lipoid-pneumonia concerns in principle; no systematic quantification of harms for any dinacharya practice was located in that search.
Whether the regimen transfers outside its climatic and cultural setting, given that Charaka Sutrasthana 6 itself makes suitability relative to the place of habitation.

Whether the popular modern three-part doshic day clock has any classical textual basis. No verse stating it was found in the Charaka, Sushruta and Ashtanga Hridaya material read here, but the search was limited to those texts and to the chapters named in gatheringNotes, so this is an unresolved question and not a negative finding.

What modern literature, if any, bears on fourteen of this record's seventeen enumerated limbs. This record carries no modern reference for brahma-muhurta waking, dantadhavana, anjana, nasya, dhumapana, murdha taila, karna purana, padabhyanga, udvartana, snana, vyayama, shaucha, aharya or sadvritta. The limb-by-limb position and the bounds of the search are set out in modernCoverage. For dantadhavana and snana in particular there is a large general dentistry and hygiene literature that this record did not search and does not represent.

What Bhavaprakasha's Purvakhanda dinacharya section says. It was not retrieved for this record and nothing here rests on it. It is the text most often cited for the version of the daily regimen taught in modern Indian Ayurvedic curricula alongside Ashtanga Hridaya, so its absence is a real limit on this record's coverage of the tradition's transmission.

What Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 2 says in English. No public-domain English translation of Ashtanga Hridaya was located, so this record quotes the chapter only in Sanskrit and reports its content at the level of lexical identification. Anyone needing a translation will have to use an in-copyright one, which this project cannot quote.

The standard (Trikamji) verse numbers for any passage in this record. Every classical address here is to the number printed in Kaviratna or Bhishagratna, or to a page where no number is printed. Kaviratna's numbering is known in this project to run behind the standard and to restart within some chapters; no standard-edition number has been checked for this record and none is asserted.

Whether a classical locus for jihva nirlekhana exists outside Charaka Sutrasthana 5. The Charaka passage was found during this revision; Sushruta's and Vagbhata's treatment of tongue cleaning was not searched for.

components.gloss: Rising in the last part of the night. Attested in the Sanskrit of Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 2.1, which opens the daily-regimen chapter with it. NOT present in Charaka Sutrasthana 5 or Sutrasthana 8 as retrieved for this record; neither chapter gives a waking hour.

Cleaning the teeth with a chewed stick of astringent, pungent or bitter wood, twice daily, without injuring the gums (Charaka Sutrasthana 5, Kaviratna's printed aphorisms 63-64; recommended woods at 65)

Scraping the tongue with a blunt-edged, bent scraper of gold, silver, copper, tin, lead or iron, to remove the secretions at the base of the tongue and those that obstruct respiration (Charaka Sutrasthana 5, Kaviratna's printed aphorisms 66-67). This limb was absent from the earlier version of this record even though the record cited a tongue-scraping Cochrane review.

Holding oil or other specified liquids in the mouth; Charaka's chapter summary lists 'the articles to be kept in the mouth and the object for which they are to be so kept' and 'the merits of oil when used as gargle'
Daily collyrium to the eyes; a mild daily variety and a stronger periodic one are distinguished

Oil instilled or snuffed into the nose. Charaka Sutrasthana 5, Kaviratna's printed aphorism 48, directs that such oils should be used at all times but not 'when the sky remains cloudless in these three seasons, viz., the rainy season, the autumn, and the spring'. The restriction is conditional on the cloudless sky, not a flat seasonal ban.

Inhaling medicated smoke at listed occasions (after bathing, eating, clearing the throat, sneezing, cleaning teeth, nasya, collyrium, waking), with rules on pipe construction and a stated daily frequency
Daily oiling of the head; benefits claimed include freedom from headache and baldness, clear senses, easy sleep
Daily oil into the ears; claimed to prevent vata-borne ear disorders, wry neck, lock-jaw, deafness (Charaka Sutrasthana 5, Kaviratna's printed aphorism 76)
Daily oiling of the body, justified by the doctrine that vata governs touch and touch resides in skin, so skin is the site to treat (Charaka Sutrasthana 5, Kaviratna's printed aphorisms 77-79)
Oiling and rubbing of the feet; claimed to relieve harshness, dryness, heat, fatigue and numbness (Charaka Sutrasthana 5, Kaviratna's printed aphorism 82)

Rubbing fragrant powders over the body. Sushruta Chikitsasthana 24, Bhishagratna's numbered section 28, attributes to it restoration of deranged vayu, reduction of fat and aggravated kapha, and firmness of the limbs.

Bathing, said in Charaka Sutrasthana 5 to purify the body and to develop virility and longevity. Sushruta Chikitsasthana 24 treats it at Bhishagratna's numbered sections 33-35 and gives prohibitions immediately after.

Physical exercise. Both texts prescribe it and both limit it. Charaka Sutrasthana 7 (Kaviratna's printed aphorisms 29-32) says one should have recourse to it 'in due measure' and lists the harms of excess. Sushruta Chikitsasthana 24 (Bhishagratna's numbered section 25) says it 'should be taken every day' but in the same section limits it to 'the half extent of his capacity', and lists the diseases of excess at section 26-27. The earlier version of this record set the two texts against each other on this point; the fuller passage does not support that contrast.

Keeping the bodily outlets clean, cropping hair and paring nails. Charaka Sutrasthana 8 (Kaviratna's printed aphorism 13) specifies three shaves and three nail-parings within a fortnight, and twice-daily bathing.

Clean clothes, perfumes, garlands, ornaments, shoes, umbrella and stick; itemised in Charaka's Sutrasthana 5 chapter summary and again in Charaka Sutrasthana 8, and treated in Sushruta Chikitsasthana 24

Code of speech, conduct and social behaviour. In Charaka it is not a separate topic but the continuation of the same enumeration as the physical acts: Sutrasthana 8 (Kaviratna's printed aphorisms 12-14) announces 'the practices of the good', states that observing them accomplishes preservation of health and subjugation of the senses together, and then runs oiling the head, ears, nose and feet and inhaling smoke directly into truthfulness, non-injury and the social rules. Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 2 does the same, placing its conduct code at verses 20-39 of the daily-regimen chapter. Sushruta's Chikitsasthana 24 also carries general rules of conduct.

classical.verse: chapter-summary aphorisms printed as 100, 101, 102 and 103 in Kaviratna's edition, the numbers printed after each aphorism
classical.establishes: The canonical inventory of daily-regimen acts in Charaka, given in the chapter's own summary aphorisms. Note that this chapter is titled for dietary measure, not for 'dinacharya'; the daily acts sit inside a chapter about proper quantity of food.
classical.quote: The merits of snuffing (oil), the mode of snuffing and its time, the manner in which the tooth-cleansing stick should be made and used, the merits of such sticks when made of particular plants, The articles to be kept in the mouth and the object for which they are to be so kept, the merits of oil when used as gargle, and the merits of anointing the head with oil, The merits of applying oil into the hollows of the ears, of rubbing oil over the body and over the feet, of rubbing (fragrant powders) over the body; of bathing, of clean apparel, of perfumes, and of ornaments, The merits of keeping the outlets (of the body) clean, of cropping the hair, of wearing shoes, and of using umbrellas and sticks, have been spoken of in this lesson called Matrasitiya.

classical.verse: aphorisms printed as 77, 78 and 79 in Kaviratna's edition
classical.establishes: The explicit reasoning chain offered for daily abhyanga: vata governs touch, touch resides in skin, oil benefits skin, therefore oil the skin daily. This is analogical argument from the jar, leather and axle, not observation.
classical.quote: As an earthen jar if saturated with oil, or a piece of leather if rubbed therewith, or the axle of a car or cart from application of the same substance, becomes strong and capable of resisting wear and tear, even so the body, by application of oil, becomes strong, and the skin improves, and all disorders due to wind are dispelled. Through such means the body also becomes capable of enduring exercise and fatigue. The wind is chiefly instrumental in the sense of touch. The sense of touch has the skin for its refuge. For the skin the application of oil is highly beneficial. Hence, one should daily anoint the skin with oil.

classical.verse: aphorisms printed as 63 and 64 in Kaviratna's edition
classical.establishes: Tooth cleaning is specified twice daily with a stated technique caution about gum injury. The claimed effects include appetite, which is a doshic rather than a dental rationale.
classical.quote: The stick for brushing the teeth should be either astringent or pungent or bitter. One of its ends should be chewed into the form of a brush. It should be used twice a day, taking care that the gums be not injured. The process (of washing the teeth thus) destroys bad odor and bad taste. It removes sordes from the tongue, teeth, and mouth, and quickly produces appetite and purifies the teeth.

classical.verse: aphorisms printed as 66 and 67 in Kaviratna's edition
classical.establishes: The classical locus for jihva nirlekhana, tongue scraping, which the earlier version of this record omitted from its components even while citing a tongue-scraping Cochrane review in its modern section. The rationale given is removal of accumulated secretions and of odour; no doshic mechanism is stated in this passage.
classical.quote: Tongue-scrapers should be made of gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, and iron. These should be of blunt edges and bent in form. By using the tongue-scraper the secretions that accumulate at the base of the tongue, and also those that obstruct respiration, are removed, and the mouth becoming freed from all bad odor emits an agreeable smell. For this reason the tongue should be scratched with the tongue-scraper.

classical.chapter: 8 (Indriyopakramaniya, rendered by Kaviratna as 'Analysis of the Senses')
classical.verse: aphorisms printed as 12, 13 and 14 in Kaviratna's edition
classical.establishes: Sadvritta, the code of conduct, and the physical daily acts are a single continuous enumeration in Charaka Sutrasthana 8, not two separate topics. The chapter states the purpose of the enumeration before giving it: observing these practices accomplishes 'the preservation of health and the subjugation of the senses' together. This is the limb the earlier version of this record omitted entirely, and it is the one that carries the regimen's stated moral and social content. Note also that Su 8 prescribes oil to head, ears, nose and feet, and does not prescribe whole-body abhyanga in this passage.
classical.quote: By observing such practices one simultaneously accomplishes two objects, viz., the preservation of health and the subjugation of the senses. I shall, therefore, O Agnivesa, inculcate to thee in full what the practices of the good are. They are as follows: one should worship the deities, kine, Brahmanas, seniors, aged men, persons crowned with (ascetic) success, and preceptors. [...] One should bathe twice in the day, once in the morning and once again in the evening. One should always keep one's outlets for the passage of impurities (viz., urine and excreta), and one's feet, perfectly clean and well washed. Within a fortnight one should have three shaves and thrice pare one's nails. One should every day wear clean and well-washed clothes. One should be always cheerful, and always use agreeable perfumes. One should wear handsome and decent garments, and dress one's hair (by combing and parting it.) One should every day apply oil to one's head, ears, nose, and feet. One should inhale smoke (under the restrictions and in the way indicated before). One should welcome a person one meets (without waiting to be spoken to). One should speak agreeable words with smiles. One should protect another fallen into distress. [...] One should firmly adhere to truthfulness, and lead a life of tranquillity (by abstaining from injuring any creature.) One should accustom oneself to calmly bear the harsh speeches of others. One should subdue wrath. [...] One should not yawn, or sneeze, or laugh without covering one's face.

classical.verse: aphorisms printed as 29, 30, 31 and 32 in Kaviratna's edition
classical.establishes: Charaka's definition of vyayama and his limit on it. The earlier version of this record asserted this position in its contested section without quoting it; the quote is supplied here so the position has an address.
classical.quote: That exertion of body which is productive of good consequences (to the body itself), which conduces to collectedness (of mind), and increases strength, is called physical exercise. One should have recourse to it in due measure. The consequences resulting from physical exercise are lightness of body, capacity for work, collectedness, power of enduring hardship, removal of all imperfections, and augmentation of the digestive fire. From excess of physical exercise result fatigue, faintness, loss of vigor, thirst, asthma, consumption, fever, and attacks of cold. An intelligent person should never indulge in physical exercise, laughter, talking, walking, sexual congress, and night-keeping, to excess even when these become necessary.

classical.verse: aphorisms printed as 40 and 41 in Kaviratna's edition
classical.establishes: The habituation rationale: habituation itself makes a practice tolerable, and suitability is defined relationally against place and existing disorder. This is a qualifier on the idea of a single universal daily routine.
classical.quote: That which produces happiness or yields not torture, in consequence of the system being inured to it, is known by the name of okasatmya. They that are conversant with this topic of assimilation (or suitability of practices to the system), regard that conduct and that food to be suitable which have virtues contrary to those of the place of habitation and of the disorders (to which the system is subject).

classical.verse: aphorism number damaged in the scanned Kaviratna text; it falls between Kaviratna's printed aphorisms 18 and 23 of this chapter
classical.establishes: The stated aim of the discipline puts preservation of health before treatment of disease, which is the frame within which the daily regimen chapters are read.
classical.quote: The purpose of the Science of Life is protection of the health of the hale and alleviation of disease of one that is ailing.

classical.chapter: 6 (Ritucharyadhyayam, which Bhishagratna heads 'the Chapter which treats of the characteristic features of the different seasons of the year and their influence on health and drugs')
classical.verse: no number: Bhishagratna's Sutrasthana chapter 6 is continuous unnumbered prose. The passage sits on his pages 50-51, in the run immediately after his account of the accumulation, excitation and pacification of the doshas and immediately before his passage on the properties of water and vegetables in natural and unnatural seasons.
classical.establishes: A stated parallel between the parts of the day and the seasons of the year, with the doshas running an accumulation-aggravation-subsidence cycle within the day as they do within the year. Two limits on what this passage can be used for. First, it stands in Sushruta's SEASONAL-regimen chapter, whose own heading is about the seasons of the year; Sushruta's daily-regimen material is in Chikitsasthana 24, and nothing retrieved for this record connects the two or derives any daily act from this parallel. Second, the mapping here is five-part (morning=spring, noon=summer, evening=rains, midnight=autumn, pre-dawn=hemanta), not the three-part kapha/pitta/vata clock taught in most modern popular accounts.
classical.quote: Likewise the features, which specifically mark the different seasons of the year are observed to characterise the different parts of a complete day and night, [or in other words] traits peculiar to spring time exhibit themselves in the morning; the noon is marked by all the characteristics of summer; the evening by those of the rainy season; the midnight by those of autumn; and the hours before dawn by those of Hemanta. And similarly, like the seasons of the year, the different parts of the day and night are marked by variations of heat, cold, etc. [or in other words] the deranged bodily humours such as wind, bile, etc. naturally and spontaneously accumulate, aggravate, or subside during the different parts of the day as they do in the different seasons of the year.

classical.chapter: 24 (rules of hygiene and the prophylactic measures)
classical.verse: Bhishagratna's own numbered section 25, with the harms of excess at his sections 26-27
classical.establishes: Sushruta's version of the daily regimen is a much longer chapter than Charaka's and is framed explicitly as prophylaxis. On exercise it prescribes daily practice AND caps it at half capacity AND lists the diseases of excess, all within the same stretch of text.
classical.quote: What is (popularly) known as physical exercise is (nothing but) a sense of weariness from bodily labour, and it should be taken every day. After taking physical exercise, the whole body should be shampooed, until it gives rise to a comfortable sensation in the limbs. It makes the body stout and strong, helps the symmetrical growth of the limbs and muscles, improves the complexion and the digestive powers, prevents laziness and makes the body light and glossy, firm and compact. [...] A man seeking his own good should take physical exercise every day only to the half extent of his capacity (Valardha), as otherwise it may prove fatal. [section 26-27:] Consumption, haemorrhage (Rakta-pitta), thirst, phthisis, aversion to food, vomiting, illusiveness, weariness, fever, cough and asthma are the diseases, which are likely to originate from excessive physical exercise, and is, therefore, forbidden after a meal and the fatigues of sexual intercourse, in a fit of vertigo and in respect of persons suffering from haemorrhage, phthisis, cachexia, cough, asthma and ulcer.

classical.chapter: 24 (rules of hygiene and the prophylactic measures)
classical.verse: Bhishagratna's own numbered sections 22-24
classical.establishes: The explicit exclusions on anointing. Sushruta's immediately preceding section 21 also makes anointment conditional: it 'should be prescribed by an intelligent person with due regard to one's habit, congeniality and temperament and to the climate and the season of the year as well as to the preponderance of the deranged Dosha or Doshas in one's physical constitution'. Daily oiling is therefore not unconditional in Sushruta.
classical.quote: Anointments of the body simply with (unmedicated) Sneha are strictly forbidden in cases of undigested (Ama) Doshas (as long as the aggravated Doshas of the body continue in an unassimilated or undigested state and in their full virulence and intensity). Anointment should not be resorted to in cases of acute fever and indigestion, nor after the exhibition of emetics and purgatives, nor after an application of a Nirudha-Vasti. Anointment in the first two cases (acute fever and indigestion) serves to make the diseases curable with difficulty and even incurable, while that made on the same day after the application of purgatives, emetics, or a Nirudha-Vasti, tends to impair the digestive capacity, etc. Anointment is similarly prohibited in diseases due to Samtarpana (repletion, etc).

classical.verse: 2.1, 2.8 and 2.9; the chapter's conduct code runs 2.20 to 2.39
classical.establishes: Vagbhata gives the daily regimen its own dedicated chapter, second in the Sutrasthana, immediately before the seasonal-regimen chapter. This is the structural source of the modern teaching order 'daily regimen then seasonal regimen'. Three things were read directly off the Sanskrit and are reported at the level of lexical identification rather than translation, because no public-domain English rendering is available. (a) Verse 1 opens the chapter with brāhme muhūrte, the brahma muhurta, and uttiṣṭhet, the optative 'should rise', with svasthaḥ, one in health, and rakṣārtham āyuṣaḥ, for the sake of protecting lifespan. This is the verse to which the brahma-muhurta rule is commonly attributed in the secondary literature, and the rule is in fact here. (b) Verse 8 contains abhyaṅgam ācaren nityaṃ, and verse 9 contains varjyo 'bhyaṅgaḥ followed by a compound naming kapha-affected, post-purification and a-jīrṇin states, so the chapter prescribes daily abhyanga and immediately excludes cases, matching Sushruta rather than the unconditional reading. (c) Verses 20 to 39 are the chapter's conduct code, and it contains close parallels to Charaka Sutrasthana 8, including nā-saṃvṛta-mukhaḥ kuryāt kṣuti-hāsya-vijṛmbhaṇam at 2.35, not sneezing, laughing or yawning with the face uncovered. The chapter's running order, verses 1 to 19, is rising, tooth cleaning, collyrium, nasya and gandusha and dhumapana, abhyanga, vyayama, udvartana, snana, and then food. No claim is made here about the chapter's title or about any verse not listed in this entry.
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

modern.title: The effect of oil pulling in comparison with chlorhexidine and other mouthwash interventions in promoting oral health: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
modern.establishes: Jong, Ooi and Teoh, International Journal of Dental Hygiene 22(1). Systematic review with meta-analysis of randomised trials of oil pulling, the closest modern analogue of gandusha/kavala. Oil pulling improved Modified Gingival Index scores relative to non-chlorhexidine mouthwash; chlorhexidine remained superior for plaque index.
modern.quality: The methodologically strongest item this record carries for any dinacharya component, and the authors themselves grade the overall body of evidence as very low certainty. Trials were small, short, largely single-centre, and used surrogate indices rather than clinical endpoints. Note that the trials test a coconut-or-sesame oil swish as a mouthwash substitute; they do not test the classical gandusha procedure, its timing, or its doshic rationale.

modern.title: Effect of oil pulling on plaque induced gingivitis: a randomized, controlled, triple-blind study.
modern.establishes: Asokan, Emmadi and Chamundeswari, Indian Journal of Dental Research. Randomised, controlled, triple-blind trial in adolescents with plaque-induced gingivitis; sesame oil pulling reduced plaque index, modified gingival index and aerobic colony counts.
modern.quality: A genuine randomised trial, but very small, single-centre, short, and limited to surrogate oral indices in adolescents. It is the most-cited empirical support for an Ayurvedic daily-regimen practice in the sources this record consulted, and it carries most of the weight of that claim, which is a warning about how thin the base is.

modern.title: WITHDRAWN: Tongue scraping for treating halitosis.
modern.establishes: Outhouse and colleagues, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews: 'Tongue scraping for treating halitosis'. Two trials with a combined 40 participants were included; evidence for a small reduction in volatile sulphur compounds was rated weak and unreliable, and neither trial reported the review's primary outcomes.
modern.quality: A Cochrane review, so high methodological standard, but with almost no data to work on. It was subsequently WITHDRAWN (this 2016 record is the withdrawal notice) pending replacement by a wider halitosis protocol, and no replacement was located in this record's searches. Tongue cleaning is one of the most widely promoted dinacharya items and its best evidence has been formally retired from the Cochrane library.

modern.title: Pilot study investigating the effects of Ayurvedic Abhyanga massage on subjective stress experience.
modern.establishes: Basler, Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine 17(5). Single-dose one-hour abhyanga in 20 healthy adults reduced a validated subjective stress score and heart rate; blood pressure fell only in the pre-hypertensive subgroup. The author states explicitly that providers make unsubstantiated claims and that no prior attempt at verification existed.
modern.quality: An uncontrolled pre-post pilot with n=20, no control group, no blinding, single session, and outcomes that are highly susceptible to the non-specific effects of an hour of touch and rest. It cannot distinguish abhyanga from any massage, and it says nothing about a daily regimen.

openQuestions: The GRETIL Astangahrdayasutra transcription carries a 1997 transcription copyright (R. P. Das, R. E. Emmerick). The underlying Sanskrit verses are classical and this project's rule is that Sanskrit originals are quotable, but the transcription's licence has not been read. Resolve before publication, or re-key the three quoted verses from a pre-1929 printed Sanskrit edition.

The devanagari and iast values added for 'dinacharya' are standard orthography supplied editorially, not quoted from a terminological standard. Address them to the WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda or an equivalent before publication, per the project's no-assertion-without-an-address rule.

Kaviratna's printed numbers are now given throughout with the standard numbers never asserted. That is honest but makes the record hard to cross-reference against any modern citation. A separate pass against a Trikamji edition would let the record carry both, and would also settle the size of the offset in Sutrasthana 8 (Kaviratna 12-14 against the critic's reported 17-18).

records.title: Disease classification in Ayurveda (vyadhi-vibhaga)
records.summary: Ayurveda does not use one disease taxonomy but several overlapping axes applied to the same illness at once. Charaka sorts diseases by origin into nija (constitutional, arising from vitiated dosha) and agantu (accidental, arising from trauma, poison, spirits, weapons or curses); by seat into sharira (bodily) and manasa (mental); by dosha into vataja, pittaja and kaphaja, with stated counts of 80, 40 and 20 nanatmaja disorders; and by the numeric enumerations of the Ashtodariya chapter, which tallies named diseases by the number of their varieties. Sushruta gives a four-way origin classification (agantuka, sharira, manasa, svabhavika) in the opening chapter and, in the chapter on the classification of diseases, a seven-way scheme running from parental-seed defect through congenital, doshic, traumatic, seasonal, providential and spontaneous causes, which he maps onto the older three-fold adhyatmika, adhibhautika and adhidaivika division. Across all of these Charaka asserts a unifying claim: however classified, constitutional disease never escapes vata, pitta and kapha.
records.evidenceState:
This is the one concept in this cluster where the situation is not simply that evidence is absent, because part of the relevant evidence has actually been collected and it is unflattering. The studies that make that sentence true are named here, with their figures, so that the claim can be checked rather than taken on trust.

PMID 30653338 (Kessler et al. 2019, J Altern Complement Med) nested a reliability study of 30 knee osteoarthritis patients and four Ayurvedic experts inside a randomised controlled trial. Raw agreement was high, 95 percent consensus agreement on the main diagnosis, and the chance-corrected figures were not: the abstract reports kappas that "largely yielded fair-to-poor inter-rater agreement kappas for central diagnostic aspects such as prakriti and agni (kappa values between 0 and 0.4)", and adds that "agreement on disease-related entities was better than that on constitutional entities". PMID 24191170 (Kurande et al. 2013, Evid Based Complement Alternat Med) had fifteen registered Ayurvedic doctors with 3 to 15 years of experience independently examine twenty healthy subjects, and computed weighted kappa for all 105 doctor pairs: average pairwise kappa was 0.07 for pulse, 0.17 for tongue and 0.28 for prakriti, with the null hypothesis of random rating rejected for only twelve of the 105 pairs on prakriti, one pair on pulse and no pair on tongue. That study's own qualification has to travel with those numbers: it also found "significant evidence against random rating by software and questionnaire use" and concluded that "Prakriti assessment appears reliable when questionnaire and software assessment are used, while other diagnostic methods have room for improvement". The unflattering result is therefore about unaided expert judgement, not about every instrument, and this record does not claim more than that. PMID 23930037, the same group's methodological overview, gives the field's assessment of itself in 2013: "reliability studies in Ayurveda are in the preliminary stage".

What none of the three measures is the classificatory axes this record is about. Between them they cover pulse, tongue, prakriti, agni and a final named diagnosis in one condition. No located study reports an agreement figure for assigning a disease to nija or agantu, to sharira or manasa, to a doshaja subtype, to one of the 80, 40 and 20 nanatmaja lists, or to one of Sushruta's seven bala-pravritta types. The classificatory schemes themselves are well documented in the primary texts and can be reported with confidence as doctrine; what remains unmeasured is whether two physicians apply them the same way.

On prediction the record states only what it has looked for. A PubMed search on 2026-10-06 for ayurved*[tiab] AND (classification[tiab] OR nosolog*[tiab] OR vyadhi[tiab]) AND (prognos*[tiab] OR predict*[tiab] OR "treatment response"[tiab]) returned 24 records whose titles were screened, and none of them tests whether assigning a disease to an Ayurvedic class predicts treatment response or prognosis better than the symptom description the assignment is derived from. That is a keyword search on title and abstract and would miss a study that does not use those words, so it supports "none located" and not "none exists".

Institutionally the picture has moved faster than the evidence, and this project now holds the artefact. The sibling repository file data/enrichment/icd-tm2.json in ayurveda-atlas is a snapshot of the ICD-11 TM2 content at release 2026-01, fetched 2026-09-17, containing 709 entities, 61 blocks and 648 categories. Five blocks bear directly on Ayurvedic disease classification: "Functional elements and humoral derangement patterns (TM2)", "Physical constituent derangement patterns (TM2)", "Power derangement and chronic accumulation patterns (TM2)", "Body constitution and temperament patterns (TM2)" and "External factors disorders (TM2)". Two facts about that chapter matter more than its size. The first is that its statistical standing is narrower than the word classification suggests: PMID 41180267 describes Chapter 26 as "a supplementary, morbidity-only chapter, enabling dual coding of traditional medicine concepts alongside conventional diagnoses", with dual coding "optional", Module I in force from 1 January 2022 and "Module II (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani) was added in 2025". Morbidity-only means the codes are excluded from mortality statistics; the same source says Chapter 26 carries "the potential to support morbidity statistics", so it is not correct to say TM2 is excluded from morbidity statistics too. The second is that the pattern-level categories were adopted ahead of their own validation: the same source states that "The validity and reliability of Chapter 26 require dedicated study", that "Within-system reliability should be tested through interrater and test–retest assessments among traditional medicine clinicians", and that "validity is not guaranteed: even within the same system, different practitioners may not agree when assigning traditional medicine patterns". A bounded PubMed search on 2026-10-06 for "ICD-11"[tiab] AND ("traditional medicine"[tiab] OR ayurved*[tiab]) returned 19 records, titles screened, none of which reports field-testing or coding-reliability results for the ASU module. NAMASTE (PMID 37541078) stands on the same footing: the initiative report establishes that standardised ASU morbidity codes exist and who built them, not that the categories behind them have been validated or that coders apply them reliably.

The constitution-genomics literature does not close the gap, and this record says so explicitly rather than omitting it while neighbouring records cite it. PMID 18782426 (Prasher et al. 2008) and PMID 26511157 (Govindaraj et al. 2015) are the two most-cited molecular results in the field. Both classify persons, not illnesses: Prasher profiled healthy individuals of extreme vata, pitta and kapha type and framed the conclusion as "differential disease predisposition", a hypothesis about susceptibility in the well, while Govindaraj correlated 52 SNPs with prakriti group membership in 262 screened males. Neither assigns a disease to a class, neither tests whether such an assignment is reproducible, and neither tests whether it predicts anything. Transfer to disease classification would require the disease axes to be derived from or validated against constitution, and the texts do not derive them that way: nija and agantu, sharira and manasa, and the doshaja triad classify the disturbance, not the person, and prakriti is the baseline a vikriti is read against rather than the vikriti itself. The one empirical hint about how the two levels behave points away from transfer, since PMID 30653338 found agreement on disease-related entities better than on constitutional entities. A replicated genomic correlate of prakriti would therefore still license no claim about vyadhi-vibhaga.

There is also a textual problem that no amount of modern work addresses: Charaka and Sushruta each give more than one classification, the schemes are structurally incompatible, both authors then subordinate everything to the doshas on grounds that are stated in unfalsifiable terms, and the identification of the enumerated Sanskrit disease names with modern entities was flagged as unreliable by the public-domain translators themselves.

contested.question: How many classifications are there, and which is primary?
positions: Charaka Sutra 11.44 gives three (physical, accidental, mental).
Charaka Sutra 20.2 gives four (accidental plus the three doshaja) and then immediately gives two by cause and two by substratum.
Sushruta Sutra 1 gives four (agantuka, sharira, manasa, svabhavika).
Sushruta Sutra 24 gives seven bala-pravritta types mapped onto three older ones.
The texts present these as complementary; they are not structurally reconcilable, and which is treated as primary varies by author and by clinical context.

contested.question: Is the nija/agantu distinction stable?
positions: It is presented as the fundamental causal division.

Charaka himself states in Ashtodariya that each converts into the other on aggravation, and in Maharoga that all four classes follow one another when aggravated, which means the distinction holds only early in the course.
Since both classes are said to share the same three inducing causes (Sutra 20.9), the distinction rests on the proximate agent alone.

contested.question: Are the nanatmaja counts of 80, 40 and 20 a taxonomy or a mnemonic?
positions: Traditional exposition treats the lists as exhaustive enumerations of dosha-specific disorders.
