Kaviratna noted that the lists differ between printed editions and that he compiled his from two texts, and that identification of the names with modern entities may not be accurate in every instance.
Some scholars read the numeric enumerations of Ashtodariya and Maharoga as pedagogical devices for memorisation rather than as claims about the number of diseases.

contested.question: Should Ayurvedic categories be mapped into ICD, or kept separate?
positions: The NAMASTE and ICD-11 traditional medicine module position is that standardised coding enables morbidity statistics, insurance and research on traditional medicine.

The ethnopharmacology methodological position (Staub and colleagues 2015) is that forcing indigenous categories into a clinical-examination-based biomedical taxonomy destroys exactly the categories that carry the local explanatory content, and that patient-perception-based systems such as ICPC map better.
The practitioner-side critique visible in the ICD-11 Chapter 26 revision literature is that even a harmonised traditional classification satisfies none of the traditions it merges.

contested.question: Does a classification that always terminates in the doshas classify anything?
positions: The classical position, stated in Charaka's bird-and-shadow verse and in Sushruta's fatherhood-of-all-maladies verse, is that doshic reduction is the deepest truth about disease.

The criterion Sushruta actually offers, that doshic symptoms can be detected in a disease of whatsoever type, is not falsifiable as stated, so the reduction cannot be tested by the means the text provides.
Charaka's own reservation, that agantu disease is initially distinguished therefrom, preserves a class that is not doshic in origin.

contested.question: Does the constitution-genomics line bear on disease classification at all?
positions: The ayurgenomics position, as stated in Prasher et al. 2008 (PMID 18782426), is that Ayurvedic phenotypic classification "allows us to uncover genes that may contribute to system level differences in normal individuals which could lead to differential disease predisposition", and in Govindaraj et al. 2015 (PMID 26511157) that "the phenotypic classification of India's traditional medicine has a genetic basis". Both claims are about prakriti.

This record's position is that the claims do not transfer to vyadhi-vibhaga, because the classified object differs: prakriti classifies the person and is assessed in the healthy, while the axes in this record classify the illness. Neither study assigns a disease to a class or tests such an assignment for reproducibility or prediction.

The one relevant empirical observation runs against transfer in the direction that matters: Kessler et al. 2019 (PMID 30653338) reported that "agreement on disease-related entities was better than that on constitutional entities", so the two levels are not interchangeable even in reliability behaviour.

A position this record does not hold but cannot rule out: if a doshaja disease assignment were shown to be derived from or constrained by prakriti, the genomics work would become relevant. No located study establishes that derivation.

notKnown: Whether two independent Ayurvedic physicians agree on nija versus agantu, on doshaja subtype, or on Sushruta's seven bala-pravritta types. The located reliability studies test other things: PMID 30653338 tested prakriti and agni among other central diagnostic aspects and returned kappa between 0 and 0.4, and PMID 24191170 tested pulse, tongue and prakriti and returned average pairwise kappa of 0.07, 0.17 and 0.28. No agreement figure for any of the classificatory axes in this record has been located.

Whether any Ayurvedic disease classification predicts treatment response or prognosis better than the symptom picture alone. No study establishing this has been located. The search behind that statement, run on 2026-10-06, was PubMed for ayurved*[tiab] AND (classification[tiab] OR nosolog*[tiab] OR vyadhi[tiab]) AND (prognos*[tiab] OR predict*[tiab] OR "treatment response"[tiab]), 24 records returned and titles screened. It is a keyword search in one database and would miss a study phrased differently, so this is a located-nothing statement and not a non-existence claim.

Whether the ICD-11 traditional medicine module covering Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani has been field-tested for coding reliability. No such results have been located, and WHO's own Bulletin (PMID 41180267) says the work is still to be done rather than reporting it: "The validity and reliability of Chapter 26 require dedicated study", with interrater and test-retest assessment named as what is needed. The searches behind the negative, both run on 2026-10-06, were PubMed for "ICD-11"[tiab] AND ("traditional medicine"[tiab] OR ayurved*[tiab]), 19 records with titles screened, and ("TM2" OR "Module 2" OR "Module II") AND "ICD-11", which returned nothing.

How the TM2 pattern blocks held in this project's snapshot map onto the classical axes in this record. The snapshot carries no definition text for any of its 709 entities and no entity in it mentions Ayurveda, so the correspondence between, for example, "Functional elements and humoral derangement patterns (TM2)" and Charaka's doshaja triad cannot be read off the data. No crosswalk is asserted here, and the BY-ND licence on TM2 would in any case forbid an adapted one.

How many TM2 categories there are. This project's source register and Indian government press material both give 529 disorder categories, while the 2026-01 snapshot held in the sibling repository contains 648 categories and 61 blocks. The figures have not been reconciled; the difference may be release drift, a difference between disorder and pattern counts, or a counting convention, and none of those has been established.

How many of the 80 vataja, 40 pittaja and 20 kaphaja named disorders can be identified with any modern entity with agreement between scholars. Kaviratna flagged his own identifications as possibly inaccurate.
Whether the readings of the nanatmaja lists differ enough between manuscript traditions to change the counts, given that Kaviratna compiled his list from two printed texts that differed.

How Kaviratna's verse numbering in the passages quoted here corresponds to standard Trikamji numbering. Every verse number in the classical array is labelled "(Kaviratna)" for that reason and no Trikamji equivalence is asserted. The correspondence has not been checked against a Sanskrit edition for Sutrasthana 11, 19 and 20 or Vimanasthana 1, and Kaviratna is known in this project to run one behind Trikamji elsewhere in the text.

What clinical consequence, if any, follows from assigning a disease to Sushruta's adi-bala (parental seed) versus janma-bala (congenital) class, which is the closest classical approach to a hereditary versus developmental distinction.

Whether the manasa class as defined, arising from non-attainment of the desired and accession of the disliked, picks out anything distinguishable from the psychiatric categories now used in the same settings.

Whether practitioners in different Indian states and schools use the same classification in the same way. No multi-centre concordance study has been located; PMID 23930037, the field's own methodological overview, described Ayurvedic reliability work as being "in the preliminary stage" in 2013 and set out the designs that would be needed.

How svabhavika conditions such as hunger, thirst and sleep are meant to function as a disease class rather than as normal physiology, and what makes their untimely occurrence pathological in operational terms.

Whether anything in the constitution-genomics literature bears on disease classification. The record's position is that it does not, for the reasons given in evidenceState and in the contested entry on the question, but that position is an argument from what the two studies did, not a result. No study testing whether prakriti constrains or predicts a disease-class assignment has been located.

components.gloss: Charaka's primary origin axis: constitutional disease arising from one's own vitiated doshas, versus accidental disease from an external agent. The two are said to convert into each other when aggravated
Seat axis: body and mind as the two substrata of disease. Charaka gives mental disease its own etiology, namely non-attainment of what is desired and accession of what is disliked
Vataja, pittaja and kaphaja disease, with enumerated counts of 80, 40 and 20 nanatmaja (dosha-specific) disorders in Charaka Sutra 20
Disorders arising from a single dosha alone versus those arising from any dosha or combination. Charaka's Ashtodariya chapter enumerates the general ones and Maharoga the dosha-specific ones

Agantuka (traumatic or extraneous), sharira (bodily, from diet, blood or humours), manasa (mental, from anger, grief, fear, joy, envy, pride, greed, lust), svabhavika (natural, including hunger, thirst, decrepitude, sleep, death)

Adi-bala (parental seed defect), janma-bala (congenital, from maternal conduct in gestation), dosha-bala (humoral), sanghata-bala (traumatic), kala-bala (seasonal), daiva-bala (providential, including epidemic and sporadic subtypes), svabhava-bala (spontaneous, timely or untimely)
The older three-fold division of affliction by locus of cause, onto which Sushruta maps his seven types
Prognostic axis of curable and incurable, cited at Charaka Vimana 6/3 alongside the somatic and psychological division
The five diagnostic limbs (nidana, purvarupa, rupa, upashaya, samprapti) which classify the evidence for a disease rather than the disease itself; systematised in Madhava Nidana chapter 1

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson XI (Tistraishaniya), verse 44 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 44 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: A three-way classification with each class given its own etiology, and a definition of mental disease in terms of desire and aversion rather than of dosha.
classical.quote: Diseases are of three kinds, viz., Physical, Accidental, and Mental. Physical diseases are those that arise from some abnormal condition of the body. Accidental are those that arise from the action of spirits, of poison, of wind, of fire, of acts of violence done to the body, such as beating, etc. Mental diseases are those that arise from non-attainment of objects desired or coveted, or from accession of those that are disliked.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson XIX (Ashtodariya), verse 47 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 47 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The unifying doctrine underneath all the classificatory axes: every nija disease reduces to vata, pitta and kapha. The bird-and-shadow simile is the standard proof-text for this.
classical.quote: All constitutional diseases that affect oneself never spring from any other source than one's wind, bile, and phlegm. Even as a bird, roving wheresoever it likes, can never transgress its own shadow, after the same manner all the diseases that afflict a person, born of the disorders of his own constituent elements, can never transgress his own wind, bile, and phlegm. Intelligent physicians observing the especial seat or place, the indications, and the exciting causes, of wind, bile, and phlegm, refer all diseases as caused by disorders of wind, or bile, or phlegm.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson XIX (Ashtodariya), closing verses
classical.verse: closing verses 1-2 of the chapter (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: That the nija/agantu boundary is permeable in both directions once disease is aggravated, which qualifies the classification substantially.
classical.quote: All the numerous diseases that appear in the body, arising from the disorders of one's constituent elements, are not separable from (disorders of) bile, phlegm and wind. All diseases, however, that are accidental, are distinguished therefrom. The Accidental becoming aggravated, follows the Constitutional disease; similarly the Constitutional, becoming aggravated, follows the Accidental. Hence, ascertaining properly the adjunct and the cause, the work of treatment should be commenced.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson XX (Maharoga), verses 2-6 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 2-6 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The explicit statement that several classifications (four-way, two-way by cause, two-way by substratum) are applied simultaneously to the same set of diseases, and that the number of resulting varieties is innumerable.
classical.quote: The diseases that occur are of four kinds: They are 1. Accidental, 2. those born of wind, 3. those born of bile, and 4. those born of phlegm. Though distributed into four kinds, their character as disease is of one kind, in consequence of the common element being present in all of them of producing affliction or pain. In consequence, again, of diseases being distributed into two kinds, viz., Accidental and Constitutional, their causes are of two kinds. In consequence, again, of the distinction between mind and body, the substrata of disease are of two kinds. The modifications, again, of those four are innumerable, in consequence of the differences in respect of causes, seats, symptoms, areas, and varieties, being innumerable.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson XX (Maharoga), verse 9 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 9 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: That the three general causes cut across the classification rather than aligning with it: all classes of disease share the same three inducing causes.
classical.quote: The inducing causes of both Accidental and Constitutional diseases are injudicious correlation of objects with the senses, want of wisdom or foresight, and time.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson XX (Maharoga), verse 18 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 18 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The canonical nanatmaja counts of 80, 40 and 20. The numbered lists that follow are of Sanskrit disease names whose identification with modern entities Kaviratna himself flagged as uncertain.
classical.quote: The diseases of Wind are of Eighty kinds; those of Bile are of forty kinds; those of Phlegm are of twenty kinds.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Vimana Sthana, Lesson I, verse 2 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 2 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The nidana-panchaka elements in Charaka: nimitta (inducing cause), purvarupa (premonitory indication), rupa (symptom) and upashaya (applicability of medicine, diet and conduct), glossed individually in Kaviratna's note to this verse.
classical.quote: Without doubt, having carefully noticed the particulars relating to inducing causes, premonitory indications, symptoms, applicability of medicine, diet and course of conduct, the varieties of diseases, the predominance of wind or bile or phlegm in diseases, the class under which the disease falls, the precise measures in which the faults have been excited, strength, and age or season, the physician, with concentrated mind, should specially attend to the knowledge (analysis) of the tastes, articles, faults, derangements, medicine, country, season, strength, body, diet, predominance of constituent elements (of the body, such as skin, blood, etc.), assimilability, mind, constitution, and age.

classical.text: Sushruta Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Chapter I
classical.establishes: Sushruta's four-way origin classification and his definition of disease, which differs from Charaka's by adding svabhavika as a fourth class and by counting hunger, thirst and sleep as derangements.
classical.quote: The Purusha (man) is the receptacle of any particular disease, and that which proves a source of torment or pain to him, is denominated as a disease. There are four different types of disease such as, Traumatic or of extraneous origin (Agantuka), Bodily (Sharira), Mental (Manasa) and Natural (Svabhavika). A disease due to an extraneous blow or hurt is called Agantuka. Diseases due to irregularities in food or drink, or incidental to a deranged state of the blood, or of the bodily humours acting either singly or in concert, are called Sharira. Excessive anger, grief, fear, joy, despondency, envy, misery, pride, greed, lust, desire, malice, etc. are included within the category of mental (Manasa) distempers; whereas hunger, thirst, decrepitude, imbecility, death, sleep, etc. are called the natural (Svabhavika) derangements of the body.

classical.text: Sushruta Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Chapter XXIV (Vyadhi-samuddeshiya)
classical.establishes: Sushruta's seven-way causal classification and its mapping onto the older three-fold division of affliction. Note that this is a third scheme, incompatible in structure with both his own Chapter I four-way scheme and Charaka's.
classical.quote: It has been stated before that anything that afflicts either the body or the living personality-self, or both, is called disease. This pain or affliction may be either physical in its character (Adhyatmikam), or due to any disturbance in the physical environments of a man (Adhibhautikam), or to the acts of God (Adhidaivikam) etc. This three-fold pain may be ultimately transformed into any of the seven kinds of diseases such as, the Adi-vala-pravritta, Janma-vala-pravritta, Dosha-vala-pravritta, Sanghata-vala-pravritta, Kala-vala-pravritta, Daiva-vala-pravritta and Svabhava-vala-pravritta.

classical.text: Sushruta Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Chapter XXIV, closing on the primacy of the doshas
classical.establishes: That Sushruta, having given a seven-way classification, then subordinates all of it to the doshas, matching Charaka's bird-and-shadow claim. The argument offered is that doshic symptoms can be detected in any disease type, which is an unfalsifiable criterion as stated.
classical.quote: The deranged bodily humours such as, Vayu, Pittam and Kapham should be looked upon as the primary sources of all diseases, inasmuch as symptoms characteristic of each of them may be detected in the case of a disease of whatsoever type, (which usually abates with their corresponding subsidence), and also because the Shastras have ascribed to them the fatherhood of all maladies that assail the human frame.

classical.establishes: Cites Charaka Vimana Sthana 6/3 for both the somatic/psychological division and the curable/incurable division. Located, not quoted.

classical.text: Madhava Nidana, chapter 1, systematises the nidana-panchaka as the five limbs of diagnosis and is the standard reference work for Ayurvedic disease description
classical.establishes: The classical framework for diagnostic evidence. No public-domain English translation exists, so nothing is quoted and no verse is asserted beyond the chapter. The Bulletin of the Indian Institute of History of Medicine carried two short papers specifically on the definition of nidana-panchaka in this chapter (PMID 12585278 and PMID 12572581).

modern.title: Reliability of Ayurvedic Diagnosis for Knee Osteoarthritis Patients: A Nested Diagnostic Study Within a Randomized Controlled Trial.
modern.establishes: Four Ayurvedic experts independently diagnosing 30 knee osteoarthritis patients, nested in an RCT, with a nominal group technique as the consensus procedure. High raw agreement on main diagnostic entities (95 percent consensus agreement on the main diagnosis) was not reflected in the kappa values, which "largely yielded fair-to-poor inter-rater agreement kappas for central diagnostic aspects such as prakriti and agni (kappa values between 0 and 0.4)". The authors also note that "agreement on disease-related entities was better than that on constitutional entities".
modern.quality: The single most useful empirical study for this concept. Properly designed reliability study nested in an RCT, international collaboration, appropriate statistics. Limits: 30 patients, one disease, four raters, a setting where a consensus procedure was available. The gap between raw agreement and kappa is the key finding and is often misreported.

modern.title: Interrater reliability of diagnostic methods in traditional Indian ayurvedic medicine.
modern.establishes: Fifteen registered Ayurvedic doctors with 3-15 years of experience independently examined twenty healthy subjects; weighted kappa was computed for all 105 doctor pairs. Average pairwise kappa was 0.07 for pulse (nadi), 0.17 for tongue (jivha) and 0.28 for body constitution (prakriti). The null hypothesis of random rating was rejected for only twelve of the 105 pairs on prakriti, one pair on pulse and no pair on tongue. The abstract's own qualification travels with those figures: there was "significant evidence against random rating by software and questionnaire use", and the authors conclude that "Prakriti assessment appears reliable when questionnaire and software assessment are used, while other diagnostic methods have room for improvement". So the finding is against unaided expert judgement, not against every instrument.
modern.quality: The most direct chance-corrected reliability figures in the Ayurvedic literature and correctly analysed. Small (20 subjects), healthy volunteers only, single site, and confined to pulse, tongue and constitution. It measures none of the classificatory axes this record is about: it does not test nija versus agantu, sharira versus manasa, doshaja subtype, the nanatmaja lists, or Sushruta's seven bala-pravritta types. Cited here for what reliability has been measured and for the boundary of that measurement, not as evidence about disease classification.

modern.title: Reliability studies of diagnostic methods in Indian traditional Ayurveda medicine: An overview.
modern.establishes: The same group's methodological overview of reliability study design for Ayurvedic diagnosis. It states the field's own position on itself: "The investigation of the reliability of traditional Chinese, Japanese and Sasang medicine diagnoses is in the formative stage. However, reliability studies in Ayurveda are in the preliminary stage." It sets out the designs and statistics that future studies would need, and names classification (explicitly prakriti classification) as one of the places where reliability is crucial.
modern.quality: A methodological overview, not primary evidence, and written by the group that then produced the reliability data, so it is the field's self-assessment rather than an independent audit. Cited for that self-assessment and for the fact that no reliability programme covering disease classification had been laid out as of 2013.

modern.title: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and data gaps in traditional medicine.
modern.establishes: Bulletin of the WHO perspective on the institutional standing of ICD-11 Chapter 26 and on what traditional medicine data the ICD does and does not capture. Four statements are quoted in this record: Chapter 26 "is a supplementary, morbidity-only chapter, enabling dual coding of traditional medicine concepts alongside conventional diagnoses"; the chapter "enables optional dual coding of traditional medicine disorders and patterns alongside conventional diagnoses" with "the potential to support morbidity statistics"; "ICD-11 took effect on 1 January 2022 with Module I (East-Asian systems)" and "Module II (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani) was added in 2025"; and on validation, "The validity and reliability of Chapter 26 require dedicated study", "Within-system reliability should be tested through interrater and test–retest assessments among traditional medicine clinicians", and "validity is not guaranteed: even within the same system, different practitioners may not agree when assigning traditional medicine patterns; and across systems, the underlying concepts may not align. Validity must be demonstrated before multinational comparisons are relied upon."
modern.quality: Policy perspective piece, not research. No abstract, no data, and its authors are writing from inside the institution whose product they are describing. It is nonetheless the best available peer-reviewed address for the statistical standing of Chapter 26 and for the statement that its validity and reliability have yet to be studied, which is why it now carries those facts instead of government press material. Not cited as evidence about Ayurvedic nosology itself.

modern.title: Initiatives: National Ayush Morbidity and Standardized Terminologies Electronic (NAMASTE) Portal.
modern.establishes: Describes the National Ayush Morbidity and Standardized Terminologies Electronic (NAMASTE) portal, India's standardised terminology and morbidity coding system for Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani.
modern.quality: Short initiative report, no abstract, no evaluation data. Establishes that the coding system exists and who built it. It does not establish that codes are applied reliably or that the classification has been validated. NAMASTE is treated here as a comparator, not as a source of definitions.

modern.title: A Proposed Revision of the International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision, Chapter 26.
modern.establishes: Argues that ICD-11 Chapter 26, the traditional medicine chapter, is a union set of harmonised Chinese, Japanese and Korean pattern classifications and proposes a structural revision.
modern.quality: Single-author proposal paper, not empirical. Included because it documents that even the better-established traditional medicine module in ICD-11 is contested in structure and terminology by practitioners of the traditions it encodes. Note that Chapter 26 Module 1 covers the East Asian traditions; the Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani content sits in Module 2, released later.

modern.title: Classifying diseases and remedies in ethnomedicine and ethnopharmacology.
modern.establishes: Systematic comparison of ICD, the Economic Botany Data Collection Standard and ICPC for classifying disease in ethnomedical systems, concluding that ICD's reliance on clinical-examination-based categories makes it a poor fit and that ICPC, being built on patient-reported categories, maps better onto ethnomedical reality.
modern.quality: Methodological analysis rather than an empirical study, but a careful and directly relevant one. It makes explicit the general problem that the Ayurvedic case instantiates: translating an indigenous nosology into a biomedical one loses the categories that did the original explanatory work.

modern.title: Definition of Nidana Pancaka (first chapter of Madhavanidana).
modern.journal: Bull Indian Inst Hist Med Hyderabad
modern.establishes: Short historical paper on the definition of nidana-panchaka in the first chapter of Madhava Nidana.
modern.quality: Historical and philological note in a low-circulation journal, no abstract available through PubMed, no DOI. Cited for textual provenance only.

modern.title: Whole genome expression and biochemical correlates of extreme constitutional types defined in Ayurveda.
modern.establishes: Genome-wide peripheral blood expression profiling plus biochemical and haematological measurement in healthy individuals selected as extreme vata, pitta and kapha types in an Indian population of Indo-European origin. Reports differences between the groups and enrichment of differentially expressed genes in transport, regulation of cyclin-dependent protein kinase activity, immune response and regulation of blood coagulation. The conclusion is framed as susceptibility, not diagnosis: the phenotyping "allows us to uncover genes that may contribute to system level differences in normal individuals which could lead to differential disease predisposition".
modern.quality: A genuine molecular study and the foundation of the ayurgenomics line, but small, single-population, with prakriti assignment by the hypothesis-forming team, a multiple-comparison burden inherent in microarray work, and no independent replication of the expression signature. Carried here only to support the record's explicit statement that the constitution-genomics line does not transfer to disease classification: the subjects are healthy, the classified object is the person and not the illness, and no disease is assigned to a class anywhere in the study. It is a comparator, not evidence about vyadhi-vibhaga.

modern.title: Genome-wide analysis correlates Ayurveda Prakriti.
modern.establishes: Genome-wide SNP analysis (Affymetrix 6.0) of 262 well-classified male individuals screened from 3,416 subjects across the three prakritis. 52 SNPs differed at p <= 1x10^-5 after 10^6 permutations and control for stratification; principal component analysis on those SNPs separated the 262 individuals into their prakriti groups irrespective of ancestry; the finding was then checked against 297 Indian population samples of known ancestry; PGM1 was reported as correlating with the pitta phenotype.
modern.quality: Methodologically the strongest study in the area: large screening, permutation testing and explicit stratification control. Caveats that bear on how far it can be pushed: males only, extreme-phenotype selection (262 of 3,416), the PCA separation is computed on SNPs selected in the same sample, which inflates apparent classification power, the single-gene narrative link to a Charaka phenotype description is interpretation rather than result, and the 52-SNP set has not been independently replicated in a separate prakriti cohort. Like Prasher 2008, it classifies persons and not diseases, and is carried here as the comparator behind the record's non-transfer statement.

records.title: Dosha-dushya-sammurchana (a modern Ayurvedic term for the meeting of disturbed dosha and susceptible tissue)
records.domain: Ayurvedic theory of health and disease: pathogenesis
records.summary: Dosha-dushya-sammurchana is a compound used in modern Ayurvedic teaching and journal writing for the step at which a disturbed, circulating dosha is said to meet and combine with a susceptible tissue element (dushya) at a particular site, so that a specific disease takes form there rather than anywhere else. The compound, not the mechanism, is what this record is about, and its textual standing is weak. The 2025 JAIMS review that is the principal English-language treatment of the term gives two classical addresses for it, Charaka Chikitsasthana 28/20-23 and Sushruta Sutrasthana 15/18. Both were retrieved for this revision. The Charaka passage is a list of the signs produced by aggravated vata; the Sushruta verse is the rule that an excessively increased dhatu increases the one after it, so that reduction is beneficial. Neither speaks of a union of dosha with dushya. What is securely classical are separately named doctrines that cover much of the same ground and can be quoted from public-domain translations: sthana-samshraya in Sushruta Sutrasthana 21, where the same spread doshas produce gulma in the abdomen, prameha in the bladder, kushtha in skin and blood and granthi or arbuda in fat according to where they are 'incarcerated'; the tissue-by-tissue list at Charaka Sutrasthana 28; and the Charaka passages that make the manifestation of disease depend on the particular characteristics of nidana, dosha and dushya taken together (Nidanasthana 4) and on the difference of the dushya vitiated (Vimanasthana 6). Those doctrines carry their own names and their own records in this lexicon. In modern teaching the step named by this compound is placed at the sthana-samshraya stage of shat-kriyakala and paired with khavaigunya, the notion of a pre-existing local defect in a channel, which is itself a commentarial and textbook term rather than a phrase with a retrievable Samhita verse.
records.evidenceState:
Read this as a record about a term, not about a demonstrated mechanism. The compound dosha-dushya-sammurchana was not found in the mula text of either Samhita in this pass, and this revision stopped trying to make up for that by pointing at doctrines that are attested under other names.

The term's advertised addresses do not survive retrieval. The 2025 JAIMS review that is the principal English-language treatment gives two: Charaka Chikitsasthana 28/20-23 and Sushruta Sutrasthana 15/18. Both were retrieved for this revision. The Charaka passage is a running list of the signs produced by aggravated vata, closing with the line that aggravated vata produces signs of these kinds. The Sushruta verse states that an excessively increased dhatu increases the one after it, so that reduction of over-increased dhatus is beneficial, and Bhishagratna prints it as metrical text in the same sense. Neither passage speaks of dosha combining with dushya. Other addresses circulate (Charaka Nidana 1, Charaka Vimana 5/3, Ashtanga Hridaya Nidana 1, Ashtanga Samgraha, Madhava Nidana, Sushruta Sutra 21) and were not all retrieved; the mutual inconsistency of the set is the point, and it is recorded in contested rather than resolved.

What is attested, and what each attestation is for. Sushruta Sutra 21 gives sthana-samshraya and the site-specific disease lists. Charaka Sutra 28 gives the same site-specificity principle with a tissue-by-tissue list. Sushruta Sutra 21/29-30 and Charaka Sutra 28/31-33 give lodgement and latency, which is the classical material behind the modern khavaigunya doctrine. Charaka Nidana 4 makes the manifestation, non-manifestation or partial manifestation of disease depend on the particular characteristics of nidana, dosha and dushya together, and states that unless the three unite in sequence and with force the disease does not appear, or appears late, weakly or partially. Charaka Vimana 6/7 makes the variety of diseases a function of the difference of the exciting cause and the difference of the dushya. Each of those is cited here under the name its own sources use, and each carries attestsCompound: false. The compound does not inherit their standing, and a reader who wants the textual case for site specificity should go to them and not to this headword.

On the word itself: saṃmūrcchita does occur in Charaka, at Sutra Sthana 24/48 in the Trikamji-based text retrieved, of various strong liquors commingled, which Gangadhara glosses as militāni, 'mixed'. That is a pharmaceutical sense. The dictionaries give the noun saṃmūrchana as congealing, thickening, accumulating, spreading, and as fainting or insensibility. The pathological-union sense is supplied by modern Ayurvedic usage, and mūrchana in Rasa Shastra and in oil and ghee pharmacy is a third thing again.

Empirically the concept is untested. There is no operational criterion for declaring that sammurchana has occurred in a given patient, no measurement of whether clinicians agree on which dushya is involved, no marker of khavaigunya, and no prospective demonstration that an assigned dosha-dushya pair predicts anything. The literature located in this pass consists of narrative reviews in non-indexed or low-indexed Ayurvedic journals (the papers that dominate this topic appear in JAIMS and similar outlets with DOIs but no PubMed indexing), one 1989 uncontrolled biochemical correlation study, and reliability and consensus studies whose results are unfavourable. PubMed returned nothing for the compound in the term-record pass, which is a finding about that string in that index.

A reader should treat dosha-dushya-sammurchana as explanatory vocabulary for site specificity: not a mechanism that has been demonstrated or measured, and not a classical term.

contested.question: Where does the compound 'dosha-dushya-sammurchana' come from?
positions: Modern reviews present it as a classical Ayurvedic concept and cite Samhita verses for it.

The cited verses differ between reviews and none of them contains the compound as a defined term: a 2025 JAIMS review cites Charaka Chikitsa 28/20-23 and Sushruta Sutra 15/18, other sources point to Sushruta Sutra 21 or to Ashtanga Hridaya Nidana 1. The pattern is consistent with a later scholastic or textbook coinage summarising a classical principle rather than a Samhita term.

Added in this revision: the two addresses the JAIMS review gives were retrieved and are about other subjects, which moves this from a pattern argument to a checked result for those two loci. The commentarial candidates (Madhukosha on Madhava Nidana, Chakrapani on Charaka, Dalhana on Sushruta) remain unread, so the origin is unestablished rather than disproved.

contested.question: Is sammurchana a distinct event, or just a name for the sthana-samshraya stage?
positions: Most modern teaching places sammurchana at sthana-samshraya, the fourth kriyakala, making it the mechanism of that stage.

Other presentations treat sammurchana as spanning localisation and manifestation, or as the phase producing premonitory symptoms, which makes it a description of a stage boundary rather than an event. Sources do not settle this.
One modern source attaches the term to two different kriyakala stages, sthana-samshraya and vyakti, within a single article (recorded in data/terms/dosha-dushya-sammurchana.json).

contested.question: What determines the site of lodgement?
positions: The khavaigunya position: a pre-existing local defect in a channel, from injury, heredity, prior disease or repeated strain, decides where the dosha can settle.

The Sushruta passage itself attributes lodgement more simply to where the humours happen to be 'incarcerated', comparing it to rain clouds pouring in the quarter of the sky where they form, with no requirement of a pre-existing defect. The khavaigunya requirement is an added explanatory layer, not a quoted premise.

Charaka Nidana 4 states a different condition again: not a defect at the site, but a joint requirement on nidana, dosha and dushya, with a predominance strong enough for manifestation. The three accounts are not the same claim and the sources do not reconcile them.

contested.question: Is dosha alone sufficient, or is a susceptible dushya necessary?
positions: The sammurchana doctrine holds that disease requires the combination; dosha in a healthy tissue passes without producing disease.

This is difficult to reconcile with classical statements elsewhere that disturbed dosha permeating the whole system produces fever and generalised disease. The sources do not explain what makes a dushya susceptible or how susceptibility could be detected in advance.

Charaka Nidana 4's conjunction requirement is the strongest classical support for the first position, and it still does not say what makes a dushya susceptible, only that the characteristics of the three factors must coincide.

contested.question: What does sammurchana mean?
positions: Modern Ayurvedic usage: the pathological union, intermixing or fusion of disturbed dosha with a susceptible tissue. Some writers gloss it as alivyapti, intermixing.
The Sanskrit dictionaries give congealing, thickening, accumulating, spreading, and fainting or insensibility; Monier-Williams has no pathogenesis sense.

The one occurrence located in a Samhita mula in this pass, Charaka Sutra 24/48, uses sammūrcchitāni of strong liquors commingled, glossed militāni by Gangadhara. On the retrieved evidence the pathological sense is modern usage rather than inherited vocabulary, though a single located occurrence cannot settle the history of the word.

contested.question: Should the headword be kept at all?
positions: Retire it: an unanchored compound with no retrievable defining verse and no operational criterion should not head a record, and the material belongs under sthana-samshraya, khavaigunya and dushya-vishesha, which are attested.

Keep it, scoped: the term is in active use in teaching and in the journal literature, readers meet it first and meet it undefined, and the most useful thing a lexicon can do is say exactly what it rests on. This revision takes the second course and marks the headword's status explicitly in headwordStatus rather than letting the classical block imply an anchor.
This is an editorial decision, and by the project's own rule it belongs to the drafting phase, not to gathering. It is recorded as unresolved.

notKnown: Whether the compound term appears in any of the three brihat-trayi Samhitas at all, and if so where. Secondary sources cite it to mutually inconsistent loci and none supplies a defining verse.
What observable state constitutes sammurchana having occurred, as distinct from dosha merely being present at a site. No source gives a criterion.

Whether clinicians agree on which dushya is involved in a given patient. Never measured. The nearest data (PMID 30653338) shows fair-to-poor agreement on the neighbouring judgements of prakriti and agni.

Whether khavaigunya can be detected before disease appears. No marker, imaging finding, or test has been proposed and validated, which means the central predictive claim of the concept is untestable as currently stated.

Whether the site-specific disease lists in Sushruta Sutrasthana 21 and Charaka Sutrasthana 28 agree with each other. I retrieved both but no source compares them systematically, and their tissue-to-disease mappings are not obviously identical.

Whether any biological correlate of dosha-dushya combination exists. The single attempt I found (PMID 22557650, 1989) asserts biochemical correlation in vivax malaria without controls or pre-specified mapping, and has not been replicated.
Whether treatment directed at the dushya rather than at the dosha changes outcomes. The doctrine implies it should; no trial has compared the two strategies.

Where the compound first appears, if it is commentarial. The candidates named in the literature and in this project's term record are the Madhukosha of Vijayarakshita and Srikanthadatta on Madhava Nidana, Chakrapani's Ayurveda Dipika on Charaka, and Dalhana's Nibandha Sangraha on Sushruta Sutrasthana 21. None was read in this pass: no commentarial text was retrieved, and searching for the Devanagari compound returned only modern Ayurvedic teaching material. The record therefore cannot name a locus for its own headword, and says so instead of supplying one.

Whether any mula verse defines dūṣya by enumerating the seven dhatus plus the three malas. The word dūṣya is attested in Charaka (Nidana 4, in nidāna-doṣa-dūṣya-viśeṣebhyaḥ) and Sushruta Sutra 15 names dosha, dhatu and mala as the three classes of bodily constituent, but the equation of dushya with sapta dhatu plus trimala comes, in what was retrieved, from Kaviratna's footnote at Nidana IV, from modern glossaries, and from WHO ISTA ITA-2.2.2. A verse that makes the enumeration under that name has not been located.

Whether 'sammurchana' with the sam- prefix is also a technical term in Rasa Shastra, as one critic finding states. What was retrieved is mūrchana, the swooning or trituration samskara of parada and the pre-treatment of oils and ghee. The disambiguation is therefore written on the form that could be verified, and the sam- prefixed Rasa Shastra usage is recorded as unconfirmed.

Whether the Charaka Nidana 4 conjunction requirement and the Charaka Vimana 6/7 dushya-vishesha claim are one doctrine or two, and whether the modern compound merges them. Nothing retrieved addresses the question.

Whether Ashtanga Hridaya or Ashtanga Samgraha carries the compound. Neither was retrieved, and neither has a public-domain English translation, so any future citation has to rest on the Sanskrit mula.
Whether NAMASTE, the AYUSH standardised-terminology portal, codes the term. The portal could not be queried without a browser session, so its coverage is unknown rather than absent.

components.gloss: The disturbed functional factor (vata, pitta or kapha, and in Sushruta's scheme also rakta) that has already accumulated, aggravated and spread.

The tissue element that is spoilt. Literally 'that which is to be vitiated'. The word is attested in Charaka's own text (Nidanasthana 4, in the compound nidana-dosha-dushya-vishesha); its identification with the seven dhatus (rasa, rakta, mamsa, meda, asthi, majja, shukra) plus the malas comes, in the sources retrieved here, from a translator's footnote, from modern glossaries and from WHO ISTA, not from a verse that enumerates them under that name.

Defect or weakness in a channel or site, which is held to determine where the circulating dosha can lodge. A commentarial and textbook term rather than a phrase with a single retrievable Samhita verse.
The channel system through which dosha travels and in which the lodgement occurs; srotodushti (channel vitiation) is the stated mode of that lodgement.

The combining or intermixing itself, in modern Ayurvedic usage: dosha and dushya are said to form a pathological entity that neither was alone. This sense is supplied by modern usage. The dictionaries give the noun saṃmūrchana as congealing, thickening, accumulating, and as fainting or insensibility; the one occurrence of the word located in the Samhitas in this pass (Charaka Sutrasthana 24/48, sammūrcchitāni ... madyāni) is of strong liquors commingled, which Gangadhara glosses as militāni. See distinguishFrom.
The resulting seat of disease, the anatomical location that gives the disease its name and its clinical picture.

classical.verse: within the sthana-samshraya section; the Bhishagratna page carries no verse numbers, and this project's verification pass (research/citation-verdicts-c1.json, entry 63) matched the passage to the Sanskrit numbered 29-33, the sthana-samshraya statement itself closing at ||33||
classical.establishes: Site specificity: the same spread doshas produce entirely different diseases according to where they are 'incarcerated'. The passage continues site by site, naming prameha and urinary stone for the bladder, fistula and haemorrhoids for the anal region, erysipelas and kushtha for flesh, skin and blood, and granthi, apachi, arbuda and galaganda for fat. This is a reference for sthana-samshraya, which has its own record (data/concepts/shat-kriyakala.json, data/terms/sthanasamshraya.json). It does not contain the compound dosha-dushya-sammurchana and is not offered as evidence for it.
classical.quote: Now we shall enumerate the names of the peculiar diseases, which are originated by the deranged and expanded humours, incarcerated in the different parts of the body. These humours, confined in the abdomen, give rise to Gulma (abdominal glands) tumours, internal abscesses (Vidradhi), abdominal dropsy, impaired digestion in the bowels, constipation (anaha), cholera (Visuchika) and dysentery.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916, public domain)

classical.verse: closing passage of the chapter; no number printed on the retrieved page. This project's verification pass (research/citation-verdicts-c1.json, entry 64) places the chapter's closing Sanskrit verse at 21.40 and identifies the 'concourse of deranged humours' clause as Bhishagratna's connective rendering of the preceding sannipata material at 21.38-39
classical.establishes: Kept as an exhibit of a translator's word, not as a parallel for sammurchana. The earlier version of this record described 'concourse of deranged humours' as the closest public-domain English wording to sammurchana in the Samhita text. That claim is withdrawn: the verification pass found the clause to be Bhishagratna's own connective phrasing over the chapter's sannipata material, and sannipata is the union of the doshas with one another, not of dosha with dushya. The object defined here is also a wound or ulcer specifically, not disease in general. Treating 'concourse' as the English of sammūrchanā would be the translator's voice absorbed as doctrine, which is the defect this project has already recorded three times.
classical.quote: A concourse of deranged humours, affecting and appearing in a particular part of the body, is called a boil or an ulcer (Vrana) which is derived from the root "Vri" to cover and is so called from the fact of its covering a particular part of the body or from its leaving a cicatrix which remains the whole life-time of the patient.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916, public domain)

classical.verse: no number printed on the retrieved page; matched by this project's verification pass (research/citation-verdicts-c1.json, entry 65) to the Sanskrit verses 29-30
classical.establishes: Disease arises where the dosha lodges, and a dosha that lodges without producing disease can lie latent in a channel and produce disease later when re-agitated. Note what the passage does not say: it does not use the word khavaigunya and does not require a pre-existing defect at the site. This is a reference for khavaigunya's classical background (data/concepts/khavaigunya.json), not for this headword.
classical.quote: The aggravated, or the abnormally irritated deranged humours, whether permeating the whole or half of the system or restricted to any particular part or member of the body, give rise to disease in the place of their incarceration, like rain clouds pouring down in the quarter of the sky where they are formed. The deranged humours, not excessively (slightly) aggravated, lie inoperative coating the internal passages (Margas) of the body and thus bring about a fresh disease, if subsequently agitated by any disturbing causes.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916, public domain)

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorism 15, his number printed after the aphorism; in Trikamji numbering the two sentences straddle the closing clause of 28.7 and 28.8, per this project's verification pass (research/citation-verdicts-c1.json, entry 66), which quotes both Sanskrit sentences. The earlier version of this record mapped it to 28.8 alone
classical.establishes: Charaka's statement of the site-specificity principle, followed in the chapter by a tissue-by-tissue list: anorexia, tastelessness, hiccup, heaviness, fever and lassitude from dosha excited in rasa; kushtha, erysipelas, bleeding disorders, splenomegaly and jaundice from dosha excited in rakta; and so on through meda, asthi, majja and shukra. A reference for the principle under its own description, not for the compound.
classical.quote: Through these causes, the wind, bile, and phlegm, being excited in particular parts of the body, produce different diseases. The faults becoming excited in particular places such as the food-fluids and others, produce particular diseases. We shall now, O Agnivesa, declare which diseases arise from which places becoming the seats of the excited faults.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorisms 39-40, his numbers printed after the aphorisms; Sanskrit 28.31-33, per research/citation-verdicts-c1.json, entry 67, which quotes 28.31, 28.32 and the opening of 28.33
classical.establishes: The latency claim: what has reached a channel may sit there without producing disease, waiting for a provoking cause. This is the classical material behind the modern idea that a defective site plus a trigger, not dosha alone, produces disease. A reference for that latency doctrine, not for the compound.
classical.quote: Arrived at the ducts they sometimes stay there, unimpelled by any other force. Unless the region and the time be undisposed thereto, they do not become excited, for they await some cause of excitement.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorism 3, his number printed after the aphorism. The Sanskrit clause is numbered 4 in the Trikamji-based text retrieved (carakasamhitaonline, Prameha Nidana): Kaviratna runs one behind here, as this project has documented elsewhere. The Sanskrit sentence continues beyond the clause quoted
classical.establishes: Added in this revision. The nearest classical statement retrieved to the content the modern compound names, and the locus the record previously lacked for the dushya half: dūṣya stands here in Charaka's own text, in a three-term compound with nidāna and doṣa, and the manifestation, non-manifestation or partial manifestation of disease turns on the particular characteristics of all three. Kaviratna's inline gloss, 'the ingredients or dhatus composing the body', is his, not the text's. The verse does not contain sammūrchana and does not say that dosha and dushya fuse.
classical.quote: Here (in the world), verily, from the particular characteristics of 'Nidana' or causes, 'doshas' or faults, and 'dushyas' or the ingredients or 'dhatus' composing the body, arise the manifestation, the non-manifestation, and the partial manifestation of diseases in general.
classical.sanskrit: iha khalu nidānadoṣadūṣyaviśeṣebhyo vikāravighātabhāvābhāvaprativiśeṣā bhavanti

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorism 4, continuing the same passage. No modern verse number is asserted: the retrieved Trikamji-based page prints verse 4 in abbreviated form and I did not establish where that edition ends it
classical.establishes: Added in this revision. The explicit conjunction requirement: unless cause, dosha and dushya come together in sequence and with sufficient force, disease does not manifest, or manifests late, weakly or partially. This is the classical sentence closest to what modern writers mean by the compound, and it is worth noticing that it names no fusion and no defect in the site, only a joint condition on three factors. ('manifestion' is as the Kaviratna OCR prints it.)
classical.quote: When these three, viz., the characteristics of causes, faults, and ingredients, are not united in sequence, no manifestion of disease takes place. Or, when they, through absence of predominance, unite as weak factors, no manifestation occurs of disease ; or there is lateness in manifestation ; or the manifestation takes place in a weak form ; or all the symptoms laid down do not show themselves.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorism 10, printed after a block of several sentences. The quoted sentence corresponds to the Sanskrit numbered 6.7 in the Trikamji-based text retrieved (carakasamhitaonline, Roganika Vimana). Kaviratna bundles several Trikamji verses under one aphorism number here, so the two numbering systems must not be mixed and no one-to-one mapping is asserted
classical.establishes: Added in this revision. Disease variety is generated by two differences, that of the exciting cause and that of the dushya vitiated. Kaviratna renders dūṣyaviśeṣāt as 'difference of the elements vitiated' and supplies the word dushya only in his footnote, where he also notes that the correct reading is dūṣyaviśeṣāt and not dravyaviśeṣāt. This is the strongest classical warrant retrieved for the claim that which tissue is involved helps fix which disease appears; it contains no term for a union of dosha with dushya.
classical.quote: When excited, the faults, in consequence of difference of exciting causes as also of difference of the elements vitiated, generate innumerable diseases.
classical.sanskrit: prakupitāstu khalu te prakopaṇaviśeṣāddūṣyaviśeṣācca vikāraviśeṣānabhinirvartayantyaparisaṅkhyeyān

classical.verse: opening of the chapter. No verse number is asserted: Bhishagratna prints no Sanskrit verse numbers, and this is the chapter's introductory sentence
classical.establishes: Added in this revision for the dushya half of the compound. Sushruta's own framing names three classes of constituent, dosha, dhatu and mala, and the chapter title is built from them. It is this triad that modern usage partitions into dosha on one side and dushya (dhatu plus mala) on the other. The passage does not use the word dushya and does not make that partition itself. Retrieved twice independently: the wisdomlib reproduction of Bhishagratna and the archive.org scan of the printed translation, where the wording is identical.
classical.quote: Since the human body is constituted of humours, (Doshas), excretions (Mala), and the fundamental principles (Dhatus) of blood, marrow, etc., hear me discourse on the features which are peculiar to each of them.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916, public domain)

modern.title: Reliability of Ayurvedic Diagnosis for Knee Osteoarthritis Patients: A Nested Diagnostic Study Within a Randomized Controlled Trial.
modern.establishes: Four Ayurvedic experts assessing the same 30 knee osteoarthritis patients reached only fair-to-poor chance-corrected agreement (Fleiss and Cohen kappa between 0 and 0.4) on core diagnostic components including prakriti and agni, although percentage agreement on the final consented diagnosis was 95 percent, and agreement on disease-related entities exceeded agreement on constitutional entities.
modern.quality: Empirical inter-rater reliability study nested in an RCT; small (30 patients, 4 raters), single condition. It does not measure agreement on dosha-dushya assignment specifically, but it is the best available evidence on whether the judgements that feed such an assignment are reproducible, and the answer is that several are not.

modern.title: Myth and reality of "theory-driven individualised practice" in Ayurveda: Mapping physicians' approaches using case-based scenarios.
modern.establishes: 141 experienced Ayurveda practitioners answering five clinical vignettes showed significant lack of consensus on diagnoses, on interventions and on their understanding of pathophysiology, with conflicting opinions; the authors conclude theoretical constructs do not uniformly determine prescriptions or individualisation.
modern.quality: Empirical cross-sectional vignette survey. Convenience sample and hypothetical cases are real limitations, but it is direct evidence that practitioners do not converge on a single dosha-dushya account of the same case.

modern.title: Critical appraisal of Doshavaha Srotas.
modern.establishes: Conceptual appraisal of doshavaha srotas, arguing for correlating vatavaha, pittavaha, kaphavaha and sarvavaha sira with corresponding srotas, in order to explain how doshas reach and vitiate particular sites.
modern.quality: Textual and conceptual review with no empirical component. It is exegesis of the channel doctrine underlying sammurchana, not evidence for it.

modern.title: Correlation of certain biochemical changes with dosha-dushya intolvement in some vishamajwaras (p.vivax malaria) and its therapeutic utility.
modern.establishes: Reports biochemical changes before and after treatment in 180 cases of anyedyushka and tritiyaka vishamajwara (identified with P. vivax malaria) and attempts to correlate those changes with the dosha-dushya involvement assigned in each case.
modern.quality: Weak. Old (1989), in a journal with no DOI recorded for the article, uncontrolled, no blinding, no pre-specified mapping, no chance-corrected statistics, and the correlation is asserted rather than tested. It is nonetheless one of the very few attempts anywhere to attach a measurement to a dosha-dushya assignment, which is itself a statement about how thin this literature is.

modern.title: Tongue coating, severity of Ama, and disease activity in patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis: A pilot study.
modern.establishes: Pilot study relating tongue coating, scored by the Winkel tongue coating index from smartphone images, to Ama severity by a validated Ama instrument and to disease activity (CDAI) in rheumatoid arthritis, treated as the prototype of amavata.
modern.quality: Small empirical pilot, and one of the few studies that operationalises a pathogenesis component at all. It addresses ama rather than dosha-dushya-sammurchana directly, is a pilot without a confirmatory study, and the PubMed record carries a DOI that does not match the article, so only the PMID is given.

modern.establishes: Suthar OP, Gupta, Marolia, Prakash, 'Dosha Dushya Sammurchana in Disease Manifestation - A Review', J Ayurveda Integr Med Sci 10(6). Retrieved for this revision to read its reference list. It gives Charaka Chikitsasthana 28/20-23 and Sushruta Sutrasthana 15/18 as its classical loci for the compound, cites Ashtanga Hridaya, Ashtanga Samgraha and Madhava Nidana Part II, and quotes no Sanskrit verse containing the compound.
modern.quality: Weak as evidence, decisive as a record of usage. Narrative review, no method section, journal not PubMed-indexed. It is cited here for what it cites, not for what it concludes: the two classical addresses it supplies were retrieved and do not support the term, which is the central finding of this revision.

openQuestions: Does the Madhukosha on Madhava Nidana 1 contain the compound, and at what locus? Needs a Sanskrit commentarial text this pass could not retrieve.
Where does the Trikamji-based verse 4 of Charaka Nidana 4 end, so that Kaviratna's aphorism 4 can be mapped to a modern number?
Can the Charaka Sutra 24 numbering discrepancy (Kaviratna 49-50 against the retrieved Sanskrit 48) be resolved against a printed Trikamji edition?

records.title: Kala-parinama (time, season and ripening as causes of disease)
records.summary: Kala-parinama is the Ayurvedic category for disease caused by time. It covers three distinguishable things that the texts run together: the seasonal cycle and its abnormalities, the internal clock of the day, night and digestive phases, and the irreversible ripening of the organism into old age and death. Charaka names time as one of the three general causes of disease and states that its pathological forms are the same three as for any other cause, namely deficiency, excess and perversity of the expected seasonal character. In the epidemic chapter Charaka ranks time as the most potent of the four collective vitiating factors, on the practical ground that a person can leave a place or avoid a water source but cannot step out of the season. Sushruta gives time its own disease class, kala-bala-pravritta, subdivided according to whether the season behaves naturally or contrarily. Charaka also treats the effects of pure ripening, decrepitude and death, as a subclass that has no remedy.
records.evidenceState: Separate the premise from the doctrine, because the record previously did not. THE PREMISE. That human physiology varies with season and with time of day is supported by work outside Ayurveda. Dopico and colleagues 2015 (PMID 25965853) found seasonal expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and in adipose tissue across several cohorts, and Wucher and colleagues 2023 (PMID 36745672) found day-night and seasonal expression differences across many tissues in a different design. That is the limit of what those papers do for this record. THE DOCTRINE. Kala-parinama is not the claim that physiology varies with time. It is the claim that time-transformation is one of three general causes of disease, operating through season-specific dosha accumulation, aggravation and subsidence, and correctable by season-specific regimen. Neither Dopico nor Wucher measured a dosha, tested the six-ritu partition, tested the morning-noon-evening kapha-pitta-vata sequence, or evaluated any ritucharya prescription. Citing them in support of the doctrine would be borrowing the credibility of a literature that never tested it, and the earlier version of this paragraph did exactly that: it said the premise was 'independently and robustly established' and then let that sentence stand as the evidential footing for the whole category. It is not. A separate inference has to be blocked too. Several conditions have well-documented seasonal incidence, including cardiovascular events, respiratory infection and affective disorder. Establishing that a disease is seasonal does not establish the mechanism the texts assign to it. A seasonal incidence curve is consistent with the classical dosha assignment, with pathogen ecology, with indoor crowding, with vitamin D, with temperature effects on vascular tone, and with several other accounts at once, and it discriminates between none of them. The record makes no claim that any seasonal disease pattern supports the dosha-seasonal mechanism. WHAT THE PREMISE ITSELF WILL NOT CARRY. 'Robustly established' was also too strong for the seasonal-transcriptomics result taken on its own terms, and the strongest objection is in the primary paper. Dopico and colleagues state in their own abstract that the seasonal change in blood cell composition 'could explain the gene expression periodicity', and in their discussion that the PBMC transcriptional landscapes 'appear to be predominantly driven by annual changes in the cellular composition of blood'. On the authors' own reading, much of the headline signal is a shift in which cells are in the sample rather than a seasonal programme inside a given cell. They also report fewer seasonal genes and a less similar seasonal pattern in their Icelandic donors, and write that 'the impact of living at higher latitudes requires further exploration'. So the premise is supported, and it is supported with live internal caveats about cell composition and about latitude. Wucher and colleagues 2023 is a useful second design because it works from postmortem tissue rather than from circulating PBMCs, and so is not exposed to the same blood-composition confound; it is exposed to others, which its entry records. THE DOCTRINE'S OWN EVIDENCE. On the specific content of kala-parinama, the searches run for this record (described in gatheringNotes) located two narrative reviews, one ethnographic study, one small cross-sectional study of season and constitution against lipids, one randomised open-label trial of a ritucharya-derived intervention (PMID 33935439), one registered single-arm protocol for seasonal purification with no results yet (PMID 42748372), and one cross-sectional survey bearing on the daily-time limb (PMID 42519781). On that set: the one randomised trial tests a single seasonal adjuvant in one season in one region against no-treatment control, open-label, n=60, with disease-frequency and quality-of-life endpoints, which is evidence about that preparation in that setting and not about the six-ritu scheme, the dosha-seasonal mechanism, or ritucharya as a system. The protocol paper is a protocol: single-arm, no control, explicitly 'hypothesis-generating'. The record does not claim that this is the whole literature. It is what the searches named in gatheringNotes returned, and a bounded search cannot support a statement that nothing else exists. What the record does claim is that it located nothing that tests the dosha-seasonal mechanism itself, and the specific gaps are itemised in notKnown rather than summarised away here. A LAST POINT ABOUT THE CATEGORY. Within the classical scheme, time absorbs both the genuinely periodic (intermittent fevers, seasonal illness) and the residual (idiopathic disease, ageing, death), so the category does explanatory work as a default attribution as well as a causal one, and the two uses are not separated in the sources. That is a structural observation about the texts, not an evidential claim, and it is the one thing in this paragraph that does not depend on the modern literature at all.

contested.question: Which mechanism does time act by?
positions: Charaka Sutra 6 gives a physical mechanism: solar desiccation and lunar or rain-driven moistening acting on the whole environment and thence on the body.
Charaka Vimana 3 gives an astral and moral mechanism: perverse conditions of constellations, planets, sun, moon and wind, rooted ultimately in collective adharma.
Sushruta Sutra 24 gives a narrowly meteorological mechanism: variation of atmospheric heat and humidity, with no astral or moral element.
These are not reconciled in the sources, and modern Ayurvedic writing usually silently adopts the Sushruta version.

contested.question: Is ageing and death a disease category or an exclusion from it?
positions: Charaka Sharira 1.122 says decrepitude and death come naturally and that what nature brings about has no remedy, which excludes them from therapeutics.
Sushruta Sutra 24 classes them as a disease type, svabhava-bala-pravritta, and then splits them into timely and untimely, which makes the untimely form modifiable by conduct.
The rasayana literature elsewhere in Charaka treats ageing as at least partly modifiable, which sits uneasily with Sharira 1.122.

contested.question: Is time a coordinate cause or the dominant one?
positions: Sutra 11.43 presents the three general causes symmetrically.
Vimana 3.13 ranks time above place, water and air, but the argument given is unavoidability of exposure rather than strength of effect, which is a different claim.
Sharira 1 subordinates time to prajnaparadha by making faults of the understanding the root of the epidemic chain.

contested.question: How many seasons, and whose calendar?
positions: The six-ritu scheme is tied to a north Indian lunisolar calendar with a monsoon.

The same scheme is applied without adjustment in temperate, equatorial and southern-hemisphere settings in contemporary practice and in the reviews, with no discussion of whether the mapping survives transplantation.
Sushruta's criterion, natural versus contrary seasonal features, is calendar-independent in principle but is not operationalised anywhere.

notKnown: Whether any measured human rhythm corresponds to the classical morning-kapha, noon-pitta, evening-vata clock. The searches named in gatheringNotes located no study testing this against actigraphy, cortisol, core temperature, melatonin or any other established circadian marker. The nearest located work, PMID 42519781, asks shift workers to report their own digestive state and measures no circadian marker, so it does not close this gap. Reworded in the 2026-10-06 revision: the earlier version asserted that no study had tested it, which a bounded search cannot support.
Whether seasonal dosha accumulation and aggravation, the chaya-prakopa-prashama cycle, predicts anything about symptom onset in a prospective cohort.

Whether following a ritucharya regimen as a system changes any clinical outcome. One randomised trial of a single ritucharya-derived preparation was located, PMID 33935439, and it is open-label, n=60, one season, one region, with no season-mismatched comparison arm, so it tests the preparation and not the seasonal principle. One registered seasonal-purification study was located, PMID 42748372, and it is a single-arm protocol with no results and no off-season comparison. Corrected in the 2026-10-06 revision: the earlier version asserted that no randomised trial existed, which was an exhaustiveness claim and was also false.
How ritucharya is to be adapted, if at all, outside the monsoon-calendar regions the texts were written for.
Whether the classical criteria for a vitiated season, deficient, excessive or contrary seasonal character, can be applied by independent observers with any agreement, or against meteorological data.

Whether the well-documented seasonality of specific conditions (cardiovascular events, respiratory infection, affective disorder) has any relationship to the classical seasonal disease assignments beyond coincidence.
Where the boundary lies between time as a genuine cause and time as the residual category for disease with no identified cause, given that Sharira 1.122 assigns both to it.
Whether the untimely form of the svabhava-bala class, that is premature ageing from unhealthy living, is distinguishable in practice from ordinary accumulated risk-factor exposure.

Whether the seasonal-transcriptomics result survives adjustment for blood cell composition. The authors of PMID 25965853 state that composition changes 'could explain the gene expression periodicity' and that their PBMC signal 'appear[s] to be predominantly driven' by them, and call for work in purified immune cell subsets. The record located no such follow-up in purified subsets. Added in the 2026-10-06 revision, because the record previously carried the premise without this caveat.

Whether any independent reanalysis or formal methodological critique of the human seasonal-transcriptomics literature has been published. The searches run for this revision (PubMed, terms combining seasonal and transcriptome or gene expression with deconvolution, cell composition, confounding and reanalysis) returned no such paper, and the strongest objections the record can cite are therefore the primary authors' own. This is a gap in the record's coverage and is stated as one rather than filled with a general remark; it is not a claim that no critique exists.

What the registered seasonal-regimen and seasonal-Panchakarma trial landscape actually contains. The Clinical Trials Registry-India was not searched directly for this record: no public API or bulk export was located and its search interface is form-driven. The two registered interventions cited here, PMID 33935439 and PMID 42748372, were reached through PubMed, which indexes only registered trials that have also been published. PMID 35370375 describes CTRI's Ayurveda holdings in general but does not enumerate seasonal-regimen trials. So the number, design and results status of registered-but-unpublished ritucharya and seasonal-purification trials is unknown to this record.

Whether the specific mainstream literatures adjacent to this concept bear on it at all, because the record has not surveyed them. Chronobiology, chronotherapy and chronopharmacology, and the epidemiology of seasonal disease onset are each large fields. The modern section here is a purposive selection chosen against the record's own classical claims, not a survey, and it should not be read as a representative sample of any of those fields. Added in the 2026-10-06 revision in response to the thinness finding; see stillOpen for why this is declared rather than remedied.

Whether seasonal purification as practised, that is Vamana in vasanta and Virechana in sharad, has any effect distinguishable from the acute effects of emesis, purgation, oleation, fomentation and the controlled post-procedure diet. The one registered study located, PMID 42748372, is single-arm by design and so cannot make that distinction, and it has not reported.

components.gloss: The six seasons of the Indian year: hemanta, shishira, vasanta, grishma, varsha, sharad
The two solar half-years, adana-kala (the taking period, northward course, drying and weakening) and visarga-kala (the giving period, southward course, moistening and strengthening)
Seasonal abnormality in the same three modes as any other cause: ayoga (the season's character deficient), atiyoga (excessive), mithyayoga (perverse, showing another season's character)

The recurring daily and prandial clock: kapha in the morning, pitta at noon, vata in the evening, with the same sequence across night watches and across the phases of eating, digesting and post-digestion
Time in respect of the accession of a specific disease, including the periodicity of intermittent fevers at one, two, three and four day intervals
Decrepitude and death as the pure ripening of time, which Charaka says arrive naturally and admit of no remedy
Literally ripening or transformation; Charaka states explicitly that this is another name for kala in the etiological triad
Sushruta's dedicated disease class for time-caused illness, subdivided by whether the season exhibits natural or contrary features

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson XI (Tistraishaniya), verse 42 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 42 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The operational definition of pathological time as ayoga, atiyoga and mithyayoga of the season's expected character, and the explicit identification of kala with parinama.
classical.quote: Heat, cold, and rain, or autumn, summer, and rain, constitute the indications of the year. That is also called Time. When the particular indication of a particular period of Time manifests itself in excess, that is called excess of correlation in respect of Time (as excess of cold in winter, or excess of heat in summer, or excess of rain in the rainy season). When such indication manifests itself in a measure less than normal, that is called want or absence of correlation (such as want of cold in winter or of heat in summer). When indications, that are the reverse of those which are normal, are manifested, that is called improper correlation (such as heat in winter or cold in summer). ... Thus are the three subjects treated of, viz., the improper contact of objects of sense with the Mind, faults of the Understanding, and Time or Parinama.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson XI, verse 43 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 43 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The three-by-three structure of the general etiology, and that time in judicious proportion is a cause of health rather than a neutral background.
classical.quote: These three, (viz., the improper contact of objects of sense with the Mind, faults of the Understanding, and Time,) each sub-divided into three kinds, constitute the causes of disease. Connection therewith in normal or judicious proportions is the cause of health.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson VI (Tasyashitiya), verse 1 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 1 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The premise of ritucharya: matching conduct and diet to season is presented as a determinant of strength, complexion and lifespan.
classical.quote: Of him who is acquainted with the opportuneness of conduct and food with seasons, strength and complexion (and happiness and period of life) increase, in consequence of his food, etc., (being taken with propriety).

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson VI, verses 2-5 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 2-5 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The adana/visarga half-year scheme and its stated mechanism, solar and wind-driven desiccation versus lunar and rain-driven moistening, which is the physical model underlying the seasonal dosha cycle.
classical.quote: For the purposes of this lesson, the year should be known as consisting of six portions, divided according to the seasons. Of these, the three seasons commencing with the season of dews and ending with summer constitute the period when the Sun travels in the region lying to the north of the equinoctial. That is again the period when the Sun takes (i.e., sucks up the liquid portion of every earthly object). The three other seasons commencing with the season of rains and ending with Hemanta constitutes the period of the Sun's southerly course. That is, besides, the time when the Sun gives (or yields moisture to all earthly objects). ... In the period of Taking, the Sun, by means of his rays, sucks up the moisture of the universe; and keen and rough winds also dry up the same.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verses 117-120 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 117-120 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The full scope of kala-samprapti: it spans seasonal, circadian, prandial and disease-periodicity time in a single category. The intermittent-fever periodicities are the one component with an obvious external referent (malarial tertian and quartan patterns).
classical.quote: In the Lesson on the causes, in brief, of diseases, time in respect of the accession of disease has been explained.
