This includes the topics, as previously explained, of the accession, excitement, and alleviation of bile and the rest, the seasons ending with the rainy, marked by characteristics that are false, excessive, or attenuated, as causes of diseases; rules about timeliness and untimeliness in respect of food eaten or in course of digestion or after digestion; forenoon, noon, and afternoon, and the three divisions, called yamas, of the night; particular diseases which spring up in particular times laid down; fevers which appear on every alternate day; those which appear with intervals of two days between successive paroxysms; and those which appear with intervals of three or four days between successive paroxysms.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verse 122 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 122 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: That svabhava-bala time effects, ageing and death, are explicitly placed outside therapeutics. Also that idiopathic disease is assigned to time by default.
classical.quote: With the development of Time, decrepitude, death and such diseases as are not due to known and defined causes, are seen to come naturally. That which is brought about by Nature has no remedy.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Vimana Sthana, Lesson III (Janapadoddhvamsaniya), verse 9 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 9 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: The diagnostic criterion for vitiated time at population scale, stated in the same three modes as at Sutra 11.
classical.quote: As regards Time, that should be known as baneful which discovers symptoms contrary to those which properly belong to the season (that is running), or symptoms that are aggravated or attenuated in comparison thereto.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Vimana Sthana, Lesson III, verses 12-13 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 12-13 (Kaviratna)
classical.establishes: That time is ranked the most potent of the four collective vitiating factors, and the explicit reason given, unavoidability, which is an argument about exposure rather than about mechanism.
classical.quote: Among these four, viz., Place, Time, Atmosphere, and Water, when they have all become perverted, explanations are subjoined as to which is more potent than which and for what reasons. Guided by the consideration of unavoidability, one conversant with the topic should hold that Water is a more potent cause than Air; Place a more potent cause than Water; and Time a more potent cause than Place, by nature.

classical.text: Sushruta Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Chapter XXIV (Vyadhi-samuddeshiya)
classical.verse: not numbered in Bhishagratna's rendering of this passage
classical.establishes: Sushruta's independent disease class for time, with a narrower and more physical mechanism than Charaka's, namely variation of atmospheric heat and humidity.
classical.quote: The Periodical type (Kala-vala-pravritta) includes diseases that are brought about by the variation of atmospheric heat or humidity with the change of the seasons, and admits of being grouped under two different sub-heads, according as the seasons, which usher these changes in, exhibit natural or contrary features.

classical.text: Sushruta Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Chapter XXIV, on the svabhava-bala-pravritta class
classical.establishes: The timely/untimely distinction, which is the closest classical approach to a premature-ageing concept and the point at which the otherwise fatalistic time category becomes modifiable by conduct.
classical.quote: The Natural or the Spontaneous (Svabhava-vala-pravritta) type includes such natural organic phenomena as, decrepitude, death, hunger, thirst, sleep, etc. These phenomena are either Kalakrita (timely) or Akalakrita (untimely). They are called Kalakrita when they occur at the proper time in persons who strictly observe the rules of health, and Akalakrita, when they appear at the improper time (morbid or premature) as the effects of unhealthy living.

classical.establishes: Standard-numbering locations for the same doctrine: kala as a fundamental padartha at Sutra 1/48-49, kala in clinical examination at Sutra 1/52, seasonal qualities at Sutra 6/3, parinama at Sutra 11/42 and Vimana 8/48, kala as etiological factor at Sutra 11/43 and Sutra 25/25. Located, not quoted.

modern.title: Widespread seasonal gene expression reveals annual differences in human immunity and physiology.
modern.establishes: Seasonal expression in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells and adipose tissue, in several cohorts. Quoted from the paper: 'Here we find more than 4,000 protein-coding mRNAs in white blood cells and adipose tissue to have seasonal expression profiles, with inverted patterns observed between Europe and Oceania.' The headline proportion belongs to one cohort, not to humans generally: 'Strikingly, we found ~23% of the genome (5,136 unique genes out of 22,822 genes tested) to show significant seasonal differences in expression in the BABYDIET data set.' The hemisphere inversion was seen in asthmatic PBMC samples: 'Summer and winter BABYDIET genes maintained their seasonal expression patterns in the asthmatic PBMC samples, with their patterns inverted in Australia.' The authors also report seasonal change in blood cell counts, and state in the abstract that these changes 'could explain the gene expression periodicity'. In the Gambian cohort the seasonal finding reported is in cell numbers, not in the transcriptome: 'In this data set, seasonal peaks in cell numbers correlated with the rainy season (June to October), during which time the infectious disease burden is at its highest levels.'
modern.quality: Corrected in the 2026-10-06 revision. Large samples, multiple cohorts, major journal, and the design is sound for its own question. Three things the earlier version of this entry got wrong or left out. First, it said 'roughly a quarter of the human genome shows seasonal expression' as a general result; the ~23% figure is from the BABYDIET cohort alone and is a proportion of the 22,822 genes tested, not of the genome. Second, it described 'a rainy-season-aligned pattern in a Gambian cohort' as if the Gambian result were transcriptomic; the Gambian result reported is seasonal variation in blood cell counts. The hemisphere inversion is Europe versus Australia. Third, and most important, it mentioned seasonal variation in cell composition as an additional observation rather than as the confound the authors themselves identify. The authors write that the PBMC transcriptional landscapes 'appear to be predominantly driven by annual changes in the cellular composition of blood', and that 'although our data suggest that cell-type numbers contribute the majority of seasonal gene expression in PBMCs, future studies of seasonal phenotypic differences within purified immune cell subsets are likely to reveal an additional layer of complexity in the human immune system'. They further note the latitude limit: 'Fewer seasonal genes were identified in Icelandic donors, and common seasonal genes had a less similar seasonal pattern in this data set. If a seasonal photoperiodic clock exists in humans, the impact of living at higher latitudes requires further exploration.' Caveat for honest use, restated and strengthened: this study establishes that season tracks measurable differences in human blood and adipose tissue, and on the authors' reading much of that is cell-composition shift. It says nothing whatever about doshas, about the six-season scheme, or about ritucharya prescriptions. It supports the general premise of kala-parinama and none of its specific content. Included deliberately as an outside comparator, not as Ayurvedic evidence.

modern.title: Impact of season and constitution on lipid parameters.
modern.establishes: In 54 healthy volunteers, lipid profile values were reported as higher in winter, and higher in kapha and pitta prakriti participants during winter.
modern.quality: Weak. Very small single-centre observational study, no control for diet, physical activity or body mass, prakriti assignment by unvalidated method with no reported inter-rater agreement, multiple comparisons unaddressed, conclusions about cardiovascular risk drawn from a single cross-sectional lipid measurement. Of the studies the searches named in gatheringNotes returned, this is the strongest located that is directly on the season-and-constitution claim, which is itself the finding. Reworded in the 2026-10-06 revision: the earlier phrasing said it was close to the strongest that exists, which a bounded search cannot establish.

modern.title: Ritucharya: Answer to the lifestyle disorders.
modern.establishes: Compiles the classical ritucharya prescriptions and argues they address modern lifestyle disorders.
modern.quality: Narrative review, explicitly so. No systematic search, no data, no outcome. Widely cited within the Ayurvedic literature, which inflates its apparent authority.

modern.title: Understanding COVID - 19 pandemic - A comprehensive Ayurvedic perspective.
modern.establishes: Applies the janapadodhvamsa framework, in which time is the most potent vitiating factor, to COVID-19, and proposes staged management.
modern.quality: Narrative conceptual paper. Proposes a mapping and a treatment scheme without testing either. Useful as evidence of how the kala doctrine is deployed in practice, not as evidence that the doctrine is correct.

modern.title: Patient Assessment and Chronic Pain Self-Management in Ethnomedicine: Seasonal and Ecosystemic Embodiment in Ayurvedic Patient-Centered Care.
modern.journal: Int J Environ Res Public Health
modern.establishes: Ethnographic description of how seasonal and ecological reasoning actually enters Ayurvedic clinical encounters in chronic pain care.
modern.quality: Qualitative study, appropriate methods for its question, no claim of efficacy. Valuable because it documents the clinical use of kala reasoning rather than asserting its validity.

modern.title: Day-night and seasonal variation of human gene expression across tissues.
modern.establishes: Day-night and seasonal transcriptomic variation across many human tissues, in a design independent of circulating-PBMC sampling. From the abstract: 'We used the time and season of death of 932 individuals from GTEx to jointly investigate transcriptomic changes associated with those cycles across multiple tissues. Overall, most variation across tissues during day-night and among seasons was unique to each cycle. Although all tissues remodeled their transcriptomes, brain and gonadal tissues exhibited the highest seasonality, whereas those in the thoracic cavity showed stronger day-night regulation.' And: 'Seasonal variation of expression affected multiple pathways, and it was enriched among genes associated with the immune response, consistent with the seasonality of viral infections.'
modern.quality: Added in the 2026-10-06 revision, as the counterweight the record previously lacked on the premise side. Large, peer-reviewed, open access, and methodologically distinct from Dopico 2015: it reads postmortem tissue from GTEx rather than circulating PBMCs, so it is not exposed to the blood cell-composition confound that the Dopico authors say drives most of their signal. That independence is the reason it is here. It is exposed to confounds of its own, which the paper's design makes unavoidable: season and hour of death are not randomly assigned, they correlate with cause of death, with agonal state and with postmortem interval, and the inference runs from time of death to tissue expression rather than from a sampled living rhythm. That reading of the design is the gatherer's, not a statement the authors make. What it does for this record is narrow and should not be stretched: it strengthens the premise that both the daily and the annual cycle leave a measurable trace in human tissue, and it reports that the two cycles are largely distinct from each other, which is at least structurally interesting against a doctrine that runs the same kapha-pitta-vata sequence through the day, the night and the year. It does not measure a dosha, does not test the six-ritu partition, does not test the morning-noon-evening assignment, and contains no Ayurvedic content of any kind.

modern.title: Efficacy of Rituharitaki (seasonal adjuvant of Haritaki) on disorders of Varsha Ritu (monsoon) w.s.r. to quality of life: An open labelled randomized controlled clinical trial.
modern.establishes: A randomised controlled trial of a ritucharya-derived intervention, which the record previously said did not exist. From the abstract: 'Administration of Haritaki with suitable vehicle as per season (Rituharitaki) is a simple, cost-effective preventive measure which can be used for such conditions.' Method: 'From 82 participants, based on inclusion criteria, 60 participants were selected and randomly allocated into trial and control group of 30 each using a computer generated random number table. Intervention given was Rituharitaki (Terminalia chebula Retz) in tablet form-3 tablets of 1g each and Saindhava (rock salt) 1g with lukewarm water at 6.30 am on empty stomach to the participants of trial group for 60 days in Varsha Ritu in Kerala.' Result: 'Significant results were obtained in the trial group in reducing the severity and frequency of common cold (p < 0.001), cough (p < 0.05), and fever (p < 0.001).'
modern.quality: Added in the 2026-10-06 revision because the record's own notKnown asserted that no randomised trial of ritucharya existed, which was both an exhaustiveness claim a bounded search cannot support and, as it turns out, false. The trial is real and it is randomised. It is also weak on the points that matter most for the doctrine. It is open-label, so every symptom endpoint is unblinded self-report against an untreated control, which is the design most vulnerable to expectation effects; n=60 in one centre in one season in one region; no placebo; the primary endpoints are symptom frequency and severity plus WHOQOL-BREF domains, with haematological parameters reported alongside and no stated correction for the number of comparisons made. What it tests is one preparation given at one time of year. It does not test the six-ritu partition, does not measure dosha accumulation or subsidence, and does not compare season-matched against season-mismatched administration, which is the comparison that would actually test the ritucharya principle rather than the drug. A positive result here is consistent with Haritaki having an effect in any season. It is cited to replace a false negative claim with a located positive study and its limits, not as support for the doctrine.

modern.title: Evaluation of Vamana and Virechana as Interventions to Decelerate the Aging Process in Healthy Adult Volunteers: Protocol for an Exploratory Single-Arm Clinical Trial.
modern.establishes: A CTRI-registered seasonal-purification intervention study aimed at the ageing limb of kala-parinama, published as a protocol. From the abstract: 'Ritu sodhana (seasonal purification) imparts rejuvenation in healthy individuals. However, its efficacy for health span and decelerating the aging process in healthy individuals remains a gray area.' Registration and design: 'The study was prospectively registered in the Clinical Trial Registry-India (CTRI; CTRI/2024/02/062176), uses a pre-posttest study design, and includes 53 participants 35 years to 65 years old. The study is exploratory and lacks a control group.' Intervention: 'The interventions include emesis in the spring and purgation in the autumn season.' Status and claim: 'Recruitment began in March 2025... Data analysis is pending' and 'The study will provide hypothesis-generating evidence, and the data will serve as a necessary precursor to adequately powered, confirmatory trials on the aging process.'
modern.quality: Added in the 2026-10-06 revision to answer the critic finding that the record cited no seasonal-Panchakarma intervention literature. It is the clearest located example of that literature and it is registered, which is what the finding asked for. It carries no result. It is a protocol: single-arm, no control group, 53 participants, surrogate endpoints only (serum malondialdehyde, total superoxide dismutase, telomerase activity) measured before and shortly after the procedure, and the authors themselves describe the output as hypothesis-generating and a precursor to adequately powered trials. Measuring an oxidative-stress marker before and after a purgative, with no control arm, cannot distinguish a rejuvenating effect from the acute physiological consequences of emesis, purgation, oleation, fomentation and a controlled post-procedure diet, nor from regression to the mean. It also does not test seasonality: the spring-emesis and autumn-purgation timing is fixed by the protocol, so there is no off-season comparison and the seasonal element of ritu shodhana is untested by construction. The CTRI number is quoted as the protocol paper prints it. It was not independently confirmed against the CTRI register; see notKnown on why CTRI itself was not searched.

modern.title: A cross-sectional survey to evaluate the status of digestion in rotating- and fixed-shift workers.
modern.establishes: The nearest located empirical work on the daily-clock limb of kala-parinama, which the record previously left with no modern reference at all. From the abstract: 'The state of Jatharagni is influenced by several physiological factors, including season, time of day, age, constitution, dosha balance, and the quality and quantity of food consumed.' Method: 'A comparative, cross-sectional study was conducted among Information Technology (IT) employees... 350 employees were selected, comprising 175 fixed-shift workers and 175 rotating-shift workers (alternating between day and night shifts monthly) using a convenience sampling technique. Agnibala was assessed using a validated questionnaire.' Result: 'The study indicated that most fixed-shift workers had an Agnibala status consistent with their Prakriti. In contrast, 61.7% of rotating-shift workers reported a change in their Agni status due to their job nature, with many shifting to Vishamagni during their night shifts.' The authors' own closing caveat: 'These observations indicate a possible relationship between shift work, circadian rhythm disruption, and digestive health.'
modern.quality: Added in the 2026-10-06 revision. Cited for one thing: it is the closest located attempt to put an Ayurvedic time-governed function against a real disruption of the daily clock, and it is included because the record's dosha-kala component otherwise had no modern reference whatever. It is weak and it does not test what the record most needs tested. Cross-sectional, convenience sample from one technology park, and the outcome is a self-report questionnaire, so the headline 61.7% is workers reporting a change in their own digestion, not a measured change; the rotating-shift workers were assessed twice and the fixed-shift workers once, which is an asymmetry between the arms. No circadian marker was measured: no actigraphy, no cortisol, no core temperature, no melatonin. Crucially, it does not test the morning-kapha, noon-pitta, evening-vata assignment, and it does not test whether agni follows the classical daily sequence; it tests whether people whose schedule is inverted say their digestion has changed, which is compatible with the classical doctrine and with the ordinary chronobiology of shift work equally well. notKnown item 1 therefore stands unanswered and has been reworded rather than removed.

records.title: Manas and the triguna: mind, sattva, rajas and tamas in health
records.summary: Ayurveda treats the mind (manas) as a substratum of health and disease alongside the body, not as a separate domain. Charaka states that body and mind together are where health and disease inhere (Su. 1.55) and that while vata, pitta and kapha are the doshas of the body, rajas and tamas are the two doshas of the mind (Su. 1.57, Sha. 4.34); Vagbhata states the same twofold locus and the same two mental doshas (AH Su. 1.21). Sattva is not counted among the doshas, and Sharira 4.36 calls the shuddha (sattvika) mind adosha, faultless. It does not follow from this that mental disorder is simply an excess of rajas or tamas, and the record does not assert it: the chapters that actually describe mental disease give a dosha-mediated pathogenesis, with the aggravated bodily doshas reaching the heart and obstructing the channels through which the mind operates to produce unmada (Ni. 7.4-5), and with apasmara setting in when sattva is destroyed by rajas and tamas while the heart is overwhelmed by the doshas (Ci. 10, Kaviratna's aphorisms 2-3). How that sits with Su. 11.45, which defines mental disease in purely motivational terms, is carried in contested rather than resolved here. Charaka classifies mind into three kinds (shuddha or sattvika, rajasa, tamasa) at Sha. 4.36, names sixteen types across Sha. 4.37-39 and summarises them at Sha. 4.40 on an avowedly analogical scheme of deities, demons and animals; the predominance principle that makes such a classification workable is stated in the mula at Sha. 3.13. Disease is classified as threefold, nija (endogenous), agantu (exogenous) and manasa (mental), the last arising from failure to obtain what is desired or from contact with what is disliked (Su. 11.45), and one of the three classes of therapy, sattvavajaya, is defined as restraint of the mind from unwholesome objects (Su. 11.54). What that restraint looks like in the treatment chapter is wider and harsher than the modern reading of it as psychotherapy suggests: Chikitsa 9 prescribes consolation and the deliberate use of opposite emotions, and also binding, whipping, confinement and induced terror.
records.evidenceState:
This concept has two distinct bodies of evidence and they should not be merged. The triguna construct has been genuinely operationalised: multiple psychometric instruments exist and are cited here with resolved identifiers (Vedic Personality Inventory, Wolf 1999, DOI 10.2466/pr0.1999.84.3c.1379; Mysore Triguna Scale, Shilpa and Venkatesha Murthy 2012, SAGE Open, DOI 10.1177/2158244012436564; MHAS-TG, 2025, PMID 40774071), and at least one empirical study has compared guna profiles between diagnosed psychiatric patients and matched controls with plausible results (PMID 36818072). That is more than most concepts in this cluster have. But the instruments do not agree with each other, none is an accepted reference standard, the strongest validation among the papers retrieved here is convergence with another self-report wellbeing questionnaire rather than any clinical outcome, and none of the retrieved papers shows that guna scores predict anything established psychometrics do not already predict. The guna-versus-diagnosis findings are cross-sectional, so they cannot distinguish a stable mental constitution from the current state of an active illness, which is the single question that matters for the classical claim.

The other body of evidence, on sattvavajaya as therapy, is poor, and the first problem with it is not design but definition. Across the three trials retrieved, sattvavajaya names three different interventions: asana, pranayama, chanting and counselling (PMID 26170589), relaxation techniques (PMID 32398908), and trance or clinical hypnosis (PMID 23049189). A fourth record, the only one on a depressive disorder found in the searches named in gatheringNotes, is a single case report in which sattvavajaya was given together with oral medicines and viddhakarma (PMID 41016220). The trials are small, open-label or unblinded, use unvalidated outcome scales devised for the study, confound the intervention with yoga and counselling, and compare two active arms with no inert control. They report benefit; their designs cannot establish it. The identification of sattvavajaya with psychotherapy, and the comparison with cognitive behavioural therapy, rests in the literature on assertion rather than trial: the most-cited statement of it (PMID 23858273) is a narrative supplement article with no method, no data and no comparison.

What this record does NOT say is that sattvavajaya has never been trialled. That claim, in the form the gathering-pass critic quoted, is not in this record and is not made here. What is said instead is bounded: the searches this record can name (see gatheringNotes) returned eleven unique PubMed records for sattvavajaya across two spellings, of which three are the comparative studies cited here, one is the case report, and the remainder are narrative or historical pieces. No controlled trial in anxiety was among them, and no scoping or systematic review in AYU or JAIM was among them. AYU and several Indian Ayurveda journals are not fully indexed in PubMed, so none of this is evidence that such studies do not exist; it is a record of what a named search found.

Two conceptual points, both now sourced rather than asserted. First, the classical taxonomy of sixteen sattva types is explicitly analogical in the text's own wording, Sha. 4.40 giving the types sattvanukarena, after the manner of the mind of, and classifying by behavioural resemblance to deities, demons and animals; no instrument retrieved here attempts to measure it. Modern triguna work measures three continuous dimensions and drops the sixteen-type scheme, and the classical construct it is in fact closest to is not that scheme at all but the graded sattva sara of Vimana 8 (classical[18]), which the modern literature retrieved here does not cite. Second, the claim that rajas and tamas are doshas of the mind in the same sense that vata, pitta and kapha are doshas of the body has no empirical content in any paper retrieved here. It is not, however, merely a structural parallel asserted and repeated: the nosology chapters added in this revision give it mechanical content, with the aggravated bodily doshas obstructing the manovaha srotas to produce unmada (Ni. 7.4) and with sattva destroyed by rajas and tamas named alongside dosha involvement in apasmara (Ci. 10). That content is textual, and it is untested.

contested.question: Is sattva a guna, a dosha, or the mind itself?
positions: Charaka counts only rajas and tamas as manasa doshas, so sattva is the mind's undisturbed nature and not a dosha

Charaka also uses sattva as a synonym for manas itself (shariram sattvasamjnam cha), and separately as a term for mental endurance or strength, so the word carries at least three senses in the same text
Modern triguna instruments treat all three as symmetrical measurable dimensions, which flattens a distinction the classical text is careful about

Added on revision: a fourth sense is now cited, sattva as one of the eight saras in Vimana 8 (classical[18]), where it is a graded measure of strength standing in a list otherwise made of bodily tissues. Whether this is the endurance sense or a fourth thing again is not stated in the passage.

contested.question: Is mental constitution a fixed trait or a current state?
positions: Classical position: manasika prakriti, like sharirika prakriti, is determined at conception and fixed

State position, implied by the finding that guna profiles differ systematically between people in acute psychiatric illness and controls: what the instruments measure may be current mental state, not constitution
No study separating these was found in the searches named in gatheringNotes, and no longitudinal guna measurement through illness and recovery was among the retrieved records

Added on revision: the texts themselves pull both ways. Sha. 3.13 says the kinds of sattva are all present in one person and that one is named only by preponderance, which is state-like; Ni. 7.4 names upaklishta-sattva, afflicted sattva, as a susceptibility, which treats a guna state as a modifiable risk factor rather than a fixed type.

contested.question: What is sattvavajaya, operationally?
positions: Literally as Charaka defines it: restraint of the mind from unwholesome objects, closer to deliberate abstention than to a therapy (Su. 11.54)
As modern Ayurvedic psychiatry practises it: an umbrella covering counselling, psychoeducation, yoga, pranayama, chanting and behavioural advice, which is far broader than the classical definition

As a near-equivalent of cognitive behavioural therapy, a comparison frequently asserted and, in the records retrieved here, never tested head to head. The assertion is now sourced to PMID 23858273, which makes it with no method, no data and no comparison.

Added on revision: in the trial literature the word does not pick out one intervention. It was delivered as asana, pranayama, chanting and counselling in PMID 26170589, as relaxation techniques in PMID 32398908 and as trance or clinical hypnosis in PMID 23049189. Three studies, three interventions.

Added on revision: Charaka's own non-drug repertoire for unmada is wider and harsher than any of these. Ni. 7.8 lists vadha, bandhana, avarodhana, vitrasana, vismapana and vismarana, and Chikitsa 9 prescribes consolation with words of dharma and artha and the deliberate induction of an opposite emotion, and also whipping, goading, binding, solitary confinement and terrifying the patient with defanged snakes, tame lions and elephants, armed men, and officers threatening death on the king's order (classical[14], classical[15]). Any claim that sattvavajaya is the classical name for psychotherapy has to say what it is doing with these.

contested.question: Does the manasa disease category require dosha involvement?
positions: Charaka Su. 11.45 defines manasa roga purely by thwarted desire or imposed aversion, with no mention of dosha

Elsewhere the texts describe unmada and apasmara through dosha vitiation of the mind, implying manasa roga is dosha-mediated after all. This is now cited rather than referred to: Ni. 7.4 (classical[13]) and Ci. 10 (classical[16]).

Revised on this pass. The gathering pass said a reconciling reading that distinguishes the cause (motivational) from the pathogenesis (dosha-mediated) is 'a modern harmonisation' because 'the texts do not state this'. That overstated the case and has been corrected: Ni. 7.4 puts both halves in a single sentence, naming kama, krodha, lobha, harsha, bhaya, shoka, chinta and udvega among the susceptibilities AND the aggravated doshas obstructing the manovaha srotas as the mechanism, and Ci. 10's pathogenesis sentence is explicitly joint. What remains genuinely modern is the tidy two-level cause/pathogenesis schema; the raw material for it is in the texts.

The tension with Su. 11.45 is not thereby dissolved. Su. 11.45 is a definition of a disease class and mentions no dosha; Ni. 7.4 and Ci. 10 are accounts of two particular diseases. Whether the class is defined dosha-free while its members are all dosha-mediated is not something the texts retrieved here address.

contested.question: Do the sixteen sattva types have any modern referent?
positions: Some authors map them onto personality typologies or temperament dimensions
Others treat them as culturally specific analogies with no translatable content, noting they classify by resemblance to gods, demons, birds, snakes, fish and trees
No instrument among those retrieved here measures them, so in practice the modern literature retrieved here has abandoned them while continuing to cite the chapter they come from

Added on revision: the text's own wording supports the second position more than the first. Sha. 4.37-39 introduce each type with vidyat, 'one should know (a man of such traits) as X', and Sha. 4.40 gathers them sattvanukarena, after the manner of the mind of, so resemblance is the stated criterion and not an interpretation imposed on it.

contested.question: Is the graded sattva of Vimana 8 the same construct as the triguna of Sharira 4?
positions: New question added on revision, raised by the material the critic asked for. Sharira 4 gives kinds of mind, named by analogy and assigned by predominance. Vimana 8 gives sattva as the eighth sara, a quantity of mental strength measured for the assessment of bala, in a list whose other seven members are skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow and shukra.
A reading that makes them one construct has to explain why one is typed and the other graded, and why sattva appears in Vimana 8 among tissues.
A reading that makes them two has to explain the single word.

The texts retrieved here do not address the relation, and neither does any paper retrieved here. The modern instruments measure a graded quantity, which is formally the Vimana 8 shape, while citing the Sharira 4 chapter.

notKnown: Whether guna scores are stable within a person over time, or whether they track current mood and symptom state. No longitudinal study was found in the searches named in gatheringNotes.
Whether triguna assessment adds predictive or explanatory information beyond established personality and wellbeing psychometrics. No incremental-validity study was among the retrieved records.
Why the different triguna instruments (VPI, Mysore Triguna Scale, MHAS-TG) yield different factor structures, and which if any should be preferred.

Whether sattvavajaya has any effect beyond attention, expectancy and the yoga practices it is usually bundled with. None of the three retrieved trials isolates it, and the three do not deliver the same intervention, so there is at present no single thing to isolate.
Whether the OCD exception in the guna-diagnosis findings (patients not differing from controls on sattva) reflects something real about OCD or is a small-sample artefact.
What the relation is between manasika prakriti and sharirika prakriti. The texts assert both; no retrieved study measures their association.
Whether the sixteen sattva types can be measured at all, and whether anyone has tried. No instrument among those retrieved here attempts it.

Whether rajas and tamas behave like doshas in any testable sense, for example showing increase and decrease with identified causes and responding to opposite-quality interventions. Ni. 7.4 and Ci. 10 give the doctrine a mechanism (obstruction of the manovaha srotas, destruction of sattva by rajas and tamas) which is in principle the sort of claim that could be operationalised; nothing retrieved here operationalises it.

Whether the classical claim that mental disease requires non-drug therapy (knowledge, fortitude, memory, withdrawal) has ever been tested against pharmacotherapy in a comparative trial. No such trial was among the retrieved records.
Whether guna-based screening identifies people missed by standard mental health screening, or simply re-identifies the same people.

ADDED ON REVISION. Whether sattvavajaya scoping or systematic reviews exist in AYU or JAIM, as the critic's missing finding states. The two PubMed searches named in gatheringNotes returned eleven unique records and no review of that kind. Those journals are not fully indexed in PubMed, so this is not evidence that no such review exists; it is a record that the searches run here did not find one, and that no such reference could therefore be cited under this project's no-quote-no-citation rule.

ADDED ON REVISION. Whether controlled trials of sattvavajaya in anxiety and in depression exist, as the critic's overclaimed finding states. None in anxiety was found in those searches; the only depression record found was a single case report (PMID 41016220). The same indexing caveat applies.

ADDED ON REVISION. The standard-edition (Trikamji) verse numbers for three of the passages quoted here are not established: Chikitsa 9 (classical[15]), Chikitsa 10 (classical[16]) and Vimana 8 (classical[18]). Kaviratna's own aphorism numbers are given instead. For Vimana 8 the discrepancy is specific and unexplained: the critic addresses sattva sara to 8.110 and Kaviratna prints 123 at that paragraph, so the one-behind offset established elsewhere in this project for Vimanasthana 8 does not hold at this point in the chapter.

ADDED ON REVISION. Whether Kaviratna's 'subjecting them to control' at Sharira 1.21 renders svasya nigrahah, the mind's restraint of itself, or the restraint of the senses. The Sanskrit reads naturally as the former and his English as the latter, and the record does not resolve it. Because it is unresolved, this record does not use Sha. 1.21 as the textual root of sattvavajaya.

ADDED ON REVISION. The swastha definition (prasannatmendriyamanah, a person of pleasant atman, indriyas and manas), which the gathering-pass summary leaned on, is commonly cited to Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 and is not held in this record. No Sushruta citation was retrieved on this pass, so the sentence that rested on it has been removed from the summary and no claim here depends on it.

ADDED ON REVISION. Charaka Nidana 8 (apasmara nidana) and the remainder of Chikitsa 9 and Chikitsa 10 beyond the passages quoted are not covered. Only the definition and pathogenesis sentences are cited, because those are what bear on this concept's claims; the therapeutic detail of the apasmara chapters is outside the scope this record keeps.
ADDED ON REVISION. Whether Charaka Sharirasthana 4's sixteen types and Vimanasthana 8's graded sattva sara are one construct or two. See contested, question 6.

components.gloss: Mind: in Charaka's account the factor whose presence or absence explains why knowledge arises when self, sense and object are already in contact (Sha. 1.18), and whose two named gunas are anutva, minuteness, and ekatva, oneness (Sha. 1.19). The further inference that cognitions must therefore be successive rather than simultaneous is Chakrapani's reasoning in the Ayurveda Dipika on Sha. 1.18-19, repeated at length in Kaviratna's footnote; the mula does not state it, and this record does not record it as doctrine.

The mind's clear, unvitiated quality: lightness, clarity, discernment. Not a dosha. Also used as a synonym for manas itself, and as a term for mental strength or endurance, which is the sense carried by sattva sara in Vimana 8.
A manasa dosha: agitation, passion, craving, wrath. Vitiates the mind by activity
A manasa dosha: inertia, stupefaction, delusion, heedlessness. Vitiates the mind by obscuration

The threefold classification of mind as shuddha (pure/sattvika), rajasa and tamasa, by which quality predominates (Sha. 4.36). That any one person carries all the kinds and is named for the one that predominates is stated in the mula at Sha. 3.13, prayovrittya.

The sixteen sattva types: seven sattvika (brahma, arsha, aindra, yamya, varuna, kaubera, gandharva) at Sha. 4.37, six rajasa (asura, rakshasa, paishacha, sarpa, praita, shakuna) at Sha. 4.38, three tamasa (pashava, matsya, vanaspatya) at Sha. 4.39, summarised by name at Sha. 4.40. The names are given there with anukarena, after the manner of, so the scheme is analogical in the text's own wording and not only in modern description.

Mental disease, classified at Su. 11.45 as arising from non-attainment of the desired or contact with the disliked, distinct from nija and agantu disease. The nosology chapters add a pathogenesis the Su. 11.45 definition does not mention: see Ni. 7.4-5 for unmada and Ci. 10 for apasmara.

The third of the three classes of therapy: restraint or subjugation of the mind, withdrawing it from harmful objects (Su. 11.54). Treated in modern Ayurveda as its psychotherapy; what that identification does and does not carry over is in contested, question 3.

Mind as the eighth of the eight saras, the predominating essences by which a person's strength is measured in Vimana 8. This is sattva in the sense of mental strength and it is graded rather than typed, so whether it is the same construct as the triguna of Sharira 4 is an open question the texts do not settle: see contested, question 6.

Vagbhata's prescription for the doshas of the mind at AH Su. 1.26: dhi (discernment), dhairya (fortitude) and atmadi-vijnana, knowledge of the self and so on. The compound ends in adi, and so on, which leaves the list open; calling it a closed triad, as the gathering pass did, reads the adi away and that has been corrected.

classical.establishes: That mind is a substratum of health and disease on the same footing as body, which is the structural basis for the whole psychosomatic architecture of the system. Sattva is used here as a name for manas, which is one of the three senses of the word tracked in contested, question 1.
classical.quote: Body and mind are regarded as the subjects in which health and disease co-inhere; parity of correlation being the cause of health.

classical.establishes: The two manasa doshas, rajas and tamas, set in explicit parallel to the three sharira doshas. Sattva is conspicuously not counted as a dosha.
classical.quote: Wind, bile, and phlegm have been said to be the causes of all bodily diseases. The qualities of Passion and Darkness have, again, been indicated to be the causes of mental diseases.

classical.establishes: That mental disease is assigned a categorically different therapeutics from bodily disease: knowledge, fortitude, memory and withdrawal of the mind rather than drugs. Kaviratna's 'the abstraction of the mind from all worldly objects' is his rendering of samadhi and should not be read as a separate item of doctrine.
classical.quote: The first kind (i.e., bodily disease) is cured by medicines founded upon acts in respect of the deities and upon reason. Mental disease is cured by knowledge of the soul, knowledge of the scriptures, (exercise of) patience and memory, and the abstraction of the mind from all worldly objects.

classical.establishes: The threefold nija / agantu / manasa disease taxonomy, and a definition of mental disease in purely motivational terms, thwarted desire or imposed aversion, with no reference to dosha at all. This is the verse the nosology chapters cited at classical[13] and classical[16] sit in tension with.
classical.quote: Diseases are of three kinds, viz., Physical, Accidental, and Mental. Physical diseases are those that arise from some abnormal condition of the body. Accidental are those that arise from the action of spirits, of poison, of wind, of fire, of acts of violence done to the body, such as beating, &c. Mental diseases are those that arise from non-attainment of objects desired or coveted, or from accession of those that are disliked.

classical.establishes: The threefold therapeutics (daivavyapashraya, yuktivyapashraya, sattvavajaya) and the classical definition of sattvavajaya as withdrawal of the mind from harmful objects. This is the definition against which the breadth of modern sattvavajaya practice should be read.
classical.quote: Medicines are of three kinds; those that depend for their action upon the deities and invisible influences; those that depend for their application and action upon knowledge and reason; and those that appertain to the subjugation of the mind. ... The subjugation of the mind by withdrawing it from every kind of injurious or harmful acts and objects of the senses, constitutes medicine of the third kind.

classical.establishes: The clearest statement of the two-mental-dosha doctrine, here in an embryological context about how vitiation of body and mind produces defects. The Sanskrit added on this pass shows the mula says only that the two vitiate sattva and that vikriti arises from the two being vitiated; it does not say that mental disorder is nothing but their excess.
classical.quote: In this connection it should be stated that there are three faults of the body. They are Wind, Bile, and Phlegm. (When excited) they vitiate the body. Again, the faults of the mind are two. These are Rajas (Passion) and Tamas (Darkness). These two vitiate the mind.
classical.sanskrit: तत्र त्रयः शरीरदोषा वातपित्तश्लेष्माणः, ते शरीरं दूषयन्ति; द्वौ पुनः सत्त्वदोषौ रजस्तमश्च, तौ सत्त्वं दूषयतः। ताभ्यां च सत्त्वशरीराभ्यां दुष्टाभ्यां विकृतिरुपजायते, नोपजायते चाप्रदुष्टाभ्याम्॥३४॥

classical.establishes: The threefold classification of mind and, importantly, that only the sattvika type is called adosha, faultless. The verse does not by itself establish a predominance model; for that see classical[9].
classical.quote: The mind, verily, is of three kinds, viz., 1. pure, 2. predominated by passion, and 3. predominated by darkness. Amongst these, that (mind) which is pure, is (otherwise) called faultless, because of its being made up of Goodness. That which is predominated by Passion is regarded as faulty, because of its being made up of wrath (or passion). So, that which is predominated by Darkness is also regarded as faulty, because of its being made up of stupefaction (or heedlessness).
classical.sanskrit: त्रिविधं खलु सत्त्वं- शुद्धं, राजसं, तामसमिति। तत्र शुद्धमदोषमाख्यातं कल्याणांशत्वात्, राजसं सदोषमाख्यातं रोषांशत्वात्, तामसमपि सदोषमाख्यातं मोहांशत्वात्। ... ॥३६॥

classical.establishes: Where the sixteen types are actually described and named: seven shuddha types at 4.37, each named at the end of its own sentence (ब्राह्मं, आर्षं, ऐन्द्रं, याम्यं, वारुणं, कौबेरं, गान्धर्वं), six rajasa at 4.38 (आसुरं, राक्षसं, पैशाचं, सार्पं, प्रैतं, शाकुनं) and three tamasa at 4.39 (पाशवं, मात्स्यं, वानस्पत्यं), with the closing summation of each group quoted above. Each type is given as a list of behavioural traits introduced by विद्यात्, 'one should know (a man of these traits) as X', which is the textual basis for saying the criterion is behavioural resemblance.
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

classical.establishes: The sixteen sattva types as a single summary list, and the avowedly analogical basis of the taxonomy: the Sanskrit says सत्त्वानुकारेण, after the manner of the mind of, which is exactly what Kaviratna's 'after the manner of' renders, so the analogical character is the text's own and not a modern gloss. The closing clause कथं च यथासत्त्वमुपचारः स्यादिति makes the purpose of the list the fitting of upachara to sattva.
classical.quote: Of the pure mind the seven varieties are those that are after the manner of the minds possessed by Brahman the Rishis, Cakra, Varuna, Yama, Kuvera, and the Gandharvas. Of the Rajas-pervaded mind the six varieties are those that are after the manner of the minds possessed by Daityas, Rakshasas, Picachas, Snakes, Pretas, and birds. Of the Tamas-pervaded mind the three varieties are those that are after the manner of the minds of beasts, fishes, and trees. The practices (or conduct) of a person will, somehow, accord with the variety of mind he may possess.
classical.sanskrit: इत्यपरिसङ्ख्येयभेदानां त्रयाणामपि सत्त्वानां भेदैकदेशो व्याख्यातः; शुद्धस्य सत्त्वस्य सप्तविधो ब्रह्मर्षिशक्रयमवरुणकुबेरगन्धर्वसत्त्वानुकारेण, राजसस्य षड्विधो दैत्यपिशाचराक्षससर्पप्रेतशकुनिसत्त्वानुकारेण, तामसस्य त्रिविधः पशुमत्स्यवनस्पतिसत्त्वानुकारेण, कथं च यथासत्त्वमुपचारः स्यादिति॥५.४.४०॥

classical.establishes: That the predominance model is in the mula and not only in a translator's footnote: the kinds of sattva are many, all of them are present in one and the same person, they are not present at one and the same time, and one is spoken of प्रायोवृत्त्या, by preponderance. This is the textual warrant for reading the Sharira 4 typology as a predominance scheme rather than a set of exclusive types.
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

classical.verse: 13 (translator's note, on Kaviratna's aphorism 23)
classical.establishes: How Kaviratna himself read the predominance model, which matters because modern triguna instruments score all three gunas continuously on this same logic. It is quoted as translator's commentary and nothing in the record rests on it: the doctrine itself is carried by the mula at classical[9].
classical.quote: It cannot, however, be true that one having a Sattwika mind is possessed of the attribute of Sattwa alone; or, in other words, that he has no grain or admixture of Rajas and Tamas. Nor can it be true that a Tamasika mind has Tamas alone for its characteristic to the total exclusion of the two other attributes in any measure. When, however, we say that one has a Sattwika mind, all that we intend by it is that the attribute of Sattwa predominates in his mind.

classical.establishes: The two gunas of manas, anutva and ekatva, and the lakshana by which manas is known: that knowledge is sometimes absent even when self, sense and object are in contact. This sources the Manas component gloss, which the gathering pass carried without any citation.
classical.quote: Subtility and oneness have been regarded as the two attributes of the mind.
classical.sanskrit: लक्षणं मनसो ज्ञानस्याभावो भाव एव च। सति ह्यात्मेन्द्रियार्थानां सन्निकर्षे न वर्तते॥१८॥ वैवृत्त्यान्मनसो ज्ञानं सान्निध्यात्तच्च वर्तते। अणुत्वमथ चैकत्वं द्वौ गुणौ मनसः स्मृतौ॥१९॥

classical.establishes: The karma of manas: apprehension of objects through the senses, स्वस्य निग्रहः, ūha and vichāra, after which buddhi operates. It is cited here only for what it says, that restraint stands among the functions of mind.
classical.quote: Seizure of objects by means of the senses, subjecting them to control, comparison, and ratiocination, are the functions of the mind. After this the understanding begins to work.
classical.sanskrit: इन्द्रियाभिग्रहः कर्म मनसः स्वस्य निग्रहः। ऊहो विचारश्च, ततः परं बुद्धिः प्रवर्तते॥२१॥

classical.establishes: The mental-disease nosology the record previously had no citation for. Two things at once: unmada is defined at 7.5 as the derangement of manas, buddhi, samjna, jnana, smriti, bhakti, shila, cheshta and achara, and 7.4 gives a pathogenesis in which the motivational factors of Su. 11.45 (kama, krodha, lobha, harsha, bhaya, shoka, chinta, udvega) appear as predisposing causes while the proximate mechanism is the aggravated doshas reaching the heart and obstructing the manovaha srotas. It also names upaklishta-sattva, one whose sattva is afflicted, as a susceptibility, which is the nearest the texts come to treating a guna state as a risk factor.
classical.quote: Of these, the four that are born of the faults quickly afflict men that are of the following descriptions. They are, — Those who are timid or subject to fear; Those, in whom the attribute of 'Sattwa' is afflicted by 'Rajas' and 'Tamas;' Those in whom the faults have been attenuated to proportions below what are regarded as normal; ... Those whose minds have been affected by lust, wrath, cupidity, joy, fear, grief, cares, and anxieties, or, Those who have been afflicted with wounds, The wind being afflicted, and the understanding being disturbed, the faults become aggravated and provoked; then reaching the heart, and obstructing the ducts through which the mind operates, they beget Insanity. Insanity, it should be known, is the derangement of the mind, understanding, knowledge, memory, devotion, behaviour, acts, and practices.
classical.sanskrit: tatra doṣanimittāś catvāraḥ puruṣāṇām evaṃvidhānāṃ kṣipram abhinirvartante tadyathā bhīrūṇām upakliṣṭasattvānām utsannadoṣāṇāṃ ... upahatamanasāṃ vā kāmakrodhalobhaharṣabhayamohāyāsaśokacintodvegādibhir bhūyo 'bhighātābhyāhatānāṃ vā manasy upahate buddhau ca pracalitāyām abhyudīrṇā doṣāḥ prakupitā hṛdayam upasṛtya manovahāni srotāṃsy āvṛtya janayanty unmādam // Car_2,7.4 unmādaṃ punar manobuddhisaṃjñājñānasmṛtibhaktiśīlaceṣṭācāravibhramaṃ vidyāt // Car_2,7.5

classical.establishes: That the classical treatment list for curable unmada runs vadha, bandhana, avarodhana, vitrasana, vismapana and vismarana, which Kaviratna renders striking, tying, confining, frightening, inspiring wonder and causing forgetfulness, set among snehana, svedana, vamana, virechana, the enemas and the rest. It is cited for one thing only: that the non-pharmacological repertoire of the texts is not confined to counsel. What this does to the modern identification of sattvavajaya with psychotherapy is argued in contested, question 3, not here.
classical.quote: Striking, tying, confining, frightening, inspiring wonder, and causing forgetfulness; Adoption of measures that lead to leanness; and Letting out blood by opening the veins.
classical.sanskrit: sādhyānāṃ tu trayāṇāṃ sādhanāni snehasvedavamanavirecanāsthāpanānuvāsanopaśamanastaḥkarmadhūmadhūpanāñjanāvapīḍapradhamanābhyaṅgapradehapariṣekānulepanavadhabandhanāvarodhanavitrāsanavismāpanavismāraṇāpatarpaṇasirāvyadhanāni bhojanavidhānaṃ ca yathāsvaṃ yuktyā yac cānyad api kiṃcin nidānaviparītam auṣadhaṃ kāryaṃ tad api syād iti // Car_2,7.8

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorisms 89, 91 and 96 (standard verse numbers not established; see numberingNote)
classical.establishes: What the non-drug half of unmada treatment actually consists of in the treatment chapter: consolation with words of dharma and artha, deliberate induction of a counter-emotion, and also whipping, goading, binding, solitary confinement and, in the aphorisms between those quoted, terrifying the patient with defanged snakes, tame lions and elephants, armed men, and officers threatening death on the king's order. This is the classical material against which the modern reading of sattvavajaya as psychotherapy, and the untested comparison with cognitive behavioural therapy, should be read.
classical.quote: Or, some friend of his should console him with words that are fraught with Piety and Profit; or, he should inform him of the loss of some beloved one, or show him some such object as is capable of exciting his wonder. ... Or, striking him with whips and goads, and binding him strongly, he should be confined in a solitary chamber. By this, his deranged mind will be quickly restored to equanimity. ... Those that have become insane through lust, or grief, or fear, or wrath, or joy, or envy, or cupidity, should be brought back to reason by the operation of opposite emotions.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorisms 2-3 (standard verse numbers not established; see numberingProblem)
classical.establishes: The second of the two mental-disease chapters the record was missing. It matters for one specific reason: the pathogenesis here is explicitly joint, sattva destroyed by rajas and tamas AND the heart overwhelmed by the bodily doshas AND the mind afflicted by chinta, kama, bhaya, krodha, shoka and the rest, in a single sentence. Any reading that makes mental disease either purely motivational or purely dosha-mediated has to account for this verse.
classical.quote: Physicians conversant with medicine say that loss of memory is called 'Apasmara' (epilepsy). ... Of persons whose tranquillity has been disturbed by the faults being excited in a large measure, and who take baneful and impure food and drink, epilepsy sets in, when their quality of Goodness is destroyed by Passion and Darkness, when their heart is overwhelmed by faults, and when their minds are afflicted by anxiety, lust, fear, wrath, grief, care and the rest.

classical.establishes: Achara rasayana, conduct itself prescribed as a rasayana, which the critic rightly called the natural classical companion to sattvavajaya. Two things are established. First, the list is almost entirely conduct and mental disposition: truthfulness, freedom from wrath, non-violence, tranquillity, compassion, absence of pride, regularity of sleeping and waking. Second, and this is why the entry runs to 36 rather than stopping at 35, the text makes the benefit conditional on first clearing the doshas of BOTH body and mind (doṣāñ chārīramānasān), so the manasa doshas appear here as something to be removed before a therapy can work, not merely as a classification of persons.
classical.quote: One that is truthful, and free from wrath, that abstains from wine and sexual indulgence, that has no animosity, that undergoes only such labour as involves no fatigue, that is tranquil and of amiable speech, that is accustomed to the silent recitation of sacred texts, and is pure (in body and mind), that is endued with gravity and firmness, that is always charitable and engaged in penances, that honours the deities and kine and Brahmanas and preceptors and spiritual guides and men of advanced years, that is always averse to cruelty, that is always compassionate, that is regular in respect of sleep and wakefulness, that takes milk and ghee, that has knowledge of time and place as also authority, that is conversant with reasons, that is reft of pride, that is of practices which are praiseworthy, that is possessed of a liberal mind, that has senses directed towards the soul, that honours men of advanced years as also those who are endued with faith and who have their souls under control, that is devoted to the scriptures, should be known as a user of 'Rasayana.' (Further) he who, endued with these high attributes, uses 'Rasayana', enjoys all the effects enumerated of 'Rasayana.' That person who, without casting off (at least) the graver faults of both body and mind, (uses 'Rasayana'), never reaps the effects of Rasayana.
classical.sanskrit: satyavādinam akrodhaṃ nivṛttaṃ madyamaithunāt / ahiṃsakamanāyāsaṃ praśāntaṃ priyavādinam // Car_6,1.4.30 ... upāsitāraṃ vṛddhānāmāstikānāṃ jitātmanām / dharmaśāstraparaṃ vidyānnaraṃ nityarasāyanam // Car_6,1.4.34 guṇair etaiḥ samuditaiḥ prayuṅkte yo rasāyanam / rasāyanaguṇān sarvān yathoktān sa samaśnute // Car_6,1.4.35 ... yathāsthūlam anirvāhya doṣāñchārīramānasān / rasāyanaguṇair jantur yujyate na kadācana // Car_6,1.4.36

classical.establishes: Sattva sara: mind as the eighth of the eight saras, the predominating essences by which a person's bala is measured. This is a second and quite different classical treatment of sattva from the Sharira 4 typology: here it is graded strength rather than type, and it sits in a list otherwise made of bodily tissues. It is the locus the critic named, and it is the classical source closest to what the modern instruments actually measure, a quantity of sattva rather than a kind of person.
classical.quote: Next, as to examination according to Sara (predominating essence or element): there are eight Saras of human beings. We shall lay down instructions about them for exact knowledge of the measure of one's strength. They are 1. skin, 2. blood, 3. flesh, 4. fat, 5. bones, 6. marrow, 7. vital seed, and 8. mind. ... They who have the mind for the predominating element of their constitution are possessed of happiness, power, health, wealth, honors, and offspring; they are endued with strong memory, as also with great reverence (for deities and seniors); they are very grateful, possessed of wisdom and purity (both external and internal); they have great energy and perseverance, much cleverness and considerable patience; they fight with great prowess in battle; they are never cheerless or melancholy. They are always firm. Their understandings and hearts are deep and grave.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: That Vagbhata states the same twofold locus of disease by the division of body and mind, and names rajas and tamas as the two doshas of the mind. It corroborates Charaka Su. 1.57 and Sha. 4.34 in a second author.
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

classical.establishes: Vagbhata's parallel to Charaka Su. 1.58: the supreme medicines for the doshas of the body are enema, purgation, emesis, oil, ghee and honey, and for the doshas of the mind it is dhī, dhairya and ātmādi-vijñāna. Read with the preceding verse 25, which announces the shodhana/shamana division and the paramaushadha of the bodily doshas, it is the clearest statement in Vagbhata that the two classes of dosha take two classes of remedy.

modern.title: A Psychometric Analysis of the Three Gunas
modern.establishes: Wolf's psychometric analysis of the three gunas, which produced the Vedic Personality Inventory, the most widely used instrument for measuring sattva, rajas and tamas.
modern.quality: The foundational instrument paper. It is a psychometric study of item structure in a convenience sample, establishing internal consistency and a three-factor structure. It does not validate the gunas against any external criterion, and the sample was not Indian, which raises an unaddressed question about whether the constructs travel. Everything downstream that uses the VPI inherits these limits.

modern.title: Development and Standardization of Mysore Triguna Scale
modern.establishes: Development and standardisation of the Mysore Triguna Scale, an alternative triguna instrument developed in an Indian population.
modern.quality: Instrument development and standardisation. The existence of multiple competing triguna scales with different item pools and factor structures, none established as the reference standard, is itself the finding: there is no agreed measurement of the construct, so results across studies are not directly comparable.

modern.title: Composition of yoga-philosophy based mental traits (Gunas) in major psychiatric disorders: A trans-diagnostic approach.
modern.establishes: Cross-sectional comparison of guna profiles (Vedic Personality Inventory) in 113 patients with DSM-5 diagnoses against 113 matched healthy controls. Controls had higher sattva than patients (except in OCD), and distinct guna configurations were reported per diagnosis: high sattva-rajas and low tamas in anxiety and OCD; high sattva-tamas and low rajas in depression; high tamo-rajas and low sattva in psychosis.
modern.quality: Reasonable sample, matched controls, standard diagnostic criteria, validated symptom scales. This is among the better empirical work on triguna. But it is cross-sectional, so it cannot separate guna profile from state effects of active illness; the OCD exception is unexplained; and per-diagnosis subgroups (n=16 to 30) are small for the configuration claims. It shows association with illness state, not that gunas are a trait-level construct or that they add information beyond existing psychometrics.

modern.title: Development of an instrument for screening mental health based on Ayurvedic concept of Triguna.
modern.establishes: Development of MHAS-TG, a 38-item triguna-based mental health screening instrument, with test-retest ICC 0.8, Cronbach's alpha 0.9, and criterion validation against the WHO Subjective Well-being Inventory giving sensitivity 75.4% and specificity 78.2%. Reports strong negative correlation between sattva and tamas scores.
modern.quality: Methodologically the most complete triguna instrument paper: it has test-retest data and an external criterion, which earlier scales lacked. The criterion is another self-report wellbeing inventory rather than a clinical outcome, so what is shown is convergent validity with an existing wellbeing measure, not that the triguna framing adds anything. Sensitivity and specificity near 75-78% against a self-report standard is modest. Single-state sampling (Kerala).

modern.title: Correlation of prakriti diagnosis using AyuSoft prakriti diagnostic tool with clinician rating in patients with psychiatric disorders.
modern.establishes: Prakriti assessment was feasible in 112 stabilised psychiatric patients, with tool-clinician ICC 0.72 (vata), 0.58 (pitta), 0.44 (kapha).
modern.quality: Relevant here because manasika prakriti and sharirika prakriti are assessed together in practice. Establishes feasibility and moderate agreement only; the kapha figure is weak and no mental-constitution component was separately validated.

modern.title: Nootropic efficacy of Satvavajaya Chikitsa and Ayurvedic drug therapy: A comparative clinical exposition.
modern.establishes: Compared sattvavajaya chikitsa (delivered as asana, pranayama, chanting and counselling, plus placebo) against Shankhapushpi tablets in 102 healthy volunteers, with Wechsler Memory Scale outcomes. The sattvavajaya arm improved immediate recall; the drug arm improved delayed recall and recognition.
modern.quality: Weak. Not blinded, no no-treatment control, healthy volunteers rather than patients, memory rather than mental health as the outcome, and the sattvavajaya arm confounds yoga practice with counselling so the active ingredient cannot be identified. Analysed with paired and unpaired t-tests on multiple subscales without correction. This is representative of the sattvavajaya evidence base rather than an outlier.

modern.title: Efficacy of Sattvavajaya Chikitsa in the form of relaxation techniques and Guda Pippalimula Churna in the management of Anidra (insomnia) - An open labelled, randomized comparative clinical trial.
modern.establishes: Open-label randomised comparison in 60 insomnia patients of sattvavajaya chikitsa as relaxation techniques versus Guda Pippalimula Churna; both improved, with sattvavajaya reported better for chinta, bhaya and krodha.
modern.quality: Weak. Open-label, no placebo or waitlist arm, outcomes scored on unvalidated symptom severity scales devised for the study, small sample, and the comparison is between two active arms so regression to the mean and attention effects are uncontrolled. Reported as effective; the design cannot support that conclusion.

modern.title: Ayurvedic concepts related to psychotherapy.
modern.establishes: The reference the modern literature leans on for the identification of sattvavajaya with psychotherapy. Its abstract states that sattvavajaya 'is the mental restraint, or a "mind control" as referred by Caraka', achieved through spiritual knowledge, philosophy, fortitude, remembrance and concentration, groups the traditional mental-health practices as swasthavritta, sadvritta and yoga, and proposes an integration of psychotherapy with Ayurveda which it names 'Psycho Veda'.
modern.quality: Assertion-level, and cited here as such. It is a narrative article in a journal supplement with no stated search strategy, no data, no patients and no comparison; PubMed types it as a journal article, not a review. It is therefore good evidence that the sattvavajaya-as-psychotherapy equation is asserted in the Indian psychiatric literature, and no evidence that the equation holds. It is added for exactly that purpose: the record's contested question 3 previously said the comparison is 'frequently asserted and never tested head to head' while citing nobody asserting it.

modern.title: Role of Sattvavajaya Chikitsa (Trance therapy) in the management of Manasa-Dosha Ajeerna.
modern.establishes: A third sattvavajaya trial, and the one that matters most for what the word means. 27 patients with Ajeerna and a significant stress score, 25 completers, randomised to Shunthi tablet or to placebo plus sattvavajaya, which here was delivered as 'Trance/Clinical Hypnosis'. Ten days. Outcomes were the classical signs and symptoms of Ajeerna and scores for Rajasika and Tamasika manobhavas. The abstract reports the Shunthi arm improving vataja and kaphaja symptoms and the sattvavajaya arm pittaja symptoms, with both arms moving the manobhava scores.
modern.quality: Weak as efficacy evidence, and that is not why it is here. Ten days, 25 analysable patients, no inert-only arm, a digestive complaint rather than a mental disorder as the target, and outcome scales that are classical symptom checklists rather than validated instruments. Its value to this record is that sattvavajaya is operationalised here as clinical hypnosis, where PMID 26170589 operationalised it as asana, pranayama, chanting and counselling and PMID 32398908 as relaxation techniques. Three studies, three different interventions, one word. That is a measurement problem that sits logically before any question of efficacy.

modern.title: A holistic Ayurvedic approach to manage persistent depressive disorder, Vishada-A case report.
modern.establishes: What the sattvavajaya-in-depression literature consists of at the top of the PubMed searches named in gatheringNotes: a single case report. One patient meeting DSM-5 criteria for persistent depressive disorder, treated for six months with sattvavajaya chikitsa plus shamana oral medicines plus viddhakarma, Hamilton Depression Rating Scale falling from 16 to 5 and the improvement reported as sustained through a non-interventional follow-up.
modern.quality: A single uncontrolled case with three interventions given together, so it cannot attribute the change to any of them, and a six-month uncontrolled observation of a chronic fluctuating condition cannot separate treatment from course. PubMed types it as a Case Report. It is included because the critic's overclaimed finding pointed at the anxiety and depression literature, and this record should show what was found when that literature was searched rather than describe it in general terms.
