records.title: Nidana-panchaka (the five-fold diagnostic frame)
records.summary: Nidana-panchaka is the name modern Ayurvedic teaching gives to a group of five things a physician is told to establish about a disease: its cause, its premonitory signs, its manifest signs, its response to a trial of contrary medicine, diet or regimen, and its pathogenic sequence. Charaka's Nidana Sthana 1 lists those five in a single prose line as what a disease is apprehended from, and defines each in the lines that follow; it does not group them under a name or call them five. The grouping as a named pentad appears in commentary, in Chakrapani's hetvadi-pancaka, and the five-fold formulation as a verse is Madhava Nidana's, whose first chapter is titled Pancha-nidana-lakshanam and is built around it. As a working device it structures a clinical history towards a disease name plus a dosha-and-tissue account of how the disease came about. It is not a test with an accuracy figure; the classical texts quoted here give no procedure for resolving disagreement between two physicians who apply it to the same patient; and the record found no study measuring whether two physicians applying it to the same patient reach the same conclusion. Contemporary sources describe it as the standard diagnostic reasoning template and samprapti as the element that individualises treatment; this record reports those as claims made, not as findings, and the one empirical test it found (PMID 39183608) ran against the second of them.
records.evidenceState: Nidana-panchaka rests on classical exegesis. Precisely what is and is not attested, since the gathered record flattened this: Charaka Nidana Sthana 1 lists the five items and defines each, and those lines are quotable in a public-domain English translation, Kaviratna's, which does contain the Nidana Sthana (classical[0] to classical[3]; the contrary finding is declined in stillOpen[0] with the evidence). What is NOT in Charaka is the group as a named or counted unit. The naming is commentarial, in Chakrapani's hetvadi-pancaka, and the five-fold formulation as a verse with a chapter titled for it is Madhava Nidana's. 'Well-attested textual construct', the gathered record's phrase, has been dropped: what is well attested is the five items; the pentad is a construct with a datable history, and the record now gives the three steps of that history with an address for each. The record also no longer claims the frame organises the modern BAMS curriculum, which was asserted with no citation anywhere in the record and is now in notKnown. What does not exist, so far as a bounded search can say, is evidence that applying the frame yields reproducible conclusions. No study was found measuring whether two physicians given the same patient agree on the nidana, the purvarupa, the rupa set, the result of an upashaya trial, or the samprapti. The nearest empirical evidence is negative: a 2024 case-vignette survey of 141 practitioners found substantial disagreement on diagnosis and on the samprapti of identical cases, and a 2019 nested reliability study found chance-corrected agreement between 0 and 0.4 on constitutional components that feed the frame, even though the same experts reached 95 per cent raw agreement on a consensus final label; a 2021 prakriti study adds ICCs of 0.72, 0.58 and 0.44. No diagnostic accuracy study was found, no prospective cohort in which purvarupa predicted later disease, and no controlled test of upashaya against any reference standard; the one paper found on purvarupa's predictive use calls for such work rather than reporting it. On PubMed on 2026-10-06 the phrase search "nidana panchaka" returned three records: the two Bulletin of the Indian Institute of History of Medicine philological notes that are modern[4] and modern[5], and PMID 41106206, a 2025 single-case report of Ayurvedic management of a vocal cord carcinoma, which is not cited in this record because an n-of-1 case report establishes nothing about the frame. 'upashaya' returned one record and 'anupashaya' none. Those counts are counts of those queries on that date, not a statement about the world's literature; the full query log is in gatheringNotes.

contested.question: Is the five-limbed set canonical, or a later editorial convention?
positions: The five items are stated as a group in Charaka Nidana Sthana 1/6 itself, in one prose line, and each is defined in 1/7 to 1/12, so the material of the frame is samhita-period (classical[0] to classical[3]).

The group as a NAMED unit is not in Charaka. The earliest naming this record can address is Chakrapani's Ayurvedadipika on Vimana 1/2, 'jnata-hetvadi-pancakasya', eleventh century (classical[5]); the five-fold formulation as a verse, with a chapter titled Pancha-nidana-lakshanam, is Madhava Nidana 1/4, 'roganam pancadha smrtam' (classical[8]), and that is the text modern teaching inherits it from. On this reading the items are early and the pentad is a later organising convention.

Not settled by this search, and the two positions above are compatible: nothing found dates the practice of treating the five together, as opposed to the act of naming them so. The record takes no view on which reading is correct and the summary has been written to assert only what the three addresses support.

contested.question: Is rupa the third limb, or is it linga?
positions: Charaka's own wording at Ni. 1/9 is 'linga', with rupa listed as one of seven words of the same import (classical[0]).

Madhava Nidana and modern teaching use 'rupa', which is why the mnemonic reads nidana-purvarupa-rupa-upashaya-samprapti; the Madhava Nidana verse 4 line as retrieved reads purvarupani / rupani (classical[8]). The substitution is terminological rather than doctrinal, but it means quotations attributed to 'the fivefold rupa' may not match the Charaka text.

contested.question: Does samprapti individualise treatment in actual practice?
positions: Standard Ayurvedic pedagogy holds that samprapti-vighatana, breaking the pathogenic sequence, is what makes each prescription patient-specific. The record carries this as a position held, and has not found a citable primary statement of it in the classical sources quoted here; Charaka's Ni. 1/12 gives samprapti analytic headings and says nothing about individualising a prescription.

The 2024 case-scenario survey (modern[0]) found that stated theoretical constructs including samprapti did not uniformly determine prescriptions, and that practitioners disagreed with each other about the samprapti of the same case; the authors raise the possibility that the framework is weak rather than merely variably applied.

contested.question: Is upashaya a diagnostic instrument or an early therapeutic trial?
positions: Chakrapani, and Kaviratna following him, treat it as a means of ascertaining the disease that should not be mistaken for treatment. In Kaviratna this is explicitly a translator's footnote, marked '-T.', not a rendering of the verse (classical[1], translatorVoice).

Operationally it is indistinguishable from an n-of-1 therapeutic trial. Charaka's definition at Ni. 1/10 specifies the objects (medicine, diet, regimen) and the two modes (contrary, or contrary in effect) but no duration, no dose, and no rule for reading a partial response, which makes the distinction hard to sustain.

contested.question: Is samprapti subdivided into five headings or six?
positions: Five. The Sanskrit of Ni. 1/12 compounds strength and time into one member, 'sankhya-pradhanya-vidhi-vikalpa-balakala-visesair bhidyate', the definitional run that follows defines five, the fifth being 'balakalavisesah', and Charaka's Vimana 1/3 uses the same compound, '...vikalpabalakalavisesan' (classical[3], and GRETIL's Car_3,1.3 quoted at classical[5]'s source).
Six. Kaviratna's English reads 'number (or enumeration), predominance, kind (or order), solution of doubt, strength (or intensity), and Time', six items, and much modern writing follows that count.

contested.question: What is the relation between nidana-panchaka and Sushruta's shatkriyakala?
positions: They touch at two points that can be shown from text: Sushruta's fourth treatment-occasion is the appearance of purvarupa (Su.Su. 21/33) and his fifth is full manifestation (21/34), which is Charaka's rupa. To that extent the frames describe the same disease in the same order.

They are not reducible to each other. Sushruta's first three stages, sanchaya, prakopa and prasara, and his sixth, bheda, have no counterpart among the five limbs; the five limbs' nidana and upashaya have no counterpart among the six occasions; and the two lists do different work, one enumerating what to establish about a disease and the other when to intervene in it.

Whether either is a staging of the other, or whether samprapti simply narrates the six occasions, was not settled here. The common teaching claim that samprapti and shatkriyakala are the same content differently cut is a claim this record has not found a classical statement of, and has not tested.

notKnown: No published study was found reporting inter-rater agreement on any individual limb of nidana-panchaka taken separately.

Whether purvarupa lists have any predictive value: no prospective cohort was found in which listed prodromes were recorded and later disease incidence measured. The nearest item found, modern[7], proposes that the prameha purvarupa be explored as a basis for identifying pre-diabetes and calls the work urgent, which is a statement that it has not been done.

Whether upashaya-based reasoning improves outcomes compared with diagnosis without it; no trial was found that randomised on this. The term is also almost absent from the indexed literature: on 2026-10-06 a PubMed search for 'upashaya' returned one record, the Madhava Nidana philological note at modern[5], and 'anupashaya' returned none.

How disagreement between limbs is to be resolved when, for example, the rupa point to one disease and the upashaya response to another; the classical passages quoted here give no decision rule and no modern source supplying one was found.
What counts as a complete samprapti statement; no agreed minimum data set was found, so two samprapti accounts of the same patient cannot be systematically compared.
Whether the frame performs differently across conditions; the reliability data found come from knee osteoarthritis, from psychiatric inpatients and from healthy volunteers.
Whether any of the five limbs maps onto a measurable biological quantity; no biomarker proposed and validated for any of them was found.

ADDED on revision. The commentators' six-fold and eighteen-fold analyses of upashaya, which the critic asked for, are not in this record. Charaka's own Ni. 1/10 supports three objects by two modes, and that is now in the record as classical[1]. The arithmetic that yields six (hetu-viparita, vyadhi-viparita, hetu-vyadhi-viparita and the three corresponding viparitarthakari forms) and then eighteen (those six across medicine, diet and regimen) is attributed in modern teaching to the Madhukosha. It is excluded because it could not be sourced to a quotable text: no public-domain English Madhukosha exists, and the 1920 Sanskrit scan used at classical[8] has a Devanagari OCR text layer too damaged to quote a commentary passage from with confidence. The gap is stated rather than filled with a paraphrase.

ADDED on revision. Whether the frame organises the modern BAMS curriculum. The gathered record asserted this in both summary and evidenceState and cited nothing for it anywhere. No CCIM or NCISM syllabus document was retrieved and the claim has been removed rather than left standing on nothing. Likewise, that contemporary teaching presents the frame as the standard diagnostic reasoning template is reported in summary as a claim made about teaching, and no syllabus, textbook or curriculum document is cited for it in this record.

ADDED on revision. Whether Madhava Nidana applies the five-fold frame disease by disease through the rest of the work. The gathered record asserted this. Only chapter 1, its title and its verse 4, has been verified here (classical[8]); the rest of the 1920 scan was not read for this purpose and no translation of it is lawfully quotable.

ADDED on revision. Whether the compound nidana-panchaka itself occurs in any samhita. It was not found in the Charaka Nidana Sthana 1 and Vimana 1 and 4 passages or the Sushruta Sutrasthana 21 and 35 passages read here, and a commentarial pancaka and a Madhava chapter title were found instead. The search was bounded to those passages and to the two public-domain English translations plus GRETIL's partial Sanskrit Charaka; it cannot support a claim that the compound occurs nowhere.

ADDED on revision. Whether the three means of knowing at Vi. 4/3, aptopadesha, pratyaksha and anumana, stand in any stated relation to the five limbs. Both lists are in Charaka (classical[0], classical[6]). No passage was found in which the five are said to be reached by means of the three, so the common framing that the three are the epistemology the five sit inside is not asserted by this record.

ADDED on revision. Whether the literature is thin or the search was thin, for the areas the queries did not reach. The queries run are logged in gatheringNotes; no hand-searching of Ayurvedic journals outside PubMed, no AYUSH Research Portal or DHARA search, and no Indian-language literature search was done, and three of those are known to index Ayurvedic clinical work that PubMed does not.

components.gloss: The cause or causes. Charaka gives eight words as bearing the same sense (hetu, nimitta, ayatana, kartri, karana, pratyaya, samutthana, nidana) and three classes of cause: union with objects of the senses that are not assimilable, faults of judgement, and the developments in course of time of past acts. Charaka's own definition of the limb is a back-reference, 'Nidana (Hetu) is the cause, as said at the outset'.

Premonitory indications, appearing before the disease is manifest. Charaka's definition is one clause: those indications which manifest themselves before the appearance of the disease. The worked example that follows in the same chapter is the prodrome list for fever. Sushruta uses the same term and makes the appearance of purvarupa the fourth of his six treatment-occasions (classical[7], Su.Su. 21/33), which is the one point at which the two frames can be shown to touch from text rather than by assertion.

The manifest signs. Charaka's word for the limb is linga, defined as those symptoms which manifest themselves on the appearance of the disease, with linga, akriti, lakshana, chihna, samsthana, vyanjana and rupa given as words of the same import. Modern teaching and Madhava Nidana put rupa in the third slot, which is why the mnemonic reads nidana-purvarupa-rupa-upashaya-samprapti; see contested[1].

Diagnosis by therapeutic trial. Charaka's definition has an internal structure that the record previously omitted: the thing prescribed may be medicine, diet or regimen (aushadha, anna, vihara), and it qualifies as upashaya either by being contrary (viparita) to the cause or to the disease, or by producing an effect contrary to them without itself being contrary (viparitarthakari); relief must follow. That is three objects by two modes in the text itself. Its opposite, anupashaya, is aggravation on trial. Kaviratna's translator's note says the act is diagnostic and should not be mistaken for treatment; that is the translator speaking, and the record keeps it as such, not as doctrine. The commentators' arithmetic that turns this into a six-fold or eighteen-fold scheme could not be verified from a quotable text; see notKnown.

Pathogenesis: the sequence by which the causes disturb dosha and tissue to produce this disease. Charaka gives jati and agati as words of the same import, and subdivides it. How many subdivisions is itself contested and the record previously got it wrong: the Sanskrit of Ni. 1/12 reads sankhya-pradhanya-vidhi-vikalpa-BALAKALA-visesha, compounding strength and time into one member, and the definitional run that follows defines five, not six. Kaviratna's English lists 'strength (or intensity), and Time' separately, which is where the widely repeated 'six considerations' comes from. The five are: sankhya, enumeration (eight fevers, five tumours, seven leprosies); pradhanya, which dosha is stronger or strongest; vidhi, class (two as natural or accidental, three by dosha, four by curable, incurable, mild, violent); vikalpa, the measure in which combined doshas have been excited; and balakala, strength and time together, read off season, day, night and the hours of eating. See contested[4].

classical.verse: Ni. 1/5-1/9 in the Trikamji numbering; the five-fold line itself is Ni. 1/6. Kaviratna prints this whole run as his single aphorism 3.
classical.establishes: That Charaka's Nidana Sthana 1 names the five items as what a disease is apprehended from, and defines three of them in the same run. It does NOT establish that Charaka names them as a set or calls them five: there is no collective noun and no 'pancadha' in this passage. For the named pentad see classical[5] and classical[8].
classical.quote: The ascertainment of disease is to be had from 'Nidana', 'Purvarupa', 'Linga', 'Upaçaya', and 'Samprapti.' Amongst these, 'Nidana' (Hetu) is the cause, as said at the outset. 'Purvarupa' implies those indications which manifest themselves before the appearance of the disease. (These are the symptoms of the period of incubation). By 'Linga' is meant those symptoms which manifest themselves on the appearance of the disease.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna, Charaka-Samhita translated into English, Calcutta: Dass, issued in parts; public domain

classical.verse: Ni. 1/10 in the Trikamji numbering; Kaviratna's aphorism 4
classical.establishes: That upashaya is defined as the prescribing of medicine, diet or regimen that is either contrary to cause or disease, or contrary in effect without being contrary in itself, with relief following. Three objects by two modes, in the text. It establishes the structure of the limb; it does not establish that the act is diagnostic rather than therapeutic, which is a reading, not a statement of the verse; see contested[3].
classical.quote: In this connection, 'upaçaya', again, is the prescribing, followed by happiness (or recovery) as the result, of medicines, diet, and practices, that are contrary to cause and disease, or contrary, as regards their effects, to the same.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna, Charaka-Samhita translated into English, Calcutta: Dass, issued in parts; public domain

classical.verse: Ni. 1/11-1/12 in the Trikamji numbering; Kaviratna's aphorisms 5-6
classical.establishes: That samprapti has jati and agati as words of the same import, and that Charaka gives it a list of analytic headings. NOTHING MORE. The gathered record's establishes field added 'which is the structural basis of the modern claim that samprapti individualises treatment'; that clause has been cut. The quote says nothing about individualisation, and the record's own contested[2] and modern[0] run against the claim, so the citation was being made to carry a conclusion it does not reach.
classical.quote: 'Samprapti', 'jati', and 'agati' of disease, are words of the same import. 'Samprapti' is distinguished by these considerations, viz., number (or enumeration), predominance, kind (or order), solution of doubt, strength (or intensity), and Time.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna, Charaka-Samhita translated into English, Calcutta: Dass, issued in parts; public domain

classical.verse: Ni. 1/12 in the Trikamji numbering, whose sub-parts carakasamhitaonline numbers 12.1 to 12.5; Kaviratna's aphorisms 7-10
classical.establishes: Each of samprapti's subdivisions defined in Charaka's own words. This is the material the critic's 'missing' finding asked for, and retrieving it also showed the record's count of six to be wrong.
classical.quote: By Number or (or enumeration) is meant such as these : Eight kinds of Fevers, Five kinds of tumours, Seven kinds of leprosy, and so on. Predominance, again, applies to faults, and consists in judging which is the stronger or the strongest. The comparative relates to two, the superlative to three. Kind (or Order) is as follows : — Diseases are of two kinds, as natural and accidental. They are of three kinds, according to the particular fault that has been excited among the three that exist (viz., wind, bile, and phlegm). They are of four kinds, considering curability, incurability, mildness, and violence. Solution of doubt (Vikalpa), in this connection, means the ascertainment of the measure in which the faults, existing in a state of union, have been excited. The distinctions of Strength and Time (in respect of disease) are dependant on the season (in which the disease has happened), day, night, the hours of eating, &c.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna, Charaka-Samhita translated into English, Calcutta: Dass, issued in parts; public domain

classical.verse: aphorism 2 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.establishes: Charaka also gives a longer list (adding pradhanya, vidhi, vikalpa, bala, kala) in which the five limbs are embedded, showing the 'five' is one enumeration among several rather than a fixed canonical set.
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

classical.text: Ayurvedadipika of Chakrapanidatta, the commentary printed with the Charaka Samhita
classical.verse: Commentary on Vi. 1/2, first gloss (GRETIL's Car_3,1.2, Ayurvedadipika segment 1)
classical.establishes: That the word pañcaka is applied to these five by a commentator: the Āyurvedadīpikā of Chakrapanidatta, glossing Charaka Vi. 1/2, opens 'nidāne jñātahetvādipañcakasya', naming the group as a pentad of hetu-and-the-rest already known from the nidāna chapter. That is the whole of what this one clause carries, and it is why the record builds nothing further on it. It still corrects the record's earlier claim that the five are Charaka's own set AS A SET, since the word pañcaka here is the commentator's and not the samhita's, and it remains commentary rather than samhita. WITHDRAWN IN THIS REVISION: the further claim that the gloss 'partly corrects the critic' by making the naming older than Madhava's verse. A clause in an eleventh-century commentary cannot establish priority of naming at all, and the record asserted the relation backwards while dating Chakrapani to the eleventh century itself. Nothing is now claimed from this passage about when the five were first named, in either direction; the critic's dating is neither corrected nor endorsed here, because this citation is not evidence about it.
classical.sanskrit: nidāne jñātahetvādipañcakasya cikitsopayogitayā doṣabheṣajādiviśeṣajñānam apekṣitaṃ bhavati ato vakṣyamāṇadoṣabheṣajādiviśeṣajñāpakaṃ vimānasthānaṃ brūte
classical.partWithheld: no English translation of this passage has been cleared for reproduction
classical.translator: none; no public-domain English of the Ayurvedadipika was found
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: Vi. 4/3 in the Trikamji numbering; Kaviratna's aphorism 2
classical.establishes: That Charaka gives a three-fold epistemology of how a disease is known at all, by authoritative instruction, by direct observation and by inference, in a separate chapter from the five limbs. This is the material the critic's 'missing' finding called 'the epistemology the five terms sit inside'. What it establishes is that both lists exist in Charaka. It does not establish the nesting relation itself: no passage quoted here says the five limbs are to be reached by means of the three, and that reading is not asserted by this record. See notKnown.
classical.quote: After this we shall expound the Lesson on the three especial means of ascertainment of disease. Thus said the illustrious son of Atri. There are three especial means of ascertaining disease. They are : — 1. The Instructions of the inspired or wise, 2. Observation, and 3. Inference.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna, Charaka-Samhita translated into English, Calcutta: Dass, issued in parts; public domain

classical.verse: Su.Su. 21/18, 21/27, 21/32, 21/33, 21/34, 21/35 mark the six stages in order; the summary couplet is 21/36
classical.establishes: That Sushruta stages the disease process in six marked steps and names all six in one summary couplet. This is the material the critic's 'missing' finding asked for. Scope limits, deliberately: this record cites the frame and does not expound it, because shat-kriyakala has its own record. The one relation this record asserts is the textual overlap at Su.Su. 21/33, where the fourth occasion is the appearance of purvarupa, and at 21/34, where the fifth is full manifestation, Charaka's rupa. Beyond those two points, whether the frames are rival, complementary or incommensurable is in contested.
classical.sanskrit: sañcayaṃ ca prakopaṃ ca prasaraṃ sthānasaṃśrayam | vyaktiṃ bhedaṃ ca yo vetti doṣāṇāṃ sa bhavedbhiṣak ||36||
classical.translation: The physician, who fully knows about the accumulation (Sanchaya), disturbance or aggravation (Prakopa), expansion (Prasaram), and differentiating traits of the deranged humours (Bheda), and is well conversant with the specific localities in which they are respectively confined in the course of their expansion (Sthana-samshrayam), and with the symptoms which they respectively exhibit in connection with the incidental disease (Vyakti), is alone worthy of that epithet.

classical.establishes: Sushruta handles the same material (cause, prodrome, primary vs secondary disease) without packaging it as a five-limbed set, which is evidence that the 'panchaka' formulation is a later organising convention.
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

classical.text: Madhava Nidana (Rugvinishchaya) of Madhavakara, with the Madhukosha of Vijayarakshita and Shrikanthadatta and the Atankadarpana of Vachaspati
classical.verse: 4, in the 1920 Sanskrit edition
classical.establishes: That the first chapter of Madhava Nidana is titled for the pentad and that its opening verse 4 states the knowledge of diseases to be five-fold, 'roganam pancadha smrtam'. Together with classical[0], which shows Charaka listing the same five without counting them, and classical[5], which shows a commentator naming them a pancaka, this is what the transmission claim in summary and contested[0] now rests on. It does NOT establish that Madhava Nidana applies the frame disease by disease through the rest of the work; that was asserted in the gathered record and only the chapter 1 verse has been verified here. See notKnown.
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

modern.title: Myth and reality of "theory-driven individualised practice" in Ayurveda: Mapping physicians' approaches using case-based scenarios.
modern.establishes: Emailed case-vignette survey of 141 registered Ayurveda practitioners (152 responses) across five clinical scenarios, asking for diagnosis, treatment plan and the Ayurvedic principles driving the choice. Found a significant lack of consensus on clinical diagnoses, on interventions and on the samprapti (pathophysiology) of the same case, with conflicting opinions common; the authors conclude that theoretical constructs including samprapti do not uniformly determine prescriptions or individualisation.
modern.quality: Empirical and directly on point, and among the very few studies that test whether the nidana-panchaka framework actually drives practice. Limitations are real: convenience sampling, self-selected email respondents, paper vignettes rather than live patients, no measure of chance-corrected agreement. It is a cross-sectional survey, not a diagnostic accuracy or reliability study, and it is published in a journal whose framing is critical of Ayurvedic practice.

modern.title: Reliability of Ayurvedic Diagnosis for Knee Osteoarthritis Patients: A Nested Diagnostic Study Within a Randomized Controlled Trial.
modern.establishes: Nested inter-rater reliability study, 30 knee osteoarthritis patients diagnosed sequentially by 4 Ayurvedic experts using a semi-structured history form. High raw percentage agreement on the consensus final diagnosis (95%) but Fleiss'/Cohen's kappa between 0 and 0.4 for central diagnostic components including prakriti and agni; agreement on disease-related entities was better than on constitutional entities.
modern.quality: Genuine empirical reliability study with appropriate chance-corrected statistics, which is rare in this literature. Small (30 patients, 4 raters), single condition, single centre, and the experts had gone through a consensus procedure beforehand, which should have inflated rather than deflated agreement.

modern.title: Understanding the etiopathogenesis and diagnosis of malignancy in the framework of Ayurveda: A review based on experience of working in an institute of oncology.
modern.establishes: Proposes a samprapti (pathogenic sequence) for malignancy on the basis of clinical observation of 400 cancer patients at an oncology institute, and concludes that modern cancer diagnosis cannot be equated with any single Ayurvedic disease entity.
modern.quality: Presented as a review based on clinical experience. No control group, no blinding, no predefined outcome, no inter-observer check; the samprapti proposed is an expert construction, not a tested hypothesis. It is honest about the absence of expert agreement in this area, which is its main value.

modern.title: Ayurvedic concept of Shatkriyakala: a traditional knowledge of cancer pathogenesis and therapy.
modern.establishes: Narrative review of shatkriyakala, Sushruta's six stages of disease progress, located by the authors in 'Varnaprashnadhyaya', applied as a staging framework for carcinogenesis. The abstract states that the review 'describes the six stages of Shatkriyakala in detail, with an emphasis on research areas to validate the concept', which is an author's statement that the concept is not yet validated.
modern.quality: A review, not evidence. No data, no patients, no reliability or accuracy measurement. Cited here for one narrow purpose: it is the only PubMed-indexed paper found that takes shatkriyakala as its subject, and it is the reason the newly added classical[7] is accompanied by a modern reference rather than standing alone. Its correlations between Sanskrit categories and cancer biology are proposals; this record does not adopt any of them. Note that the paper's chapter attribution matches the chapter name verified independently at classical[7], Vrana-prashna.

modern.title: Definition of Nidana Panchaka (first chapter of Madhavanidana).
modern.journal: Bull Indian Inst Hist Med Hyderabad
modern.establishes: Philological note on the nidana-panchaka of Madhava Nidana chapter 1. Its own title spells the term 'Nidana Panchaka (first chapter of Madhavanidana)', which is the earliest indexed attestation this record has of the modern compound, and of its attachment to Madhava rather than to Charaka. The abstract states that Madhavakara assembled etiopathogenesis, clinical pathology and diagnosis for a large number of diseases 'together at one place from classical sources'.
modern.quality: Historical and textual scholarship, not clinical evidence. Useful only for the textual lineage. CORRECTION to the gathered record, which said of this entry 'no abstract indexed': an abstract is indexed and was retrieved on 2026-10-06. The accessibility complaint stands, the bulletin is not widely held, and no full text was obtained, so nothing beyond the abstract is claimed from it.

modern.title: Definition of Nidana Pancaka (first chapter of Madhavanidana).
modern.journal: Bull Indian Inst Hist Med Hyderabad
modern.establishes: The continuation of modern[4], named as such in its own abstract, which states that it 'deals with Nadana, Purvarupa, Rupa, Upashaya and Samprapti as described in the first Chapter of Madhavanidana' and gives the earlier part's citation as Bulletin of the Indian Institute of the History of Medicine, Volume XXVII, No. 2, July 1997, pp. 163-171. It is independent confirmation that chapter 1 of Madhava Nidana defines the five, which is the claim this record can no longer get from an English translation.
modern.quality: Same character and same limits as modern[4]. Promoted from a bare mention inside modern[4]'s establishes field in the gathered record to an entry of its own, because it is doing independent work. 'Nadana' in the quoted abstract is the indexed abstract's own spelling and is reproduced, not corrected.

modern.title: Correlation of prakriti diagnosis using AyuSoft prakriti diagnostic tool with clinician rating in patients with psychiatric disorders.
modern.establishes: Inter-rater reliability of prakriti assessment in 112 psychiatric inpatients, comparing the AyuSoft software tool against two Ayurveda physicians examining the same patients. Reported as ICC 0.72 for vata, 0.58 for pitta and 0.44 for kapha, described by the authors as moderately strong, good and comparatively weak respectively. The authors also state that they 'could not find any literature regarding reliability of a prakriti diagnostic tool in patients with psychiatric conditions'.
modern.quality: A real reliability study with chance-corrected statistics, which is rare here. But it measures prakriti, which is NOT one of the five limbs; it is a constitutional entity that feeds the reasoning. It is cited for that reason only, to show that where agreement on the inputs has been measured it has come out moderate at best, and the pattern matches modern[1]. Single centre, one tool versus two raters rather than rater-versus-rater throughout, and a psychiatric sample whose generalisability to the frame at large is unknown. It is not evidence about nidana-panchaka and is not counted as such.

modern.title: Predicting and preventing diabetes: Translational potential of Ayurveda information on pre-diabetes.
modern.establishes: The only paper found that addresses the predictive use of purvarupa. It PROPOSES that 'Ayurveda account of prameha purvarupa (subclinical features of diabetes) may be proposed as the foundation upon which clinic-based pre-diabetes identification and subsequent prevention may be explored', and closes that the approach 'has a huge translational potential warrants an urgent exploration'. Its own framing is therefore that the predictive value of a purvarupa list has not been established.
modern.quality: A proposal paper, not a study: no cohort, no follow-up, no incidence data, no measure of sensitivity or specificity for any prodrome. Its value to this record is precisely that it is a proposal. It converts notKnown's claim about purvarupa from the record's own assertion of absence into something an indexed author also treats as open, which is a stronger and more checkable footing than an unsupported negative. It does not close the gap and the notKnown item stands.
