records.title: Ojas and the Ayurvedic Account of Resistance to Disease
records.summary: Ojas is described in the classical texts as the refined essence distilled from all seven bodily tissues, seated principally in the heart, pervading the body, and responsible for strength (bala), steadiness of the sense organs, complexion, voice and the capacity to withstand disease (vyadhikshamatva). Its depletion is said to produce fearfulness, weakness, emaciation, loss of lustre and, at the extreme, death. Three modes of derangement are distinguished: displacement from its seat (visramsa), corruption by vitiated humours (vyapat) and wasting (kshaya), and Sushruta supplies a sign list and a prognosis for each. The concept is the usual point of contact between Ayurveda and modern immunology, but the correspondence is an interpretive one: ojas as described covers reproduction, morphogenesis, mood and vitality as well as resistance to illness, and the classical sources do not agree among themselves on what ojas actually is. In Kaviratna's wording Charaka calls it, in one aphorism of Sutrasthana 17, a quantity of pure blood "which is slightly yellowish" residing in the heart, and forty aphorisms later identifies it with normal phlegm, while Sushruta calls it the quintessence of all the dhatus. The reddish-yellow description that circulates widely is Vagbhata's and is recorded here under Vagbhata, not under Charaka. This record makes no claim about how much modern evidence exists for or against the identification with immunity; it states what the searches named in gatheringNotes returned.
records.evidenceState:
This is the clearest case in the cluster of a concept resting on classical exegesis with a modern literature that proposes rather than demonstrates. Within what this record retrieved there is no assay for ojas, no reference range, no validated clinical instrument, and no study in which anything called ojas was measured before and after an intervention. A PubMed query for ojas in title or abstract restricted to clinical trial or randomised controlled trial publication types returned nothing on 2026-10-06, which is the search that licenses that sentence.

On biochemical identification the record previously said that two proposals exist. That was a census a bounded search cannot support, and it was also wrong. Three are now retrieved: steroids and steroid classes in 1995 (PMID 7705867), kapha read as the degree of gene expression and "correlated with the ojas of the body or total body defence mechanism" in 2000 (PMID 11272402), and cholesterol with HDL-C as surrogate for healthy apara ojas in 2025 (PMID 41289791). All three are hypothesis or review papers whose authors say so, and none has been followed by a validation study in what was retrieved here. The searches run were: ojas in title; ojas in title or abstract with biomarker, biochemical or immunity; ojas with ayurveda; ojas with immunoglobulin, glycoprotein, albumin or albumen; ojas with thermodynamic, entropy or agni; and author searches on Hankey and on Patwardhan. The critic expected a Hankey thermodynamic account of agni and ojas and Patwardhan immunity-concept papers to turn up; the Hankey author query with ojas or agni in title or abstract returned nothing, and the Patwardhan immunity results retrieved are botanical immunomodulation studies rather than identifications of ojas. An immunoglobulin or glycoprotein reading was searched for by name and not retrieved. That is a statement about these searches and not about the world; a different search, and in particular one outside PubMed and into Ayurvedic journals that PubMed does not index, could find more.

Bhishagratna's "albumen" is deliberately not counted among those proposals. It is a translator's gloss carried silently through his whole rendering of Sushruta Sutrasthana 15, and his own footnote says the term is used "primarily" for protoplasmic matter in cells and "secondarily" for albumen. Counting it as a biochemical identification would be absorbing the translator's voice as doctrine, which this project has had to correct three times already. It is recorded as a position in contested, attributed to the translator.

Beyond the proposals, the indexed literature retrieved here consists largely of narrative reviews that restate the classical doctrine in immunological vocabulary and stop. The quantitatively strongest item located, the Chyawanprash prophylaxis meta-analysis (PMID 39544586), is null on every efficacy endpoint with severe heterogeneity, and tests a formulation rather than the construct. The post-2020 Ayurvedic COVID literature was searched on this pass as the critic asked, and it changes the shape of the gap rather than closing it. Immune parameters were measured: a randomised placebo-controlled pilot trial quantified IL-6, TNF-alpha and hs-CRP (PMID 33596494), and a multicentric randomised AYUSH-64 trial reported faster clinical recovery (PMID 36928877) while a second AYUSH-64 randomised trial reported no difference in RT-PCR conversion (PMID 34908795). In none of them was ojas the exposure, an outcome, or measured at all. So the honest statement is not that nobody has measured immunity under an ojas-framed intervention, it is that nobody has measured ojas alongside the immunity, which leaves the identification exactly where it was. One retrieved paper does operationalise a mode of ojas derangement: a prospective DMD cohort scored ojovisramsa as a staging variable and found it differed significantly between ambulation stages (PMID 42161239), with no reliability data.

Compounding all of this, the classical sources do not agree on what ojas is. Charaka's Sutrasthana 17 calls it a slightly yellowish pure blood in the heart at the aphorism Kaviratna prints as 74 and identifies it with normal phlegm at 114, while Sushruta calls it the quintessence of all seven dhatus and Bhishagratna's own footnote records authorities who deny that ojas and vitality are identical at all. Kaviratna's footnote to the anjali list in Sharirasthana 7 adds a fourth layer: a variant reading that makes ojas a kind of phlegm, which Gangadhara's commentary adopted and which Kaviratna rejects by declaring, in his own voice, that ojas is "the blood of blood". A construct whose primary sources define it several incompatible ways cannot be operationalised until that is resolved, and no modern paper retrieved here resolves it.

One thing the record previously got wrong in the other direction is worth stating plainly. It reported that the half-anjali quantity of ojas could not be found in either public-domain translation. It is there, in Charaka Sharirasthana 7, and it is now quoted. What is still unlocated is the para/apara vocabulary and the eight-drop figure. So the quantities are not all commentarial; one of them is scriptural and the division they are usually hung on may not be.

The correct overall statement is that ojas is a rich and internally detailed classical account of vitality and resistance, that its identification with immunity is an interpretive overlay rather than a finding, and that no operational definition of it has been validated in anything this record retrieved.

contested.question: What is ojas, materially?
positions: Sushruta Sutrasthana 15: the quintessence of all seven dhatus from rasa to shukra, identical with vital power.
Charaka Sutrasthana 17, at the aphorism Kaviratna prints as 74: a quantity of pure, slightly yellowish blood residing in the heart.

Charaka Sutrasthana 17, at the aphorism Kaviratna prints as 114: normal phlegm (kapha) itself. Three aphorisms earlier the same chapter says "The phlegm that is normal is called strength of the body", which is how this identification reaches bala.
A fourth position recorded in Bhishagratna's note to Sutrasthana 14: certain authorities hold ojas to be the eighth and culminating dhatu, produced from the thin fraction of shukra.

A fifth, recorded in Bhishagratna's footnote to Sutrasthana 15: 'Several authorities hold a contrary view stating that Ojas (albumen) forms only one of the essentials of vitality and that the two are by no means identical.'

A sixth, and it is the translator rather than the text: Bhishagratna renders ojas throughout as "albumen", and his footnote to Sutrasthana 15 says the term means "primarily ... protoplasmic matter as found in cells (Vindus)" and "secondarily ... albumen". This is a nineteenth-century biochemical reading embedded in the translation itself. It is listed here as a position held by the translator, and it is excluded from any count of proposals in the indexed modern literature for that reason.

A seventh, textual rather than doctrinal: Kaviratna's footnote to the anjali list in Sharirasthana 7 reports a variant reading of the ojas line which Gangadhara read as "the particular kind of phlegm known as ojas", so the kapha identification has manuscript support outside Sutrasthana 17. Kaviratna rejects it and asserts in his own voice that ojas is "the blood of blood, the most vital dhatu in the body", which is the translator settling a question the text leaves open.

contested.question: Is there a para/apara division, and what are the quantities?
positions: The standard modern teaching distinguishes para ojas (a very small fixed quantity in the heart, commonly given as eight drops) from apara ojas (a larger circulating quantity, commonly given as half an anjali), and the 2025 biomarker paper builds directly on this division.

On the quantities the record's earlier negative result was half wrong and is corrected here. The half-anjali measure IS in the retrieved public-domain Kaviratna, in Charaka Sharirasthana 7, where the anjali list gives marrow one anjali, brain half an anjali, and semen and ojas "the same (as above)". So that figure is scriptural. Charaka introduces the list as known by inference rather than direct perception, and Kaviratna's footnote to the ojas line records a variant reading at exactly that point, so it is a disputed line even within the edition that carries it.

The eight-drop figure was searched for again on 2026-10-06 in both full texts and not located. Neither was the para or apara vocabulary as applied to ojas: the only Para and Apara in Kaviratna are the Nyaya categories Paratwa and Aparatwa in Sutrasthana 25, which are about priority and inferiority of place, season and age, not about two kinds of ojas.

So the honest position is that one of the two quantities is scriptural, the other is not located, and the two-kinds division that organises them is not attested in either translation searched. Whether the division is commentarial, or later, or simply a modern teaching convenience, this record does not establish.

contested.question: What is the modern correlate of ojas, if any?
positions: Steroids and steroid classes (Walton and Pugh 1995, PMID 7705867).
Kapha read as the degree of gene expression as protein synthesis, "correlated with the ojas of the body or total body defence mechanism" (Mishra and colleagues 2000, PMID 11272402).
Cholesterol and its products, with HDL-C as surrogate for healthy apara ojas (Sumantran and Nair 2025, PMID 41289791).

General immune competence, immunoglobulins or innate immunity, the commonest framing in clinical and popular Ayurvedic writing. A search for an immunoglobulin or glycoprotein identification by name retrieved none, so the framing is widespread in practice and not argued for in what was retrieved from the indexed literature.
That there is no single correlate, because ojas as described spans reproduction, foetal morphogenesis, mood, strength and resistance, and no one molecule does all of that.

contested.question: Is ojas equivalent to immunity at all?
positions: The equivalence is assumed in most clinical writing and in public health messaging, and vyadhikshamatva is routinely translated as 'immunity'. PMID 26195903 is a clean specimen: its authors gloss ojas as "immune strength" in the conclusion of a trial that measured blood sugar.

Against this: the classical functions of ojas include conception, foetal development, complexion, voice, sensory and intellectual function and courage, most of which have no immunological content, while the immune system's central features (specificity, memory, self and non-self discrimination) have no classical counterpart under ojas.

A separate point, raised by the Charaka Sutrasthana 28 passage added in this revision: the clearest classical statement about differential resistance to disease does not mention ojas at all. It makes resistance a function of the adequacy of flesh, blood and bone, of strength, and of the measure of food. If that is where the corpus locates vyadhikshamatva, then ojas and vyadhikshamatva are related but not identical even inside the classical frame, and the modern habit of treating the two terms as one may be importing a unity the texts do not assert.

contested.question: Is ojo-kshaya at its extreme truly incurable?
positions: Sushruta states it directly, and the sentence before it states the converse: visramsa and vyapat are to be treated by "elixirs and remedies possessed of rejuvenating properties", while a patient who has lost consciousness from excessive ojas waste is to be given up by the physician. Both sentences are now quoted in full.

This has never been tested in anything retrieved here, and as a prognostic claim it is unfalsifiable as stated, since the diagnosis of terminal ojo-kshaya is itself made from the moribund state it is meant to predict.

notKnown: No assay for ojas was located, so none of the three published proposals for a molecular correlate (PMIDs 7705867, 11272402, 41289791) can be checked against the thing it claims to mark.
No reference range or normal value is defined for any candidate ojas marker in an ojas frame.

Ojo-visramsa, ojo-vyapat and ojo-kshaya have sign lists in Sushruta Sutrasthana 15, now quoted, but no case definition another team could apply, and no interrater reliability data was located. The flat statement in the previous version of this record, that they have no operational criteria and no reported prevalence in any population, was too strong: PMID 42161239 scored ojovisramsa in a 67-participant DMD cohort and reported it differing significantly between ambulation stages. What remains unknown is whether that scoring is reproducible, whether it transfers outside a rare neuromuscular disease, and what prevalence any of the three modes has in a general population.
No study has shown that any intervention changes a putative ojas marker in parallel with a clinical outcome; the 1995 and 2025 proposals are both untested.

The para/apara distinction is not established from the public-domain translations. The half-anjali quantity IS, for ojas without qualification, at Charaka Sharirasthana 7, which corrects this record's earlier negative result. The eight-drop quantity was searched for again and not located, and neither was any para or apara vocabulary applied to ojas. Whether the division itself is commentarial, later, or a modern teaching convenience is not resolved by any source retrieved here.
Whether the three incompatible classical definitions describe one thing, three things, or a term that shifted meaning across recensions is not resolved by any source I found.
The claim that ojas passes between mother and foetus in the eighth month has no identified referent and has never been investigated.
What the clinician is actually judging when assessing ojas at the bedside - and whether two clinicians judge it the same way - has not been measured.

Whether Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 11 is a parallel locus for the three derangement modes, and at which verses, is not established. There is no public-domain English translation of the Ashtanga Hridaya, no Sanskrit text of it was retrieved on this pass, and the verse range 37-40 that circulates in secondary sources is unverified. The sign lists this record carries are sourced to Sushruta Sutrasthana 15, which was retrieved and quoted, so nothing in the record now depends on the Vagbhata locus; whether Vagbhata says the same thing is simply not covered here.

Whether the aphorism numbers Kaviratna prints for the passages used here (Sutrasthana 11 at 31, Sutrasthana 17 at 74 and 114, Sutrasthana 28 at 13, Sutrasthana 30 at 6-10, Sharirasthana 4 at 31) correspond to the standard Trikamji numbers is not established. The off-by-one offset documented for this translation was established for Chikitsasthana 15 and Vimanasthana 5 and 8, and has not been checked for these chapters, so no standard-edition number is asserted for any of them.

Why Kaviratna's printed aphorism number for the eighth-month ojas passage (31) differs from the number the Sanskrit source used in this record gives for what appears to be the same passage (Sharirasthana 4.24) is not resolved. The two numbering systems have not been reconciled.

No study was located in which ojas was measured alongside an immune parameter. Immune parameters have been measured under Ayurvedic interventions (IL-6, TNF-alpha and hs-CRP in PMID 33596494), and clinical outcomes under AYUSH-64 (PMIDs 36928877, 34908795), but in none of the retrieved studies was ojas an exposure, an outcome, or measured. The question the previous version of this record asked, whether ojas status correlates with any measured immune parameter, therefore remains open because the studies that measure the second thing do not measure the first.

Whether the identification of ojas with vyadhikshamatva is supported by the corpus at all is not settled here. The clearest classical statement on differential disease resistance located in this gathering (Charaka Sutrasthana 28, quoted) makes no mention of ojas, and the record has not searched the corpus systematically for a passage that joins the two terms explicitly.

Whether the half-anjali measure is reproducible as a reading is not established. Charaka introduces the anjali list as known by inference rather than direct perception, and Kaviratna's footnote at the ojas line records a competing manuscript reading that Gangadhara followed, so the line this record now quotes is itself textually disputed.

components.gloss: The refined essence of all seven dhatus; the substance whose presence sustains life and whose loss ends it.

The 'superior' ojas, said in modern teaching to reside in the heart in a very small fixed quantity, loss of which is fatal. Neither the term para ojas nor the eight-drop quantity could be located in the two public-domain translations searched in full text, so no chapter and verse is asserted for either. Charaka's cardiac seat of "the foremost Ojas" (Sutrasthana 30, quoted below) is the nearest retrieved anchor, and it carries no quantity.

The 'ordinary' ojas, a larger circulating quantity distributed through the body and responsive to diet, drugs and regimen. The half-anjali measure IS in the retrieved public-domain Charaka: Sharirasthana 7 (Sharira-sankhya) gives the measure of ojas as half an anjali, quoted below. What is not in the retrieved text is the attachment of that measure to a term apara ojas, or any para/apara division at all; the earlier statement in this record that the half-anjali figure could not be located was wrong and is corrected.

Strength, in the classical usage covering physical capacity, resistance and resilience; often used as the observable proxy for ojas. Charaka divides it three ways, by nature, by season and by exertion, in Sutrasthana 11 (quoted below), and Charaka Sutrasthana 30 says flatly that "The Ojas is the strength of the body."
The capacity both to resist the onset of disease and to withstand it once present. The term closest in function to 'immunity', though broader.

Displacement of ojas from its seat: looseness of joints, inertness, fatigue, dislodgement of the doshas, suppression of bodily and mental function. Sourced to Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 in Bhishagratna's rendering, quoted below.

Corruption of ojas by contact with vitiated humours: numbness and heaviness of limbs, dropsical swelling attributed to deranged vayu, discoloured complexion, malaise, drowsiness and somnolence. Sourced to Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 in Bhishagratna's rendering, quoted below; this sign list was an uncited assertion in the previous version of this record.

Wasting of ojas: fainting, emaciation, mental distraction, delirium, loss of consciousness, death. Declared incurable at the extreme. Sourced to Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 in Bhishagratna's rendering, quoted below.
Injury, chronic wasting disease, anger, grief, worry, exertion and hunger - a list mixing physical insult with sustained emotional and metabolic strain.

The class of rejuvenative therapy prescribed to restore ojas. Sushruta assigns it specifically to visramsa and vyapat and withholds it from advanced kshaya, in the sentence quoted below. It is the practical intervention arm of the concept, and the arm where trials have been run, though the trials test formulations rather than the construct.
The heart, described as the receptacle of ojas and the root of the ten great vessels that carry it throughout the body.

Charaka's measure-by-palmful list in Sharirasthana 7 assigns ojas half an anjali, the same measure as brain and semen, an anjali being the hollow of the two joined palms. The list is introduced by Charaka himself as known by inference rather than by direct perception, and Kaviratna's footnote to the ojas line records a variant reading that would have made ojas a kind of phlegm, which Kaviratna rejects in his own voice.

classical.verse: prose section; Bhishagratna's rendering carries no verse numbers
classical.establishes: Sushruta's definition of ojas as the distilled essence of the whole tissue sequence rather than a distinct substance, in a lawfully quotable public-domain translation.
classical.quote: The quintessence of all the fundamental principles of the body, starting with lymph chyle and ending with semen, is called the Ojas, which is identical with what is termed 'vital power.'

classical.verse: prose section
classical.establishes: The functional scope claimed for ojas: tissue integrity, vitality, voice, complexion and sensory and cognitive function. Note how much wider this is than immune competence.
classical.quote: This Ojas (albumen) or strength-giving principle serves to impart a firm integrity to the flesh (and the muscles), exercises unbounded control over all acts of vitality, improves the voice and complexion, and helps both the external (operative) and the internal (intellectual) sense organs, in duly performing their natural functions.

classical.verse: prose section on the causes and modes of derangement
classical.establishes: The aetiology of ojas depletion, which places emotional strain (anger, grief, anxiety) alongside physical insult and starvation, and the claim that ojas is converted into bala radiating from the heart.
classical.quote: A blow, a persistent wasting disease, anger, grief, cares and anxieties, fatigue and hunger, are the causes to which should be ascribed the wasting or disappearance of this strength-giving principle (albumen) of the body. The bodily albumen, through the agency of the abovesaid causes, is wasted through the channels carrying the different fundamental principles of the body. Albumen is transformed into strength which radiates from the heart.

classical.verse: 'Authoritative verses on the subject', prose section
classical.establishes: The threefold classification of ojas derangement and the clinical signs of the first mode - the nearest thing in the corpus to diagnostic criteria for an ojas disorder.
classical.quote: A deranged state of albumen is marked by the three abovesaid properties of dislodgment from its proper seat (Visransha); by a change of its natural virtues through contamination (Vyapad) and by wasting (Kshaya). The first of these properties (Visransha) is characterised by looseness of the joints, by an inert state of the body, by a sense of fatigue, by a dislodgment of the deranged humours from their natural seats, and by a suppression of the bodily and intellectual functions.

classical.verse: prose section, continued
classical.establishes: The signs of ojo-kshaya and the explicit prognostic declaration of incurability at its extreme - a clinical claim, and one that has never been evaluated.
classical.quote: The loss or waste of Ojah (albumen) is marked by such symptoms as fits of fainting, emaciation of the body, bewilderment and distraction of the mind, delirium and loss of consciousness and ultimately death. ... A patient who has lost all consciousness (owing to an excessive loss or waste of albumen) should be given up by a physician (as incurable).

classical.verse: 73-74 (as printed; the OCR of this fascicule renumbers irregularly around these lines)
classical.establishes: Charaka's clinical picture of ojas depletion - and, crucially, his identification of ojas with a slightly yellowish pure blood residing in the heart, which is materially a different claim from Sushruta's essence-of-all-dhatus.
classical.quote: When the element called Ojas becomes attenuated, the patient yields to causeless fears, becomes weak, indulges in anxious thoughts ceaselessly, and feels pain in all his senses. His body again loses its splendour; he becomes cheerless; a dryness pervades the whole system; and a languor comes over him so that he feels fatigue upon the slightest exertion. There resides in the heart a quantity of pure blood, which is slightly yellowish. This blood in the body is called Ojas. Through attenuation of this blood or its loss, even death may overtake the man.

classical.verse: 114 (as printed)
classical.establishes: A third and incompatible identification of ojas, with normal kapha, appearing in the same chapter of the same text some forty verses after the heart-blood definition. This internal inconsistency is the single most important fact about the classical account.
classical.quote: It is the phlegm that is also called the Ojas in the system. When its normal condition becomes altered, it becomes a source of evil.

classical.verse: 6-10 (as printed; the OCR renders some superscript numerals unreliably)
classical.establishes: The cardiac seat of ojas, its distribution through the ten great vessels, and the breadth of its remit - conception and foetal development as well as strength and life itself. This is the passage showing ojas is not a synonym for immunity.
classical.quote: The heart is the seat (or receptacle) of the foremost Ojas. It is also the seat of supreme Brahman. For these reasons the heart is called Mahat (Great) and Artha (precious possession), by physicians. Because the heart or Mahat is the root of the ten ducts, therefore these are called Mahamula (having the Great for their root). These bear the Ojas and run into every part of the body. All embodied creatures, vivified by the Ojas, move about or act. Without it, the life of all creatures becomes extinct. The Ojas operates in the first place as the essence of conception. ... Dwelling in the heart, it sustains or supports life. The Ojas is the strength of the body. The body and the life-breaths are established in it.

classical.verse: translator's footnote to verse 74, recording a couplet present only in some recensions
classical.establishes: The sensory description of ojas (ghee-coloured, honey-tasting, smelling of parched grain) that later biomarker proposals lean on when arguing it is a lipid - and the fact that the translator flags it as present only in some texts, so the description is not firmly part of the received text.
classical.quote: That which is called Ojas at first appears in the bodies of embodied creatures, endued with the color of clarified butter. In taste it resembles honey. Its scent resembles that of fried paddy. As honey is gathered by bees from diverse kinds of flowers and fruits, even so is the Ojas of men gathered by the wind, bile, and phlegm from the several elements mentioned above.

classical.establishes: The doctrine that ojas passes back and forth between mother and foetus in the eighth month, the classical explanation for eighth-month prematurity - and an example of an ojas claim with a testable-looking form that has never been examined.
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

classical.verse: in the region of 37-40 per secondary sources; not asserted
classical.establishes: Vagbhata's account of ojas - its location chiefly in the heart, its unctuous and slightly reddish-yellow character, the causes of its decrease (anger, hunger, worry, grief, exhaustion) and the resulting fear, weakness and emaciation. Located only: there is no public-domain English translation of the Ashtanga Hridaya, so this may be paraphrased but never quoted, and the verse numbers circulating in secondary sources are not verified here.

classical.verse: 'Authoritative verses on the subject', prose section; Bhishagratna prints no Sanskrit verse numbers
classical.establishes: The sign list for ojo-vyapat, which component 7 of this record asserted without a citation until this revision. The same six signs appear in the prose a page earlier, but in a different order ("numbness and heaviness of the limbs, dropsy due to the action of the deranged bodily Vayu, discoloured or changed complexion, feeling of malaise, drowsiness and somnolence"), dropsy standing second in the prose and last in these verses, and malaise fourth in the prose and second here. The set of six signs is therefore doubly attested within the chapter, while the sequence is not. What this citation establishes is which six signs Sushruta assigns to the Vyapad; it establishes nothing about any order or priority among them.
classical.quote: Numbness and heaviness of the limbs, malaise, a discoloured complexion, drowsiness, somnolence and dropsical swelling brought about by a deranged state of the bodily Vayu, should be considered as natural consequences of the Vyapad (change of the natural virtues of albumen through contamination).
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: prose section following the 'Authoritative verses'; no verse numbers in this translation
classical.establishes: The treatment rule and the prognosis together, in the order the text gives them: rasayana for visramsa and vyapat, abandonment for kshaya that has reached loss of consciousness. The record previously quoted only the second sentence while its establishes field leaned on the first, which is the defect the critic identified.
classical.quote: The medical treatment in cases of dislodgment or flowing out external secretion of albumen from its natural seat (Visransha), as well as in the event of it becoming contaminated by the vitiated principles of the body, should consist in improving its quantity by elixirs and remedies possessed of rejuvenating properties, tending to increase the quantity of such fluid (albumen) in the body. A patient who has lost all consciousness (owing to an excessive loss or waste of albumen) should be given up by a physician (as incurable).

classical.verse: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 28 (Vividhashitapitiya). In Kaviratna's numbering, which prints the aphorism number after the aphorism: aphorism 13 plus the opening sentence of aphorism 14, since 13 is printed after 'are incapable of resisting diseases' and 14 after the following 'mild or virulent, quickly-arising or slow in generation' sentence, which this citation does not quote. Printed pp. 395 to 396. In the Trikamji vulgate numbering the whole quoted span sits inside a single prose sutra, Ca.Su. 28/7, verified against the GRETIL Carakasamhita e-text at '// Car_1,28.7'.
classical.establishes: The clearest classical statement of differential resistance to disease that this gathering has retrieved, and the one that ties resistance to the adequacy of the dhatus and to a measure less than normal rather than to ojas by name. It is the bridge between the tissue-quantity doctrine and vyadhikshamatva. It also sets the limit of the bridge: ojas is not named in it, so it supports a claim about dhatu adequacy and resistance, not a claim that ojas is what resistance consists of.
classical.quote: Those bodies which are very fat, or which are very lean, or which are made up of flesh, blood and bones that are either undeveloped or of measure less than normal, or which are destitute of strength, or which are supported by such kinds of food as are not agreeable to them, or which depend upon a very small measure of food, or which are endued with very little vitality, are incapable of resisting diseases. These bodies which are the reverse of those described above are capable of resisting diseases.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: 31 as printed by Kaviratna, after the aphorism; the standard-edition number is not established here
classical.establishes: The threefold division of bala, constitutional, seasonal and acquired, in a lawfully quotable public-domain English rendering. Because Charaka elsewhere says the ojas is the strength of the body, this division is the closest the corpus comes to saying that resistance has a fixed component and a modifiable one, which is the structural claim the para/apara teaching is usually used to carry.
classical.quote: There are three kinds of strength, viz., that which is due to one's nature, that which is due to a particular season (of life or the year); and that which is due to exertion (such as physical exercise, the use of invigorating food and spices and liquors, &c). Natural strength implies that kind of strength which inheres to the very nature of one's body and mind. By the second kind of strength is meant that strength which depends upon either a particular season of life (such as youth, manhood, &c.), or of the year (as spring, summer, &c), The third kind of strength is that due to the use of particular kinds of food and physical exercise

classical.verse: prose list of anjali measures; the marginal aphorism numerals on these lines are OCR-destroyed and are not reconstructed
classical.establishes: The half-anjali measure of ojas, in the retrieved public-domain Charaka. This overturns this record's own earlier negative result, which reported that the half-anjali figure could not be located in either public-domain translation. It is scriptural, not commentarial. What it does not establish is the para/apara reading: the list gives one measure for ojas and uses no para or apara vocabulary, and Charaka introduces the whole list as known by inference rather than by direct perception.
classical.quote: Of the Marrow the measure is 1 'anjali.' Of the Brain the measure is half an 'anjali.' Of the Semen the measure is the same (as above). Of the Ojas the measure is the same (as above).

classical.verse: Kaviratna's footnote to the ojas line of the anjali list, signed "T."
classical.establishes: Two things, and the second is the more important. First, that a textual variant exists at this point under which ojas is a kind of phlegm, which Gangadhara's commentary adopted, so the kapha identification is not confined to Sutrasthana 17.114. Second, that Kaviratna then settles the question in his own voice, calling ojas "the blood of blood, the most vital dhatu in the body". That is the translator asserting a doctrine, not Charaka, and it is the exact failure mode this project has recorded three times. Any modern claim that Charaka identifies ojas with blood should be checked against this note before it is attributed to the text.
classical.quote: Some texts read '[transliteration OCR-destroyed in the scan and not reconstructed].' Gangadhara, following this reading, explains it as meaning 'the particular kind of phlegm known as ojas.' This can be hardly correct. The 'ojas' has been before described. It is not regarded as any kind of phlegm. On the other hand, it is the blood of blood, the most vital 'dhatu' in the body. The reading is evidently incorrect.

classical.verse: 31 as printed by Kaviratna, after the aphorism; the Sanskrit source used elsewhere in this record numbers the same passage 24, and the discrepancy is not resolved here
classical.establishes: The eighth-month ojas exchange between mother and foetus, in a lawfully quotable public-domain English rendering. This is the doctrine for which the record previously had only a Sanskrit original, on the stated ground that Kaviratna does not reach Sharirasthana. He does, and this is the passage. The claim itself remains untested, which is recorded in notKnown.
classical.quote: In the eighth month the foetus draws from the mother, and the mother draws from the foetus, through the juice-bearing ducts, again and again, that ingredient (dhatu) which is called ojas. Indeed, each takes it from the other (at successive moments of time). ... Hence, at this stage of pregnancy, the life of the child in the womb becomes fraught with danger in consequence of the inconstancy of the ojas. Beholding this, the eighth month is not counted by those who are skilled (in the science of obstetrics).

modern.title: Stress, steroids, and "ojas": neuroendocrine mechanisms and current promise of ancient approaches to disease prevention.
modern.establishes: The first sustained modern proposal for a biochemical identity of ojas: Walton and Pugh argue that specific steroids and steroid classes are the likely candidates for the 'ordinary' and 'superior' types of ojas, and situate the concept within stress and neuroendocrine research on homeostasis.
modern.quality: Narrative review with an embedded hypothesis, in Indian J Physiol Pharmacol. No experiment, no cohort, no measurement of anything called ojas. The authors are candid that the linkage was made possible by a particular interpretive tradition, and the paper's affiliation (Maharishi International University) is disclosed on its face. Thirty years on, the steroid proposal has not been tested.

modern.title: Can cholesterol and its products serve as biomarkers for ojas?
modern.establishes: The most recent biomarker proposal: Sumantran and Nair argue that cholesterol and its downstream products (steroid hormones, bile acids, vitamin D, myelin) are candidate biomarkers for ojas, with HDL-C as a possible surrogate for healthy apara ojas, reasoning from five classes of correspondence.
modern.quality: Hypothesis paper, not an empirical study. The authors describe their own evidence as 'correlative, potentially causal, and clinical' and their conclusion as a hypothesis with 'candidate' biomarkers; the correspondences are drawn from existing cholesterol literature and mapped onto classical descriptions of ojas. No ojas was measured, no cohort was assessed, no assay was developed or validated. Its main value for this record is as documentation that after thirty years the field is still at the proposal stage.

modern.title: A short review on deciphering Vyadhikshamatva: insights from HLA-B27-ankylosing spondylitis relation.
modern.establishes: An attempt to read vyadhikshamatva against a concrete immunogenetic finding, the HLA-B27 association with ankylosing spondylitis.
modern.quality: Short narrative review. It maps classical categories onto an established immunological association rather than generating or testing a prediction from the Ayurvedic side. Representative of the genre: modern immunology supplies the content, the Ayurvedic vocabulary supplies a restatement.

modern.title: Safety and Efficacy of Chyawanprash as a Prophylaxis Treatment for COVID-19: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Control Trials.
modern.establishes: The best available quantitative test of an ojas-restoring intervention. A systematic review and meta-analysis of five randomised controlled trials of Chyawanprash as COVID-19 prophylaxis, pooling 153,343 participants, reporting odds ratios of 0.45 (95% CI 0.06-3.08) for COVID-19 positivity, 0.37 (95% CI 0.01-12.86) for symptomatic positivity, 0.95 (95% CI 0.18-5.04) for healthcare resource use and 0.94 (95% CI 0.63-1.40) for adverse events.
modern.quality: A genuine meta-analysis of RCTs, so methodologically the strongest item here, and its result is null: every confidence interval crosses 1, with severe heterogeneity (I-squared 80% and 83% for the two efficacy outcomes). The authors themselves note high heterogeneity and bias and call for further research. It also tests a formulation, not the construct - a null result says nothing about whether ojas exists, and a positive one would not have shown that it does. The safety signal (no excess adverse events) is the most secure finding.

modern.title: Role of Kasahara Dashemani Vati in Kasa and Vyadhikshamatva in children with special reference to recurrent respiratory tract infections.
modern.establishes: A small clinical study explicitly framed around vyadhikshamatva, evaluating Kasahara Dashemani Vati in children with recurrent respiratory tract infections.
modern.quality: Small single-centre trial in Ayu. Uses recurrent infection frequency as a proxy for vyadhikshamatva without validating that proxy, and provides no measure of the construct independent of the clinical outcome it is meant to explain.

modern.title: An observational study on acceptability, palatability, and safety of Ayurveda immunity booster kit for the prevention of COVID-19 in frontline workers in Jaipur, India.
modern.establishes: An observational study of an 'Ayurveda immunity booster kit' in frontline workers during COVID-19, reporting on acceptability, palatability and safety.
modern.quality: Observational, and explicitly not an efficacy study - no control group and no immune endpoint. Included here as an honest illustration of how the 'immunity' framing has been deployed in practice: the outcome measured was whether people would take it, not whether it did anything.

modern.title: Molecular approach to ayurveda.
modern.establishes: A third proposal in the indexed literature for a molecular correlate, earlier than either of the two the record previously carried. Mishra, Singh and Dagenais propose monitoring the doshas through free-radical and signalling parameters, with kapha read as the degree of gene expression as protein synthesis, and state that this "can be correlated with the ojas of the body or total body defence mechanism". Its existence is why the record no longer says there are two proposals.
modern.quality: Narrative review in Indian J Exp Biol proposing objective parameters for the doshas. No experiment, no measurement, no cohort, and the ojas sentence is a single clause at the end of a dosha-focused argument rather than a developed identification. It is weak evidence for anything about ojas, and that is the point: it is strong evidence that a census of two was wrong.

modern.title: Conceptualization and design of an Ayurveda framework for the diagnosis of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy: insights from a prospective cohort study.
modern.establishes: The one retrieved study in which a mode of ojas derangement was operationalised as a variable and scored in a cohort. A three-year prospective observational cohort of 67 participants with molecularly confirmed Duchenne muscular dystrophy, not on steroids, assessed with Ayurvedic staging; the authors report that under rogavastha significant differences between ambulation stages were observed in Sarvagatavata, Asthimajjagatavata and Ojovisramsa.
modern.quality: Cross-sectional baseline data from a cohort study, in J Ayurveda Integr Med. It is a framework paper: the Ayurvedic categories are the instrument, not the thing being validated, and the paper reports no interrater reliability for the ojovisramsa judgement, no case definition that another team could apply, and no comparison against an external standard. So it shows that ojovisramsa can be scored and that the scores track a disease stage in one rare-disease cohort; it does not show that the scoring is reproducible or that it measures ojas. It is cited here because the previous version of this record said flatly that the three derangement modes have no operational criteria and no reported prevalence in any population, and that was too strong.

modern.title: Randomized placebo-controlled pilot clinical trial on the efficacy of ayurvedic treatment regime on COVID-19 positive patients.
modern.establishes: The retrieved answer to the question the record's notKnown asked, namely whether any trial of an ojas-restoring regimen measured an immune parameter. This one did: a placebo-controlled randomised double-blind pilot trial in asymptomatic COVID-19 (CTRI/2020/05/025273) of Giloy Ghanvati, Swasari Ras, Ashwagandha and Tulsi Ghanvati with Anu taila, quantifying serum IL-6, TNF-alpha and hs-CRP by chemiluminescent immunometric assay on day 1 and day 7, and reporting average fold changes in the treatment group 12.4, 2.5 and 20 times lower than placebo at day 7.
modern.quality: A real randomised placebo-controlled trial with real immune endpoints, and it still says nothing about ojas, which is the finding. Ojas was not the exposure, not an outcome, and not measured; the abstract does not use the word. The design is a pilot, the regimen is a four-drug combination so no component is isolated, recovery was assessed by RT-qPCR clearance in an asymptomatic population where most recover anyway, and the inflammatory markers are reported as average fold changes rather than with confidence intervals. Its value to this record is precise and limited: the post-2020 literature did measure immune parameters under Ayurvedic interventions, so the gap in the ojas account is not that nobody measured immunity, it is that nobody measured ojas alongside it.

modern.title: Co-administration of AYUSH 64 as an adjunct to standard of care in mild and moderate COVID-19: A randomized, controlled, multicentric clinical trial.
modern.establishes: The AYUSH-64 evidence the critic asked to be searched. A randomised, controlled, assessor-blind multicentric trial of AYUSH 64 added to standard of care in 140 hospitalised adults with mild to moderate COVID-19, reporting mean time to clinical recovery 6.45 versus 8.26 days (95% CI of the difference -3.02 to -0.59, P = 0.003 per protocol, P = 0.002 on intention to treat), 48 adverse events in each arm and no deaths.
modern.quality: Methodologically the stronger of the two AYUSH-64 trials retrieved and a positive result on a clinical endpoint, which makes it the right test of the critic's expectation. It carries no immune endpoint at all and no ojas or vyadhikshamatva measurement, so a positive result here is evidence about a polyherbal formulation in COVID-19 and not evidence about the construct. The open-label design with an assessor blind, the convenience sample and the single pandemic wave are its main limits. A second AYUSH-64 randomised trial (PMID 34908795, Ayu 2022, n = 60) found no significant difference in RT-PCR conversion, which is why no direction of effect is claimed here.

modern.title: A clinical study on the Naimittika Rasayana effect of Silajatu and Mamajjaka in type-2 Diabetes Mellitus.
modern.establishes: How the ojas-as-immunity equation is actually used in clinical research: a three-arm clinical study of Silajatu and Mamajjaka as naimittika rasayana in 84 followed-up patients with type 2 diabetes, whose authors frame Prameha patients as carrying "impaired Agni and depleted Ojas status, that is, hypometabolic and immuno-compromised state" and conclude that the drugs promote "Agni (biofire) and Ojas (immune strength) status".
modern.quality: Small open study in Ayu with modern-drug comparison, outcomes reported as subjective and objective response and post-prandial blood sugar. Ojas appears in the framing and in the conclusion and nowhere in the measurements; the gloss "Ojas (immune strength)" is asserted, not derived. Included as an exhibit of the interpretive slide the record describes, not as evidence for it.

Why Kaviratna's aphorism numbering diverges from the Sanskrit source's for the eighth-month passage (31 against 24) is unresolved, and so is whether the documented off-by-one offset in this translation extends to Sutrasthana 11, 17, 28 and 30 and Sharirasthana 4 and 7. records.title: Panchakarma rationale
records.summary: Panchakarma is the name used for a set of five eliminative procedures that constitute internal shodhana, together with the preparatory and recovery phases that surround them. The stated rationale is sequential and mechanical: aggravated doshas that have lodged in the tissues must first be loosened and brought back to the gut by internal and external oleation (snehana) and heat (swedana), then expelled by the route appropriate to the dosha and its seat, then followed by a graded re-feeding regimen (samsarjana krama) while digestive capacity is weak. Each of those three steps is now cited to an operative passage: Sushruta's emesis-and-purgation chapter states the loosening step and makes it mandatory, distinguishes the upward from the downward route by the behaviour of the drug, and grades the dose to the bowel type; Sushruta's post-procedure chapter and Charaka's Sutrasthana 15 give the graded re-feeding. The claimed payoff is durability, since Charaka holds that faults subdued by correctives cannot reappear and Sushruta compares a purged body to a tank baled dry, and preparedness, since Sushruta holds that rejuvenative therapy given to an uncleansed body is like dyeing a dirty cloth. Both payoffs are argued by analogy rather than by a mechanism. What the five procedures are is not settled and this record does not settle it: the enumerations it can actually source do not agree with each other, and in Sushruta a commentator is recorded disputing the ordinary reading of the word. The record cites procedural passages for emesis, purgation, both enemas, nasal administration and the graded re-feeding. It cites none for bloodletting and quotes no Vagbhata at all; both limits are stated in notKnown rather than left silent.
records.evidenceState: The classical rationale is well attested and, after this revision, cited at the level of the operative procedures rather than only at the level of the principle. The sequencing detail is specific enough to be checkable: three days of oily food after oleation before purgation and one before emesis (Ca.Su.13.80-81), seven days between a purgative and the oil enema and the oil enema before the decoction enema (Bhishagratna's Chikitsa XXXVII.2 and XXXVIII.1), a purgative dose set by the threefold koshtha (XXXIII.15), and a gruel count set by the measured volume expelled (XXXIX.3-4). It is not internally consistent, and this revision withdraws the claim that it is. Three inconsistencies sit inside the record's own sources. The membership of the five cannot be settled from them: the one passage in the retrieved material that enumerates a group of five names oleation, purgation, emesis, asthapana and anuvasana, which matches neither scheme the record previously contrasted, and it does so in the translator's gloss rather than in the text. Charaka Sutrasthana 16 counts increase of the digestive fire among the signs of a properly purified body while Sushruta's recovery chapter opens by saying the digestive fire grows dull after exactly these procedures, a tension Bhishagratna resolves in a footnote of his own. And Bhishagratna records Dallana reading the word 'panchakarma' in Sushruta Chikitsa 13 as something else entirely. On top of that, the two stated payoffs, durability and preparation for rasayana, are both argued by analogy: faults subdued by correctives cannot reappear (asserted), a purged body is a tank baled dry, an unprepared body is sapless wood, an uncleansed body is dirty cloth. The one passage that offers something closer to a mechanism, XXXIII.21-22, explains the two routes by whether the drug is digested, which is a claim about the drug and not about the dosha. The modern evidence does not test the central claims, on the evidence this record searched, and the searches are now named in gatheringNotes rather than left implicit. No systematic search was run and none is claimed. Within those searches: the strongest study, Peterson et al. 2016, is a real controlled metabolomic study with proper multiple-testing correction, but the intervention it tested was a six-day residential programme combining herbs, vegetarian diet, meditation, yoga and massage, so its finding of altered plasma phosphatidylcholines cannot be attributed to the eliminative procedures, and the paper makes no clinical outcome claim. The clinical trials that do isolate a procedure are small, unblinded, lack a no-procedure arm, and confound the procedure with a follow-on palliative drug. The most obvious modern mechanistic hypothesis, that these are gut-directed interventions acting through the microbiome, is described in a 2024 review as nascent with too few studies to support categorical conclusions. A 2026 registered protocol from an Ayurvedic university is still single-arm with surrogate endpoints, which is itself a fair index of where the field stands. On safety, this revision stops asserting that nothing was found. The search found one prospective single-centre pharmacovigilance survey that attributes 23 of 52 confirmed adverse drug reactions in a hospital year to panchakarma, with no per-procedure denominator, and one 15-patient before-and-after study of serum electrolytes after purgation. Neither gives an adverse-event rate. A 2008 JAMA assay of internet-sold Ayurvedic medicines, which found detectable lead, mercury or arsenic in a fifth of 193 products, is recorded as context for the safety of orally administered classical preparations and explicitly not as evidence about the drugs used in panchakarma, which it did not sample. The honest summary is that panchakarma is a well-documented and elaborately specified traditional procedure, specified down to the dose and the meal count, whose central claims of durability and preparation for rasayana have not been tested in anything this record located, whose one respectable piece of biochemical data does not bear on those claims, and whose own textual tradition does not agree on what the five procedures are.

contested.question: What are the five karmas?
positions: Charaka's set is usually given as vamana, virechana, niruha (decoction) basti, anuvasana (oil) basti and shirovirechana/nasya, with the two enemas counted separately and bloodletting excluded. UNSOURCED IN THIS RECORD: the Charaka passage that enumerates them is in Siddhisthana, which is not in the Kaviratna volume this record reads, and Ca.Su.2.34-35 names 'the five acts' without listing them. The position is retained as the standard report, not as a sourced claim.

Sushruta and Vagbhata are usually said to count raktamokshana (bloodletting) among the five and to treat the enemas as one. UNSOURCED IN THIS RECORD: no passage in Bhishagratna Volume II that was read enumerates such a set, and no Vagbhata is quoted anywhere in this record. The gathering pass supported this position with a verse attribution for Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 14 taken from an unnamed chapter summary; that attribution has been removed as unverifiable. The position is retained as the standard report and is flagged so that nothing downstream treats it as cited.

A third enumeration is actually retrievable, and it matches neither. At Sushruta Sarira Sthana, Bhishagratna's chapter II, sections 5-12, the group named is oleation (sneha-karma), purgatives, emetics, asthapana and anuvasana, and in the next paragraph Bhishagratna glosses the Sanskrit 'oil etc., purgatives etc.' as '(Pancha-karma)', with a footnote supplying those members. Oleation is inside the five here and nasal administration is not. This is the translator reading the term, not Sushruta enumerating it, and it is recorded as such.

Bhishagratna's footnote to Sushruta Chikitsa 13, section 7 records that Dallana, the standard Sushruta commentator, glosses the term in that passage as something other than the five eliminative measures, taking it to mean the measures used against kushtha affecting bone as the fifth dhatu. The word was not univocal even in the commentarial period.

The consequence, which this record states rather than resolves: the referent of 'panchakarma' is not stable across the sources this record can quote, and a record that picked one would be choosing rather than reporting.

contested.question: Do the preparatory steps have an independent rationale or are they part of the eliminative act?
positions: The classical sequencing rules treat snehana and swedana as mandatory precursors with specified intervals (Ca.Su.13.80-81), and Sushruta states the mobilising function outright: oleation, heat and secretion-producing food so that the doshas 'would be loosened and dislodged from their seats' (Bhishagratna's Chikitsa XXXIII.3).

The reason Sushruta gives for the preparation being mandatory is an analogy, not a mechanism: a body given a purgative or emetic without prior oleation and heat 'breaks up like a piece of sapless wood at the time of bending it' (XXXIII.33). The same chapter also makes the preparation repeatable and conditional, requiring a second oleation and heat before purgation after an emesis (XXXIII.14) and a drying phase first in those habituated to oily food (XXXIII.29-30), which reads as an independently managed step rather than a formality.

No study located by the searches named in gatheringNotes separates the preparatory phase from the eliminative phase, so whether snehana and swedana contribute anything beyond the diet and rest they entail is untested here.

Bhishagratna's own note on Sushruta Chikitsa 32 warns that 'sveda' does not necessarily mean producing sweat, which undercuts readings of the step as a diaphoretic or detoxifying measure in the modern sense. The warning is the translator's, about his own English, and is used here only as that.

contested.question: Does purification kindle the digestive fire or dull it?
positions: Charaka Sutrasthana 16, at Kaviratna's aphorisms 14 to 16, lists 'the increase of the digestive fire' first among the signs of one whose system has been properly purified, and makes improved digestive capacity one of the blessings of proper purgation; Sushruta says the same at Bhishagratna's Chikitsa XXXIII.18.

Sushruta's recovery chapter opens by stating the reverse: 'The digestive fire (Kayagni) of a person naturally grows dull after the exhibition of emetics and purgatives, after the administration of a Niruha-Vasti, after the internal application of a Sneha and after blood-letting' (Bhishagratna's Chikitsa XXXIX.2). The whole graded diet is built on that premise.

Bhishagratna harmonises the two in a footnote at that point, saying the fire is ultimately kindled by these measures but immediately afterwards becomes dull and sluggish. ATTRIBUTION: that resolution is the translator's. Neither passage as retrieved says it. It is recorded here because it is a plausible reading and because this project has three times absorbed a translator's harmonisation as doctrine, so the attribution is the point.

What follows for the record: the two statements are both in the sources and the reconciliation is not, so the claim that the classical account is internally consistent has been withdrawn from evidenceState.

contested.question: Is panchakarma a treatment, a preparatory measure, or a seasonal health practice?
positions: Charaka Su.16 frames it as definitive treatment with durable effect, and Sushruta's benefits-of-purgation passage (Bhishagratna's Chikitsa XXXIII.18) does the same with a different analogy.

Sushruta Chikitsa 27.2 frames it as a precondition for rasayana to work, and Bhishagratna's Chikitsa XXXVII.2 frames the oil enema as requiring prior purification in the same way, so the preparatory framing is internal to the procedure set and not only a bridge to rasayana.

Contemporary practice and the 2026 protocol frame seasonal purification (ritu shodhana) in healthy people as a healthspan measure, a use for which the protocol itself concedes the evidence remains a gray area.

contested.question: What does the Peterson 2016 metabolomic finding show?
positions: It is widely cited as biochemical evidence that panchakarma produces measurable physiological change.

The intervention was a multi-component residential programme, so the same data are equally consistent with six days of vegetarian diet, meditation and rest producing the phosphatidylcholine shift with no contribution from the eliminative procedures. The paper does not claim otherwise.

contested.question: What can be said about the safety of panchakarma?
positions: The classical texts describe the harms of over-administration in clinical detail and make them the operator's responsibility: Charaka Su.16 (Kaviratna 7-9) describes graded over-purgation up to dark-blue blood and then tells the patient to seek a learned physician, and Sushruta states flatly that 'purgatives administered by ignorant physicians to persons who ought not to be purged (often) prove fatal' (Bhishagratna's Chikitsa XXXIII.19).

The modern safety literature the search named is thin but not empty. A prospective single-centre pharmacovigilance survey (PMID 27011712) attributes 23 of 52 confirmed hospital ADRs in one year to panchakarma, mostly mild to moderate and mostly gastrointestinal or cutaneous, with an overall ADR incidence of 1.14 percent in the hospital's patient population. A 15-patient study of serum electrolytes after purgation (PMID 24696575) found deviations within the normal range.

Neither of those is an adverse-event rate for the procedure. The pharmacovigilance denominator is the hospital population rather than the people who underwent a procedure; spontaneous reporting under-counts; and 23 of 52 is a share of reactions, not a risk. The record states this as an open gap rather than letting the two studies stand in for one.

A separate and distinct safety question is the composition of the preparations administered. A 2008 JAMA assay (PMID 18728265) found detectable lead, mercury or arsenic in 20.7 percent of 193 internet-purchased Ayurvedic medicines, with no difference by country of manufacture and no protection from a GMP claim. It sampled none of the drugs used in panchakarma, so it bears on the class of product and not on this procedure, and the gap it leaves is recorded in notKnown.

notKnown: Whether the eliminative procedures contribute anything beyond the diet, rest and practitioner contact that accompany them. No study located by the searches named in gatheringNotes has a component-controlled design.

Whether effects of panchakarma persist. No study located by those searches includes a follow-up period adequate to test the durability claim at Ch.Su.16.20 or its Sushruta counterpart at Bhishagratna's Chikitsa XXXIII.18.

What, if anything, is eliminated. No study located by those searches characterises the material removed by vamana or virechana, or shows that its removal relates to any measured outcome. Sushruta measures the quantity expelled in volumetric units (prastha, adhaka) and grades the recovery diet by it (Chikitsa XXXIX.3-4), so the tradition treats the quantity as meaningful; nothing retrieved here identifies what it consists of.

Whether snehana and swedana are necessary. The waiting intervals in Ch.Su.13.80-81 and the seven-day interval at Bhishagratna's Chikitsa XXXVII.2 are precise enough to test and no test of them was located.

The adverse-event rate of panchakarma under ordinary practice conditions. The classical texts describe over-administration harms in detail and name misapplication as sometimes fatal. The modern searches named in gatheringNotes found one prospective hospital pharmacovigilance survey (PMID 27011712) and one 15-patient electrolyte study (PMID 24696575), neither of which yields a rate per procedure: the pharmacovigilance denominator is the hospital's whole patient population, and spontaneous reporting under-counts. This record makes no claim about whether a prospective safety cohort exists. The register where Indian Ayurvedic trials are registered, CTRI, was not searched: it was reached today but its search interface returned no results to the queries attempted, so no CTRI search can be reported and no conclusion drawn from its absence.

Whether the single CTRI registration this record names, CTRI/2024/02/062176, says what the JMIR protocol paper says it says. The number is quoted from that paper's abstract and has not been checked against the register.

How much procedural variation exists between practitioners and centres for the same named karma, and whether outcomes differ accordingly. Sushruta's own chapters show the scope for it: the dose varies with koshtha, the retention time is given in matras with commentators disagreeing on how many (Bhishagratna's Chikitsa XXXVIII cites Agnivesha and Parashara against each other), and Dallana is repeatedly cited for variant readings.

Whether the classical eligibility criteria identify anything that predicts response or harm. The criteria are now cited rather than merely named: the threefold koshtha and its dosing rule at Bhishagratna's Chikitsa XXXIII.15, and the exclusion lists at XXXIII.11 and XXXIII.19. The 2026 protocol uses madhyama koshtha, vamanarha and virechanarha as inclusion criteria. No study located here tests whether any of them predicts anything.

Whether the drugs actually administered during panchakarma carry the heavy-metal contamination found in Ayurvedic products on open sale. PMID 18728265 assayed internet-purchased oral products in 2005 and found detectable lead, mercury or arsenic in 20.7 percent of them, concentrated in rasa shastra preparations; it sampled no emetic, purgative, enema or nasal preparation as dispensed in a panchakarma unit, and no study that does so was located. This record therefore has no basis for a statement either way about the drugs its subject uses.

SCOPE LIMIT, bloodletting. This record cites no procedural passage for raktamokshana and no passage enumerating it among the five. Sushruta's operative material on bloodletting and leeches sits in Sutrasthana, which is in Bhishagratna's Volume I and was not consulted. Nothing in this record should be read as a claim about raktamokshana beyond its appearance in a list of procedures after which digestion is dull (Bhishagratna's Chikitsa XXXIX.2).

SCOPE LIMIT, Vagbhata. This record quotes no Ashtanga Hridaya. The project can publish quotations only from Kaviratna's Charaka and Bhishagratna's Sushruta, the two public-domain English translations it has settled on; no public-domain English Ashtanga Hridaya was found, and quoting an in-copyright translation or paraphrasing one as though it were a citation are both barred. The chapter-level address is retained and marked unsourced. Nothing here is evidence about Vagbhata's scheme, including the usual report that he counts bloodletting among the five.

SCOPE LIMIT, numbering. No standard-edition crosswalk was established for any of the Sushruta citations in this record. Bhishagratna prints no Sanskrit verse numbers, only his own section numbers, and his chapter order for the two enemas (XXXVII anuvasana, XXXVIII niruha) was not checked against a standard edition's. The Sushruta locations here are therefore reproducible in his printing and nowhere else until that crosswalk is done. For Charaka, both numbering systems are now recorded on every entry, and the drift is not uniform: Kaviratna runs two behind in Sutrasthana 2, two behind at Sutrasthana 15.16 while matching exactly at 15.6 and 15.7, and three behind at Sutrasthana 16.20.

components.gloss: Preparatory oleation, internal (graded doses of medicated ghee over days) and external, held to loosen dosha from the tissues. Sushruta's operative chapter (Bhishagratna's Chikitsa XXXIII, sections 3 and 33) states the loosening claim and makes the step mandatory before either emesis or purgation.

Preparatory sudation or heat application, divided by Sushruta into direct heat, vapour, poultice and heated fluid, held to liquefy and mobilise the loosened dosha. Bhishagratna's own note warns that 'sveda' means the application of heat whether or not sweating follows.

Therapeutic emesis; the upward (urdhva) route, principally directed at kapha. Operative passage: Bhishagratna's Sushruta Chikitsa XXXIII, sections 3-13, with the route difference explained at sections 21-22 by the emetic being undigested and so forcing its way up.

Therapeutic purgation; the downward route, principally directed at pitta. Operative passage: Bhishagratna's Sushruta Chikitsa XXXIII, sections 14-20, including the threefold koshtha assessment that sets the dose.

Decoction enema. Operative passage: Bhishagratna's Sushruta Chikitsa XXXVIII, which places it after the oil enema and requires oleation and sudation first. Charaka's scheme is usually said to make this the principal measure against vata; this record cites no Charaka passage for that and does not assert it.

Oil enema, treated as a procedure distinct from the decoction enema. Operative passage: Bhishagratna's Sushruta Chikitsa XXXVII, section 2, which sets it seven days after a purgative and forbids it in a body not already cleansed.

Nasal administration, treated as cleansing of the head and neck region. Operative passage: Bhishagratna's Sushruta Chikitsa XL, section 18, which divides nasya into shiro-virechana and snehana and then into five named forms.

Bloodletting. Routinely listed among the five in later and in modern accounts. This record cites no classical passage that enumerates it among the five and no procedural passage for it: Sushruta's operative material on bloodletting sits in Sutrasthana, which is in Bhishagratna's Volume I and was not consulted here. See notKnown and contested.

The graded post-procedure diet, from thin gruel upward, held to rebuild digestive capacity; treated as part of the procedure, not an afterthought. Operative passages: Charaka Sutrasthana 15 (Kaviratna's aphorism 18, standard 15.16), which gives a twelve-meal progression, and Bhishagratna's Sushruta Chikitsa XXXIX, sections 2-4, which proportions the diet to the quantity eliminated.

classical.verse: standard 2.34-2.35; Kaviratna prints 32 and 33 after the two aphorisms
classical.establishes: That the group of five (pancha karma) is treated as an organising category for materia medica this early in the Sutrasthana, and that the same drugs are deliberately re-presented from the standpoint of the five procedures. It does not enumerate the five: Kaviratna's text names purgation and vomiting and then abbreviates.
classical.quote: Thus have been mentioned the eight and twenty varieties of Gruel. The drugs, in brief, have also been spoken of, that are used in the five acts, (viz., purgation, vomiting, &c.). Those drugs that were spoken of before for imparting a knowledge of roots and fruits have been mentioned again for imparting a knowledge of how they are used in connection with the five acts.

classical.verse: standard 13.80-13.81; Kaviratna prints 76 after the first aphorism and leaves the second unnumbered, the next number in his sequence being 77
classical.establishes: The sequencing rule that makes panchakarma a staged procedure rather than a single act, including a specific and differential waiting interval between oleation and the two main eliminative routes.
classical.quote: One who, after having taken Oils, wishes to take a purgative, should wait for three days, eating during that period food that is oily, liquid, and warm, and that is mixed with the juice of meat. One who, after having taken Oils, wishes to take an emetic, should wait for one day after having eaten the same kind of food ( as is mentioned in the last Verse ) during that day.

classical.verse: standard 16.20; Kaviratna prints 17 after the aphorism
classical.establishes: The durability claim that is the primary justification offered for undertaking panchakarma rather than a drug regimen. It is asserted, not argued.
classical.quote: The faults of the system, if subjugated by fasts and Pachanas, may reappear. If subjugated by correctives, they cannot reappear.

classical.verse: standard 16.9-16.10 and 16.12; Kaviratna prints 7 after the first part of the quote and 9 after the second, with his 8 falling inside the ellipsis
classical.establishes: That the classical tradition itself treats these procedures as carrying real and describable harm when over-administered, and conditions their use on operator skill. Relevant to any modern safety assessment.
classical.quote: The indications of an excessive or over administration of purgatives are evacuation, in the first instance, of stools, bile, phlegm, and wind in due order, and then the discharge of blood that looks like liquified fat or broth of meat, and after this, the discharge of pure water without any phlegm or bile being mixed with it, and then blood of a dark blue. The other symptoms are thirst and pain in consequence of the obstruction of wind. ... Hence, in the matter of the administration of purgatives and emetics for purifying or correcting the constitution of its faults, an intelligent man should seek a learned and skilful physician for his help, one, that is, who will bestow upon him both long life and happiness.

classical.verse: standard 15.16; Kaviratna prints 18 after the aphorism
classical.establishes: The samsarjana krama itself, which this record previously named as a component and cited nowhere. Charaka specifies a twelve-meal progression after emesis: thin rice gruel (manda) for meals one to three, a thicker jelly-like preparation for four to six, soft rice with mudga soup for seven to nine, rice with meat decoction for ten to twelve, then the same diet for a week before the ordinary regimen resumes. The graded diet is given as a numbered procedure, not as general advice.
classical.quote: The patient should then, in the evening of that day, or on the next day, be caused to bathe in lukewarm water. Take then a little quantity of red Cali rice, boil it in water and make a manda of it. The Liquid portion that is to be obtained after the manda has settled down is the gruel that should be administered, while still agreeably warm, to the patient. Marking the strength of his appetite, similar food should be administered to him when the time comes for his second as also his third act of eating. ... After that, the same kind of diet should be continued for a week in succession. On the expiry of a week, however, the patient may betake himself to his usual regimen.

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section 2
classical.establishes: The classification of the preparatory heat phase into four kinds.
classical.quote: Sveda (calorification, fomentation, diaphoretic measures, etc.) may be divided into four groups such as, the application of direct heat (Tapa-sveda), fomentation (Ushma-sveda), poulticing (Upanaha sveda) and the application of heated fluids (Drava-sveda). All kinds of diaphoretic measures (Sveda) belong to one or the other of these groups.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916), public domain

classical.verse: translator's footnote attached to Bhishagratna's section 7
classical.establishes: That the referent of the word 'panchakarma' is disputed inside the classical commentarial tradition. Dallana, the standard commentator on Sushruta, is reported here as reading it in this passage as something other than the five eliminative procedures. This is evidence that the word was not univocal, and it is deliberately recorded as a translator's footnote reporting a commentator, not as a statement of the text.
classical.quote: Some take the term in its ordinary sense to mean the five measures of emetics, purgatives, etc. ; but Dallana would explain it as the measures adopted in the treatment of the Kushtha affecting the bone which is the fifth Dhatu in the system.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916), public domain

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section 2
classical.establishes: The second major rationale for panchakarma beyond direct treatment: it is held to be a precondition for rasayana to work at all. The justification offered is an analogy (dye on dirty cloth), not a mechanism.
classical.quote: A person whose system has not been (previously) cleansed (Sodhana) with the proper purifying remedies (emetics and purgatives) should not, in any case, have recourse to such tonics inasmuch as they would fail to produce the wished-for result, just as the application of a dye to a piece of dirty cloth will prove non-effective.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916), public domain

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's sections 2 and 3
classical.establishes: The core mechanical rationale, in the operative chapter rather than inferred from the preparatory ones: oleation, then heat, then secretion-producing food, for the stated purpose of loosening and dislodging dosha from its seat before it is expelled. This is the passage the record's summary was describing and had never cited.
classical.quote: The principal maxims to be followed are to augment the loss or deficiency, to pacify the aggravation and reduce the increment of the Doshas and maintain them in a state of healthy equilibrium. Emetics and purgatives are the principal remedies in cleansing the system of all the Doshas (morbific principles). Now hear me, therefore, discourse on the mode of their administration. The body of the patient should be first anointed with a Sneha (oil, etc.) and Sveda should then be applied thereto. He should then be made to partake of meals which would produce internal secretions from the system, so that all the Doshas (morbific diathesis, etc.) accumulated in the organism would be loosened and dislodged from their seats.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916), public domain

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section 15
classical.establishes: The classical eligibility and dosing assessment that the record's notKnown names (koshtha assessment) and had never cited. The threefold koshtha is not a descriptive aside: it sets the purgative dose. The same category appears as an inclusion criterion in the 2026 registered protocol recorded under modern, which requires madhyama koshtha.
classical.quote: Koshtha (bowels) may be grouped under three heads as mild or easily movable (Mridu), middling or moderately constipated (Madhya) and hard or constipated (Krura). The first kind (Mridu) of the Koshtha should be ascribed to the abundance of Pitta therein and can be moved even with milk only ; the last (Krura) is ascribable to the action of an abundance of Vayu and Kapha and can be moved only with the greatest difficulty ; while the second, Madhayama, should be held as the product of a condition of equilibrium among the (three) Doshas and this is the most general type. Purgatives should be administered in small doses to persons of lax bowels (Mridu Koshtha), in moderate doses to those of moderately constipated bowels (Madhayama Koshtha), and in large doses to persons of extremely constipated bowels (Krura Koshtha).
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916), public domain

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section numbered 18 (see verificationNote: his numbering around this point is printed 18-A, 18-B and 18)
classical.establishes: Sushruta's version of the durability claim, parallel to Charaka Sutrasthana 16 but argued by a different analogy: the purged body is a drained tank in which nothing can live.
