The emesis counterpart in the same chapter at Bhishagratna's 9-10 uses a felled tree drying up with its twigs and fruit. Both are analogies offered in place of a mechanism, which is the point this record needs them for.
classical.quote: Clearness and expansion (Prasada) of the intellect, firmness of the organs and of the Dhatus (root-principles) of the body, increase of energy (Bala), improved digestive capacity and a late or delayed old age are the blessings which follow a proper administration of purgative remedies. The deranged Pitta of the system, having been fully removed (with the help of a purgative), precludes the possibility of the existence of any Pitta-origined complaint, just as the waters of a tank or any other reservoir of water, having been fully baled out, bar against the possibility of the existence of all aquatic animals and plants living therein.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916), public domain

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section 19
classical.establishes: The exclusion criteria for purgation and the explicit statement that misapplied purgation kills. Together with Charaka Sutrasthana 16 this gives the classical side of the safety question a procedural address, and it establishes that the texts make eligibility, not just technique, the operator's responsibility. The parallel exclusions for emesis stand in the same chapter at Bhishagratna's 11.
classical.quote: Exhibition of purgatives are prohibited in respect of persons of impaired digestion, or of those treated with an excessive application of any emulsive remedy (Sneha-Karma), or of those who are exceedingly corpulent, too old, fatigued, thirsty or intoxicated, or of those suffering from any ulcer. ... A purgative medicine should not be administered before the digestion of a meal previously taken, neither in the diseases due to an abuse of wine, nor in acute catarrh and acute fever or to a newly parturient woman and persons not previously treated with a Sneha (oil or Ghrita). A mild purgative may, however, be administered (in cases of emergency) to a person of extremely Pitta-predominant temperament. Purgatives administered by ignorant physicians to persons who ought not to be purged (often) prove fatal.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916), public domain

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's sections 21-22
classical.establishes: The reason the tradition gives for there being two routes rather than one: the two classes of drug share their active properties and differ only in whether they are digested, so the direction of expulsion follows from the drug's own behaviour. This is the nearest thing in the retrieved classical material to a stated mechanism rather than an analogy, and it is a mechanism about the drug, not about the dosha.
classical.quote: Emetic and purgative remedies, in spite of their possessing in common the powers of motion (Saratva), subtlety, keenness, expansiveness and heat-making properties, tend to remove the injurious and deranged morbific principles (Doshas) of the body in (two) different ways by virtue of their respective inherent qualities (Prakriti). A purgative, in the course of its digestion, carries down with it all the Doshas from the system (loosened and dislodged by virtue of its own specific properties). An emetic, on the other hand, is not digested, owing to (its lightness due to) its inherent extraordinary qualities, but it soon forces its way up with the Doshas (to be) removed.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916), public domain

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section 33
classical.establishes: That the preparatory phase is not optional in Sushruta's scheme and that the reason given for it is an analogy (sapless wood snapping when bent) rather than a mechanism. This is the passage that makes the record's contested question about whether snehana and swedana have an independent rationale a real question in the text and not only in the modern literature. The same chapter's closing aphorism is the one that states it.
classical.quote: The body (health) of a patient to whom a purgative or emetic medicine is administered without first applying Sneha and Sveda thereto breaks up like a piece of sapless wood at the time of bending it. The aggravated Doshas dislodged from their seats in the organism through the effects of Sneha and Sveda and stirred by emollient food are easily expelled by emetics and purgatives.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916), public domain

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section 2
classical.establishes: The operative passage for the oil enema, and with it a second instance of the staging rule: the enema waits seven days on a purgative, is dosed as three-quarters of the decoction enema, and is barred outright in a body not already purified. The stated reason is absorption, which is a mechanism of a kind, though no evidence is offered for it.
classical.quote: An Anuvasana-vasti should be applied to a patient fit to be treated therewith, seven days after the administration of a purgative and after he has regained his strength and taken his meal of rice. Three-quarter-parts of the medicinal solution enjoined to be used in connection with a Niruha-vasti (dry or oilless) in consideration of the age and temperament of the patient form the (full) dose of a Sneha vasti. An enema (Vasti) should be applied after the emission of stool, flatus and urine from the system, since they resist the penetration of the Sneha into the bowels. A Sneha-vasti (emulsive or oleaginous enema) should not be applied to a person whose organism has not been previously cleansed (by an appropriate emetic and purgative). The potency of the Sneha would be able to easily infiltrate into a system previously cleansed in the manner before indicated.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916), public domain

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's sections 1 and 2-A
classical.establishes: The operative passage for the decoction (niruha / asthapana) enema, and the ordering of the two enemas relative to each other: the oil enema comes first and the decoction enema follows it. It also shows the preparatory pair applying to the enemas and not only to emesis and purgation, which the record previously asserted as a general rule without citing it anywhere.
classical.quote: Now we shall discourse on the mode of applying as well as on the treatment with a Nirudha-vasti (Nirudhopakrama-Chikitsitam). The application of an Anuvasana-vasti (enema) should be followed by that of one of the Asthapana class. The body of the patient should be first anointed (with a Sneha) and fomented. Previous to the application of a vasti, the bowels and bladder should be relieved of all (foecal) accumulations (flatus and urine). The clyster (Vasti) should be applied at noon in a well-cleansed chamber, devoid of any gust of wind, and the patient should be laid on his left side on a spacious bed not furnished with any pillows, but a little raised up there where his buttocks would rest, and there should be attendants at his feet.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916), public domain

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section 2
classical.establishes: The rationale for the recovery phase, stated in its own chapter: the procedures themselves leave digestion weak, so the diet that follows is part of the procedure. It is also the one retrieved classical passage that lists bloodletting alongside the four other procedures as something after which this applies, which is suggestive about the membership question but does not enumerate a set of five.
classical.quote: The digestive fire (Kayagni) of a person naturally grows dull after the exhibition of emetics and purgatives, after the administration of a Niruha-Vasti, after the internal application of a Sneha and after blood-letting. It is further lessened by the eating of extremely heavy (difficult of digestion) articles of fare, just as a low or dull fire is extinguished by a heavy load of fuel. Light meals taken in small quantities, on the other hand, increase the digestive fire under these circumstances, just as light fuel in small quantities serves to re-kindle a low fire.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916), public domain

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's sections 3 and 4
classical.establishes: Sushruta's graded re-feeding, and the rule that grades it: the number of gruel meals is set by the measured volume of what was expelled, after which the diet moves on to vilepi. This is the Sushruta counterpart to Charaka's twelve-meal progression, and it makes the recovery phase quantitative rather than merely cautious.
classical.quote: The quantity of diet should be proportionate to the Dosha (morbific diathesis) eliminated from the organism. The quantity of the Dosha or Doshas eliminated consists of three measures, viz., one Prastha, half an Adhaka or an Adhaka (at most). The first is the lowest, the second is the intermediate and the last named measure (one Adhaka) should be deemed as the highest quantity (of the Dosha that can be eliminated under the circumstances). Yavagu (gruel) prepared with a small quantity of rice (Tandula) should be given once, twice or thrice respectively in cases of the eliminated Dosha being a Prastha, half an Adhaka or an Adhaka in quantity.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916), public domain

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section 18
classical.establishes: The operative passage for nasal administration, which the record listed as a component and cited nowhere. It also supports the component gloss: one of the two broad kinds is explicitly S'iro-Virechana, cleansing of the head, which is why nasya is grouped with the eliminative procedures rather than with local treatment. This section goes no further than naming nasya and classifying it, twofold into S'iro-Virechana and Snehana and fivefold into Nasya, S'iro-Virechana, Pratimarsha, Avapida and Pradhamana; it does not describe how a nasya is given, and no claim about the procedure rests on it. In the same chapter, and read verbatim in the same scan, Bhishagratna's section 19 is the S'iro-Virechana drug list with its Kaphaja indications, his section 20 is the timing of administration, and the procedure, including the preparatory fomentation of neck, cheek and forehead, is at his section 21, not at sections 19-20 as this record previously said.
classical.quote: The term "Nasya" (Snuff) is so called from the fact of its being composed of the powders of any drugs or of any Sneha (oleaginous substance) cooked with such drug or drugs, to be stuffed into the nostrils. It may be broadly divided into two kinds, viz. : Siro-Virechana (errhines) and Snehana (contributor of oleaginous principles) ; and may, however, be further grouped under five specific heads, viz. : Nasya, Siro-Virechana, Pratimarsha (a medicated Sneha poured into the nostrils to be discharged into the mouth), Avapida (the expressed juice of any drug put into the nostrils in drops by pressing it with the palms then and there) and Pradhamana (a medicinal snuff blown into the nostrils with the help of a blow pipe). Of these, the Nasya (snuff) Siro-Virechana (errhines) are pre-eminently the most effective.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916), public domain
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's sections 5-12, and the sentence he numbers next
classical.establishes: A third enumeration, and the reason the membership question cannot be settled from this record's sources. The group of procedures named here is oleation, purgation, emesis, asthapana and anuvasana: five, with oleation counted in and with neither nasal administration nor bloodletting present. That is not Charaka's usually reported set and not the set usually attributed to Sushruta. It must be read with care, because the word 'Pancha-karma' appears here as Bhishagratna's parenthetical gloss on an 'etc.' in the Sanskrit and his footnote supplies the members ('The word "Adi" in the text includes emetics, purgatives, Anuvasanam and Asthapanam measures according to their specific Doshas'). So this entry is evidence that the translator read the word as naming this set; it is not evidence that Sushruta enumerated it.
classical.quote: In all cases of seminal disorders as well as in menstrual anomalies, Uttara-Vasti (uretheral or vaginal injection) should be made after having recourse to the application of medicated oil etc. (Sneha-karma), purgatives, emetics, Asthapana and Anuvasana measures. ... In all the four cases when the catamenial blood would be found to be vitiated (by the deranged Vayu, Pittam, Kaphah or Sonita), the preliminary remedial measures of the application of oil etc. purgatives etc. (Pancha-karma) should be first employed
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907-1916), public domain

classical.establishes: Chapter-level address only. Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 14 is the chapter on the two kinds of therapy, and Sutrasthana 18-20 are usually cited as the operative chapters on emesis and purgation, enema and nasal administration. This record makes no claim about what any of those chapters contains. It quotes no Vagbhata, and nothing in this record should be read as evidence about Vagbhata's scheme.

modern.title: Identification of Altered Metabolomic Profiles Following a Panchakarma-based Ayurvedic Intervention in Healthy Subjects: The Self-Directed Biological Transformation Initiative (SBTI).
modern.establishes: In 65 healthy adults undergoing a six-day panchakarma-based residential programme versus 54 controls, a set of 12 plasma phosphatidylcholines decreased with adjusted p below 0.01 after Bonferroni correction, with 57 further metabolites differing at 10 percent FDR. The most-cited piece of hard biochemical data associated with panchakarma.
modern.quality: Empirical with a control group and appropriate multiple-testing correction, published in Scientific Reports, and it carries a published corrigendum. But the intervention bundled herbs, a vegetarian diet, meditation, yoga and massage, so nothing in the design attributes the metabolomic shift to the eliminative procedures rather than to six days of diet change and residential routine. The paper reports a difference in metabolite abundance; it does not test any classical claim about dosha elimination, durability, or clinical benefit, and there is no follow-up.

modern.title: Ayurvedic Therapies to Target the Microbiome: Evidence and Possibilities.
modern.establishes: Review of Ayurvedic therapies as microbiome interventions. Concludes that research connecting Ayurvedic interventions and the gut microbiome is at a nascent stage, and that the small number of studies of virechana and basti prevents categorical conclusions about panchakarma's microbiome effects.
modern.quality: Narrative review, not an empirical study and not a systematic review with a protocol. Its value here is entirely as an honest negative statement from within the field about how thin the mechanistic evidence is for the most obvious candidate mechanism.

modern.title: Evaluation of Vamana and Virechana as Interventions to Decelerate the Aging Process in Healthy Adult Volunteers: Protocol for an Exploratory Single-Arm Clinical Trial.
modern.establishes: Registered protocol for an exploratory single-arm study of seasonal vamana and virechana in 53 healthy adults aged 35 to 65, measuring serum malondialdehyde, total superoxide dismutase and telomerase activity. The abstract records the registration as CTRI/2024/02/062176 and states the design 'is exploratory and lacks a control group'. Its inclusion criteria are classical: madhyama koshtha assessed by questionnaire, and vamanarha and virechanarha status.
modern.quality: A protocol with no results, explicitly single-arm with no control group, on surrogate biomarkers. Recorded because it states from inside the field that the rejuvenative effect of seasonal purification in healthy individuals 'remains a gray area', and because a single-arm design in 2026 indicates the state of the evidence base. The CTRI number reaches this record through this paper's abstract and has not been checked against the CTRI register itself; see notKnown.

modern.title: Efficacy of Virechana and Basti Karma with Shamana therapy in the management of essential hypertension: A comparative study.
modern.establishes: Open randomised comparison of virechana versus basti (both followed by the same palliative preparation) in 33 patients with essential hypertension, reporting greater blood-pressure relief in the virechana arm.
modern.quality: Weak. Small, unblinded, no arm without a panchakarma procedure, both arms confounded by the shared shamana drug, and results given as percentage relief without effect sizes or confidence intervals.

modern.title: Effectiveness, safety, and standard of service delivery: A patient-based survey at a pancha karma therapy unit in a secondary care Ayurvedic hospital.
modern.establishes: Patient-based survey of effectiveness, safety and service delivery at a panchakarma unit in a secondary-care Ayurvedic hospital.
modern.quality: Uncontrolled patient survey, subject to selection and courtesy bias, and not a measure of efficacy. Included as one of the few sources that looks at panchakarma as it is actually delivered rather than as an idealised protocol.

modern.title: Ayurvedic PG education and Panchakarma.
modern.establishes: Editorial from a panchakarma department head on the state of postgraduate panchakarma education.
modern.quality: Editorial, no abstract, no data. Recorded only as documentation that concerns about the standardisation of panchakarma training and practice are raised inside the discipline; it should not be cited for any factual claim about procedure or outcome.

modern.title: Pharmacovigilance study of Ayurvedic medicine in Ayurvedic Teaching Hospital: A prospective survey study.
modern.establishes: Prospective one-year adverse-drug-reaction monitoring study at an Ayurvedic secondary-care teaching hospital in Belgaum, by spontaneous and intensive monitoring, June 2010 to May 2011. Of 84 reported adverse drug events, 52 were confirmed as ADRs, an overall incidence of 1.14 percent in the patient population. Of those 52, the abstract attributes 23 (44.23 percent) to panchakarma, 13 (25.00 percent) to herbal formulations and 6 (11.53 percent) to rasa aushadhi. Gastrointestinal (24) and skin (15) were the commonly affected systems; 30 reactions were moderate and 20 mild in severity, and most patients recovered.
modern.quality: This is the closest thing the searches named in gatheringNotes found to an adverse-event rate for panchakarma under ordinary practice conditions, and it is why the record's previous unbounded negative on that point has been withdrawn. It is still not an adverse-event rate for panchakarma: it is a single-centre, single-year pharmacovigilance survey whose denominator is the hospital's whole patient population rather than the people who underwent a procedure, so no per-procedure rate can be read off it. It depends on spontaneous reporting, which under-counts. The 44.23 percent is a share of confirmed ADRs, not a risk. The authors' own framing is that systematic documentation of ADRs in Ayurveda is lacking and that the work is a step toward pharmacovigilance, not a measure of it.

modern.title: Clinical study to evaluate the effect of Virechanakarma on serum electrolytes.
modern.establishes: Before-and-after measurement of serum electrolytes in 15 patients undergoing virechana, undertaken to ask whether therapeutic purgation causes the electrolyte disturbance that diarrhoeal fluid loss would predict. The authors report the deviations as remaining within the normal range and read that as suggesting virechana is safely applied.
modern.quality: Weak, and recorded for what it attempts rather than what it shows. Fifteen patients, single arm, no control, no blinding, a surrogate endpoint, and a conclusion stated as suggestive by the authors themselves. It is included because it is one of the few retrieved studies that measures a specific harm mechanism the procedure would be expected to produce, which is a different and more testable question than overall safety, and because leaving it out would have left the safety gap looking emptier than the search found it.

modern.title: Lead, mercury, and arsenic in US- and Indian-manufactured Ayurvedic medicines sold via the Internet.
modern.establishes: Of 193 Ayurvedic medicines bought from 25 internet vendors in August to October 2005 and assayed by x-ray fluorescence, 20.7 percent (95 percent CI 15.2 to 27.1) contained detectable lead, mercury or arsenic. Prevalence did not differ between US-manufactured (21.7 percent) and Indian-manufactured (19.5 percent) products (P = .86). Rasa shastra products, which combine herbs with metals and minerals by design, had a higher prevalence (40.6 versus 17.1 percent, P = .007) and higher median lead (11.5 versus 7.0 microg/g) and mercury (20,800 versus 34.5 microg/g) concentrations. All metal-containing products exceeded at least one standard for acceptable daily intake, and 75 percent of them carried Good Manufacturing Practices claims.
modern.quality: A strong study of the thing it studied, in JAMA, with a sampling frame, confidence intervals and a stated assay method. It is cited here with a sharp limit, because the distance between it and this record's subject is the whole of its relevance. It sampled oral products sold to the public over the internet in 2005. It did not sample the emetic, purgative, enema or nasal preparations administered during panchakarma, did not sample medicated ghee, and measured no outcome in any patient. It therefore cannot be read as an adverse-event rate for panchakarma, and it does not tell this record anything about the contamination status of the specific drugs panchakarma uses. What it does establish is that contaminant content in Ayurvedic medicines on open sale was substantial and was not predicted by country of manufacture or by a GMP claim, which is the context any safety discussion of orally administered classical preparations has to sit in. The record carries a notKnown entry for the gap it leaves open. It also carries a published erratum (JAMA 2008 Oct 8;300(14):1652) and a published comment with author reply (JAMA 2009 Jan 21;301(3):271-2), neither of which was retrieved.

records.title: Prajnaparadha (error of judgement as a cause of disease)
records.summary: Prajnaparadha is the Ayurvedic category for disease caused by a failure of judgement rather than by an external agent or by the passage of time. Charaka defines it as the aggregate of harmful acts committed by a person whose dhi (comprehension), dhriti (restraint) and smriti (memory) have lapsed, and lists the acts concretely: forcing or suppressing natural urges, reckless exertion, sexual excess, acting against known self-interest, and conduct driven by envy, pride, fear, anger, greed, delusion and conceit. It is one of the three general causes of disease in Charaka's scheme, alongside unwholesome sensory contact and time, and Sutra 11/43 names the three together. The claim is causal and moral at once. Sharira 1/102 calls prajnaparadha sarvadosha-prakopana, which Kaviratna's own footnote reads as covering both the three bodily doshas and transgressions from duty generally, so how much physiology that compound carries is not settled by the word itself. Sutra 7/51 extends the category even to disease arising from poison, fire, weapons and assault, and in the epidemic chapter at Vimana 3/20 it is placed at the root of the chain that ends in vitiated air, water, land and season. The category also does clinical work in at least one place: at Nidana 7/10 prajnaparadha is given as the cause of exogenous insanity, expressly against the view that acts of a previous life are the cause. Unlike a diagnosis, it is not a named disorder; it is an attributed cause, and Sharira 1/109 locates it in the mind rather than in the body. Everything in this paragraph reports what the classical text asserts. The record makes no claim that any of it has been tested, and the evidence paragraph below states what has not.
records.evidenceState:
WHAT THE CLASSICAL MATERIAL SUPPORTS. The classical claims in this record are quoted and located, in a public-domain English translation for the English and in the Sanskrit original for the Sanskrit. That establishes what Charaka's text says about prajnaparadha. It establishes nothing about whether what the text says is so.

WHAT THE MODERN REFERENCES ARE AND ARE NOT. The earlier version of this paragraph opened by saying that the concept 'rests on classical exegesis alone', while the record's own reference list contained empirical studies. That sentence is withdrawn as self-contradictory. The accurate division is this. Three of the references are exegesis: DOI 10.21760/jaims.v3i4.13295, 10.47468/csne.2021.e01.s09.046 and 10.47070/ayushdhara.v13i1.2545, all non-indexed or non-empirical, all restating the Charaka verses in psychological or neurobiological vocabulary and asserting equivalences with health-risk behaviour, cognitive distortion, akrasia, executive dysfunction or reward pathways, none reporting data, participants or any measurement of prajnaparadha. Two further references are about prajnaparadha and are also not empirical: PMID 22557014, a narrative argument linking the concept to AIDS prevention, and PMID 11611678, a 1982 history-of-medicine paper whose text this record has not read. The remaining three references are genuine empirical work and none of them is about prajnaparadha: PMID 40774071 builds an instrument for triguna, PMID 24191170 and PMID 30653338 measure diagnostic agreement for pulse, tongue, prakriti and agni. They are carried here as comparators for neighbouring constructs, and labelled as such in their own quality fields. So the honest statement is narrower than the old one: no empirical study of prajnaparadha itself was found in the searches named below, and the empirical studies cited here are about other things.

ON RELIABILITY, A CORRECTION. The earlier paragraph asserted that there is 'no inter-rater reliability estimate'. That was wrong at field level and is withdrawn. Inter-rater reliability of Ayurvedic diagnosis has been estimated more than once, and the estimates are low. Kurande and colleagues report average pairwise weighted kappa of 0.07 for pulse, 0.17 for tongue and 0.28 for prakriti across all 105 pairs of fifteen doctors (PMID 24191170). Witt and colleagues report kappa between 0 and 0.4 for prakriti, agni and related constructs in knee osteoarthritis patients (PMID 30653338). What survives of the original point is this: neither study rated prajnaparadha, and no reliability estimate for prajnaparadha turned up in the searches named below.

THE SEARCHES THAT WERE ACTUALLY RUN, on 2026-10-06. PubMed esearch on 'prajnaparadha' returned one record, PMID 22557014, which is a narrative piece on achara rasayana and sadvritta in AIDS prevention and not a study of prajnaparadha. PubMed esearch on 'prajna-aparadha', 'prajnaaparadha' and 'prajna+aparadha' each returned one record, PMID 11611678, Krishan 1982, which is on the concept; so the earlier sentence that a PubMed search returns a single record about a different subject was wrong on the variant spellings and is corrected. PubMed esearch on 'pragyaparadha' returned nothing. Crossref resolved the three exegetical DOIs and confirmed their titles, journals and years. A web search for a validated prajnaparadha assessment instrument returned development and validation work for prakriti and for triguna, and returned no instrument for prajnaparadha. Kaviratna's Charaka was searched in full OCR for the term and for its English renderings.

THE NEGATIVES, SCOPED TO THOSE SEARCHES AND TO NOTHING WIDER. Within what was searched, the record found no operational definition of prajnaparadha, no instrument that measures it, no reliability estimate for it, no prospective cohort in which it is scored at baseline and outcomes are counted, and no trial in which an intervention targeting it is compared against a comparator. These are findings about a bounded search, not about the world. PubMed and Crossref do not index Indian MD and PhD dissertations, and CTRI, Shodhganga, the AYUSH Research Portal and DHARA were not searched for this record. The record therefore does not claim that no prajnaparadha scale or trial exists anywhere; it claims that it found none, and names where it did not look. The corresponding gaps are listed in notKnown rather than left implied here.

TWO ADJACENT OBSERVATIONS WORTH KEEPING IN VIEW. First, the sub-class with the most obvious physiological reading, deliberate forcing or suppression of natural urges at Sharira 1/103, is in principle testable, and nothing found here tests it at the level the doctrine claims. Second, where Ayurvedic mental and constitutional constructs have been operationalised in the literature found here, it has been triguna and prakriti, and measured agreement for the better-developed of those was poor to fair. The record offers no estimate of how a construct as broad and as morally loaded as prajnaparadha would fare, and declines to predict that it would fare worse, because it has no basis for the prediction.

STATING IT PLAINLY. In the literature found here, prajnaparadha is an attribution, not a finding.

contested.question: How wide is the category? Charaka gives two definitions that do not obviously coincide.
positions: Sharira Sthana 1 defines it narrowly as the acts of a person whose dhi, dhriti and smriti are specifically impaired (Sharira 1/102, Kaviratna 109), which makes the impairment the diagnostic entry point.
Sutra Sthana 11 defines it as the mithyayoga of speech, mind and body, that is, any harmful voluntary exertion whatever (Kaviratna's Sutra 11, verse 41), which makes the category nearly unbounded.
Sutra 7/51 widens it again in a different direction, to disease arising from poison, fire, weapons and assault, which are not voluntary acts of the sufferer at all.

Commentators generally harmonise the first two by treating the second as the operational test and the first as the mechanism, but the texts themselves do not say this, and this record has not read a commentary in a quotable edition.

contested.question: Is prajnaparadha genuinely independent of the other two general causes?
positions: The classical position treats the three as a coordinate triad of distinct causes, stated as such at Sutra 11/43: asatmyendriyartha-samyoga, prajnaparadha and parinama, 'each subdivided into three kinds, constitute the causes of disease'.

Kaviratna, translating in 1896-1913, objected in his own footnote to Sharira 1.135 that the first and third causes 'are scarcely exclusive of each other' and that diseases under the second may be due to the same causes as the first and the third, concluding 'Altogether, the classification does not seem to be scientific'. This is a contemporaneous internal criticism from within the translation tradition, not a modern one, and it is the translator's voice rather than the text's.
Modern Ayurvedic authors generally treat prajnaparadha as the superordinate cause on the strength of Vimana 3, which makes the triad asymmetric rather than coordinate.

contested.question: Is prajnaparadha a moral category, a cognitive one, or both?
positions: The Vimana 3 chain runs through adharma and prior sinful acts, which reads as moral and karmic.

Sharira 1/109 (Kaviratna 116) locates it entirely in the mind, manaso gocaram hi tat, and Kaviratna's note to that verse excludes the physical element of the act, which reads as cognitive. The exclusion is his gloss, not the verse's words.
Nidana 7/10 sets prajnaparadha against the view that acts of a previous life cause exogenous insanity, which cuts the other way: here the text prefers a present cognitive fault over a karmic one.
Contemporary authors usually recast it as health-risk behaviour or lifestyle error, which drops both the karmic and the faculty-impairment content without acknowledging the substitution.

contested.question: Does prajnaparadha make Ayurvedic etiology unfalsifiable? Added in this revision in answer to a critic finding.
positions: The case that it does, assembled from this record's own quoted material: the enumeration of acts closes with 'These and such other acts' (Kaviratna Sharira 1.115), so no act is specified as falling outside the category; Sutra 11, verse 41 sweeps in 'everything, in brief, that is an injurious or harmful exertion of speech, mind and body, though omitted in the above enumeration'; Sutra 7/51 extends the category to disease from poison, fire, weapons and assault; and Vimana 3/20 extends it to vitiated air, water, land and season. On that reading there is no disease and no treatment failure that the category cannot absorb after the fact, and no observation that could count against an attribution.

Kaviratna reached a related verdict from inside the translation tradition, in his footnote to Sharira 1.135: the classification 'does not seem to be scientific'. His ground was overlap between the causes rather than unfalsifiability as such, so this supports the objection without being the same objection.

What would settle it in the other direction is an operational definition that specifies, in advance, what would NOT count as prajnaparadha. The record has not found one; see the evidence paragraph and notKnown.

A defence is available to the tradition, that the category is prescriptive and preventive rather than predictive, which would make falsifiability the wrong test. Sutra 7/53 is prescriptive in exactly that way. The record records this as an available reading and not as a sourced position, because it has not found it argued in print; the gap is listed in notKnown.

contested.question: Does the category import blame onto the sick, and is it clinical or moral in use? Added in this revision in answer to a critic finding. This sharpens the moral-or-cognitive question above into a question about who is held at fault.
positions: That it does locate fault in the sufferer: Sutra 7/51 assigns even diseases from poison, fire, weapons and assault to the patient's own prajna erring, prajna tesv aparadhyati. On the face of the verse, the victim of an assault is the party whose judgement is at fault.

That the fault is collective rather than personal: in Vimana 3 the agents are the foremost inhabitants of a country, city, town or village who 'transgressing righteousness, set the example of unrighteousness', and the sick are the population that suffers the consequence. Read that way the chapter is closer to a social-determinants argument than to patient blame.

That its use at Nidana 7/10 is clinical rather than moral: there it functions as the hetu that distinguishes agantuja unmada from the dosha-born varieties, which is diagnostic work, and it is preferred over the past-life-karma account. Whether substituting a present fault for a past-life fault lessens the blame or merely relocates it is not something the text addresses.

The record has not retrieved a source that argues the ethical question directly. The one indexed paper that engages the karma question by title is PMID 11611678, and its text was not retrieved, so nothing is attributed to it.

contested.question: Is prajnaparadha one of three parallel causes, or the cause of the other two? Added in this revision in answer to a critic finding.
positions: Parallel: Sutra 11/43 states the three as a coordinate triad, trayas trividha-vikalpa hetavo vikaranam, three causes each threefold, with no priority among them. Sharira 1/98 likewise lists the three together as the causes of duhkha.

Upstream: Sharira 1/102 calls prajnaparadha sarvadosha-prakopana; Sutra 7/51 makes it the fault behind agantu disease, which is the territory of the other causes; and Vimana 3/20 makes it the yoni, the source, of adharma and of prior acts, and so of vitiated season and element, which is the territory of kala.

A structural observation that can be read either way: Sharira 1 lists the three causes once at 1/98 and then explains only prajnaparadha at length, 1/99 to 1/109. That is either emphasis or subordination, and the chapter does not say which.
Kaviratna's footnote to Sharira 1.135 observes the same asymmetry from the translator's side, that the causes are not mutually exclusive, without resolving the architecture.
The texts gathered here do not state which architecture is intended, and this record does not choose.

notKnown: Whether prajnaparadha can be scored reliably by two independent trained examiners at all. No kappa for prajnaparadha was found in the searches named in evidenceState. Kappas have been published for other Ayurvedic constructs: 0.07, 0.17 and 0.28 for pulse, tongue and prakriti (PMID 24191170), and between 0 and 0.4 for prakriti, agni and related constructs (PMID 30653338).
Whether any measurable outcome follows from a prajnaparadha attribution that does not follow equally from ordinary behavioural risk-factor assessment.
Whether the specific classical claim that habitual suppression of natural urges causes the enumerated downstream disorders holds up in any controlled observation.
How prajnaparadha is to be distinguished in practice from the mithyahara-vihara (dietary and behavioural error) named in disease-specific nidana chapters, since the act lists overlap heavily.

Whether the dhi/dhriti/smriti triad corresponds to any separable cognitive functions, or whether it is one faculty described three ways. The only sourced statement this record has on the point is Kaviratna's footnote to Sharira 1.105, in his own voice: 'Dhi, Dhriti, and Smriti are explained by the Commentators as implying only different functions of the Understanding or buddhi.' That is the translator reporting the commentators collectively, with none of them named at that point, and the earlier version of this record stated flatly that 'Charaka's own commentators say the latter', which went further than the source allows.

Whether Chakrapani and Gangadhara in fact disagree over whether the dhi/dhriti/smriti triad is a psychological faculty model or a soteriological one. A critic finding asserts this is a live disagreement between them. The record could not verify it and does not assert it either way. What was checked: Kaviratna's public-domain Charaka, which names Gangadhara and Chakrapani frequently elsewhere but, at Sharira Sthana 1, reports the commentators only collectively and only on the faculty question. No public-domain English translation of the Ayurveda Dipika or of Gangadhara's Jalpakalpataru is available to quote, and the Sanskrit of neither commentary was retrieved for this record.

Whether the epidemic claim of Vimana 3, that collective moral failure precedes vitiation of air, water, land and season, is intended literally, allegorically, or as a social-determinants argument. The sources do not settle this. The Sanskrit of 3/20 does carry va, 'or', in tanmulam va'satkarma purvakrtam, which loosens the chain the English presents as fixed, but it does not settle the register.
What, if anything, distinguishes an act of prajnaparadha from an act simply done in ignorance, given that the definition requires impaired judgement rather than culpable knowledge.

Whether sarvadosha-prakopana at Sharira 1/102 means the three bodily doshas, transgressions from duty generally, or both. Kaviratna's footnote takes it both ways and then says Charaka 'has his eye, however, on wind, bile, and phlegm in particular'. That is a translator's judgement on an ambiguous compound and the record does not promote it to doctrine, so how much physiology the claim carries is open.

Whether Ashtanga Hridaya and Ashtanga Sangraha carry this doctrine, and in what form. The earlier version of this record asserted that both 'carry the same triad of general causes and the same dhi-dhriti-smriti definition in abbreviated form', with no chapter, no verse and no quote. That assertion is withdrawn and the citation removed; see citationsRemoved. Two things point against it as stated: Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 1 organises the causes of disease as the hina, mithya and ati yoga of kala, artha and karma, which is a different scheme from Charaka's named triad, and the prajnaparadha locus attributed to Vagbhata by wisdomlib is Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 4.33-34, in the chapter on prevention, which parallels Charaka's Sutra 7/53 rather than the Sharira 1 definition. Neither was verified against a Sanskrit edition for this record and no public-domain English translation of Vagbhata exists to quote, so this record now asserts nothing about Vagbhata. The locus to check first is Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 4.33-34.

Whether the unindexed Indian MD and PhD dissertation literature contains prajnaparadha assessment scales. A critic finding states that several theses develop them. The record cannot confirm or deny it: Shodhganga, the AYUSH Research Portal and DHARA were not searched for this record, and PubMed and Crossref do not index those theses. This gap is the main reason the negatives in evidenceState are scoped to named searches rather than stated absolutely.
Whether CTRI holds any registered trial with prajnaparadha as an eligibility criterion, an exposure or an outcome. CTRI was not searched for this record.

Whether the defence that prajnaparadha is a preventive and prescriptive frame rather than a predictive one has been argued anywhere in print, which is what would be needed to turn it from an available reading into a sourced position at contested question 4.

What Krishan 1982 (PMID 11611678) argues. It is the one indexed paper found whose subject is the concept itself, it carries no abstract in PubMed, and its full text was not retrieved. Its contents are therefore unknown to this record and nothing is attributed to it.

components.gloss: Lapse of comprehension: applying the mind injudiciously to what is permanent and what is changeable, to good and evil
Lapse of restraint: the mind, drawn to objects, can no longer be held back from harmful courses
Lapse of memory: the mind overwhelmed by passion and heedlessness swerves from what it knows to be true
Forcing natural urges before they arise and suppressing them when they are pronounced; the most concrete and most often cited class of prajnaparadha acts
Rash or violent exertion, including sexual excess
Undertaking acts injudiciously and postponing acts that ought to be done
Envy, pride, fear, anger, greed, delusion, arrogance and error, and any act arising from them or injurious to the body
In Charaka Vimana 3 the chain runs prajnaparadha to adharma to vitiation of air, water, land and time, making prajnaparadha the root of collective as well as individual disease

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson VII (Inadvisability of suppressing the urgings of Nature / Naveganadharaniya), verse 49 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 49 (Kaviratna); the same verse is numbered Sutra 7/51 in the standard numbering printed by carakasamhitaonline, where the Sanskrit was verified
classical.establishes: That the category reaches beyond voluntary self-harm: diseases classed as agantu (exogenous), including those from poison, fire, weapons and assault, are referred to the sufferer's own prajna erring. The Sanskrit says prajna tesv aparadhyati, 'the prajna errs in respect of these'. This is the widest causal extension of the concept found in the material gathered here, and it is the textual basis for the objections recorded in contested questions 4, 5 and 6.
classical.quote: Regarding those extraneous diseases of men that arise from the action of superhuman beings and planets, of poison, of (hot and unhealthy) winds, of fire, and of blows and weapons, (and of curses and incantations), people's own understandings are to blame.
classical.sanskrit: ये भूतविषवाय्वग्निसम्प्रहारादिसम्भवाः। नृणामागन्तवो रोगाः प्रज्ञा तेष्वपराध्यति॥५१॥

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson VII, verse 50 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 50 (Kaviratna, printed in the scan as a damaged '60'); standard Sutra 7/52
classical.establishes: That the manovikaras (mental disturbances) are themselves said to be prajnaparadha-born. The Sanskrit compound prajnaparadhaja appears here in the verse body, which matters because Kaviratna's English never transliterates the term.
classical.quote: Jealousy, grief, fear, wrath, pride, malice, and such other mental derangements have all been said to arise from faults of the understanding.
classical.sanskrit: ईर्ष्याशोकभयक्रोधमानद्वेषादयश्च ये। मनोविकारास्तेऽप्युक्ताः सर्वे प्रज्ञापराधजाः॥५२॥

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson VII, verses 51-52 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 51-52 (Kaviratna, printed in the scan as a damaged '51-62'); standard Sutra 7/53
classical.establishes: The preventive protocol attached to the category: abandonment of prajnaparadha, quieting of the senses, memory, knowledge of place, time and self, and following the conduct of the good. Note a divergence between the two columns that bears directly on this project's translator-voice problem: the Sanskrit opens tyagah prajnaparadhanam, 'abandonment of the prajnaparadhas', while Kaviratna renders the same words 'the abandonment of unrighteous practices' and drops the term. Kaviratna's English conceals prajnaparadha here rather than inventing it.
classical.quote: The abandonment of unrighteous practices, the restraint of the senses, the cultivation of the memory, knowledge of place, of time, and of one's own self, and treading in the footsteps of the righteous, constitute the method that is laid down for the prevention of all extraneous diseases of even those whose understandings are vitiated by faults. As regards the man of intelligence, he should, prior to the appearance of disease, accomplish all those acts which he regards to be beneficial for himself.
classical.sanskrit: त्यागः प्रज्ञापराधानामिन्द्रियोपशमः स्मृतिः। देशकालात्मविज्ञानं सद्वृत्तस्यानुवर्तनम्॥५३॥

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson XI (Tistraishaniya), verse 41 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 41 (Kaviratna). This revision could not pin a single standard verse number to it. carakasamhitaonline carries the karma / vak-manah-sharira-pravritti definition with its atiyoga, ayoga and mithyayoga at Sutra 11/39, and Kaviratna's verse 41 is the closing sentence of that definitional block; the earlier version of this record asserted no standard number here and this revision does not invent one.
classical.establishes: A second definitional locus for prajnaparadha in Sutra Sthana, distinct from the Sharira Sthana one. What it establishes is that prajnaparadha, Kaviratna's 'faults of the Understanding', is predicated of karma, the exertion of speech, mind and body, under all three degrees of correlation and not of mithyayoga alone: 'Correlation, as shown above, is of three kinds. These three kinds of acts or exertions are regarded as faults of the Understanding.' What this aphorism adds to the enumeration that precedes it is a catch-all for the third degree only, that any 'injurious or harmful exertion of speech, mind and body, though omitted in the above enumeration, should be taken as falling within injudicious correlation in respect of those three'. The record therefore should not call this a definition of prajnaparadha as mithyayoga, and should not call it wider on that ground. It should be read instead as the act-based definition: prajnaparadha is karma of speech, mind and body in all three vikalpas, standing as one of the three causal heads that Kaviratna's next aphorism names alongside the improper contact of sense-objects with the mind and Time or parinama. Verified as body text, not footnote: it stands in the running translation with Kaviratna's aphorism number 41 printed after it.
classical.quote: Without referring to excess of correlation in respect of these, everything, in brief, that is an injurious or harmful exertion of speech, mind and body, though omitted in the above enumeration, should be taken as falling within injudicious correlation in respect of those three. Correlation, as shown above, is of three kinds. These three kinds of acts or exertions are regarded as faults of the Understanding.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana, Lesson XI (Tistraishaniya), verses 42-43 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 42-43 (Kaviratna); standard Sutra 11/43 for the second sentence, where the Sanskrit was verified. In this chapter Kaviratna's number and the standard number coincide.
classical.establishes: The trividha hetu stated as a coordinate triad, each member threefold, with prajnaparadha named in the Sanskrit. Added in this revision because this is the verse that makes the three causes parallel, and it is therefore the counterweight to Sutra 7/51, Sharira 1/102 and Vimana 3/20, which make prajnaparadha upstream. The tension between them is contested question 6.
classical.quote: Thus are the three subjects treated of, viz., the improper contact of objects of sense with the Mind, faults of the Understanding, and Time or Parinama. These three, (viz., the improper contact of objects of sense with the Mind, faults of the Understanding, and Time,) each subdivided into three kinds, constitute the causes of disease. Connection therewith in normal or judicious proportions is the cause of health.
classical.sanskrit: इत्यसात्म्येन्द्रियार्थसंयोगः, प्रज्ञापराधः, परिणामश्चेति त्रयस्त्रिविधविकल्पा हेतवो विकाराणां

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I (Katidhapurushiya), verse 105 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 105 (Kaviratna); standard Sharira 1/98, confirmed in this revision by matching the Sanskrit of 1/98 against this rendering
classical.establishes: The trividha hetu as stated in Sharira Sthana: the three general causes of duhkha are lapse of dhi/dhriti/smriti, time, and unwholesome contact of sense objects. The Sanskrit says duhkha-hetavah, causes of sorrow or suffering, which is what Kaviratna renders; the chapter does not say vyadhi-hetavah here.
classical.quote: Loss of Understanding, of Firmness, and of Memory, time in respect of the accession of disease and of the administration of correctives, as also the accession of objects unaccordant with the senses, these should be known as the causes of sorrow.
classical.sanskrit: धीधृतिस्मृतिविभ्रंशः सम्प्राप्तिः कालकर्मणाम्| असात्म्यार्थागमश्चेति ज्ञातव्या दुःखहेतवः||९८||

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verses 106-108 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 106-108 (Kaviratna); standard Sharira 1/99-101 as located by carakasamhitaonline
classical.establishes: The three lapses defined one by one. Added in this revision because the first three entries of this record's components array glossed dhi-vibhramsha, dhriti-vibhramsha and smriti-vibhramsha with no citation behind them; this is the passage they were glossing. Kaviratna's footnote to verse 105 adds, in his own voice and not Charaka's, that the commentators explain dhi, dhriti and smriti as 'implying only different functions of the Understanding or buddhi', which is the sourced basis for the notKnown item on whether the triad is three faculties or one.
classical.quote: An injudicious attention to what is unchangeable and what is changeable, as also to good and evil, is regarded as loss of understanding, since the understanding implies a judicious application to things. The mind that is prone to earthly objects is incapable of being restrained from evil courses owing to loss of firmness, for firmness implies restraint of inclinations. The swerving of the mind of a person who is overwhelmed by passion and heedlessness from the knowledge of truth, is known as loss of memory, for that which should be remembered (viz., the knowledge of truth) dwells in memory.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verse 109 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 109 (Kaviratna); standard Sharira 1/102, confirmed in this revision against the Sanskrit
classical.establishes: The formal definition of prajnaparadha as the asubha karma of a person whose dhi, dhriti and smriti are vibhrashta, and the claim that it is sarvadosha-prakopana. How much that compound carries is open: Kaviratna's footnote to this verse states, in his own voice, that 'Dosha' in sarvadoshaprakopanam 'has reference as much to the faults, (wind, bile and phlegm) as to all trangressions from duty', and that Charaka 'has his eye, however, on wind, bile, and phlegm in particular'. That is the translator reading an ambiguity, not the text resolving it, and this record does not treat the physiological reading as settled.
classical.quote: The evil acts which a man who has lost understanding, firmness, and memory, perpetrates, should be known to constitute what is called fault of judgment. This (fault of judgment) is provocative of all the faults.
classical.sanskrit: धीधृतिस्मृतिविभ्रष्टः कर्म यत् कुरुतेऽशुभम्| प्रज्ञापराधं तं विद्यात् सर्वदोषप्रकोपणम्||१०२||

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verse 110 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 110 (Kaviratna); standard Sharira 1/103
classical.establishes: The concrete opening of the enumerated list of prajnaparadha acts. The urge-forcing and urge-suppression items are the ones with the most obvious physiological reading, which is why they are singled out in the evidence paragraph as the testable residue.
classical.quote: The expulsion (by force) of urine and stools and other excreta (before the calls are distinct), suppression of the same (when the urgings are pronounced), indulgence in acts of rashness, over-indulgence in women,

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verses 114-115 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 114-115 (Kaviratna); standard Sharira 1/107-108
classical.establishes: That the category is open-ended: the enumeration closes with 'and such other acts', so prajnaparadha is not a closed list. This is the textual basis for the unfalsifiability objection recorded at contested question 4.
classical.quote: Envy, pride, fear, wrath, cupidity, stupefaction, arrogance, and errors, or all baneful acts arising from these, and all acts injurious to the body: These and such other acts which arise from passion and stupefaction, are regarded by sages as disease-producing faults of judgment.

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Sharira Sthana, Lesson I, verse 116 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 116 (Kaviratna); standard Sharira 1/109, confirmed in this revision against the Sanskrit
classical.establishes: That prajnaparadha is of the manas: manaso gocaram hi tat. Separately, and in his own voice rather than Charaka's, Kaviratna's footnote to this verse says 'Acts have two elements, viz., mental and physical. The physical element is excluded. Acts that are faults of judgment are, the Rishi says, all mental.' The exclusion of the physical element is Kaviratna's gloss and is cited here as his, not as doctrine.
classical.quote: Injudicious apprehension of things by the understanding, as also a setting of one's self to injudicious acts, should be known as fault of judgment. That which is called fault of judgment really concerns the mind.
classical.sanskrit: बुद्ध्या विषमविज्ञानं विषमं च प्रवर्तनम्| प्रज्ञापराधं जानीयान्मनसो गोचरं हि तत्||१०९||

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Nidana Sthana, Lesson VII (Nidana of Insanity / Unmada), verse 13 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 13 (Kaviratna); standard Nidana 7/10, matched in this revision by comparing the Sanskrit of 7/10 with Kaviratna's rendering
classical.establishes: The one place in the material gathered here where prajnaparadha does clinical work rather than general etiological work: it is given as the hetu of agantuja unmada, the fifth and exogenous variety of insanity, and is set expressly against the rival view that acts of a previous life are the cause. Added in this revision; the earlier version of this record cited no Nidana locus and so carried the claim that prajnaparadha is 'not a diagnosis' without the counter-instance in view.
classical.quote: Some say that the evil acts of previous lives are the cause of this variety of Insanity (viz., that which is called Accidental). But the illustrious Punarvasu of Atri's race declared that fault of judgment is the cause.
classical.sanskrit: तस्य च हेतुः प्रज्ञापराध एवेति भगवान् पुनर्वसुरात्रेयः

classical.text: Charaka Samhita, Vimana Sthana, Lesson III (Janapadoddhvamsaniya), verse 23 in Kaviratna's numbering
classical.verse: 23 (Kaviratna); standard Vimana 3/20, confirmed in this revision against the Sanskrit
classical.establishes: That prajnaparadha is made the ultimate root of epidemic disease, through adharma and through the vitiation of air, water, land and season. This is the strongest and most sweeping causal claim made for the concept in the material gathered here. One qualification visible in the Sanskrit and flattened in the English: tanmulam va'satkarma purvakrtam carries va, 'or', so the prior-acts link is offered as an alternative root rather than a second term in a fixed chain. A second qualification from the surrounding verses: the agent in this chapter is collective, the leading inhabitants of a region, which is the basis for the social-blame position at contested question 5.
classical.quote: Unto him the illustrious son of Atri said, O Agnivesa, the perversity that arises of all these, viz., air and the rest, has unrighteousness for its root. That unrighteousness has for its root sinful acts committed before. The source of both these (viz., unrighteousness and sinful acts), is faults of the understanding.
classical.sanskrit: सर्वेषामप्यग्निवेश! वाय्वादीनां यद्वैगुण्यमुत्पद्यते तस्य मूलमधर्मः, तन्मूलं वाऽसत्कर्म पूर्वकृतं; तयोर्योनिः प्रज्ञापराध एव|

classical.text: Charak Samhita New Edition (carakasamhitaonline.com), encyclopedic entry 'Prajnaparadha', DOI 10.47468/csne.2021.e01.s09.046
classical.establishes: Standard-numbering locations of the same material. This revision independently verified, by matching Sanskrit against Kaviratna's rendering, the following: Sutra 7/51, 7/52 and 7/53; Sutra 11/43; Sharira 1/98, 1/102 and 1/109; Nidana 7/10; Vimana 3/20. The following are recorded as located by this source and NOT independently verified here: the threefold cause at Sutra 20/5, Sutra 28/7 and Nidana 1/3; the dhi/dhriti/smriti definitions at Sharira 1/99, 1/100 and 1/101; and the mithyayoga definition at Sutra 11/39. The page prints the enumerated acts as the range Sharira 1/102-108, which includes the definition verse; on the verse-by-verse matching done here the acts run standard 1/103-108 with 1/102 the definition and 1/109 the mind verse. The underlying full English text on this site is the 1949 Gulabkunverba translation and is in copyright, so nothing English was quoted from it; the Devanagari and IAST verses quoted in the entries above are the Sanskrit original and were taken from this site's verse headers.

modern.establishes: Argues that prajnaparadha is the root cause of mental disorder and maps it onto contemporary psychiatric categories.
modern.quality: Narrative conceptual review, not an empirical study. No data, no participants, no measurement of prajnaparadha. Published in a non-indexed Ayurvedic journal; the DOI resolves in Crossref to 'Contemplating the relevance of Prajnaparadha as a root cause of Mental Disorder', Journal of Ayurveda and Integrated Medical Sciences, 2018, and the title was confirmed there in this revision. It restates classical doctrine in modern vocabulary, which is the dominant pattern for this concept. Exegesis, not evidence about the world.

modern.establishes: The most careful exposition of the concept found in this revision's searches, with full classical referencing and a survey of commentarial positions.
modern.quality: Encyclopedic exegesis with a registered DOI, produced under an Ayurvedic academic consortium; Crossref resolves it to 'Prajnaparadha', Charak Samhita New Edition, 2021. It is a secondary textual resource, not evidence about the world. Valuable for locating verses and for Sanskrit, and this revision used it for exactly that. Worthless as clinical evidence. Its English translation layer is the in-copyright 1949 Gulabkunverba text and was not quoted.

modern.establishes: Proposes a correlation between prajnaparadha, triguna and the neurobiology of addiction.
modern.quality: Narrative correlative review in a non-indexed journal; Crossref resolves it to 'Ayurvedic Conceptualization of Addiction: A Correlative Study of Prajnaparadha, Triguna, and Neurobiological Reward Pathways', AYUSHDHARA, dated 15 March 2026, confirmed in this revision. It proposes the mapping rather than testing it; no neurobiological data are generated and no operational definition of prajnaparadha is offered. Exegesis, not evidence about the world.

modern.title: The meaning of prajnā-aparādha and karma in Ayurveda.
modern.journal: Bull Indian Inst Hist Med Hyderabad
modern.establishes: That PubMed does index one article whose subject is prajnaparadha itself: Krishan Y, 'The meaning of prajna-aparadha and karma in Ayurveda', Bulletin of the Indian Institute of History of Medicine (Hyderabad) 1982;12(1-4):28-33. Added in this revision because the earlier evidence paragraph stated that a PubMed search on the term returns a single record about a different subject, and that was wrong once the variant spellings were tried.
modern.quality: Bibliographic record only. Retrieved by PubMed esearch on 'prajna-aparadha', 'prajnaaparadha' and 'prajna+aparadha' and resolved by esummary on 2026-10-06; indexed for MEDLINE; no abstract is indexed, no DOI is registered, and the full text was not retrieved. The citation was independently corroborated against the Vienna Caraka research bibliography. Nothing whatever is asserted here about its argument, its conclusions or its quality, because the record has not read it. It is cited for one fact only: that such a paper exists and is indexed.

modern.title: Role of achara rasayana and sadvrta in the prevention of AIDS.
modern.establishes: The single record returned by a PubMed search on the spelling 'prajnaparadha'. It is a narrative argument that achara rasayana and sadvritta, good conduct for self and society, can prevent diseases 'basically caused by Prajnaparadha', and that prajnaparadha 'also appears responsible for the spread of AIDS'.
modern.quality: Narrative conceptual piece in Ancient Science of Life, 2001;20(3):62-4, PMCID PMC3336402. Not a study of prajnaparadha: no data, no participants, no measurement, no comparison. Added in this revision so that the search result the earlier evidence paragraph referred to is actually in the reference list and checkable, rather than being characterised in prose that the reader cannot audit. The quoted phrases are from the PubMed abstract.

modern.title: Development of an instrument for screening mental health based on Ayurvedic concept of Triguna.
modern.establishes: That a neighbouring Ayurvedic mental construct, triguna, can be turned into a 38-item self-report screening instrument with test-retest ICC 0.8 and Cronbach's alpha 0.9, validated against the WHO Subjective Well-being Inventory in 400 participants (sensitivity 75.4 percent, specificity 78.2 percent).
modern.quality: Genuine empirical psychometric work, single research group, single Indian state for the primary sample, no independent replication found here. Included as a contrast: it shows that operationalisation of an Ayurvedic mental category is possible. The instrument does not measure prajnaparadha and the paper does not claim to. The earlier version of this entry added that the study 'also shows that nobody has done this for prajnaparadha'; that inference is withdrawn, because one paper about triguna cannot establish what does not exist elsewhere. What the record can say is in the evidence paragraph, scoped to the searches named there.

modern.title: Interrater reliability of diagnostic methods in traditional Indian ayurvedic medicine.
modern.establishes: That inter-rater reliability of Ayurvedic diagnosis has been estimated, and estimated low. Fifteen registered Ayurvedic doctors independently examined twenty healthy subjects; weighted kappa was computed for all 105 doctor pairs. From the abstract: 'the pairwise kappas ranged from poor to slight, slight to fair, and fair to moderate for pulse, tongue, and prakriti assessments, respectively. The average pairwise kappa for pulse, tongue, and prakriti was 0.07, 0.17, and 0.28, respectively.' The authors conclude that 'the results demonstrate a low level of reliability for all types of assessment made by doctors', while noting that 'Prakriti assessment appears reliable when questionnaire and software assessment are used'.
modern.quality: Empirical reliability study from an Aalborg University group, published in Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine; PMID and DOI both resolved in this revision and the kappa figures are quoted verbatim from the PubMed abstract. Healthy subjects rather than patients, twenty of them, one centre. Prajnaparadha was not among the assessed items. Added in this revision for one reason: the earlier evidence paragraph asserted that no inter-rater reliability estimate exists, and that was wrong at field level. It is this study, together with PMID 30653338, that makes the corrected statement possible: reliability has been measured in Ayurvedic diagnosis, and never for prajnaparadha.

modern.title: Reliability of Ayurvedic Diagnosis for Knee Osteoarthritis Patients: A Nested Diagnostic Study Within a Randomized Controlled Trial.
modern.establishes: In 30 knee osteoarthritis patients rated by 4 Ayurvedic experts, chance-corrected inter-rater agreement for core constitutional constructs such as prakriti and agni was fair to poor, with kappa values between 0 and 0.4, despite 95 percent consensus agreement on the final diagnosis.
modern.quality: Well-designed diagnostic reliability study nested in a randomised trial, from a Charite-led group. Small sample, single disease. Prajnaparadha was not among the items rated, which is itself informative: a study specifically built to test Ayurvedic diagnostic reliability did not include it as a ratable item. Alongside PMID 24191170, this is the second of the two studies that refute the earlier absolute claim that no inter-rater reliability estimate exists in this field.

records.title: Rasayana theory
records.summary: Rasayana is the branch of Ayurveda concerned with measures taken to improve the quality of the bodily tissues rather than to remove a disease. Charaka defines it etymologically as the means of imparting superior rasa and the dhatus derived from it, and attaches a list of claimed outcomes. The exact content of that list is translation-dependent and this record now carries two renderings of it rather than one (see contested). It is delivered either as an intensive indoor regimen in a purpose-built chamber (kutipraveshika) or as a method pursued without such seclusion (vatatapika); Charaka names both at aphorism 16 of the rasayana lesson, and no statement ranking one above the other was found in Kaviratna's text of that lesson. Both classical authorities require prior purification: Sushruta compares rasayana given to an uncleansed body to dyeing a dirty cloth, and Charaka's first pada makes a cleansed bowel the physician's precondition for administering it. Vajikarana is not a separate subject appended to rasayana but is defined inside the same lesson, as the second of the two kinds of medicine that increase the ojas of a healthy person. The tradition also extends the category to conduct (achara rasayana), though on Kaviratna's text the passage describes a person whose conduct qualifies him as a user of rasayana and whose faults, uncast off, would stop rasayana working; the stronger reading, that conduct alone substitutes for the drug, is Kaviratna's footnote rather than his translation of the verses. Modern research has largely reinterpreted the category as antioxidant and immunomodulatory pharmacology of individual formulations, which is a substitution of subject matter rather than a test of the theory, though the single-herb rasayana dravyas carry a human randomised literature with cognitive and clinical endpoints that polyherbal-formulation research does not.
records.evidenceState: Rasayana has more experimental work attached than most concepts in this cluster, and the shape of that work matters more than its volume. Taking the eleven modern references in this record by design class: three are human randomised trials of classical polyherbal rasayana formulations, of which one tests a disease indication (iron deficiency anaemia) rather than the rejuvenative claim; three are systematic reviews or meta-analyses of randomised trials of single herbs (Bacopa monnieri, Withania somnifera twice); three are narrative reviews with no primary data; and two are preclinical, one in Drosophila and one in rats. The record previously presented a count of eight references without this breakdown, which overstated the coverage, and it described the tested set as 'chiefly Amalaki rasayana and Chyawanaprash', which was true of the references then gathered and not true of the literature. The single-herb rasayana dravyas do carry randomised human trials with validated cognitive endpoints, and the Withania meta-analysis pools twenty of them. That corrects the record's former position that no human work exists on the cognitive claims. It does not make the classical claim supported, for four reasons that the record now states rather than implies. The single-herb trials test standardised extracts over eight to twelve weeks, not classical formulations under a classical regimen, and none has a longevity endpoint on any relevant timescale. Whether those herbs are even the drugs the classical medhya list names depends on plant identifications that the commentarial tradition itself disputes, Kaviratna recording Gangadhara's dissent on mandukaparni in a footnote. The structural parts of the theory remain untested in anything retrieved here: the shodhana precondition that both principal texts make a gate on administration, the achara rasayana passage, and whether the classical grouping picks out drugs sharing any property. And the yardstick is stated plainly in the texts now quoted, which promise a hundred years of retentive memory, verbatim recall on a single hearing, and in one place five hundred years of life. Against that, a 45-day improvement in a DNA repair assay and an SMD of 0.52 on memory tests are not small results in the wrong direction; they are results about a different question. The honest position is that several rasayana substances have genuine randomised human evidence on short-term cognitive, anxiety and sleep endpoints, that one classical formulation has a single good placebo-controlled trial on a cellular surrogate, and that rasayana theory as a theory remains untested.

contested.question: Is prior shodhana actually necessary for rasayana to work?
positions: Sushruta's chapter 27 states it categorically, with the dyed-cloth analogy as justification. Charaka's first pada states it too, and now with a quote: the physician administers the formulation having ascertained that the bowels have been properly cleansed (Kaviratna aphorism 27). The record previously asserted the Charaka parallel without a citation; it is now sourced.
The rasayana trials located here administered the formulation or extract without prior purification, and several reported positive results, which is at minimum in tension with the classical rule.

No study located compared rasayana with and without preceding shodhana, so the claim is neither confirmed nor refuted by the work retrieved here; that literature simply proceeds as if the rule were not there.

contested.question: Is rasayana a pharmacological category or a regimen?
positions: The classical framing makes the regimen constitutive, with the formulation as one element. The quoted Sushruta medhya chapter is explicit: prior cleansing, prescribed diet order, entry into a chamber and mantra recitation a thousand times are written into each individual preparation, not appended to it. Charaka specifies the chamber's siting, walls, windows and auspicious entry at aphorisms 17 to 23.
Modern research treats rasayana as a set of formulations or, increasingly, single standardised extracts, and studies them as drugs, discarding the regimen entirely.

Sushruta's vajikarana chapter lists the means of vajikarana as food, 'speech that gladdens the ears', touch, moonlit nights, song, company and 'a merry careless heart', with no drug among them, which is direct textual evidence that the paired category is not conceived pharmacologically either.

Achara rasayana is often cited as the sharpest evidence for the non-pharmacological reading, on the ground that conduct with no drug at all produces the effect. That reading is now contested within this record: see the following question. No study of achara rasayana as an intervention was located.

contested.question: Does achara rasayana claim that conduct replaces the drug, or that conduct conditions it?
positions: Conduct replaces the drug. This is Kaviratna's footnote to the passage: 'Such a person does not require the aid of any Rasayana of drugs. He attains, through his conduct, to all the effects of Rasayana.' It is the reading this record previously carried, in its summary, its component gloss and its contested section, attributed to Charaka.

Conduct conditions the drug. This is what Kaviratna's translation of the verses themselves says. The person of such conduct 'should be known as a user of Rasayana' (52-56); he who has these attributes AND uses rasayana enjoys all its enumerated effects (57); he who has not cast off his graver faults never reaps them (58); the combinations succeed with those cleansed in mind and body (59). On this reading achara rasayana is continuous with the shodhana requirement rather than an alternative to pharmacology.

The disagreement is a translator's footnote against the translator's own text, which is the fourth instance in this project of the defect where a translator's voice is absorbed as doctrine. It is recorded here rather than resolved. Settling it requires the Sanskrit of Charaka Chikitsasthana 1, fourth pada, which was not retrieved in this pass, and ideally Chakrapani's commentary; Kaviratna also notes at aphorism 58 that he believes Gangadhara has misunderstood the couplet, so the commentarial tradition is not unanimous either.

contested.question: Which English rendering of Charaka's rasayana outcome list is correct?
positions: The record's former summary listed: long life, memory, intelligence, freedom from disease, retained youth, lustre, complexion, voice, strength of body and senses. That wording came from the verse-numbered edition at carakasamhitaonline.com, which is in copyright and was never quoted, so the list was a paraphrase of an unquotable source.

Kaviratna's public-domain translation has: longevity of life, memory, apprehension, health, youth, brightness, complexion, excellence of voice, great strength of body and the senses, power of making speech true, bows (from others), and comeliness of features. Three items have no counterpart in the record's former list, and 'apprehension' and 'health' are materially weaker than 'intelligence' and 'freedom from disease'.

Per the project's rule that disagreement between renderings is the data rather than a problem to resolve, both are recorded and neither is adopted as the record's own. Which is closer to the Sanskrit cannot be stated from what was retrieved here: no Sanskrit text of this passage was consulted in this pass.

contested.question: What plants do the classical medhya rasayana names denote, and does the single-herb trial literature test them?
positions: Kaviratna's 1890s identifications, printed inline with the Charaka passage, are mandukaparni as Hydrocotyle asiatica and shankhapushpi as Pladera decussata. These are the translator's botanical attributions, not the text's.
Kaviratna's own footnote records that Gangadhara identifies mandukaparni as danti, Baliospermum montanum, a quite different plant, so the identification is disputed inside the commentarial tradition.

Current usage differs again: mandukaparni is generally taken as Centella asiatica and shankhapushpi most often as Convolvulus pluricaulis, while brahmi is widely identified with Bacopa monnieri and sometimes with Centella asiatica, the two names being used interchangeably in some regions and for different plants in others.

This bears directly on the modern evidence. The Bacopa systematic review and the Withania meta-analyses are the strongest designs in this record, and whether they are evidence about a classical medhya rasayana drug at all depends on which identification is right. The record does not resolve this and does not treat those trials as tests of the classical drugs.

contested.question: Do the classical rasayana formulations share any common active principle?
positions: The antioxidant hypothesis, dominant in the modern literature, treats them as a class unified by free-radical scavenging.

The classical grouping is by claimed effect, not by composition, and includes items as different as amalaki preparations, bhallataka preparations, shilajatu, metals including gold and iron, and conduct. No source located demonstrates a shared mechanism across the classical list.

contested.question: Where does the kamya / naimittika / ajasrika classification come from?
positions: It is very widely presented in contemporary Ayurvedic writing as a Charaka classification.

It was not found in the retrieved verse-numbered edition of Charaka's Rasayana Adhyaya, nor in the public-domain Kaviratna text of that lesson now read in full for this record, which is consistent with it being a commentarial or later nibandha systematisation. Sources that attribute it directly to Charaka should be treated with caution. The search behind this was a reading of one lesson in one translation plus a keyword search of its OCR, which can support 'not found here' and cannot support a claim about the whole Charaka corpus.

notKnown: Whether any rasayana produces the specific classical outcomes over the timescales the texts name. This item previously read 'No trial with a clinical longevity or cognitive endpoint over a relevant timescale was located', and the first half of that was a search failure reported as an evidence gap: randomised human trials with validated cognitive endpoints exist for single rasayana dravyas and are now cited in this record. The gap that survives is narrower and still real. Nothing located has a longevity endpoint at all, and the cognitive trials run eight to twelve weeks against texts that promise a hundred years of retentive memory.
Whether prior shodhana changes rasayana effect. Not tested in anything retrieved here, despite being a stated gate on administration in both principal texts.

Whether kutipraveshika outperforms vatatapika. This item previously described the comparison as one 'the classical texts assert'.
