No statement ranking the two methods was found in Kaviratna's text of Charaka's rasayana lesson, where the two are named at aphorism 16 and elaborated only in the translator's footnotes, so the record no longer attributes the comparative claim to the text. Whether another classical text asserts it, and whether the comparison has ever been made experimentally, are both unknown here.

Whether achara rasayana does anything. No study located. And, now, what achara rasayana claims in the first place: the drugless-substitute reading is Kaviratna's footnote and his translation of the verses reads the other way, so the question of what would even be under test is open.
Whether the effects seen with Amalaki rasayana or Chyawanaprash persist after the formulation is stopped, or reflect only nutritional repletion in the study populations.

What dose, duration and preparation method are required, and whether classical preparation procedure matters. The DNA-repair trial prepared the formulation strictly per traditional text but did not compare against a non-traditionally prepared control. The single-herb trials use standardised commercial extracts, which is a further step away from the classical preparation and makes the question harder rather than easier to answer from that literature.

Whether rasayana formulations carry long-term harms. Several classical rasayanas involve bhallataka (Semecarpus anacardium), and Kaviratna's Charaka also gives shilajatu and preparations with gold and powdered iron; no long-term safety cohort was located. The Withania meta-analyses report on safety over trial durations of weeks, which does not address this.
Whether the 'rasayana' grouping picks out any real biological kind, or is a heterogeneous list unified only by claimed benefit.

What Charaka's own vajikarana chapter (Chikitsasthana 2) says. This record establishes from Chikitsasthana 1 that rasayana and vajikarana form one unit and that Charaka sequences them, and it quotes Sushruta's vajikarana chapter, but Charaka Chikitsasthana 2 was not retrieved or read in this pass and nothing is asserted about its contents. Scoped out rather than filled with a general statement.

Whether standard Trikamji verse numbering agrees with Kaviratna's printed aphorism numbers at the locations cited here. Kaviratna prints his number after the aphorism and is documented in this project as running one behind Trikamji through at least Chikitsasthana 15 and Vimanasthana 5 and 8. At Chikitsasthana 1 his numbers for the definition passage (7-8) and the two methods (16) coincide with the numbers this record previously carried from a verse-numbered edition, and his number for the medhya drugs (34-35) does not coincide with the 1.3.30-31 commonly cited for that passage. No Sanskrit edition was consulted to adjudicate, so the record carries Kaviratna's own numbering and says so, rather than converting between systems.

What the Sanskrit of Charaka Chikitsasthana 1 says at the passages quoted here, independent of Kaviratna's English. GRETIL's Caraka coverage is selected excerpts only, and no Sanskrit text of this lesson was retrieved. This is what the two translation disagreements recorded in contested would need in order to be settled, and it is the main piece of verification this record still lacks.

components.gloss: The means of imparting superior rasa and the succeeding dhatus; a quality-of-tissue intervention rather than a disease-directed one. Charaka places it as one of the two kinds of medicine aimed at the ojas of a healthy person, the other being vrishya.

Indoor or 'hut-entering' method: administration after the patient enters a purpose-built closed chamber, whose siting, construction and auspicious timing Charaka specifies at aphorisms 17 to 23. Described as the more intensive of the two in the sense that it imposes a residential regimen the other does not. The record previously called it 'the more effective of the two'; that comparative was not found in Kaviratna's text of the lesson and has been withdrawn.

The method pursued without entering a closed chamber. Kaviratna's footnote glosses the name as exposure to wind (vata) and sun (atapa) and cautions that it does not mean the patient actually sits in sun and wind, only that he is not confined; the fourth pada's footnote gives the alternative name Sauryamarutika. The gloss is the translator's, not the text's.

Prior purification, required by both Charaka and Sushruta for rasayana to take effect. Sushruta states it categorically with the dyed-cloth analogy; Charaka's first pada makes the physician's judgement that the bowels have been properly cleansed the condition of administering the formulation.

The subset directed at intellect and memory rather than at the body generally. Charaka's third pada (Karaprachitiya) names mandukaparni, liquorice, guduchi and shankhapushpi, singling out shankhapushpi for strength of understanding; Sushruta's Chikitsasthana 28 treats the same subject at length under mandukaparni, brahmi and vacha. Which plants these names denote is contested.

Conduct-based rejuvenation: truthfulness, freedom from wrath, restraint, compassion and a long list of further attributes. On Kaviratna's text the person so described 'should be known as a user of Rasayana', and the following aphorisms make conduct the condition of the drug succeeding rather than a replacement for it. The claim that conduct alone produces rasayana effects with no drug at all appears in Kaviratna's footnote; the record previously carried the footnote's reading as the text's.

The paired eighth branch, directed at reproductive capacity. Not merely adjacent to rasayana: Charaka defines both inside the rasayana lesson as the two kinds of medicine that increase the ojas of a healthy person, and announces at aphorism 14 that rasayana will be laid down first and vajikarana after. Sushruta gives it its own chapter at Chikitsasthana 26, immediately before the three rasayana chapters.

Brahmya rasayana, Chyavanaprasha, Amalaka rasayana, Haritaki rasayana and others; the operational content of the category in practice. Kaviratna's abstract of the part lists six combinations in the first section and nine in the second, several of the latter built on bhallataka (Semecarpus anacardium).

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed aphorism number 7-8
classical.establishes: The list of claimed rasayana outcomes and the etymological definition, now quoted from a public-domain translation instead of recorded on verse numbers taken from an in-copyright edition. Kaviratna prints his aphorism number 7-8 AFTER the passage, which is the documented house style of this translation. That number coincides with the location 1.1.7-8 the record previously carried from carakasamhitaonline.com, so the one-behind divergence documented for Kaviratna elsewhere does not appear here; whether standard Trikamji numbering agrees was not independently checked against a Sanskrit edition and is recorded in notKnown. Note that Kaviratna's rendering of the outcome list is not the list the record's summary previously asserted: he has 'apprehension' where the record had 'intelligence', 'health' where the record had 'freedom from disease', and he carries three further items ('power of making speech true', 'bows (from others)', 'comeliness of features') that the record omitted. The disagreement is recorded in contested rather than resolved.
classical.quote: From the administration of 'Rasayana' one obtains longevity of life, memory, apprehension, health, youth, brightness, complexion, excellence of voice, great strength of body and the senses, power of making speech true, bows (from others), and comeliness of features. These drugs (or preparations) are called 'Rasayana' because of their capacity to impart superior 'Rasa' and other 'dhatus' (or ingredients of the body). 7-8

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed aphorism numbers 5, 9-12, 13, 14
classical.establishes: That rasayana and vajikarana are one unit of the classical architecture rather than two subjects that happen to sit next to each other. Charaka's rasayana lesson itself divides medicine aimed at the ojas of the healthy into vrishya and rasayana, defines vajikarana within that division, and sequences the two. Added in answer to the critic's finding that the record listed vajikarana as a component with no reference. Ellipses mark omitted intervening material; the omitted stretch of 9-12 continues the list of vajikarana's claimed effects (progeny, fame, prosperity) without changing the sense. The OCR prints the aphorism number for 9-12 as '9-iz'; it is read as 9-12 and that reading is an inference from the surrounding sequence, not a clean scan.
classical.quote: That which increases the ojos of a healthy person is of two kind s viz., 'Vrishya' (aphrodisiacs), and 'Rasayana (tonics). 5 ... That, again, which leads to the birth of children and children's children, that which causes immediate pleasure, that by which one is enabled to approach women, unimpededly and with the strength of a stallion, that by which one becomes the favourite of women, that by which one grows (in strength and energy), that by which the vital seed of a person who is even decrepit is seen to become inexhaustible and fruitful ... is called 'Vajikarana' (or aphrodisiac). 9-12 ... Thus have been mentioned the two kinds of medicines (viz., Rasayana' and Vajikarana) for increasing the ojos of a healthy man. ... 13 ... We shall first lay down the ordinances in respect of 'Rasayana.' Then we shall speak of 'Vajikarana.' 14

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed aphorism number 16
classical.establishes: The two modes of administration, now quoted from the public-domain translation rather than recorded on an in-copyright edition's verse number. Kaviratna's printed number is 16, matching the location the record previously carried. The scan's OCR garbles his transliteration: 'Kutipravegika' is Kutipraveshika (Kaviratna writes the palatal sibilant with a cedilla that the recogniser reads as g) and 'VatStapica' is Vatatapika. The passage names the two methods and does nothing more; it does not rank them. Kaviratna's footnote at this point, which explains kuti as a chamber and pravesha as entrance, is the translator's gloss and not part of the text.
classical.quote: The Rishis understood that there are two methods for the administration of Rasayanas.' These are 'Kutipravegika' and 'VatStapica.' 16

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed aphorism numbers 24 and 27
classical.establishes: Charaka's parallel shodhana requirement, which the record previously asserted without a quote. Purification is not a general recommendation here but the physician's gate: the formulation is given once he has ascertained that the bowels are cleansed. This is the Charaka-side support for the contested question on whether prior shodhana is necessary, and it means that question rests on both principal texts rather than on Sushruta alone.
classical.quote: Then (in that chamber), cleansed by correctives, becoming cheerful, and having gained strength, one should again have 'Rasayana' administered unto oneself. The correctives one will use I shall now lay down. 24 ... When the physicians conversant with considerations of age, nature of constitutions, and power of assimilation, having ascertained that the bowels of the person have been properly cleansed, should administer to him 'Rasayana' consisting of (proper) combinations. That should be administered to the individual which is suitable to him .27

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed aphorism number 34-35
classical.establishes: The four medhya rasayana drugs of Charaka's third pada, which the critic flagged as a component with no reference. Added in answer to that finding. Three points of translator's voice must travel with this quote. First, the section headings 'MEDHAKARA RASAYANA' and 'RASAYANA THAT INVIGORATES THE UNDERSTANDING' are Kaviratna's editorial additions. Second, the Latin binomials are his 1890s botanical identifications, not the text's, and they are not the identifications in current use: mandukaparni is now generally Centella asiatica and shankhapushpi most often Convolvulus pluricaulis. Third, Kaviratna footnotes that Gangadhara identifies mandukaparni as danti (Baliospermum montanum) instead, so the plant behind the first name is disputed inside the commentarial tradition itself. Kaviratna prints 34-35; the location usually cited for this passage in modern writing is 1.3.30-31, which was not verified against a Sanskrit edition in this pass, so only Kaviratna's own number is recorded.
classical.quote: The expressed juice of 'Mandukaparni' (Hydrocotyle Asiatica), liquorice reduced to pulv, or the juice of 'Guduchi' (Tinospora cordifolia), should be used with milk. The paste also of the roots and the blossoms of 'Qankhapushpi' (Pladera decussata) should be used with the liquid. These 'Rasayanas' promote longevity, destroy disease, increase strength, and improve digestion, complexion, and voice. They also invigorate the understanding. Of these, again, that made of 'Qankhapushpi' (Pladera decussata) especially conduces to strength of understanding. 34-35

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed aphorism numbers 52-56, 57, 58, 59
classical.establishes: Achara rasayana, quoted from Kaviratna. On his printed aphorisms 52-56 the passage characterises, through a long list of attributes, a person who 'should be known as a user of 'Ras3yana'', and the three aphorisms that follow make conduct bear on whether the drug works: he who is endued with these attributes and uses rasayana enjoys all its enumerated effects (57), he who has not cast off the graver faults of body and mind never reaps them (58), and the combinations succeed with those who are cleansed in mind and body and have their souls under control (59). What this passage establishes is therefore conduct as potentiator or precondition at 57-59. It does not establish anything against the drugless-substitute reading, and must not be cited that way, because Kaviratna's own footnote marked § at the close of 52-56 states that reading in his own words: 'This section is headed 'Achara-Rasayanam', that is, the 'Rasayana of conduct'. The- Eind of person* here described should be known as- one whose very conduct operates as a •Rasayana.' Such a person does not require the aid of any 'Rasayana' of drugs. He attains, through his conduct, to all the effects of 'Rasayana.' — T.' (OCR as printed.) That is the translator's gloss rather than the mula, and it attaches to 52-56 only; the record should carry it alongside the quote and leave the substitute question open.
classical.quote: One that is truthful, and free from wrath, that abstains from wine and sexual indulgence, that has no animosity, that undergoes only such labour as involves no fatigue, that is tranquil and of amiable speech, that is accustomed to the silent recitation of sacred texts, and is pure (in body and mind), that is endued with gravity and firmness, that is always charitable and engaged in penances ... that is devoted to the scriptures, should be known as a user of 'Rasayana.' 52-56 (Further) he who, endued with these high attributes, uses Rasayana', enjoys all the effects enumerated of 'Rasayana.' 57 That person who, without casting off (at least) the graver faults of both body and mind, (uses 'Rasayana'), never reaps the effects of Rasayana. 58 (Rasayanic) combinations, which have for their objects the lengthening of (the period of) life and the prevention of decrepitude and disease, succeed with those who are cleansed in respect of mind and body and who have their souls under control. 59
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.text: Charaka Samhita (Kaviratna translation, 1896-1913), TRANSLATOR'S FOOTNOTE, held as an exhibit and not as doctrine
classical.verse: Kaviratna's footnote to aphorisms 52-56
classical.establishes: The source of the record's former achara rasayana claim, and a fourth instance of the defect this project has documented three times: the translator's voice absorbed as doctrine. 'Such a person does not require the aid of any Rasayana of drugs' is Kaviratna's gloss, signed with his own '- T.', and it is in tension with his translation of aphorisms 57 to 59 immediately above it. The record had the footnote's reading in its component gloss, its summary and its contested section, attributed to the classical text. It is retained here as an exhibit of how the claim entered the record, which is what the lexicon exists to make visible, and not as support for the claim.
classical.quote: This section is headed 'Achara-Rasayanam', that is, the 'Rasayana of conduct'. The kind of person here described should be known as one whose very conduct operates as a 'Rasayana.' Such a person does not require the aid of any 'Rasayana' of drugs. He attains, through his conduct, to all the effects of 'Rasayana.' - T.

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's own printed section numbers 1 and 2; he prints no Sanskrit verse numbers anywhere
classical.establishes: Three things at once: the scope claim (invulnerability to disease and decay), the timing rule (youth and middle age, not old age), and the prerequisite of prior shodhana with the dyed-cloth analogy as its whole justification. The citation previously read '27.1-27.2' in a form that could be mistaken for Sanskrit verse numbers. Bhishagratna prints no Sanskrit verse numbers, only his own section numbers, so the locator is now stated as his section numbering explicitly. The content of the quote was checked against the source and is unchanged.
classical.quote: Now we shall discourse on the recipes and modes of using elixirs and rejuvinators of the human organism which will make it invulnerable to the inroads of any disease or of decay (Sarvopaghata-shamaniya-Rasayanam). 1. Metrical Texts :- A wise physician should (invariably) prescribe some sort of tonic (Rasayana) for his patients in their youth and middle age after having their systems (properly) cleansed by the applications of a Sneha and purifying remedies (emetics and purgatives). A person whose system has not been (previously) cleansed (Sodhana) with the proper purifying remedies (emetics and purgatives) should not, in any case, have recourse to such tonics inasmuch as they would fail to produce the wished-for result, just as the application of a dye to a piece of dirty cloth will prove non-effective. 2.

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's own printed section numbers 3-4; he prints no Sanskrit verse numbers anywhere
classical.establishes: The character of the claims actually being made: arrest of senescence from a combination of four ordinary dietary substances taken early in life. Useful as a check on modern restatements that soften rasayana into 'general tonic' language. Locator restated as Bhishagratna's section numbering for the same reason as the preceding entry.
classical.quote: Old age and senile decay would be arrested (lit.- perpetual or life-long youth would be secured) by drinking milk, cold water, honey and clarified butter, either severally or jointly ... in early life (just on or just before the completion of the process of organic development).

classical.chapter: 26 (Kshina-Baliya Vajikarana), printed as 'The medical treatment for increasing virility'
classical.verse: Bhishagratna's own printed section numbers 1, 2-A, 2-B and 2, in that printed order
classical.establishes: Vajikarana in Sushruta, as the chapter immediately preceding the three rasayana chapters, which is the second half of the answer to the critic's finding that vajikarana sat in the components with no reference. The 'Means of Vaji-Karana' passage is also direct evidence for the contested question of whether these categories are pharmacological or regimen-based: the means listed are food, speech, touch, moonlight, music, company and a cheerful heart, with no drug among them. Two cautions. The headings 'Definition of Vaji-Karana' and 'Means of Vaji-Karana' are Bhishagratna's editorial insertions, not the text's. And the numbering as printed runs 1, then 2-A, then 2-B, then 2, which is his own sectioning and not Sanskrit verse numbers; the apparent disorder is in the source.
classical.quote: Now we shall discourse on the medical treatment for increasing the strength and virile power of weak persons (Kshina-Valiyam Vaji-Karana). i. ... Definition of Vaji-Karana :— if duly taken, the Vaji-karana* remedies make a man sexually as strong as a horse (Vaji), and enable him to cheerfully satisfy the heat and amorous ardours of young maidens, a fact which has determined the nomenclature of this class of (^medicinal) remedies. 2-B. Means of Vaji-Karana :--Various kinds of (nutritious and palatable) food and (sweet, luscious and refreshing) liquid cordials, speech that gladdens the ears, and touch which seems delicious to the skin, clear nights mellowed by the beams of the full moon and damsels young, beautiful and gay, dulcet songs that charm the soul and captivate the mind, use of betel-leaves, wine and wreaths of (sweet-scented) flowers, and a meny careless heart, these are the best aphrodisiacs in life. 2.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.chapter: 28 (Medhayushkamiya Rasayana), printed as 'Elixirs (rasayana) to improve memory and life span'
classical.verse: Bhishagratna's own printed section numbers 1, 4 and 5; he prints no Sanskrit verse numbers anywhere
classical.establishes: The medhya rasayana material in Sushruta, quoted rather than merely located, which upgrades what this record previously carried as an unquoted chapter-contents note. Two things the quoted text supports. The prior-cleansing requirement recurs inside each individual preparation, not only in the general rule at chapter 27: 'The Doshas of the system of a person should be first thoroughly cleansed' in section 4, 'Having had the Doshas of the system duly cleansed' in section 5. And the regimen is constitutive to the extent the quoted words show it: the prescribed diet and the consecration of the dose by reciting the proper Mantras a thousand times are part of the prescription, not optional accompaniments. Seclusion is not claimed from this quote; the sentences in the chapter that would carry it fall inside the ellipses and are not quoted here. The scale of the claims is worth recording exactly, because 'a long life of a hundred years', verbatim recall of a discourse on a single hearing, the appearance of the goddess of learning in an embodied form and a life of five hundred years are what the text says; this is the yardstick against which a modern surrogate-marker result should be read, and it is the clearest reason this record treats the classical claim as untested rather than partly supported.
classical.quote: Now we shall discourse on the elixirs and remedial agents which tend to improve the memory and invigorate the mental faculties as well as to increase the duration of human life (Medhayushkamiyam Rasayana). 1. ... Manduka-parni Rasayana:- The Doshas of the system of a person should be first thoroughly cleansed (with the help of proper emetics and purgatives, etc.), and he should be advised to undergo the prescribed diet ... An adequate dose of the expressed juice of the Manduka-parni should then be stirred with milk, and should be taken after consecrating it by reciting the proper Mantras a thousand times ... This would ensure a long life of a hundred years in the full vigour of retentive memory and intellectual faculties, and would impart a god-like effulgence to the complexion. 4. Brahmi Rasayana:- ... A continuous use of the medicine for a week improves the memory, leads to the expansion of the intellectual faculties and imparts a celestical glow to the complexion. In the second week of its course it revives old and forgotten memories in the user and adds to his proficiency in the writing out of any book to be written. In the third week it enables a man to reproduce from memory as many as one hundred words if twice heard or read (at a single sitting). In the same manner a (further) use of the drug for twenty-one days removes all inauspicious features whether of the body or of the mind, the goddess of learning appears in an embodied form to the (mind of the) user, and all kinds of knowledge come rushing into his memory. A single hearing is enough to make him reproduce (verbatim from memory a discourse however lengthy), and he is enabled to live for five hundred years. 5.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: Sushruta continues rasayana past chapter 28 into Svabhavavyadhi-pratishedhaniya (printed as 'Elixirs for the prevention of death and decay') and Nivritta-samtapiya (printed as 'Elixirs to remove mental and physical distress'). The chapter headings were retrieved from the volume's chapter list and confirmed; the individual preparations named in the contents index include Svetavalguja, Krishnavalguja, Mandukaparni, Brahmi and Vacha rasayanas, of which the last three fall in chapter 28 and are now quoted in the entry above. Recorded as located: no quote is attributed from chapters 29 or 30 and no section numbers within them were confirmed. The entry previously spanned 'chapters 28-30' and has been narrowed to 29-30 because 28 is now carried as a quoted citation of its own.

Later nibandha texts carry rasayana forward and are the usual source cited for the kamya / naimittika / ajasrika three-way classification of rasayana (rasayana for desired qualities, for a specific disease, and for daily use). Note that this classification was not found in the Charaka text itself, either on the retrieved verse-numbered edition or in the public-domain Kaviratna text of Chikitsasthana 1 now read for this record, which is consistent with it being a commentarial or later systematisation. No public-domain English translation of either text has been located, so paraphrase only.

modern.title: Effect of Amalaki rasayana on DNA damage and repair in randomized aged human individuals.
modern.establishes: Randomised placebo-controlled trial of Amalaki rasayana prepared per classical text, given to healthy aged volunteers for 45 days. UVC-induced DNA strand break repair was stably maintained or enhanced in the rasayana group with no adverse effects; nucleotide excision repair and base excision repair were unchanged.
modern.quality: The best-designed study of a classical polyherbal rasayana formulation located for this record: randomised, placebo-controlled, mechanistically specific, with a negative result honestly reported on two of three repair pathways. Limitations are real: 45 days, a surrogate cellular endpoint with no clinical outcome, and the authors themselves call for further work. It tests one formulation, not rasayana theory.

modern.title: Ayurvedic Amalaki Rasayana promotes improved stress tolerance and thus has anti-aging effects in Drosophila melanogaster.
modern.establishes: Amalaki rasayana improved stress tolerance and extended measures of healthy lifespan in Drosophila melanogaster.
modern.quality: Preclinical model organism study. Methodologically sound for what it is, and useful as mechanistic support, but a fly model cannot establish the human claims made in Charaka's rasayana lesson and is not evidence about rasayana as a category.

modern.title: Evaluation of Cyavanaprāśa on Health and Immunity related Parameters in Healthy Children: A Two Arm, Randomized, Open Labeled, Prospective, Multicenter, Clinical Study.
modern.establishes: Two-arm randomised multicentre study in 702 school children (627 completers) comparing six months of Chyawanaprash plus milk against milk alone, reporting more than twofold reduction in immunity-related illness episodes and better parent-reported energy, fitness and quality of life.
modern.quality: Mixed. Large and randomised, which is unusual in this literature, and prospectively registered (CTRI/2015/02/005574). But open-label with no placebo, outcomes recorded in parent-kept diaries so wholly unblinded and subject to expectancy, and three of the authors are employed by the manufacturer, which is disclosed. The effect size should be treated as an upper bound, not an estimate.

modern.title: Clinical efficacy of Amalaki Rasayana in the management of Pandu (Iron deficiency anemia).
modern.establishes: Randomised comparison of Amalaki Rasayana against ferrous fumarate with folic acid in iron deficiency anaemia over 45 days.
modern.quality: Small single-centre trial in a low-visibility journal, unblinded, and testing a disease-specific indication rather than the rejuvenative claim. Included to show the range of what 'rasayana research' actually contains.
modern.design: human randomised trial, disease indication not rejuvenative claim

modern.title: Rasayana therapy in classical literature of Ayurveda: a review.
modern.journal: Bull Indian Inst Hist Med Hyderabad
modern.establishes: Survey of rasayana therapy as presented in the classical literature.
modern.quality: Textual review in a history-of-medicine bulletin. Not empirical, and not an evidence assessment. Useful for doctrine, not for efficacy.

modern.title: Plant-based Rasayana drugs from Ayurveda.
modern.establishes: Overview of plant-based rasayana drugs, reporting that antioxidant and immunomodulation are the most studied activities of rasayana drugs.
modern.quality: Narrative review. Its own summary is the honest datapoint: the literature has converged on two assayable activities and largely stopped there, which is a substitution of tractable pharmacology for the classical claim rather than a test of it. Note that this generalisation is about rasayana drugs as a class and sits in tension with the single-herb cognitive trial literature recorded below, which uses behavioural rather than biochemical endpoints.

modern.title: Neuronutrient impact of Ayurvedic Rasayana therapy in brain aging.
modern.establishes: Discussion of rasayana therapy as neuronutrition in brain ageing.
modern.quality: Narrative review in Biogerontology. Restates the medhya rasayana doctrine in modern neurobiological vocabulary and proposes mechanisms; no primary data and no clinical endpoint.

modern.title: Geroprotection through modulation of heart rate variability, oxidative enzymes, tissue integrity, and gene expression by an Ayurvedic herbal formulation, Amalaki Rasayana.
modern.establishes: Amalaki Rasayana supplementation in ageing male Fischer rats (36 animals, assessed at 18, 24 and 30 months) reported maintained heart rate variability, preserved antioxidant enzymes, reduced tissue degeneration and gene expression changes.
modern.quality: Preclinical rodent study with a longitudinal design, which is a genuine strength for an ageing claim. Still a single formulation in a single strain, with surrogate endpoints, and no human bridge.

modern.title: The cognitive-enhancing effects of Bacopa monnieri: a systematic review of randomized, controlled human clinical trials.
modern.establishes: Systematic review of randomised controlled human trials of Bacopa monnieri for cognitive performance in adults without dementia or significant cognitive impairment. Six trials met inclusion, all twelve weeks, three different extracts at 300-450 mg/day. Across studies Bacopa improved performance on 9 of 17 tests in the domain of memory free recall, with, in the authors' words, 'little evidence of enhancement in any other cognitive domains'.
modern.quality: Added in answer to the critic's missing-modern and overclaimed findings, both of which turned on this reference. It is a properly conducted systematic review of randomised human trials with validated cognitive endpoints, which is a stronger design class than anything else in this record. Three limits on what it can do here. It evaluates a single herb, not a classical rasayana formulation or regimen. Its own conclusion is narrow: memory free recall improved, other domains did not, and the authors describe the field as 'in its infancy'. And whether Bacopa monnieri is a drug of the classical medhya rasayana list at all depends on an unsettled plant identification, since brahmi is identified with Bacopa monnieri in much modern writing while Kaviratna's Charaka gives mandukaparni as Hydrocotyle asiatica and Gangadhara as danti; see contested.
modern.design: systematic review of human randomised controlled trials

modern.title: Effects of Withania somnifera (L.) Dunal (Ashwagandha) on cognitive and physical function in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
modern.establishes: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA, PROSPERO CRD420261292996) of randomised trials of Withania somnifera in adults, 20 studies and 1,249 participants. Reports improvement in memory (SMD 0.52, 95% CI 0.27-0.78), attention and processing speed (SMD 0.29, 95% CI 0.07-0.51), executive function (SMD -0.42, 95% CI -0.70 to -0.13), testosterone (SMD 0.33, 95% CI 0.13-0.54) and muscle strength (SMD 0.58, 95% CI 0.12-1.04), with no significant effect on body weight or body fat percentage. Risk of bias assessed with RoB 2 and certainty with GRADE.
modern.quality: Added in answer to the critic's missing-modern finding, which named the Withania RCT and meta-analytic literature specifically. Methodologically the most thorough synthesis in this record: registered protocol, RoB 2, GRADE, and botanical reporting assessed with ConPhyMP, which matters in a literature where extract identity is usually unstated. Caveats that keep it from settling anything about rasayana theory. Muscle strength was heterogeneous (I2 56.9%) and significant only in physically active subgroups. Global cognition rested on a single study. Trial durations are the eight-to-twelve-week range typical of supplement research, not a timescale on which a longevity claim could be examined. And as with Bacopa, this is one herb standardised as an extract, not a classical formulation administered under a classical regimen.
modern.design: systematic review and meta-analysis of human randomised controlled trials

modern.title: Safety and efficacy of Withania somnifera for anxiety and insomnia: Systematic review and meta-analysis.
modern.establishes: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised placebo-controlled trials of Withania somnifera for anxiety and insomnia. Five RCTs, 254 participants pooled; Hamilton Anxiety Scale reduced (MD -5.96, 95% CI -10.34 to -1.59, p = 0.008) with I2 of 98%, and sleep onset latency, total sleep time, PSQI and sleep efficiency improved while wake after sleep onset and total time in bed did not.
modern.quality: Added alongside the Frontiers meta-analysis so that the Withania literature is not represented only by its most favourable synthesis. The pooled anxiety estimate carries I2 of 98%, which is close to total heterogeneity and makes the point estimate hard to interpret whatever its confidence interval; the authors' own conclusion is that larger trials are needed to confirm the effects. Total pooled n is 254. Anxiety and insomnia are also disease-adjacent indications rather than the rejuvenative claim, so this sits in the record for the same reason as the anaemia trial: to show what the evidence base actually contains.
modern.design: systematic review and meta-analysis of human randomised controlled trials

openQuestions: A relayed statement that 'Dr. Singh has given permission' accompanied this revision with no document, scope, rights holder or date, and no entry in data/sources/. It was not used to license any quotation and was not needed. Before any in-copyright translation is quoted anywhere in this project, that permission needs a source register entry naming grantor, work, scope and date.

Charaka Chikitsasthana 2 (vajikarana) is now legible in the same public-domain Kaviratna text derivative used for this record, and reading it would close the notKnown item this revision had to open. It is out of scope for a repair of this record but is cheap to do and would also serve the vajikarana term record.

Kaviratna's Lesson I contains further quotable material not drawn on here, including the chamber specification at aphorisms 17 to 23, the bhallataka preparations of the second pada, and shilajatu and metal rasayanas in the third, which bear on the unanswered long-term safety item in notKnown.

Kaviratna's abstract of this part carries editorial claims in his own voice that should not be mistaken for the text, among them that no system of medicine except the Hindu gives such importance to the treatment of the healthy, and a footnote elsewhere glossing rasayanas as 'drugs prepared with the three myrobalans'. Flagged here because this record has already had one footnote absorbed as doctrine.

records.title: Ritucharya: the classical rationale for seasonal regimen
records.summary: Ritucharya is the classical prescription that diet and conduct be changed with the season. The rationale, as the retrieved passages state it, has three parts. First, the year is divided into two solar half-years, adana (the sun's northern course, when the sun and dry winds take up moisture and human strength declines) and visarga (the southern course, when moisture is restored and strength increases), each subdivided into three two-month seasons. The causal chain the texts give is environmental before it is doshic: solar and wind action alters the qualities of water and plants, which alters food, which alters the body. Second, the doshas are held to run a three-stage cycle keyed to season: accumulation (chaya) in one season, aggravation or manifestation (prakopa) in the next, and subsidence (prashama) in a third. Whether the regimen for a season is therefore aimed at the dosha accumulating in it or at the one manifesting in it is NOT settled by the passages retrieved here: Charaka's autumn prescription reads as anticipatory, Sushruta's chapter closes by directing that the deranged dosha be checked in the season of its prakopa before it manifests as illness, and the two are not reconciled in anything retrieved. See contested. Third, suitability is defined relationally: what is appropriate is what has qualities contrary to those of the place of habitation and of the existing disorder, though Kaviratna footnotes a textual variant at exactly that verse (see notKnown). The seasons named are those of the north Indian calendar, defined by named lunar months, and the texts do not address latitudes where that calendar does not apply.
records.evidenceState: What the modern references carried here establish is that human physiology and disease incidence vary with the time of year. That is not in dispute, and it is not an Ayurvedic proposition. Dopico 2015 found seasonal expression profiles in more than 4,000 protein-coding mRNAs in white blood cells and adipose tissue; Ter Horst 2016 found annual seasonality in stimulated cytokine responses across 534 healthy subjects; Sheth 1999 found January peaks in myocardial infarction and stroke mortality across 300,000 Canadian deaths. None of the three was designed to test ritucharya, none uses the six-season division, and none measures anything corresponding to vata, pitta or kapha. Offering them as support for 'the premise behind ritucharya' credits the classical scheme with evidence it has not been given, so this record does not offer them that way. The generic claim these papers support is one nobody disputes; the Ayurvedic claim is the specific one, that physiology varies in the particular doshic pattern Charaka Sutrasthana 6 and Sushruta Sutrasthana 6 assert, with the two half-years as the driver, and no reference here speaks to that. Two of the three point away from a calendar-fixed regimen rather than towards one. Dopico's seasonal expression pattern is inverted between Europe and Oceania, and the blood-composition changes that might explain it differ between the United Kingdom and The Gambia; an effect whose sign depends on latitude is evidence against a fixed six-season calendar anchored to north India being the operative variable. Ter Horst's cohort is single-site Dutch and carries no latitude information at all. Sheth's winter peak is a Canadian winter, in months that Sushruta's scheme splits across hemanta and shishira. Nothing retrieved here tests the scheme itself: not the six-season division, not the dosha-to-season assignments, not the chaya-prakopa-prashama sequence, not ritusandhi, not the claim of spontaneous seasonal remission, and none of the per-season dietary or behavioural prescriptions. What the searches returned is set out with dates and hit counts in modernCoverage.searchBound: a Europe PMC query for 'ritucharya' on 2026-10-06 returned 68 records, of which exactly one carries the publication type 'Controlled Clinical Trial', and that one tests a prophylactic polyherbal kit rather than a seasonal regimen; the same query restricted to publication type 'Randomized Controlled Trial' returned nothing. Sixty-seven of those 68 were read as metadata only. On that basis this record states what those searches returned and does not state that no trial exists, and the Ayurvedic-side pattern it can report is the one its own references show: narrative reviews that restate the classical scheme in the vocabulary of chronobiology or the gut microbiome, propose a biomarker or a microbiome study as future work, and stop, of which the gut-microbiome review cited here, not even PubMed-indexed, is the clearest example. The honest summary is that ritucharya is a classically coherent scheme resting on a real and generic phenomenon, with no modern test of the scheme itself, and with the one latitude-resolved modern finding pointing against its calendar being exportable.

contested.question: Where do the boundaries of adana and visarga fall, and which season starts the year?

positions.view: Charaka's Sutrasthana 6 runs adana from the dewy season (shishira) through summer, and visarga from the rains through hemanta, and describes the seasons in that order.
positions.source: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 6, prose aphorisms 1-2 in Kaviratna's edition, quoted in full in this record. Kaviratna's own footnote to this passage lists the six seasons beginning from hemanta, which is a third ordering and is the translator's, not Charaka's.

positions.view: Sushruta's Sutrasthana 6 lists the six seasons beginning with winter (Magha-Phalguna) and defines the ayanas by the sun and moon changing course at the tropics, giving a different narrative entry point. Modern textbooks reconcile these, but the two chapters are not identical in ordering or emphasis.
positions.source: Sushruta Samhita, Sutrasthana 6, Bhishagratna p. 46, unnumbered prose, quoted in full in this record; the account of the two ayanams follows immediately on p. 47.

contested.question: Does a dosha accumulating in a season need treating in that season, or only when it manifests in the next?

positions.view: Sushruta states the accumulated doshas 'should be checked as soon as they become aggravated (manifest themselves)' in the following season, which reads as intervention at prakopa.
positions.source: Sushruta Samhita, Sutrasthana 6, Bhishagratna p. 50, quoted in full in this record.

positions.view: Charaka's autumn prescription is framed as acting on pitta 'stored' during the rains, and the general logic of the chapter is anticipatory: eat contrary to the season now so that nothing accumulates. Practitioner traditions differ on whether purificatory measures are timed to chaya or prakopa.
positions.source: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 6, aphorisms 32-33 of the renumbered verse series, quoted in full in this record. No source is cited here for the practitioner traditions; that sentence rests on nothing retrieved and is retained only as a report of disagreement, not as a sourced position.

positions.view: A third reading, added during this revision from the chapter's own closing sentences: Sushruta ends by directing that the deranged kapha be checked in spring, pitta in autumn and vata in the rains, that is in the season of prakopa, 'before they develop themselves in any patent or manifest bodily ailment'. That is intervention at prakopa but ahead of overt disease, which is neither of the two positions above and does not resolve them against Charaka.
positions.source: Sushruta Samhita, Sutrasthana 6, the chapter's closing sentences immediately before the colophon, quoted in full in this record.

contested.question: How should ritucharya be applied outside the north Indian calendar and climate?

positions.view: The texts define seasons by Indian lunar months and do not address the question; Charaka's okasatmya rule, suit food and conduct to the place of habitation, arguably licenses local adaptation.
positions.source: Sushruta Samhita, Sutrasthana 6, Bhishagratna p. 46 for the month definitions; Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 6, aphorisms 40-41 of the renumbered verse series for the okasatmya and contrary-qualities rule. Both quoted in full in this record. Note the textual variant Kaviratna flags at aphorism 41.

positions.view: Modern seasonality data show the human seasonal transcriptome inverts between northern and southern hemispheres and that the underlying blood-composition changes differ again between the UK and The Gambia, which means a month-anchored regimen cannot simply be exported. No classical or modern source retrieved here resolves how to re-anchor it.
positions.source: PMID 25965853, carried in this record's modern section.

contested.question: Is 'unseasonal weather causes epidemics' a public-health observation or a moral doctrine?

positions.view: Sushruta's practical instruction, avoid contaminated water and produce during an epidemic, is sound and matches modern outbreak practice.
positions.source: Sushruta Samhita, Sutrasthana 6, Bhishagratna p. 51, quoted in full in this record.

positions.view: The aetiology he gives for the unseasonal weather itself is collective sin and malign destiny, and the passage continues into depopulation by curse, spell and demoness. Modern Ayurvedic writing generally reports the first half and omits the second; recording only the first half misrepresents the source.
positions.source: Sushruta Samhita, Sutrasthana 6, Bhishagratna pp. 51-52; the sentences on curse, anger, spell and poisonous pollens follow directly on p. 52 and were read on 2026-10-06.

notKnown: Whether following a seasonal regimen changes any clinical outcome. No trial of one was returned by the searches listed in modernCoverage.searchBound, and those searches were English-language, Europe PMC only, and did not include any trial registry.
Whether the classical dosha-to-season assignments correspond to anything measurable. No biomarker of seasonal dosha accumulation has been proposed and validated in anything retrieved here.

Whether the claim of spontaneous seasonal remission (pitta disorders easing in hemanta, kapha in summer, vata in autumn) holds for any defined modern disease category. This is a directly testable claim and no test of it was found.

How ritucharya should be adapted for southern-hemisphere, equatorial or temperate-continental climates, or for people living in climate-controlled environments year round. Charaka's okasatmya rule licenses adaptation in principle and supplies no procedure for it.
Whether the seasonal foods prescribed carry any effect beyond ordinary seasonal food availability and energy balance.

Whether the seasonality documented in immune gene expression and in stimulated cytokine responses has any causal relationship to the seasonal variation in disease incidence, let alone to Ayurvedic categories. Dopico and Ter Horst measure immune variables, Sheth measures deaths, and nothing retrieved connects them.

Whether seasonal variation in vitamin D, rather than season as such, is what drives the seasonal immune findings this record relies on. Ter Horst 2016 reports vitamin D's mediating effect as limited and alpha-1-antitrypsin as a partial mediator, in one single-site Dutch cohort. That is one result, not a settled confound. A generic Europe PMC search for the seasonal vitamin D literature on 2026-10-06 returned well over a thousand records and none of them was appraised, so this record cannot separate 'season affects immunity' from 'sunlight exposure affects immunity'.

Whether a primary interventional study of a seasonal regimen exists in the literature the searches reached. Of the 68 Europe PMC records matching 'ritucharya' on 2026-10-06, 67 were classified by publication type only and not read in full; the one typed as a controlled clinical trial (PMID 36052011) tests a prophylactic polyherbal kit, not a seasonal regimen. A primary study could be sitting in one of the 67, or in the non-English and non-indexed literature that was never searched at all.

Whether the adana/visarga mechanism as the texts state it, solar and wind action altering the qualities of water and plants and thence of the body, has ever been measured. No search for it was run. The mechanism now has quoted classical loci in this record and no modern reference whatever.

Whether Charaka Sutrasthana 6's closing rule governs qualities contrary to the PLACE only, or contrary to the place and the existing DISORDER. Kaviratna footnotes a textual variant at that aphorism, 'Doshanam' against 'Deshanam', and judges 'Deshanam' correct while translating both. No second edition, no Sanskrit original and no commentary (Chakrapani or otherwise) was consulted on the point, so the record cannot say which reading the tradition carries.

What the rest of Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 3 says. Only verse 58 was retrieved and read. Vagbhata's own seasonal prescriptions, his ordering of the seasons and his account of bala are not covered by this record, and the wisdomlib page for the chapter is Cloudflare-blocked.

Whether the Das-Emmerick e-text's verse numbering for Ashtanga Hridaya matches any printed critical edition. The ritusandhi verse is numbered 58 there and no collation was done, so 'AH Su 3.58' is reported as the e-text's address and not as a printed-edition address.

Whether Bhishagratna's chaya/prakopa vocabulary reflects Sushruta's Sanskrit or Bhishagratna's own glossing. The words naming each state as the 'excited state' of a particular dosha appear in his footnotes rather than his text, and the Sanskrit original of Sushruta Sutrasthana 6 was not consulted during this work.
Whether Charaka's and Sushruta's two orderings of the year are reconcilable in the texts themselves rather than only in modern textbooks. Nothing retrieved here reconciles them; see contested.

Whether the three-way assignment of bala to position within a half-year (strongest in hemanta and shishira, weakest in the rains and summer) has any measurable correlate. Charaka states it, Vagbhata appears to state something similar at Sutrasthana 3.7 which was seen but not read closely, and no modern reference here addresses it.

components.gloss: The six seasons of two months each: shishira (winter/dewy), vasanta (spring), grishma (summer), varsha (rains), sharad (autumn), hemanta (late autumn/cold). Bhishagratna's Sushruta names the constituent months explicitly and is quoted for it in this record.

The sun's northern course, covering shishira, vasanta and grishma in Charaka's reckoning. The sun and dry winds take up moisture; the juices generated become dry, bitter, astringent and pungent; human strength declines.
The sun's southern course, covering varsha, sharad and hemanta. The sun's power is weakened, moisture that is cool, sour, saline and sweet increases, and human strength increases.

Seasonal strength. Charaka states men are weak in the first season of visarga (rains) and the last of adana (summer), intermediate in the two middle seasons, and strongest in the last of visarga (hemanta) and the first of adana (shishira).

Accumulation. A dosha builds quietly in one season without producing disease. Sushruta: pitta accumulates in the rains, kapha in hemanta, vata in summer, and in each case by way of the qualities that water and vegetables take on in that season.

Aggravation or manifestation. The accumulated dosha is liquefied or agitated by the following season's conditions and produces disease. Sushruta: pitta in autumn, kapha in spring, vata in early rains (pravrit).

Subsidence. Sushruta states that disorders of bile, phlegm and wind are respectively ameliorated in hemanta, summer and autumn 'by natural causes', which Bhishagratna glosses in brackets as variations of temperature and rainfall.

Suitability by habituation, and the rule that suitable conduct and food are those with qualities contrary to the place of habitation and to the existing disorder. Kaviratna's own footnote to the second of these two aphorisms records a textual variant, 'Doshanam' against 'Deshanam', and he judges 'Deshanam' (of places) the correct reading while his English renders both place and disorder. The 'existing disorder' half of the rule as usually taught therefore rests on a reading Kaviratna himself rejects; no second edition or commentary was consulted here. See notKnown.

The junction of two seasons, defined as the last week of the outgoing season and the first week of the incoming one, at which the earlier regimen is to be given up and the later taken up gradually. The verse was RETRIEVED during this revision, in Sanskrit, at Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 3.58 of the Das-Emmerick machine-readable text, and is quoted in this record's classical section. The standard attribution to Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 3 therefore holds. It is still true that no public-domain English translation of Vagbhata exists, so no English quotation is offered, and that the e-text has not been collated against a printed critical edition.
Unseasonal or contrary season. Sushruta treats this as a cause of epidemic disease, and attributes the unseasonal weather itself to collective moral cause.

classical.chapter: 6 (Tasyashitiya; printed 'Tasyapitiya' in Kaviratna's own colophon and summary)
classical.verse: aphorisms printed 1 and 2 in the chapter's PROSE series, the numbers printed after each aphorism
classical.establishes: The adana/visarga frame and the six-season division, stated as the organising structure of the chapter. This is a cited locus for the two half-years themselves, not for the prescriptions derived from them. The claimed outcome is strength, complexion, happiness and lifespan.
classical.quote: Of him who is acquainted with the opportuneness of conduct and food with seasons, strength and complexion (and happiness and period of life) increase, in consequence of his food, &c., (being taken with propriety). For the purposes of this lesson, the year should be known as consisting of six portions, divided according to the seasons. Of these, the three seasons commencing with the season of dews and ending with summer constitute the period when the Sun travels in the region lying to the north of the equinoctial. That is again the period when the Sun takes (i.e., sucks up the liquid portion of every earthly object). The three other seasons commencing with the season of rains and ending with Hemanta constitutes the period of the Sun's southerly course. That is, besides, the time when the Sun gives (or yields moisture to all earthly objects).

classical.verse: aphorism printed 5 in the chapter's PROSE series, the number printed after the aphorism
classical.establishes: The adana half of the mechanism. The stated causal chain is environmental: solar and wind action alters the qualities of plants and water, which alters the qualities of food, which alters the body. The doshic account is downstream of an environmental one.
classical.quote: In the period of Taking, the Sun, by means of his rays, sucks up the moisture of the universe; and keen and rough winds also dry up the same. Besides, (both the Sun and) the winds, in the seasons of Sisira, Vasanta, and Grishma, gradually developing the property of roughness, and generating juices that are dry, bitter, astringent, and pungent, contribute to the weakness of mankind.

classical.verse: aphorism printed 6 in the chapter's PROSE series, the number printed after the aphorism
classical.establishes: The visarga half of the mechanism, in the same environmental terms as the adana half: weakened solar power and cloud-borne water change the qualities available in food and drink, and strength follows. Added during this revision so that both half-years, and not only adana, carry a quoted locus.
classical.quote: In the season, however, of rains, of Sarat, and of Hemanta, when the Sun begins his southerly course, and his powers become weakened by time, by the virtue of his track itself, by the winds generated by the clouds, and by the downpours (from the cloudy regions), when the Moon also appears with unabated vigor, and (lastly) when the heat of the universe becomes cooled by the water that falls from the clouds, moisture that is cool, sour, saltish, and sweet, increases gradually, and the strength of human beings increases.

classical.verse: aphorism printed 1 in the chapter's RENUMBERED VERSE series, the first aphorism after the words 'On this topic are the following verses'
classical.establishes: The seasonal strength (bala) sequence, which the original record asserted in its components list with no quote behind it. Note that strength here is assigned by POSITION within a half-year, not by climate description, which is part of why the scheme does not travel to other latitudes.
classical.quote: It should be said that during the first season of the Giving period, (viz., the season of rains), and the last season of the Taking period, (viz., summer), men become weak. In the two intermediate seasons of both the periods, (viz., Sarat and Vasanta), men become neither very weak nor very strong. During the last season of the Giving period, (viz., Hemanta), and the first of the Taking period, (viz., Sisira), the strength of men is at its highest.

classical.verse: aphorisms printed 32 and 33 in the chapter's RENUMBERED VERSE series
classical.establishes: The accumulate-then-manifest logic in Charaka's own words, and the derived rule that the autumn regimen targets pitta stored during the rains. This is the clearest retrieved statement that the regimen looks back at what accumulated, though it does not settle whether intervention belongs to the season of accumulation; see contested.
classical.quote: The bile of men whose bodies are exposed to the cold of the rainy season, and who suffer themselves to be suddenly exposed to the rays of the Sun, becomes stored. This bile, in the season of Sarat, becomes injurious. Those that desire their own benefit should, therefore, in the season of Sarat, take food and drink, agreeably to the proper measure, and that are sweet, light, cool, with (at times) things that are bitter and that check bile.

classical.verse: aphorisms printed 40 and 41 in the chapter's RENUMBERED VERSE series, the last two before the chapter-summary verse
classical.establishes: The relational definition of suitability, which is the third part of the rationale and the only part that licenses adapting the regimen to a different place. Added during this revision; the original record cited 'Charaka Sutrasthana 6' for it in a component gloss with no quote.
classical.quote: That which produces happiness or yields not torture, in consequence of the system being inured to it, is known by the name of okasatmya. They that are conversant with this topic of assimilation (or suitability of practices to the system), regard that conduct and that food to be suitable which have virtues contrary to those of the place of habitation and of the disorders (to which the system is subject).

classical.verse: unnumbered prose, Bhishagratna vol. I p. 46, immediately after the definition of the units of time and immediately before the account of the two ayanams
classical.establishes: The seasons are defined by named months of the Indian lunar calendar, not by climate variables. This anchors ritucharya to a specific latitude and calendar, which is the central difficulty in applying it elsewhere.
classical.quote: The twelve months such as, Magha, etc. are divided into six seasons such as, Winter, Spring, Summer, Rains, Autumn and Hemanta, each consisting of two months. The two months known as Tapas and Tapasya (Magha and Phalguna) constitute the season of winter. Spring consists of two months called Madhu and Madhava (Chaitra and Vaishaka). Summer is marked by two months known as Shuchi and Shukra (Jaistha and Ashadha). The rains or the rainy season is marked by two months called Nabhas and Nabhasya (Shravana and Bhadra). The two months known as Isha and Urja (Ashvina and Kartika) constitute what is called the season of Autumn. Hemanta is marked by two months called Sahas and Sahasya (Agrahayana and Pousha).

classical.verse: unnumbered prose, Bhishagratna vol. I pp. 49-50, the three consecutive paragraphs on the rains, Hemanta and summer that precede the summary of the triad
classical.establishes: The dosha-to-season assignments themselves, dosha by dosha, each with its stated environmental mechanism: pitta accumulates in the rains and manifests in autumn, kapha accumulates in hemanta and manifests in spring, vata accumulates in summer and manifests in pravrit. Added during this revision because the summary passage alone cannot carry these assignments: its English list order does not read respectively.
classical.quote: ... the bile originated and accumulated during the rains, is liquefied by the rays of the sun and gives rise to bilious diseases. ... Hence water and vegetables partaken of in Hemanta are divested of their properties of acid reaction after being assimilated in the human system, but they give rise to an accumulation of phlegm in the body owing to their heaviness, sliminess, and cooling and oily character. In spring, the phlegm thus accumulated in the body is liquefied and ushers in diseases due to a deranged state of that bodily humour. ... The sun's rays dry up the natural moisture of the human system, and accordingly water and vegetables largely partaken of in summer, give rise to an accumulation of wind in the system owing to their lightness, dryness, or expansive and drought-making properties. Subsequently wind thus accumulated in the summer, is agitated by the rains and cold winds in the forepart of the rainy season (Pravrit) when the ground is flooded with water and thus gives rise to diseases which are incidental to a deranged state of the bodily wind.

classical.verse: unnumbered prose, Bhishagratna vol. I p. 50, the summary of the triad, immediately before the mapping of the parts of the day onto the seasons
classical.establishes: The triad named as a triad, and the prashama assignments. It also contains the claim of seasonal remission without treatment, which is testable and has not been tested. What it does NOT by itself establish is which dosha accumulates in which season: its first sentence lists 'wind, bile, etc.' against 'the rains, Hemanta and summer' in non-matching order, so the assignments come from the preceding paragraphs, quoted separately in this record.
classical.quote: The fundamental bodily humours such as, wind, bile, etc. augmented and accumulated during the rains, Hemanta and summer, should be checked as soon as they become aggravated (manifest themselves) in autumn, spring, or in the forepart of the rainy season (Pravrit). Diseases which owe their origin to a deranged state of bile, phlegm and wind, are respectively ameliorated in Hemanta, summer, and autumn by natural causes, [such as the variations of atmospheric or earthly temperature, rainfall, etc.]. Thus far we have discussed the accumulation, excitation and pacification or alleviation of the deranged bodily humours.

classical.verse: unnumbered prose, Bhishagratna vol. I p. 51, after the mapping of the parts of the day onto the seasons and before the account of depopulation by curse, spell and poisonous pollen
classical.establishes: Seasonal derangement is the classical bridge to epidemic disease (janapadodhwamsa). It is worth recording plainly that the stated cause is collective moral fault, and the stated remedy is avoidance of contaminated water and produce. The remedy is sound public health; the aetiology is not.
classical.quote: Water and vegetables retain their natural properties when the seasons are natural, and do not exhibit contrary features, and they then tend to increase the appetite, vitality, strength, and power of the human system. Contrary or unnatural seasons are but the consequences of sin committed by a whole community and portend the workings of a malign destiny. A season, exhibiting unnatural or contrary features, affects or reverses the natural properties of water and vegetables peculiar to it, which, drunk or partaken of, cause dreadful epidemics in the country. The best safeguard lies in not using such defiled water and vegetables when an epidemic breaks out in the country.

classical.verse: unnumbered prose, the chapter's closing sentences, immediately before the colophon 'Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Sutrasthanam'
classical.establishes: How Sushruta's own chapter ends on the question the record leaves contested: the dosha is to be dealt with in the season of its PRAKOPA, but before it becomes a patent illness. That is neither the purely anticipatory reading nor treatment of established disease. Added during this revision because the original record said no retrieved passage bore on the question, and this one does, without settling it against Charaka's autumn prescription.
classical.quote: The bodily humours such as wind, etc. are disturbed and aggravated by the contrariety, excess or variations in the characteristic features of the seasons. Hence it is prudent to check the deranged phlegm in spring, to conquer the deranged bile in autumn, and to subdue the deranged bodily wind in the rains, before they develop themselves in any patent or manifest bodily ailment.

classical.verse: 58, as numbered in the Das-Emmerick machine-readable text (AH Su 3.58)
classical.establishes: The ritusandhi rule, retrieved at last. Working rendering: the last week of one season together with the first week of the next is known as the junction of seasons; there the earlier regimen is to be abandoned and the later one taken up, by degrees. This is the verse universally attributed to this chapter in modern Ayurvedic teaching, and the attribution holds. The e-text also carries a variant line at this verse, 'ṛtvor antyādi-saptāhād a-sātmya-jā hi rogāḥ syuḥ sahasā tyāga-śīlanāt', to the effect that diseases arise from unsuitability when the change is made abruptly.
classical.sanskrit: ṛtvor antyādi-saptāhāv ṛtu-saṃdhir iti smṛtaḥ | tatra pūrvo vidhis tyājyaḥ sevanīyo 'paraḥ kramāt || 58 ||
classical.translator: none. No public-domain English translation of Vagbhata exists, so no English quotation is given. The sense stated in 'establishes' is this project's working rendering of the Sanskrit, not a published translation, and is marked as such.

modern.title: Widespread seasonal gene expression reveals annual differences in human immunity and physiology.
modern.establishes: Dopico and colleagues, Nature Communications 6:7000. More than 4,000 protein-coding mRNAs in human white blood cells and adipose tissue show seasonal expression profiles, 'with inverted patterns observed between Europe and Oceania'; the blood cell-composition changes that could explain the periodicity 'differ between the United Kingdom and The Gambia'; and the immune system shows a pro-inflammatory transcriptomic profile during European winter with increased soluble IL-6 receptor and C-reactive protein.
modern.quality: A large, well-powered, multi-cohort transcriptomic study, and the strongest evidence carried here that human physiology has a genuine annual rhythm. It is a COMPARATOR, not a validation: it does not test ritucharya, does not use the Indian six-season division, and measures nothing that corresponds to vata, pitta or kapha. Its two between-population results point AGAINST a calendar-fixed regimen rather than for one: an effect that inverts between hemispheres and differs again between the UK and The Gambia is an effect whose sign depends on latitude, which is precisely what a regimen anchored to Magha-through-Pausha at north Indian latitude cannot accommodate. The original version of this record cited the confirming half of this paper in its evidenceState and left the disconfirming half in this field; both halves now appear in evidenceState.

modern.title: Host and Environmental Factors Influencing Individual Human Cytokine Responses.
modern.establishes: Ter Horst and colleagues, Cell 167(4):1111-1124, from the Human Functional Genomics Project. Cytokine responses to 19 bacterial, fungal, viral and non-microbial stimuli were measured in 534 healthy subjects. 'Annual seasonality is found to be an important environmental factor influencing cytokine production. Alpha-1-antitrypsin concentrations partially mediate the seasonality of cytokine responses, whereas the effect of vitamin D levels is limited.'
modern.quality: Added during this revision in answer to the critic's 'missing' finding on both the cytokine-seasonality literature and the vitamin D confound. Large for a functional immunology study, with stimulated-response readouts rather than resting transcriptome, so it is independent evidence that seasonality reaches immune FUNCTION and not only gene expression. Two limits matter here. It is a single-site Dutch cohort, so it carries no information about latitude and cannot be read either for or against a calendar-anchored regimen. And its vitamin D result is one cohort's mediation analysis, not a settlement of the confound: it weakens the claim that seasonal immune variation is simply sunlight acting through vitamin D, in this cohort, for these readouts. It tests nothing Ayurvedic, and alpha-1-antitrypsin is not a dosha.

modern.title: Increased winter mortality from acute myocardial infarction and stroke: the effect of age.
modern.establishes: Sheth, Nair, Muller and Yusuf, Journal of the American College of Cardiology, pp. 1916-1919. Analysis of 300,000 deaths in the Canadian Mortality Database for 1980-82 and 1990-92: acute myocardial infarction deaths peak in January (RR 1.090) and trough in September (RR 0.904); stroke deaths peak in January (RR 1.113) and trough in September (RR 0.914); the seasonal swing widens markedly with age.
modern.quality: Large and robust for what it measures, but ecological and observational, using administrative death records with no individual-level exposure data. It establishes that disease incidence really is seasonal, which is the premise ritucharya assumes. It does not establish that the classical dosha-season assignments are correct, and a Canadian January peak does not map onto Sushruta's kapha-accumulation-in-hemanta scheme in any testable way.

modern.establishes: Journal of Ethnic Foods, volume 8, issue 1, published 13 May 2021: 'Adopting seasonal regimen (Ritucharya) to modulate the seasonal variation in gut microbiome'. Proposes that seasonal diet shifts could be used to steer gut microbiota and links this to the classical concepts of shadkriyakala, agni and ama.
modern.quality: A NARRATIVE REVIEW with no primary data; the abstract describes itself as a review. It proposes a mechanism as future work and stops, which is the dominant pattern in this literature. The journal is not indexed in PubMed and the article returns no Europe PMC record, so it carries no PMID. It is recorded here because it is the most-cited modern attempt at a mechanism for ritucharya, and because its status as hypothesis rather than finding should be stated plainly.

openQuestions: Whether this project can publish the Ashtanga Hridaya Sanskrit quotation at all. The GRETIL e-text is distributed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 over a transcription marked 'Copyright 1997 R.P. Das and R.E. Emmerick'. Attribution is easy; the non-commercial and share-alike conditions are a licensing decision for the project, not a citation question, and the verse should not go to publication until that decision is made. If share-alike is unacceptable, the alternative is to quote the verse from a public-domain printed Sanskrit edition, which would also supply the collation this record says it lacks.

Whether to consult the Sanskrit of Charaka Sutrasthana 6.41 and of Sushruta Sutrasthana 6 before publication. Two of this record's notKnown entries exist only because the Sanskrit was not read: the Doshanam/Deshanam variant, and whether Bhishagratna's chaya/prakopa labelling is his or the text's. Both would likely close with one pass over a Sanskrit edition.

records.title: Roga-marga (the three pathways of disease)
records.domain: Ayurvedic theory of health and disease — topography of pathogenesis
records.summary: Roga-marga is Charaka's division of the body into three pathways along which disease settles. Shakha, the outer pathway, is rakta and the other dhatus together with the skin, and is called the bahya marga. Marma and asthi-sandhi, the vital points — Charaka's Sanskrit names basti (bladder), hridaya and murdha — together with the junctions of the bones and the snayu and kandara bound to them, form the madhyama or middle pathway. Koshtha, the great internal cavity, named in Ca.Su.11/48 as the mahasrotas, the middle of the body, the mahanimna and the amashaya and pakvashaya, is the abhyantara or internal pathway. Diseases are assigned to a pathway by where they manifest: goitre, pustules, skin disease and superficial growths to shakha; hemiplegia, convulsive disorders, facial palsy, wasting, bone and joint pain, prolapse of the rectum and diseases of head, heart and bladder to the middle pathway; fever, diarrhoea, vomiting, cholera, cough, dyspnoea, hiccup, abdominal disease and spleen disease to koshtha. Five conditions — visarpa, shvayathu, gulma, arsha and vidradhi — are named twice in the same aphorism, once as following shakha and once as following koshtha, which is the ubhaya-marga or dual-pathway group. The scheme is presented in the commentarial and teaching tradition as prognostic and therapeutic rather than merely descriptive, and the convention that the middle pathway is the hardest to cure is repeated across the modern reviews; this record was unable to locate that ranking in any verse of Charaka, Vagbhata or Sushruta that it could retrieve, and records it as commentarial convention rather than as text (see contested[3] and notKnown). Its mechanism rests on doshagati, the movement of doshas between koshtha and shakha, stated at Ca.Su.28/31-33.
records.evidenceState: Roga-marga is the best-anchored of the concepts in this cluster textually and the thinnest empirically. The classical footing is solid and now verified in three texts rather than one. Ca.Su.11/48 defines all three pathways; Ca.Su.11/49, a single aphorism, populates each with named diseases and names five of them twice, once as following shakha and once as following koshtha, which is the dual-pathway group; Ca.Su.28/31-33 supplies the doshagati mechanism by which doshas move outward from koshtha to shakha and back, with Chakrapani glossing the shakha of that chapter as the dhatus. Vagbhata states the same scheme independently at A.H.Su.12/44-49, defining shakha in Charaka's own words, agreeing with Charaka on koshtha, naming the madhyama rogamarga in the text, and splitting the dual-pathway diseases into outer-part and inner-part varieties instead of assigning them twice. Sushruta's koshtha at Su.Ci.2/12-13 is wider than either and includes the seat of blood along with the heart, unduka and lungs, which leaves the koshtha-shakha boundary genuinely unsettled rather than merely unclear, since rakta itself is assigned to shakha. What the texts do not contain, so far as this record could retrieve them, is the prognostic ranking the tradition is most often quoted for. Ca.Su.11/48-49 states membership and says nothing about difficulty of cure; A.H.Su.12/44-49 likewise. Ca.Ci.28/72-74 does attribute poor prognosis to depth of seat for a list of vata disorders that overlaps the madhyama list, but it never uses the word rogamarga and does not rank the pathways. The attributions of the ranking run to commentators, Chakrapani for the general claim that roga-marga serves prognosis and Gangadhara for the specific ruling that madhyama-marga disease is krichhra-sadhya or yapya, and neither commentary was retrieved in the original here, so neither is cited. The modern position is close to empty. A PubMed E-utilities search on 2026-10-06 returned zero records for 'rogamarga', for 'roga marga ayurveda' and for 'roga-marga'; every modern reference in this record that bears on roga-marga directly sits in non-indexed Indian Ayurveda journals, and the two PubMed-indexed references bear on the concept only by implication. That literature is dominated by narrative reviews that restate the three lists and then propose an analogy, most often to physiological compartmentalisation, without testing it. One cross-sectional study of 100 outpatients was found, and it reports a pathway distribution with an age gradient that it has no design to distinguish from ordinary epidemiology. No study was found in this search that measures whether two clinicians assign the same patient to the same pathway, whether pathway assignment predicts outcome or difficulty of cure, or whether the therapeutic rule derived from doshagati improves anything. The concept as it stands is a classical topographic taxonomy, attested in three samhitas and in continued teaching use, whose central prognostic claim is commentarial rather than textual and which has no published test of either its prognostic or its therapeutic claims.

contested.question: What exactly does shakha cover?
positions: The dhatus plus skin, i.e. a tissue compartment. This is what Ca.Su.11/48 states — 'shakha raktadayo dhatavas tvak ca' — and what Kaviratna's footnote spells out, and Vagbhata gives the identical definition at A.H.Su.12/44, 'shakha raktadayas tvak ca'. Two texts, same words.

The limbs and periphery, in the ordinary sense of the word 'branch'. This is how the term is often used loosely in clinical teaching. No source consulted here states it as the definition of the bahya rogamarga, and both texts that do define it define it the other way.

Whether the shakha of the doshagati passages at Ca.Su.28/31-33 is the same shakha as Ca.Su.11/48 is a real question, but it cannot be settled from the English. The Sanskrit uses the same word in both places, and Chakrapani on 28/31 glosses the destination as rasa and the rest, 'rasadinam shakharupatvat', which identifies it with the dhatus. On the evidence retrieved here the two uses agree.

contested.question: What is the extent of koshtha?
positions: The alimentary cavity. Ca.Su.11/48 gives mahasrotas, sharira-madhya, mahanimna, amashaya and pakvashaya. A.H.Su.12/46 gives 'antah koshtho mahasrota ama-pakvashayashrayah', which agrees. Kaviratna's footnote extends it to the bladder, the aorta, the lungs and the juices of liver and spleen, but that extension is his, not the verse's.

A wider internal territory. Su.Ci.2/12-13, now quoted at classical[7] from Bhishagratna, lists the seats of ama, agni, pakva, mutra and rudhira, plus the heart, the unduka and the lungs, as koshtha. Four of those eight are not in Charaka's or Vagbhata's definition.

The two definitions are not reconcilable at the boundary. Charaka assigns rakta to shakha and Sushruta assigns the reservoir of blood to koshtha, so on the combined reading the same tissue falls on both sides.
