Nothing retrieved here resolves which definition the roga-marga scheme is supposed to use, and the roga-marga scheme is Charaka's.

contested.question: How should the dual-pathway (ubhaya marga) diseases be understood?
positions: Membership is a property of the episode, not of the disease. Ca.Su.11/49 names visarpa, shvayathu, gulma, arsha and vidradhi twice inside one aphorism, as shakhanusarinah and again as koshthanusarinah, with no qualifier distinguishing two kinds of each.

They are separate outer and inner varieties of conditions that share a name. This is Vagbhata's reading and he states it in the text: A.H.Su.12/45 assigns the 'bahirbhaga', outer-part, varieties of durnama, gulma and shopha to shakha, and A.H.Su.12/47 assigns the 'antarbhaga', inner-part, varieties of shopha, arsha, gulma, visarpa and vidradhi to koshtha.
The category is a residue of a taxonomy that does not partition cleanly, which weakens the claim that pathway assignment is informative.

Charaka and Vagbhata therefore disagree about the same five diseases, and the disagreement is in the Sanskrit rather than in anyone's translation. Whether Vagbhata is interpreting Charaka or departing from him is not addressed by any source consulted here.

contested.question: Is the middle pathway really the hardest to cure?
positions: The standard teaching position, repeated across the modern reviews, is that madhyama-marga diseases are the most difficult, often phrased as krichhra-sadhya or yapya.

No verse stating it was located. This revision searched the three places the audit named. Ca.Su.11/48 and 11/49 were retrieved in full in the Sanskrit and quoted at classical[0], [2], [3] and [4]; they state membership and contain no prognostic term. A.H.Su.12/44-49 was retrieved in full in the Sanskrit and quoted at classical[6]; it contains no prognostic term either. Ca.Ci.28/72-74 was retrieved and is quoted at classical[8]; it does say that a list of vata disorders overlapping the madhyama list 'may or may not be cured even with effort' because of the depth of the seat, but it never uses the word rogamarga and does not rank the three pathways.

The claim's provenance is commentarial. The modern critical edition at carakasamhitaonline.com reports Chakrapani on Ca.Su.11/48 as giving the purpose of the roga-marga section as knowing prognosis, which is weaker than a ranking; the reviews attribute the ranking itself to Gangadhara. Chakrapani's commentary on Su.11 is not in the GRETIL Caraka excerpt, which covers only Sutrasthana 1-3, 5, 6 and 26-28, and Gangadhara's Jalpakalpataru was not retrievable here. Neither is quoted, so neither is cited.

Its status in this record is therefore: conventional, attributed to commentators, not located in any samhita verse retrieved, and not tested. The searches that justify the words 'not located' are the four named above and nothing wider.

contested.question: Does roga-marga correspond to any modern physiological division?
positions: Yes, to compartmentalisation — alimentary, intravascular, interstitial, intracellular (AYUSHDHARA 2023, modern[1]).
No: the three pathways group diseases by manifest site, not by any single physiological axis, and the dual-pathway group shows the taxonomy crossing whatever boundary is proposed.

Any such mapping has to choose a definition of koshtha first, and the texts do not agree on one. Charaka's and Vagbhata's koshtha is alimentary; Sushruta's includes the blood reservoir, the heart and the lungs, which would land in a different compartment on the proposed scheme.
The mapping has never been tested, so all of the above are currently assertions.

notKnown: No samhita verse ranking the three pathways by difficulty of cure was located. This is the single most-repeated clinical claim about the concept, and the searches run for it were: the full Sanskrit of Ca.Su.11/48 and 11/49, the full Sanskrit of A.H.Su.12/44-49, and Ca.Ci.28/72-74. None contains a prognostic term applied to a rogamarga. The claim is attributed in the modern literature to Chakrapani and to Gangadhara. Chakrapani's commentary on Ca.Su.11 is not in the only machine-readable Caraka commentary text available here, and Gangadhara was not retrievable at all, so whether either commentator states the ranking in the form the reviews give is unverified. A wider search of printed commentary editions would settle it and has not been run.

Whether Ca.Ci.28/74's principle, that depth of seat makes cure uncertain, was intended as the same doctrine as the roga-marga ranking is not stated by any source consulted. The verse is about vata-vyadhi sites, the overlap with the madhyama list is partial, and treating the two as one claim would be the record's inference and not a source's.

Whether two clinicians independently assign the same patient to the same roga-marga has not been measured in anything found in this search. No inter-rater agreement data for this classification were located.

Whether pathway assignment predicts prognosis, difficulty of cure, or response to a given therapy is untested in anything found. The tradition's central prognostic claim has neither a located verse nor supporting data.

Whether the therapeutic rule derived from doshagati — bring shakha-lodged doshas back to koshtha before shodhana — improves outcomes over shodhana without that step has not been trialled in anything found in this search.
The criteria by which the single cross-sectional study assigned its 100 patients to pathways are not stated in it, so what that study measured is unclear.

How a disease that occupies both pathways should be managed differently from one confined to a single pathway is not specified by the sources consulted. Vagbhata's outer-part and inner-part distinction implies that the two varieties are treated as two diseases, but he does not say so and no source consulted draws the therapeutic consequence.

Whether Charaka's double assignment of the five dual-pathway diseases and Vagbhata's bahirbhaga/antarbhaga split are the same doctrine in different words or two different doctrines is not addressed by any source consulted.

Where the boundary between koshtha and shakha actually falls is not settled. Charaka and Vagbhata give an alimentary koshtha and assign rakta to shakha; Sushruta's koshtha at Su.Ci.2/12-13 includes the reservoir of blood as well as the heart, unduka and lungs. Nothing consulted says which definition the roga-marga scheme is to be read with.

No source found reconciles the roga-marga topography with the srotas enumeration. Both are territorial schemes over the same body, and how they relate — whether a channel belongs to a pathway, or crosses several — is not addressed.

The Sanskrit text and verse number of the Sushruta koshtha definition at classical[7] were not confirmed against a primary edition. The English is quoted from Bhishagratna directly, but Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers, and the address 12-13 and the Devanagari come from two secondary web sources. This is a known gap in that citation, recorded on the citation itself.

Whether the English translation of the Ashtanga Hridaya that the modern reviews quote is a lawful source for this project is not settled, because no public-domain English translation of the text was identified. The A.H. citations here are Sanskrit only for that reason.

components.gloss: The external pathway. Charaka defines it as 'raktadayo dhatavas tvak ca', rakta and the other dhatus together with the skin (Ca.Su.11/48). Vagbhata gives the same definition in the same words, 'shakha raktadayas tvak ca', and calls it the bahya-rogayana (A.H.Su.12/44). The word literally means 'branch'; both texts use it for a tissue compartment, not for the limbs.

The middle pathway. Charaka's Sanskrit names the marmas as 'basti-hridaya-murdhadini' — bladder, heart, head and the like — and adds the junctions of the bones and the snayu and kandara bound to them (Ca.Su.11/48). Vagbhata lists 'shiro-hridaya-vasty-adi-marmani' with the joints of the bones and the sira, snayu and kandara attached to them, and names this the madhyama rogamarga (A.H.Su.12/47-48). Kaviratna's English renders basti as 'the arms' and murdha as 'the brain' in both places where they occur; the Sanskrit does not support either rendering and the gloss here follows the Sanskrit.

The internal pathway. Charaka gives it as a set of synonyms: mahasrotas, sharira-madhya (the middle of the body), mahanimna, and the amashaya and pakvashaya (Ca.Su.11/48). Vagbhata agrees almost exactly: 'antah koshtho mahasrota ama-pakvashayashrayah' (A.H.Su.12/46). Sushruta's definition is wider and does not coincide with either; see contested[1].

The dual-pathway group. Ca.Su.11/49 names visarpa, shvayathu, gulma, arsha and vidradhi twice within one aphorism: first as 'shakhanusarino bhavanti rogah' (diseases following shakha) and again as 'koshthanusarino bhavanti rogah' (diseases following koshtha). The compound 'ubhaya-marga' is not in the verse; it is the category name used by the commentarial and teaching tradition for the repetition. Vagbhata handles the same five differently, assigning their 'bahirbhaga' (outer-part) varieties to shakha and their 'antarbhaga' (inner-part) varieties to koshtha (A.H.Su.12/45, 47), which is a different doctrine about the same list. See contested[2].

The movement of doshas between pathways. Ca.Su.28/31: from koshtha to shakha through exercise, the sharpness of internal heat, and neglect of what is beneficial, driven by the quickness of vayu. Ca.Su.28/32: once there they may lie dormant, not stirred, awaiting a further cause. Ca.Su.28/33: they leave shakha and return to koshtha by increase, liquefaction, digestion, clearing of the channel mouths, and the restraining of vayu. Chakrapani's Ayurvedadipika on 28/31 glosses the destination as rasa and the rest — 'rasadinam shakharupatvat' — which identifies shakha here with the dhatus, the same sense as Ca.Su.11/48.

The tradition uses the pathway to grade difficulty of cure and to choose therapy. This record could not locate a samhita verse that ranks the three pathways by difficulty. The attribution runs through commentators: the modern critical edition at carakasamhitaonline.com reports Chakrapani on Ca.Su.11/48 as saying the purpose of describing roga-marga is to know prognosis, and the reviews attribute the specific ruling that madhyama-marga disease is krichhra-sadhya or yapya to Gangadhara. Neither commentary was retrieved in the original, so neither is quoted here. See contested[3] and notKnown.

classical.establishes: The definition of all three pathways and the contents assigned to each, in the Sanskrit, with a public-domain English alongside it whose limits are recorded above. This is the locus classicus for the concept.
classical.sanskrit: त्रयो रोगमार्गा इति- शाखा, मर्मास्थिसन्धयः, कोष्ठश्च| तत्र शाखा रक्तादयो धातवस्त्वक् च, स बाह्यो रोगमार्गः; मर्माणि पुनर्बस्तिहृदयमूर्धादीनि, अस्थिसन्धयोऽस्थिसंयोगास्तत्रोपनिबद्धाश्च स्नायुकण्डराः, स मध्यमो रोगमार्गः; कोष्ठः पुनरुच्यते महास्रोतः शरीरमध्यं महानिम्नमामपक्वाशयश्चेति पर्यायशब्दैस्तन्त्रे, स रोगमार्ग आभ्यन्तरः||४८||
classical.translation: The seats of disease are three. They are (1) Cakha, (2) vital parts and bone-joints, and (3) Koshtha. Amongst these, Cakha includes blood and the like, the humours known by the name of Dhatu, and skin. These constitute the External seat of disease. The Vital parts, again, are the arms, the heart, the brain, and the like. The Bone-joints are the joints of the different bones, and the arteries and veins attached to them. These two (viz., the vital parts and bone-joints) constitute what is called the second seat (in our enumeration) of disease. Koshtha is otherwise called the great Stream within the body. The great cavity below, the cavity containing undigested food, the cavity where digestion takes place, and other words occurring together in medical treatises and expressive of the same part of the human frame, are also used for Koshtha. Koshtha is the Internal seat of disease.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's footnote to his aphorism 47, i.e. to Ca.Su.11/48
classical.establishes: That Kaviratna read marga as seat or territory rather than as conduit, and read shakha in this context as a tissue compartment rather than the limbs. His extension of shakha to flesh, marrow, fat, bone and shukra goes beyond the verse, which says rakta and the other dhatus and the skin; the extension is his, and that is part of what this entry records.
classical.translation: The word 'Marga' literally means path or way. In medical treatises, as applied to disease, it implies seat or the parts subject to disease. 'Cakha' literally means branch. As a techinacal word in medical science, it implies, as explained in the text, blood and the like, the humours and the skin. Of course, it includes flesh, marrow, fat, bones, and seminal fluid.

classical.verse: 49, first of its three clauses
classical.establishes: The bahya-marga disease list, and immediately after it the five diseases said to follow shakha — visarpa, shvayathu, gulma, arsha, vidradhi. The same five are named again in the third clause of the same aphorism as following koshtha (classical[4]), and that repetition inside one aphorism, in the Sanskrit, is what constitutes the dual-pathway group. No reconstruction of the English is needed or used.
classical.sanskrit: तत्र, गण्डपिडकालज्यपचीचर्मकीलाधिमांसमषककुष्ठव्यङ्गादयो विकारा बहिर्मार्गजाश्च विसर्पश्वयथुगुल्मार्शोविद्रध्यादयः शाखानुसारिणो भवन्ति रोगाः
classical.translation: Bronchocele, ulcers, tubercles, indolent tumours, warts, tumours, fleshy excrescences, soft corns, leprosy, dark spots on the cheek, and other ailments of this kind, are diseases that appertain to External seats. Erysepelas, abscesses, tumours (in the stomach and the arms), piles, deep-seated abscesses, and similar other maladies are diseases that appertain to External seats.

classical.verse: 49, second of its three clauses
classical.establishes: The madhyama-marga disease list: pakshavadha, graha, apatanaka, ardita, shosha, rajayakshma, asthi-sandhi-shula, guda-bhramsha, and diseases of head, heart and bladder. The verse states membership only. It says nothing about prognosis, severity or difficulty of cure, and must not be cited for the ranking discussed in contested[3].
classical.sanskrit: पक्षवधग्रहापतानकार्दितशोषराजयक्ष्मास्थिसन्धिशूलगुदभ्रंशादयः शिरोहृद्बस्तिरोगादयश्च मध्यममार्गानुसारिणो भवन्ति रोगाः
classical.translation: Hemiplegia, pains (in different limbs), spasmodic contractions, facial paralysis, pulmonary consumption, phthisis, pains in bones and bone-joints, prolapsus ani, and other diseases of the head, of the heart, and of the arms, all appertain to the Second seat.

classical.verse: 49, third of its three clauses
classical.establishes: The abhyantara-marga disease list, and in its second sentence the second naming of visarpa, shvayathu, gulma, arsha and vidradhi, this time as koshthanusarinah. Together with classical[2] this is the whole basis of the ubhaya-marga category: the same five diseases named under both pathways within one aphorism of the Sanskrit.
classical.sanskrit: ज्वरातीसारच्छर्द्यलसकविसूचिकाकासश्वासहिक्कानाहोदरप्लीहादयोऽन्तर्मार्गजाश्च विसर्पश्वयथुगुल्मार्शोविद्रध्यादयः कोष्ठानुसारिणो भवन्ति रोगाः||४९||
classical.translation: Fever with diarrhcea, nausea, tympanitis, cholera and choleraic diarrhoea, asthma, consumption, hiccup, epistisis (suppression of urine), spleen, and other diseases of the stomach appertain to that which has been called the Internal seat. Besides these, erysipelas, intumescence, internal tumours, piles, all deep-seated abscesses, and other diseases of a similar kind, are said to appertain to the seat known by the name of Koshtka (as explained before).

classical.establishes: The mechanism underpinning roga-marga: doshas move outward from koshtha to shakha under named conditions, may lie dormant there awaiting a further cause, and return inward when the named reversals occur. This is the classical basis for the therapeutic rule that shakha-lodged doshas should first be drawn back to koshtha. Chakrapani's gloss additionally ties the shakha of this chapter to the dhatus of Ca.Su.11/48.
classical.sanskrit: vyāyāmād ūṣmaṇas taikṣṇyāddhitasyānavacāraṇāt / koṣṭhācchākhā malā yānti drutatvānmarutasya ca // 31 // tatrasthāśca vilambante kadācin na samīritāḥ / nādeśakāle kupyanti bhūyo hetupratīkṣiṇaḥ // 32 // vṛddhyā viṣyandanāt pākāt srotomukhaviśodhanāt / śākhā muktvā malāḥ koṣṭhaṃ yānti vāyośca nigrahāt // 33 //
classical.translation: Through physical exercise, through the keeness of (internal) heat, through neglect of beneficial acts and practices, the Malas pass from the Koshtha to the ducts, impelled thereto by the speed (or force) of the wind. Arrived at the ducts they sometimes stay there, unimpelled by any other force. Unless the region and the time be undisposed thereto, they do not become excited, for they await some cause of excitement. In consequence of aggravation, of escape (through liquefaction, &c.), of digestion, and of the clearance of the mouth of the duct, the Malas, leaving the ducts, return to the Koshtha, the force of the (impelling) wind having been subdued.

classical.establishes: Vagbhata's independent statement of the same three-pathway scheme, which this record previously carried as an unverified paraphrase taken from a review. Four things it settles. (1) Shakha is defined in the same words as Charaka: 'shakha raktadayas tvak ca', and is called the bahya-rogayana (12/44). (2) Koshtha is 'antah koshtho mahasrota ama-pakvashayashrayah' (12/46), which agrees with Charaka's definition and not with Sushruta's wider one. (3) The madhyama rogamarga is named as such in the text — 'madhyamah rogamargah' — and consists of the marmas, given as shiro-hridaya-vasti and the rest, the joints of the bones, and the sira, snayu and kandara bound to them (12/47-48). (4) Vagbhata handles the dual-pathway diseases by splitting them: the 'bahirbhaga' or outer-part varieties of durnama (arsha), gulma and shopha go to shakha (12/45), and the 'antarbhaga' or inner-part varieties of shopha, arsha, gulma, visarpa and vidradhi go to koshtha (12/47). That is a different doctrine from Charaka's, and it is the textual basis of position 2 in contested[2]. Nothing in 12/44-49 ranks the three pathways by difficulty of cure.
classical.sanskrit: kurvanti vividhān vyādhīn śākhā-koṣṭhāsthi-saṃdhiṣu | śākhā raktādayas tvak ca bāhya-rogāyanaṃ hi tat || 44 || tad-āśrayā maṣa-vyaṅga-gaṇḍālajy-arbudādayaḥ | bahir-bhāgāś ca dur-nāma-gulma-śophādayo gadāḥ || 45 || antaḥ koṣṭho mahā-srota āma-pakvāśayāśrayaḥ | tat-sthānāḥ chardy-atīsāra-kāsa-śvāsodara-jvarāḥ || 46 || antar-bhāgaṃ ca śophārśo-gulma-visarpa-vidradhi | śiro-hṛdaya-vasty-ādi-marmāṇy asthnāṃ ca saṃdhayaḥ || 47 || tan-nibaddhāḥ sirā-snāyu-kaṇḍarādyāś ca madhyamaḥ | roga-mārgaḥ sthitās tatra yakṣma-pakṣa-vadhārditāḥ || 48 || mūrdhādi-rogāḥ saṃdhy-asthi-trika-śūla-grahādayaḥ |
classical.translator: No public-domain English translation of the Ashtanga Hridaya exists, so no English is quoted. The Sanskrit above is the citation.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: Sushruta's definition of koshtha, which is wider than Charaka's and than Vagbhata's. It includes the seat of blood, and also the heart, the unduka and the lungs, none of which are in Ca.Su.11/48. This entry was marked 'located' and unquoted at gathering, and it is load-bearing: contested[1] and notKnown both turn on it. The boundary problem is now sourced rather than asserted, since rakta is assigned to shakha by Ca.Su.11/48 and its reservoir to koshtha here.
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

classical.establishes: Added in response to the thin finding, which asked whether Ca.Ci.28 supports the claim that the middle pathway is hardest to cure. It does not support that claim, and this entry records what it does say instead. Charaka here lists sandhi-chyuti, hanu-stambha, kunchana, kubjata, ardita, pakshaghata, anga-samshosha, pangutva, khuda-vatata, stambhana, adhyavata and the vata disorders seated in majja and asthi, and says of them 'ete sthanasya gambhiryad yatnat sidhyanti va na va' — these, by reason of the depth of the seat, may or may not be cured even with effort, and are to be treated when recent, in a strong patient, and free of complications. The principle is depth of seat, and the disease list overlaps Charaka's own madhyama-marga list at ardita, pakshaghata and the bone and joint conditions. It is adjacent evidence, not the verse the tradition cites: it is a statement about vata-vyadhi sites, it never uses the word rogamarga, it does not mention the three pathways, and it does not rank them. It is recorded here so that the claim in contested[3] can be seen to have a textual neighbour and still no text.
classical.sanskrit: सन्धिच्युतिर्हनुस्तम्भः कुञ्चनं कुब्जताऽर्दितः ||७२|| पक्षाघातोऽङ्गसंशोषः पङ्गुत्वं खुडवातता | स्तम्भनं चाढ्यवातश्च रोगा मज्जास्थिगाश्च ये ||७३|| एते स्थानस्य गाम्भीर्याद्यत्नात् सिध्यन्ति वा न वा | नवान् बलवतस्त्वेतान् साधयेन्निरुपद्रवान् ||७४||
classical.translator: No public-domain English is available for this chapter. Kaviratna's Chikitsasthana stops at his Lesson XXII and does not reach chapter 28; the scan's own closing testimonials describe the translation as complete only 'so far as it has gone'. The carakasamhitaonline English is in copyright under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and is not quoted. The Sanskrit is the citation.

modern.establishes: A single-centre cross-sectional study of 100 OPD patients classified by roga-marga. Reports abhyantara 38%, madhyama 36%, with internal-pathway disorders (amlapitta, ajirna) concentrated in the 21-30 age band and middle-pathway bone and joint disorders in the 31-50 band.
modern.quality: The only study found in this search that counts anything about roga-marga in patients, and it is weak: n=100, one outpatient department, no comparison group, no stated criteria for assigning a patient to a pathway, no inter-rater check, and publication in a non-indexed Ayurveda journal. The age gradient it reports is consistent with the ordinary age distribution of dyspepsia and of osteoarthritis, so the study provides no test that would discriminate between the roga-marga scheme carrying information and the gradient arising from background epidemiology alone. This record holds no comparison data for that OPD population and has run no analysis against one, so it does not assert that the gradient is explained by background epidemiology; it asserts only that the study cannot tell the two apart.

modern.establishes: Critical analysis of roga-marga that proposes the physiological notion of compartmentalisation (alimentary, intravascular, interstitial, intracellular) as a modern analogue of the three pathways.
modern.quality: Narrative review. The compartment analogy is offered as an interpretation and is not tested against anything; no patient data, no measurement. It is a plausible-sounding mapping with no evidence behind it.

modern.establishes: Review arguing that roga-marga functions as a clinical and therapeutic indicator, i.e. that knowing the pathway should guide prognosis and choice of therapy.
modern.quality: Narrative review in a non-indexed journal. Asserts clinical utility; presents no outcome data demonstrating it. This is also one of the reviews that attributes the prognostic ranking of the three pathways to the commentators rather than quoting a verse.

modern.establishes: Analysis of the roga-marga concept and its claimed clinical importance.
modern.quality: Narrative review, non-indexed journal. Adds textual restatement, not evidence.

modern.title: Myth and reality of "theory-driven individualised practice" in Ayurveda: Mapping physicians' approaches using case-based scenarios.
modern.establishes: Case-vignette survey of 141 experienced practitioners found significant lack of consensus on clinical diagnosis and on the pathophysiology assigned to the same case, and that theoretical constructs did not uniformly determine treatment choice.
modern.quality: Empirical and directly relevant, since pathway assignment is part of the samprapti reasoning surveyed. Limitations: convenience sample, emailed self-report, hypothetical cases, no formal agreement statistic. It does not measure roga-marga assignment as such, so it bears on the concept by implication rather than directly. Still the only study in this cluster that tests rather than restates.

modern.title: Understanding the etiopathogenesis and diagnosis of malignancy in the framework of Ayurveda: A review based on experience of working in an institute of oncology.
modern.establishes: Review drawing on examination of 400 cancer patients at an oncology institute, proposing that udara, gulma and vidradhi correspond to abdominal tumours with cancerous potential, and stating plainly that there is no common agreement among experts on the Ayurvedic pathogenesis of malignancy.
modern.quality: Framed as a review based on clinical observation rather than a designed study: no protocol, no comparison group, no reported classification criteria, findings arrived at by expert judgement. Its value here is mainly the author's own admission of disagreement among experts, and the fact that two of the three conditions it names (gulma, vidradhi) are among the five dual-pathway conditions of Ca.Su.11/49.

records.title: Sadhya-asadhya (prognosis and the decision to treat)
records.summary: Sadhya-asadhya is the classical requirement that the physician determine, before beginning treatment, whether a disease is curable, manageable but not curable, or beyond treatment. Charaka divides diseases into sadhya (curable) and asadhya (incurable), each into two: curable easily or with difficulty, and incurable but suppressible (yapya) or without treatment at all (anupakramya, pratyakhyeya). He states this at Ca.Su.10/9 and then, at Ca.Su.10/11-20, gives a graded list of criteria for each of the four. That criteria block is the most detailed prognostic rule either samhita contains, and this record did not carry it at gathering. Charaka restates the scheme at Ca.Su.18/39-41, where yapya is named in the verse and curability is crossed with mildness and violence to give four kinds. Sushruta gives three working categories, curable, yapya and incurable, at Su.Su.35, and specifies the features that make a disease yield to medicine: recent onset, absence of distressing complications, mismatch with the patient's country, season, temperament and habituation, intact digestion, and the presence of strength and fortitude. He applies the same three tiers to one disease class at Su.Su.23, where a named block of yapya ulcers admits palliation only. Vagbhata compresses the whole scheme into Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 1/29+(1) to 1/35. The classification carries a strong professional injunction. Charaka warns at Ca.Su.10/8 that a physician who treats an incurable case loses wealth, knowledge and fame and incurs the censure of the world; Sushruta at Su.Su.33 tells the physician to abandon patients with named fatal complications; and Vagbhata at A.H.Su.1/34-35 lists the patients to be given up, most of them named for reasons that are not medical at all. A parallel body of material, the arishta lakshanas of Charaka's Indriya Sthana, twelve chapters whose titles are enumerated in components, and Sushruta Sutrasthana 28 to 33, catalogues signs of impending death; Vagbhata's counterpart is Sharirasthana 5. The two bodies are joined inside the text itself, because Charaka's criteria for refusal at Ca.Su.10/20 include sarishta, the disease accompanied by arishtas, and Vagbhata's at A.H.Su.1/33 include drishta-rishta. Charaka also lays down a disclosure rule at Ca.In.12/62-64: the physician should never say unasked that death is near, should not say so even when asked if the declaration would cause harm, and should instead decline the case without saying why. The rule is asymmetric; at Ca.In.12/65-66 the physician is told to declare recovery when the contrary signs appear.
records.evidenceState: Sadhya-asadhya rests on classical exegesis, and this revision made the classical side substantially stronger while narrowing what can be said about the modern side. On the texts, the concept is now sourced in three samhitas and nineteen citations, of which eighteen carry a quote. Charaka states the fourfold scheme at Ca.Su.10/9, grades the curable again by magnitude of means at 10/10, and then gives a separate criteria list for each of the four tiers at 10/11-20, built from a recurring set of variables whose values shift across the tiers: force of causes and signs, correspondence of dosha with dushya, prakriti, season and place, number of doshas, number of pathways, depth of seat, marma and sandhi involvement, duration, complications, tolerance of medicines, and completeness of the four padas. That block is the most detailed prognostic rule in either samhita and the record did not have it at gathering, which is why it previously credited Sushruta with the nearest thing to an operational rule. Charaka restates the scheme independently at Ca.Su.18/39-41, where yapya is named in the verse. Sushruta's three tiers and his criteria are at Su.Su.35, and Su.Su.23 shows the three tiers applied to one disease class with a named yapya block. Vagbhata compresses the whole thing into A.H.Su.1/29+(1) to 1/35. The arishta material is Charaka's twelve Indriya Sthana chapters, Sushruta Su.Su.28 to 33, and A.H.Sharirasthana 5. The two bodies are joined inside the text: Charaka's refusal criteria at Ca.Su.10/20 include sarishtam, Vagbhata's at A.H.Su.1/33 include drishta-rishta, and Sushruta closes his arishta block at Su.Su.32 by saying that the physician who can read the fatal signs is honoured by the king for determining whether a disease is curable or incurable. Three separate loci therefore state the purpose of the arishta chapters to be the sadhya-asadhya judgement, which the record previously asserted as its own reading. The doctrine has an internal feature that resists testing, and it is in the Sanskrit rather than in anyone's English: Ca.In.2/5 says no arishta once arisen vanishes other than by death and no death is unpreceded by one, and 2/6 assigns both false positives and false negatives to prajnaparadha. But Vagbhata reports a qualification the record did not have. At A.H.Sha.5/3-4 he says that some hold rishta to be twofold, sthayin and asthayin, and that a mere abundance of doshas can produce a rishtabhasa, an appearance of a rishta, which subsides when the doshas are pacified, while the persistent one goes inevitably to death. That is a prospectively applicable criterion, and it narrows the self-sealing reading without dissolving it. On the modern side, nothing was found in the indexes searched that tests any part of the concept, and the searches are named in full in searchRecord rather than summarised. PubMed E-utilities was run on 2026-10-06 with seventeen strings, DHARA with ten, and the AYUSH Research Portal, which holds 30,920 Ayurveda records and is the largest relevant index, failed server-side on every attempt with its own tempdb error and has therefore not been searched at all. Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, CENTRAL, Google Scholar, any Hindi or Devanagari search, and any hand-search of non-indexed Indian Ayurveda journals were not attempted. Within those bounds: changing the search string recovered three on-topic indexed records the record had missed, so the record's previous claim that there is no modern evidence base was not merely unbounded but wrong in part. One of the three, a 1997 paper in Ancient Science of Life, states the classical ruling that kaphaja prameha is sadhya and pittaja and vataja are yapya and asadhya, and sets out to test it against insulin level; its retrievable abstract reports an aim and no results, so it establishes that the attempt exists and nothing more. Another is a commentarial study of arishta-vijnana in Dalhana and Chakrapani, which shows that the scholarly literature on the arishta material is substantial and that this record has consulted none of it in the original. The strongest material actually in hand remains indirect: the knee-osteoarthritis reliability study, which shows that Ayurvedic experts agree poorly on the diagnostic inputs a prognostic judgement would be built from, and the three oil-drop papers, of which the 2012 one is a standardisation protocol whose own premise is that the technique is crude and variable. Zero of the ten modern references report a sadhya, yapya or asadhya assignment tested against an outcome, an agreement statistic for any prognostic category, or sensitivity, specificity or a c-statistic for any arishta sign. That is the honest summary of the modern position, and it is a statement about these searches rather than about the world. This revision also added three comparators from conventional medicine, because the defensible claim is not that no evidence exists but that the test has not been done and this is what it would look like. Christakis and Lamont (2000) measured clinician prognostic accuracy directly: 20 per cent of 468 predictions accurate, 63 per cent overoptimistic, survival overestimated by a factor of 5.3. The Surprise Question meta-analysis (2017) reports pooled accuracy of 74.8 per cent over 25,718 predictions with c-statistics from 0.512 to 0.822, which is the form a single clinician-rated death sign has to be reported in to be assessable at all. The Palliative Prognostic Index meta-analysis (2025) does the same for a composite score built from weighted features, which is the form Charaka's and Sushruta's criteria lists take. Together they show that the quantity the arishta chapters claim to deliver is one conventional medicine also attempts and is measurably poor at, so the comparison is not between a tested method and an untested one; it is between a method whose error has been quantified and one whose error has not. What remains most in need of explicit treatment in any modern reference is the ethical content, and this revision sharpened it rather than softening it. Charaka's disclosure rule at Ca.In.12/62-64 directs the physician to withhold a terminal prognosis and decline the case without saying why, and at 12/65 it directs him to declare recovery with certainty when the contrary signs appear, so it is a one-way restriction and not a general reticence. Vagbhata's refusal list at A.H.Su.1/34-35 is wider still and eleven of its twelve grounds are not prognostic: political disfavour, lack of means, distraction, non-compliance, violence, grief, timidity, ingratitude, and thinking oneself a physician. Every reason the three texts give for getting the prognosis right is a reason of the physician's standing: loss of wealth and fame at Ca.Su.10/8, infamy and loss of one's own interest at A.H.Sha.5/1+(2), professional success at Su.Su.33, and the king's honour at Su.Su.32. This is the part that is incompatible with contemporary informed-consent and palliative-care practice, and no source consulted reconciles them.

contested.question: Is the classification three-fold or four-fold?
positions: Three: sadhya, yapya, asadhya. This is Sushruta's formulation at Su.Su.35 (classical[11]) and the one used in most teaching.
Four: sukhasadhya, kricchrasadhya, yapya, anupakramya/pratyakhyeya. This is Charaka's at Ca.Su.10/9 (classical[1]) and Vagbhata's at A.H.Su.1/29+(1) (classical[17]), in the same terms in both.

Charaka elsewhere crosses curability with severity to produce a different four, mild-curable, violent-curable, mild-incurable and violent-incurable, at Ca.Su.18/41 (classical[6]). The three schemes are routinely presented as one, which they are not.

Arguably more than four, since Ca.Su.10/10 divides the curable again by whether the means required are alpa, madhyama or utkrishta (classical[2]). Charaka therefore has at least five grades of sadhya-ness within the curable alone, and the record's own earlier count of four was itself a simplification.

contested.question: Is refusing an incurable case an ethical duty or professional self-protection?
positions: The texts give the reason in self-interested terms, and this revision found that all four places they do so agree. Ca.Su.10/8 lists artha, vidya, yasha, upakrosha and asangraha, all costs to the physician. A.H.Sha.5/1+(2) says treatment in one whose life-span is exhausted yields ayashas and svartha-hani, infamy and loss of one's own interest. Su.Su.33 says the physician 'with any regard to professional success' should abandon such a patient. Su.Su.32 says the physician who can read the fatal signs is honoured by the king for determining curability. Four loci, four reasons, none of them about the patient.

Modern Ayurvedic commentary reframes pratyakhyana as honesty about limits and avoidance of futile burdensome treatment, closer to a palliative-care rationale. Both readings are defensible from the text, but they are different rationales and the texts state the first.

Vagbhata's refusal list at A.H.Su.1/34-35 (classical[17]) makes the self-protection reading harder to avoid, because most of it is not about prognosis at all. The physician is to give up the patient who is hated by physicians and kings, who hates them, who is hinopakaranam (lacking means), vyagram (distracted), avidheyam (non-compliant), chandam (violent), shokaturam (grief-stricken), bhirum (timid), kritaghnam (ungrateful) or vaidyamaninam (thinks himself a physician). Only gatayusham, one whose life-span is gone, is a prognostic ground. Whatever pratyakhyana is in Charaka, in Vagbhata it is partly a rule about which patients are worth taking on.

A third reading is possible and is not the same as either: that the texts are describing a reputational economy rather than prescribing one, i.e. recording what a physician who wished to keep a practice in that setting had to do. No source consulted here argues this, and this record does not assert it; it is listed because the first two positions are usually presented as exhausting the options and they do not.

contested.question: Should a terminal prognosis be disclosed?
positions: Charaka Ca.In.12/62-64 (classical[9]): never unasked, not even when asked if harm would follow, and decline without explaining.

The rule is one-directional, which the record did not previously state. Ca.In.12/65 (classical[10]) tells the physician to declare recovery dhruvam, with certainty, when the signs contrary to the death-signs appear. So the text is not reticent about prognosis as such; it withholds bad news and gives good news positively. This makes the conflict with informed consent sharper, not softer, because the asymmetry is itself the thing modern consent doctrine objects to.

Contemporary medical ethics and the informed-consent framework under which registered Ayurvedic practitioners operate in India require disclosure to a competent patient who asks. The classical rule and current professional obligation conflict, and no source consulted resolves this.

The classical rule's own stated ground is harm, 'tatra yatropaghatakam', where it would be injurious, which is recognisably a therapeutic-privilege argument and is not simply evasion. That does not reconcile the two, because modern consent doctrine has largely rejected therapeutic privilege as a default, but it does mean the disagreement is about whether the privilege holds rather than about whether patients matter.

contested.question: Do arishta signs have prognostic content?
positions: The tradition treats them as reliable, on the strength of long clinical observation; Kaviratna's own preface remarks that experience seems to confirm many of Punarvasu's observations. That remark is the translator's and is recorded as such.

No sign has been evaluated prospectively in anything found in the searches named in searchRecord, and several arishta chapters concern dreams, omens, the conduct of the messenger sent to fetch the physician, and incidents on the road, which are not observations about the patient at all. Ca.In.12/66 confirms this directly: the signs the physician may read recovery off include the messenger, omens on the road, the patient's household and the patient's property.

The doctrine's definition is self-sealing, and this is in the Sanskrit rather than in the English. Ca.In.2/5 says no arishta once arisen vanishes other than by death and no death is unpreceded by one; Ca.In.2/6 assigns both false positives and false negatives to prajnaparadha. A.H.Sha.5/2 says the same. On that definition clinical experience cannot discriminate between true and false arishtas.

But Vagbhata reports a qualification that is not post-hoc. At A.H.Sha.5/3-4 (classical[18]) he says 'ke-cit tu tad dvi-dhety ahuh', some say it is twofold, by the division into sthayin and asthayin: an abundance of doshas can produce a rishtabhasa, an appearance of a rishta, which subsides when the doshas are pacified, whereas the persistent one goes inevitably to death. Persistence through dosha-pacification is a criterion that can be applied before the outcome is known. It does not remove the circularity, since the persistent sign is still fatal by definition, but it means the tradition is not uniformly committed to the unfalsifiable version, and the record's flat statement that it is was too strong.

What would settle it is not in dispute and has simply not been done: a prospective cohort reporting, for each named sign, sensitivity, specificity and a time horizon, in the form the Surprise Question literature uses (modern[8]). Until then the question is open rather than answered in either direction.

contested.question: Is yapya a useful category today?
positions: It maps naturally onto chronic disease management and is cited as evidence that Ayurveda distinguished control from cure long before modern medicine did.

The mapping is loose: Sushruta's eight 'hard to cure' conditions at Su.Su.33 include several (ashmari, bhagandara, some udara) that are now routinely curable surgically, so the category's membership is not stable across time.

The claim that yapya is defined only negatively, by the failure of cure, is no longer tenable in the form the record previously stated it. Ca.Su.10/17-18 gives positive criteria: remaining life-span, a small ease gained from wholesome regimen, a slight cause restarting the condition, depth of seat, many dhatus, marma and sandhi involvement, continuous presence, long duration, two doshas. Ca.Su.18/39 adds a positive functional definition, that treatment well done becomes yatrakara, enabling the patient to go on. Whether those criteria can be scored reproducibly is a separate and open question; that they exist is now sourced.

A sharper difficulty than the negative-definition one is that the criteria are time-indexed to therapeutics. 'Beyond the path of treatment' at Ca.Su.10/19 and 'needing surgery, alkali or fire' at Ca.Su.10/15 are both statements about what the available means can reach, so the boundary between kricchrasadhya, yapya and pratyakhyeya moves whenever the means change, and the texts give no updating rule. See notKnown.

Su.Su.35's second sentence adds a different instability: each of the three tiers is to be examined for whether the disease is primary, aupasargika (accessory or sympathetic to something else), or the premonitory sign of something incipient. A yapya condition that is actually aupasargika is not a stable member of the class, because its course is governed by the primary disease.

notKnown: Whether a sadhya/yapya/asadhya assignment predicts survival or recovery. NARROWED in this revision. The record previously said 'No prospective cohort has ever tested this'. One attempt was found, modern[3], a 1997 paper in Ancient Science of Life that states the classical ruling on prameha (kaphaja sadhya, pittaja yapya, vataja asadhya) and sets out to test it against insulin level; its retrievable abstract reports an aim and no design, sample size or results, and the full text was not obtained. What can be said is that no adequate test was found in the searches named in searchRecord, not that none has ever been attempted.

Whether two physicians assign the same patient to the same prognostic category. No inter-rater reliability study of prognostic classification was found in the searches run. The nearest datum, modern[6], shows poor agreement on the diagnostic inputs rather than on the prognostic output, which bounds the answer without giving it.

The sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, c-statistic or lead time of any individual arishta sign. None was found. The form such a report would have to take is now specified by comparison with modern[8], which reports exactly these quantities for a structurally similar single clinician-rated judgement.

Whether Charaka's criteria at Ca.Su.10/11-20 can be operationalised and scored reproducibly. This replaces the record's earlier item, which asked the question only of Sushruta's Su.Su.35 list because it did not have the Charaka block. The Charaka block is the harder case: it uses about a dozen variables with ordinal values and gives no weights, no thresholds and no combination rule. No instrument was found for either list. Modern[9] shows what a validated composite of this shape looks like in practice.

Whether the sthayin and asthayin distinction Vagbhata reports at A.H.Sha.5/3-4 was ever worked out into a usable rule, how long a rishta must persist through dosha-pacification to count as sthayin, and who the 'ke-cit', the some who say so, were. The verse reports the view and does not develop it, and no commentary on it was consulted here.

How the classification is meant to be revised as treatment changes. Several conditions listed as intrinsically hard to cure at Su.Su.33 are now surgically curable, and 'beyond the path of treatment' at Ca.Su.10/19 is explicitly indexed to available means. The texts give no updating rule and no source consulted supplies one.

Whether pratyakhyana as practised today leads to referral, to abandonment, or to delayed presentation to conventional care. No observational data on what actually happens to refused patients was found.

How the non-disclosure rule is handled in current practice under Indian consent law, and whether practitioners follow the classical rule, the modern rule, or something in between. No survey was found. The asymmetry now documented at Ca.In.12/65 makes this a sharper question than the record previously posed, because a practitioner could be following the classical rule precisely while appearing to disclose freely.

Whether Vagbhata's refusal list at A.H.Su.1/34-35 is read today as live guidance, as historical context, or as something to be explained away. Eleven of its twelve grounds are non-medical and one of them, hinopakaranam, is poverty. No source consulted addresses how it is taught.

Whether the oil-drop urine test measures anything. Its inter-observer reliability has still not been reported in anything found. NARROWED in this revision: the record previously said the reliability 'has never been reported', without noting that modern[2], a 2012 standardisation paper, states the problem in its own words ('the technique is very crude and there are chances of variations in the observations') and proposes a protocol intended to make observations reproducible. A protocol is not a reliability estimate, so the gap stands, but it is not an unexamined gap.

What Chakrapani's Ayurvedadipika on the Indriya Sthana, Dalhana's Nibandha Samgraha and Chakrapani's Bhanumati say about this material. Modern[4] reports that all three treat arishta-vijnana at length and that Chakrapani held Charaka's Indriya Sthana superior for it. None was read in the original here and none is cited. This is the largest classical gap left in the record, and it is the same gap recorded on the roga-marga record of this project.

Sushruta's threefold classification of ayu into dirghayu, madhyamayu and alpayu, which modern[5] reports with characteristics for each. The locus was not identified and the passage was not retrieved, so it is not cited. It is plainly adjacent to this concept, since the life-span judgement is what Ca.Su.10/17 makes yapya depend on, and it is recorded as a gap rather than paraphrased from the review.

Whether the prognostic material in Charaka's Vimana and Chikitsa Sthanas, which modern[5] names alongside Indriya and Sharira, adds anything to the four tiers. Those two sthanas were not searched in this revision.

Whether the AYUSH Research Portal holds work that would change any of the above. It holds 30,920 Ayurveda records, its search failed server-side on every attempt on 2026-10-06, and it has therefore not been searched. This is the single largest boundary on every negative statement in this record.

components.gloss: Diseases that respond to treatment. Charaka subdivides into sukhasadhya (easily curable) and kricchrasadhya (curable with difficulty) at Ca.Su.10/9, and at Ca.Su.10/10 divides the curable again by whether the means required are alpa, madhyama or utkrishta, slight, intermediate or great. Each subdivision has its own criteria list: sukhasadhya at Ca.Su.10/11-13, kricchrasadhya at Ca.Su.10/14-16.

Not curable, but controllable so that well-applied treatment prolongs life. The text's own criteria are at Ca.Su.10/17-18: the life-span being what remains, the patient has had a little ease from wholesome regimen and a slight cause sets the condition off again; the disease is deep-seated (gambhira), lodged in many dhatus, settled in marma and sandhi, continuously present, long-standing, and arising from two doshas. Ca.Su.18/39 names the category in the verse: incurable diseases called yapya, in which treatment well done is yatrakara, enabling the patient to go on. Sushruta's Su.Su.23 applies it to ulcers, where the yapya group admits palliation only. This is the closest classical analogue to chronic disease management.

components.term: Asadhya / anupakramya / pratyakhyeya (incurable, to be refused)
components.gloss: No treatment produces benefit; the physician is told to decline. Charaka states at Ca.Su.10/10 that incurable diseases that are niyata, settled, do not admit of the threefold division by means. The criteria are at Ca.Su.10/19-20: arising from three doshas, having passed beyond the path of treatment (kriyapatham atikrantam), following all the pathways, producing anxiety, stupefaction and restlessness, destroying the senses, fully grown in a weak patient, and accompanied by arishta (sarishtam). Ca.Su.18/40 adds that only the foolish strive at these and the learned physician does not.

Ca.Su.18/41 crosses curability with severity: 'sadhyash chaivapy asadhyash cha vyadhayo dvividhah smritah | mridu-daruna-bhedena te bhavanti chaturvidhah'. Diseases are of two kinds, curable and incurable, and by the division into mild and violent they become four. The verse stops there. It does not say which of the four is equivalent to yapya.

Ca.Su.10/11-20 gives a criteria list for each of the four categories, built from a recurring set of variables: the force of the causes, premonitory signs and present signs; whether the dushya, the season, the patient's prakriti and the place are favourable to the disease or not; how many doshas are involved; how many pathways; depth of seat; involvement of marma and sandhi; duration; the presence of complications; whether the body tolerates all medicines; and whether the four padas of treatment are complete. The same variables run through all four categories with their values shifted, which makes it a graded scale rather than four separate lists.

Recent onset; no distressing complications; the disease unsuited to the patient's country, season, temperament and habituation; samagni (regular and unimpaired digestion); strength, fortitude and signs of longevity; and the four commendable factors of treatment (physician, drugs, attendant, patient) present. A disease marked by the opposite features is incurable; one with traits common to both is extremely hard to cure. Su.Su.35 states the three tiers and this rule in the same chapter.

Signs of impending death. Charaka devotes the whole of his Indriya Sthana to them, twelve chapters whose titles, verified against the critical edition's chapter index, are: 1 Varnasvariyam (colour and voice), 2 Pushpitakam (odour and taste), 3 Parimarshaneeyam (touch), 4 Indriyaneekam, 5 Purvarupeeyam, 6 Katamanisharireeyam, 7 Pannarupiyam, 8 Avakshiraseeyam, 9 Yasyashyavanimittiyam, 10 Sadyomaraneeyam, 11 Anujyotiyam, 12 Gomayachurniyam. Sushruta's block is Su.Su.28 to 33, six chapters whose Bhishagratna chapter openings were read and are listed at classical[16]. Vagbhata's counterpart is A.H.Sharirasthana 5, Vikritivijnaniya. Charaka's Pushpitakam chapter likens an arishta to a flower and death to the fruit (Ca.In.2/3).

The physician's duty to decline hopeless cases, coupled with a restriction on announcing death: never unasked, not even when asked if it would injure, and declining without stating the reason (Ca.In.12/62-64). The restriction runs one way only: at Ca.In.12/65-66 the physician is told to declare recovery with certainty when the signs contrary to the death-signs appear. Vagbhata's refusal list at A.H.Su.1/34-35 is wider than Charaka's and mostly non-medical.

classical.establishes: The professional sanction behind the classification. Note what the verse gives as the loss: artha (wealth), vidya (knowledge), yasha (fame), upakrosha (censure) and asangraha (not being retained in practice). All five are costs to the physician. The verse names no cost to the patient and no duty to the patient, and this is the textual basis of position 1 in contested[1].
classical.sanskrit: अर्थविद्यायशोहानिमुपक्रोशमसङ्ग्रहम्| प्राप्नुयान्नियतं वैद्यो योऽसाध्यं समुपाचरेत्||८||
classical.translation: That physician who takes up the treatment of a disease that is incurable incurs loss of wealth, loss of knowledge, loss of fame, censure of the world, and incapacity for practice.

classical.establishes: The four-way classification in the Sanskrit and in a lawfully quotable English: sukhasadhya, kricchrasadhya, yapya, anupakrama. The verse names the four and does nothing else; the criteria that distinguish them are at 10/11-20 and are cited separately at classical[3], classical[4] and classical[5].
classical.sanskrit: सुखसाध्यं मतं साध्यं कृच्छ्रसाध्यमथापि च| द्विविधं चाप्यसाध्यं स्याद्याप्यं यच्चानुपक्रमम्||९||
classical.translation: As regards curable diseases, they are of two kinds, viz., those that are easily curable and those that are curable with difficulty. Incurable diseases, also, are of two kinds, viz., those that are capable of being suppressed, and those that have no treatment.

classical.establishes: That the curable are graded a second time by the magnitude of means required (alpa, madhyama, utkrishta), and that the settled incurable are treated as internally undifferentiated. Also, as an exhibit, two of Kaviratna's footnotes that this record previously drew doctrine from.
classical.sanskrit: साध्यानां त्रिविधश्चाल्पमध्यमोत्कृष्टतां प्रति| विकल्पो, न त्वसाध्यानां नियतानां विकल्पना||१०||
classical.translation: As regards diseases that are curable, they may again be regarded from three points of view, viz., those that are capable of being cured by the application of means that are easy, those that are curable by means neither easy nor difficult, and lastly those that are curable by means that are difficult. Incurable diseases, which have no treatment, do not admit of being looked upon from different points of view. This much on the points of view from which diseases may be looked upon.

classical.establishes: New in this revision. Charaka's criteria for sukhasadhya, the first tier of the gradation. Eleven conditions, and they are the same variables that reappear with shifted values in the other three tiers: force of the causes, premonitory signs and present signs; non-correspondence between dosha and dushya; non-correspondence with the patient's prakriti; non-correspondence with the season; a place that does not obstruct treatment; one gati or pathway; recent onset; absence of upadrava; one dosha; a body that tolerates all medicines; and the four padas complete. This entry, with classical[4] and classical[5], is the Charaka material the record was missing, and it is what makes the scheme a graded scale rather than four labels.
classical.sanskrit: हेतवः पूर्वरूपाणि रूपाण्यल्पानि यस्य च| न च तुल्यगुणो दूष्यो न दोषःप्रकृतिर्भवेत्||११|| न च कालगुणस्तुल्यो न देशो दुरुपक्रमः| गतिरेका नवत्वं च रोगस्योपद्रवो न च||१२|| दोषश्चैकः समुत्पत्तौ देहः सर्वौषधक्षमः| चतुष्पादोपपत्तिश्च सुखसाध्यस्य लक्षणम्||१३||
classical.translation: The characteristics of diseases that are easily curable are as follows. When the causes, premonitory indications, and present symptoms are slight ; when the derangement has no sympathy with the inducing causes of the disease, when the derangement that has brought about the disease is not capable of being aggravated by the constitution of the patient; when the inducing derangement is not sympathetic with the virtues of the season in which the disease has appeared ; when the treatment does not become difficult in consequence of the place where the disease occurs ; when the part affected by the disease is one ; when it is new ; when the disease is free from violent symptoms ; when the derangement that has caused the disease is concerned with only one (of the three, viz., wind, bile, and phlegm) ; when the body is such that it is capable of bearing all kinds of medicines ; and lastly, when all the four requisites are present ; diseases are said to be easily curable.

classical.establishes: New in this revision. Charaka's kricchrasadhya criteria (10/14-16) and the first of his two yapya criteria verses (10/17). The kricchrasadhya list is the sukhasadhya list with its values moved: middling force of the causes, the premonitory signs and the present signs; correspondence with any one of kala, prakriti and dushya; a vulnerable patient (pregnant or elderly woman, old man, child, on which see variantReadings); moderate complications; dependence on surgery, alkali or fire; chronicity (anavam); origin in a difficult desha (kricchradeshajam, 10/15, the moved counterpart of the sukhasadhya variable na desho durupakramah at 10/12); one pathway with the four padas incomplete; two pathways but not long standing; two doshas. Marma and sandhi involvement is not one of them. Neither marma nor sandhi occurs anywhere in 10/14-16; marmasandhisamashritam stands at 10/18, a yapya verse, which this record quotes and places correctly at classical[5]. Kaviratna's English for this block does read 'when the disease, affecting some vital limb or some joint of the body, affects only one part', but that is his gloss on kricchradeshajam and ekapatham, resting on his own commentator's footnote that desha covers 'both the division of the country and the particular part of the body'. It is the translator's voice, not the verse, and belongs with the four other translator's-voice absorptions this record already documents. 10/17 defines yapya by the remainder of the life-span, by a small ease gained from wholesome regimen, and by a slight cause setting the condition off again.
classical.sanskrit: निमित्तपूर्वरूपाणां रूपाणां मध्यमे बले| कालप्रकृतिदूष्याणां सामान्येऽन्यतमस्य च||१४|| गर्भिणीवृद्धबालानां नात्युपद्रवपीडितम्| शस्त्रक्षाराग्निकृत्यानामनवं कृच्छ्रदेशजम्||१५|| विद्यादेकपथं रोगं नातिपूर्णचतुष्पदम्| द्विपथं नातिकालं वा कृच्छ्रसाध्यं द्विदोषजम्||१६|| शेषत्वादायुषो याप्यमसाध्यं पथ्यसेवया| लब्धाल्पसुखमल्पेन हेतुनाऽऽशुप्रवर्तकम्||१७||
classical.translation: The characteristics of diseases that are curable with difficulty are as follows : when the causes, premonitory indications, and present symptoms, are of force neither slight nor very grave ; when any of these, viz., the season of the disease, its nature, and the character of those ingredients of the body which are known by the name of Dushya, is sympathetic with the derangement that induces the disease ; when the disease appertains to an elderly woman, an old man, and an infant ; when the disease is not characterised by excessively violent symptoms ; when the disease is such that it should be treated with the aid of operations by (surgical) instruments, by caustic alkali, and by fire ; when the disease is chronic ; when the disease, affecting some vital limb or some joint of the body, affects only one part; when the four principal requisites of treatment are wanting in some particular and the disease affects two parts; when the disease is not very old; and lastly when the disease has been induced by a double derangement ; such diseases should be known as curable with difficulty. Even diseases that are incurable in consequence of the exhaustion of one's allotted period of life may be kept in a suppressed state by means of regulated diet and (proper) nursing.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.establishes: New in this revision. Charaka's pratyakhyeya criteria at 10/19-20, as distinct from the yapya criteria at 10/17-18: tridosha origin, having passed beyond kriyapatha (the path of treatment), following all the margas, producing autsukya, arati and sammoha (anxiety, restlessness, stupefaction), destroying the indriyas, fully grown in a weak patient, and sarishta, accompanied by arishtas. The last of these is the joint between this concept and the arishta literature, and it is in the verse rather than in anyone's commentary: the refusal rule explicitly takes the arishta signs as one of its inputs. Vagbhata makes the same join at A.H.Su.1/33 with drishta-rishta (classical[17]).
classical.sanskrit: गम्भीरं बहुधातुस्थं मर्मसन्धिसमाश्रितम्| नित्यानुशायिनं रोगं दीर्घकालमवस्थितम्||१८|| विद्याद्द्विदोषजं,...तद्वत्प्रत्याख्येयं त्रिदोषजम्| क्रियापथमतिक्रान्तं सर्वमार्गानुसारिणम्||१९|| औत्सुक्यारतिसम्मोहकरमिन्द्रियनाशनम्| दुर्बलस्य सुसंवृद्धं व्याधिं सारिष्टमेव च||२०||
classical.translation: When the disease is deeply ingrained (into the marrow and such other constituents of the body), when it affects many of the constituent parts, when it is attached to the vital limbs and joints of the body, when it manifests itself continuously, when it is chronic and very old, when it is born of the derangement of two of the three ingredients (of wind, bile, and phlegm) or of all the three, when it is beyond the operation of treatment, when it affects all the organs, when the patient is thoroughly cheerless and despairing, when the disease is characterised by a stupefaction of the mind, when the disease weakens the strength of all the organs (of knowledge and action), when the disease has reached the highest limit of aggravation and the patient has become entirely strengthless, and lastly when the disease exhibits indications of the patient's dissolution, it should be regarded as one that should not be taken up for treatment.

classical.establishes: Charaka's second, independent statement of the scheme, in a chapter about swellings rather than about method. Three things it adds to Ca.Su.10. (1) Yapya is named in the verse itself, 'yapya-sanjnitah', and defined by its effect: treatment well done becomes yatrakara, enabling the patient to go on. (2) The refusal is put as a contrast between the foolish and the learned (balaih / vidvan), which is a different register from the loss of wealth and fame at 10/8. (3) 18/41 crosses curability with mridu and daruna, mild and violent, to give four kinds, and stops there without saying which of the four corresponds to yapya. That identification comes from Kaviratna's footnote and is quoted as an exhibit at classical[7].
classical.sanskrit: असाध्याश्चापरे सन्ति व्याधयो याप्यसञ्ज्ञिताः| सुसाध्वपि कृतं येषु कर्म यात्राकरं भवेत्||३९|| सन्ति चाप्यपरे रोगा येषु कर्म न सिध्यति| अपि यत्नकृतं बालैर्न तान् विद्वानुपाचरेत्||४०|| साध्याश्चैवाप्यसाध्याश्च व्याधयो द्विविधाः स्मृताः| मृदुदारुणभेदेन ते भवन्ति चतुर्विधाः||४१||
classical.translation: There are others (of this class) which are regarded incurable. Some, again, ( though incurable ) are capable of being suppressed. In diseases of this latter kind, well-applied treatment assists the patient to live on. There are others that are truly incurable. In them no treatment produces success. Only fools strive to treat them. The learned physician never sets his hand upon them. Diseases are of two kinds, viz., Curable and Incurable. Distributing them according to the considerations of mildness and violence, they become of four kinds.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's footnote to his verse 46, i.e. to Ca.Su.18/41. Not a verse of the samhita.
classical.establishes: Added in this revision as the source of a claim the record had mis-attributed. It establishes who said that mild-incurable means yapya, and that it is not in the verse.
classical.translation: Four kinds, such as (1) Mild and Curable, (2) Violent and Curable, (3) Mild and Incurable, and (4) Violent and Incurable. Among these, Mild and Incurable would mean Yapya or suppressible. - T.

classical.establishes: The arishta doctrine, including its unfalsifiable structure, which is now shown to be in the Sanskrit and not an artefact of the English. 2/5 says there is no vanishing of an arishta once arisen other than by death, and no death that is not preceded by an arishta. 2/6 then assigns both false positives and false negatives to prajnaparadha, the physician's error of judgement. Taken together, a true arishta is always followed by death by definition and every apparent counter-example is reclassified as misperception, so no observation can count against the rule. Vagbhata reports a variant that partly answers this; see classical[18] and contested[3].
classical.sanskrit: पुष्पं यथा पूर्वरूपं फलस्येह भविष्यतः| तथा लिङ्गमरिष्टाख्यं पूर्वरूपं मरिष्यतः||३|| अप्येवं तु भवेत् पुष्पं फलेनाननुबन्धि यत्| फलं चापि भवेत् किञ्चिद्यस्य पुष्पं न पूर्वजम्||४|| न त्वरिष्टस्य जातस्य नाशोऽस्ति मरणादृते| मरणं चापि तन्नास्ति यन्नारिष्टपुरःसरम्||५|| मिथ्यादृष्टमरिष्टाभमनरिष्टमजानता| अरिष्टं वाऽप्यसम्बुद्धमेतत् प्रज्ञापराधजम्||६||
classical.translation: As a flower is seen here to be the premonitory indication of a fruit to be, so a symptom called 'Arishta' is a premonitory indication of a person about to die. There may, indeed, be a flower that is not followed by a fruit. So also there may be a fruit that has not been preceded by a flower. For all that, there cannot be a disappearance of an 'Arishta' that has manifested itself, without death occurring (as a consequence). There cannot, again, be a death that has not been preceded by an 'Arishta.' An ignorant physician regards a symptom as an 'Arishta' which without being a real 'Arishta' only puts forth the appearance of an 'Arishta.' Similarly, such a person fails to detect an 'Arishta' in a symptom that is really so. Both these are due to a deficiency of the understanding.

classical.establishes: The classical disclosure rule, which is non-disclosure by default and refusal without explanation, now anchored to the Sanskrit: aprishtena na vaktavyam (62), prishtenapi na vaktavyam tatra yatropaghatakam (63), abruvan maranam tasya nainam icchech chikitsitum (64). This is in direct tension with modern informed-consent norms and is the most consequential ethical content of the concept. The rule is one-directional; see classical[10].
classical.sanskrit: मरणायेह रूपाणि पश्यताऽपि भिषग्विदा| अपृष्टेन न वक्तव्यं मरणं प्रत्युपस्थितम्||६२|| पृष्टेनापि न वक्तव्यं तत्र यत्रोपघातकम्| आतुरस्य भवेद्दुःखमथवाऽन्यस्य कस्यचित्||६३|| अब्रुवन्मरणं तस्य नैनमिच्छेच्चिकित्सितुम्| यस्य पश्येद्विनाशाय लिङ्गानि कुशलो भिषक्||६४||
classical.translation: The physician, even if he marks these symptoms of death which have been laid down (in the above verses) agreeably to medical scriptures and in accordance with the purpose in view, should never, unasked, say that death is near. Even when asked, he should not say so when his declaration is capable of producing injury, that is, when the patient himself or anybody else is likely to suffer pain or torture in consequence. Without telling him that his death is near, the intelligent physician should simply decline to take up the treatment of that patient in whom signs of death may become noticeable.

classical.establishes: New in this revision. The disclosure rule is asymmetric, and the asymmetry is in the verse. 12/62-64 forbid announcing imminent death; 12/65 directs the physician to declare recovery dhruvam, with certainty, when the contrary signs appear. Bad news is withheld and good news is given positively. This bears directly on contested[2]: the classical rule is not a general reticence about prognosis, it is a one-way restriction, which makes the conflict with informed consent sharper rather than softer. 12/66 also shows what the physician is allowed to read the good news off: messengers, omens on the road, the patient's household, and the patient's property. The last of these, dravya-sampatti, is the patient's means, and Kaviratna's footnote on the page glosses it as implying that 'According to Charaka, the treatment of those that are poor should not be taken up'. That gloss is his and is not quoted as doctrine here, but Vagbhata's own refusal list at A.H.Su.1/34 does include hinopakaranam, one lacking the means; see classical[17].
classical.sanskrit: लिङ्गेभ्यो मरणाख्येभ्यो विपरीतानि पश्यता| लिङ्गान्यारोग्यमागन्तु वक्तव्यं भिषजा ध्रुवम्||६५|| दूतैरौत्पातिकैर्भावैः पथ्यातुरकुलाश्रयैः| आतुराचारशीलेष्टद्रव्यसम्पत्तिलक्षणैः||६६||
classical.translation: When the physician, guided by (his observation of) messengers, inauspicious incidents occurring on his way (to the patient's house), similar incidents connected with the patient's family, the conduct and disposition of the patient, and the signs connected with the possessions of the patient, sees symptoms which are the reverse of those that are called death-indicating, he should declare the certain recovery of the patient to be at hand.

classical.establishes: Sushruta's three working prognostic categories, named in his own chapter on clinical observation. The second sentence, which the record did not previously carry, adds a cross-cutting distinction that is not a prognostic tier at all: each of the three is to be examined for whether it is a primary disease, an accessory or sympathetic one (aupasargika), or the premonitory sign of something incipient. That is a second axis, and it is relevant to contested[4], because a yapya condition that is actually aupasargika to something else is not stable as a category member.
classical.translation: All the diseases, whose names have been specifically enumerated before, may be grouped under any of the three different heads as the curable, the suppressible (Yapya) and the incurable (lit : fit to be pronounced as hopeless). Each of these different types, in its turn, should be carefully observed so as to determine whether it is a primary or an independent disease, or merely an accessory or sympathetic one, or the premonitory indication of an incipient distemper in its incubative stage.

classical.establishes: Sushruta's explicit criteria for assigning a case to curable, hard-to-cure or incurable, stated as one positive list plus two residual rules: the opposite features mean incurable, mixed features mean extremely hard to cure. The structure is worth noting because only the top tier is defined positively; the other two are defined by departure from it, which is the point made in contested[4] about yapya lacking a positive criterion.
classical.translation: A disease of recent growth or origin unattended with any distressing or unfavourable complications, and unsuited to the nature of the country, the season of the year, the temperament, and the adopted or congenial or naturalised traits of the physique of a patient with a regular and unimpaired state of digestion (Samagni), and who exhibits traits of strength, fortitude and longevity and commands the co-operation of the four commendable factors of a course of medical treatment, readily yields to medicine. A disease, which is marked by features other than those described above, should be regarded as incurable, while the one exhibiting traits common to both the abovesaid types, should be looked upon as extremely hard to cure.

classical.establishes: A named list of eight conditions treated as intrinsically hard to cure, and the complication set that converts a case to abandonment. The eight, read on the page and not quoted because the OCR garbles several of them, are Maha-vata-vyadhi, Prameha, Kushtha, Arsha, Bhagandara (printed 'Vagandara' in the scan), Ashmari, Mudha-garbha and the eight kinds of Udara. Two things in the sentence matter for contested[1]. The reason given for abandonment is the physician's professional success. And the trigger is not the disease but its complications, which means a case moves into the abandonment class by acquiring an upadrava rather than by being that disease.
classical.translation: Hear me describe, Oh child, the diseases which being attended with many a distressing and supervenient symptom, and being treated without rejuvenating and restorative medicines, speedily assume incurable character. ... A physician with any regard to professional success should abandon a patient laid up with any of the preceding diseases, marked by complications such as, emaciation of the body, loss of strength, dyspnoea, palpitation, wasting, vomiting, dysentery and hie-cough, fever and swoon.

classical.establishes: New in this revision. This entry was previously part of a bundled, unquoted 'located' entry. It matters because it is the one place found in either samhita where the three tiers are worked through for a single disease class with a named yapya block. Bhishagratna's own table of contents for the chapter lists 'Easy curability of an ulcer', 'Symptoms of difficult or incurable types, as well as of those which admit only of palliation'. The chapter grades ulcers by the patient (young, muscular, strong, resolute heal readily; old, emaciated, timid, weak heal slowly), then by anatomical site, then by comorbidity, and only then names the yapya group. The five conditions in the elided clause appear on the page as Avapathika (which the OCR corrupts, and which Bhishagratna glosses as paraphimosis), Niruddha-prakasha, Sanniruddha-guda, Jathara and Granthi; they are reported here and not quoted. The operational interest is that yapya status is assigned by the host condition and by the presence of parasites, not by the ulcer itself.
classical.translation: Ya'pya ulcers :--An ulcer incidental to, and affecting the seat of any of the following diseases, viz. ... and characterised by the germination of parasites in its interior, as well as the one appearing in the cavity of the abdomen, or affecting the mucous linings of the intestines, or brought about by the corrosive secretions of a nasal catarrh (Pratishyaya), and infested with parasites, should be considered as only admitting of a palliative treatment. Similarly palliation is the only remedy in the case of an ulcer which appears in a patient suffering from any morbid secretion from the urethra (Prameha) or from any form of cutaneous affections, marked by worms in its inside.

classical.establishes: New in this revision. One sentence, and it does two things the record needed. It states the purpose of the whole Sushruta arishta block explicitly: the fatal signs are read in order to determine whether a disease is curable or incurable, which is the sadhya-asadhya judgement. So the two bodies of material are joined on the Sushruta side as well as the Charaka side, in the text rather than by this record's inference. And it states the incentive in the same breath: the physician who can do it is honoured by the king. That is a third datum for contested[1], alongside Charaka's loss of wealth and fame at Ca.Su.10/8 and Sushruta's 'regard to professional success' at Su.Su.33. All three reasons the texts give for getting the prognosis right are reasons of the physician's standing.
classical.translation: The physician, who can detect and fully interpret these fatal indications, is honoured by the king for determining the curable or incurable nature of a disease.

classical.chapter: 28 to 33 (the arishta block), read as a body
classical.establishes: Enumerated in this revision, having previously been cited as a vague range. The six chapters and their own stated subjects, taken verbatim from Bhishagratna's chapter openings, are: XXVIII, favourable or unfavourable prognosis of an ulcer (Viparita-aviparita-Vrana-Vijnaniya); XXIX, favourable or unfavourable prognosis in diseases as known from messengers, omens and dreams (Viparita-aviparita-Duta-vijnaniya); XXX, prognosis from the perverted functions of the five sense organs (Panchendriyartha-Vipratipatti); XXXI, prognosis from the altered condition of features (Chhaya-Vipratipatti); XXXII, prognosis from the perversion of the external appearances of the body (Svabhava-vipratipatti); XXXIII, incurable diseases (Avaraniya). Two corrections to the record follow. The record previously gave the block as 'Sushruta Sutrasthana 28-33' in the summary but as 'Chapters XXVIII-XXXII' in this citation; the range is 28 to 33, with 33 being the refusal chapter rather than an arishta chapter proper, and both places now say so. And chapter XXIII, which the record bundled into this entry, is not part of the block: it is the ulcer-prognosis chapter and is now cited separately and quoted at classical[14]. The content of XXIX in particular is summarised and deliberately not quoted here, because it concerns the conduct of the messenger sent to fetch the physician and incidents on the road, and quoting it as clinical doctrine would misrepresent it.

New in this revision, replacing an unquoted placeholder. Vagbhata's whole treatment of the concept in seven verses, and it adds three things the record did not have. (1) 1/29+(1) gives the fourfold scheme in Charaka's own terms: 'sadhyo 'sadhya iti vyadhir dvidha tau tu punar dvidha | susadhyah krichchhrasadhyash cha yapyo yash chanupakramah'. (2) 1/30-33 compress the criteria: 1/30-31 for sukha (a body tolerating all medicines, a young self-controlled patient, not marma-going, slight causes and signs, no upadrava, dushya and desha and ritu and prakriti not alike, the padas complete, favourable grahas, one dosha, one marga, recent), 1/32 for krichchhra (needing surgery and the rest, or mixed) and for yapya ('sheshatvad ayusho yapyah pathyabhyasad viparyaye', yapya by what remains of the life-span and by regimen, in the contrary case), 1/33 for anupakrama (in the utterly contrary case), which includes 'drishta-rishtah', one in whom a rishta has been seen. That is Vagbhata making the same join between this concept and the arishta literature that Charaka makes at Ca.Su.10/20 with sarishtam. (3) 1/34-35 are a refusal list, and this is the part with the most weight for contested[1]. The physician should abandon the patient who is hated by physicians and kings, who hates them, who is hostile, who is hinopakaranam (lacking the means), vyagram (distracted), avidheyam (not to be directed, non-compliant), gatayusham (whose life-span is gone), chandam (violent), shokaturam (stricken with grief), bhirum (timid), kritaghnam (ungrateful), and vaidyamaninam (one who thinks himself a physician). Eleven of those twelve grounds are not prognostic at all. They are about politics, means, temperament and the patient's deference to the physician.
