On the evidence of this verse, refusal in the classical texts is not reducible to a judgement that treatment would be futile.
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

classical.establishes: New in this revision, and the locus the audit asked for by name. Four things. (1) 5/1 is Vagbhata's version of Charaka's flower-and-fruit figure, with two more analogies added: 'pushpam phalasya dhumo 'gner varshasya jala-dodayah', the flower of the fruit, the smoke of the fire, the rising of the cloud of the rain, so is rishta of death, dhruvam, certainly. (2) 5/1+(1) and 1+(2) restate the professional sanction on the same pattern as Ca.Su.10/7-8: in one who has life-span, all therapies properly applied bear fruit, bhishajam bhutyai, for the prosperity of physicians; in one whose life-span is exhausted, what is done is futile and yields ayashas (infamy), deha-samdeham and svartha-hanim, loss of one's own interest. The costs named are again the physician's. (3) 5/2 restates the unfalsifiable structure in almost Charaka's words: there is no death without arishta, no life where a rishta has been seen, and the misperception of rishta where there is none and the failure to perceive it where there is run 'a-naipunat', from lack of skill. (4) 5/3-4 is the part this record did not have and could not have inferred. Vagbhata reports an opinion, marked as an opinion, 'ke-cit tu tad dvi-dhety ahuh', but some say it is twofold: by the division into sthayin and a-sthayin, persistent and non-persistent. From a mere abundance of doshas a rishtabhasa, an APPEARANCE of a rishta, may arise; that one subsides when the doshas are pacified, whereas the persistent one goes inevitably to death. That is a criterion, prospectively applicable, for separating a true sign from a false one, and it is not post-hoc reclassification. It does not dissolve the circularity, because the persistent one is still fatal by definition, but it is a real qualification of the self-sealing reading this record states on Charaka's authority, and it is now a position in contested[3] rather than being left out.
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

modern.title: Assessment of prognostic aspects of cancer by Taila Bindu Pariksha.
modern.establishes: Pilot study of Taila Bindu Pariksha (the spread of an oil drop on a urine sample) as a prognostic indicator in 20 cancer patients about to receive radiotherapy or chemotherapy, compared with the ECOG performance scale; reports that in the majority of patients the correlation was statistically highly significant. The paper states plainly that there is no direct description of a method to ascertain cancer prognosis in the Ayurvedic classics.
modern.quality: Weak. Single group of 20, no blinding of the oil-drop reader to the patient's clinical state, no inter-observer agreement reported for the drop-shape reading, ECOG itself is a coarse clinician-rated scale, and the analysis is a correlation with no prespecified hypothesis or correction. The finding should be treated as hypothesis-generating at most. Its most useful content is its own admission that the classics contain no prognostic method for this.

modern.title: A study on Tailabindu pariksha - An ancient Ayurvedic method of urine examination as a diagnostic and prognostic tool.
modern.establishes: Earlier study of Taila Bindu Pariksha as a diagnostic and prognostic tool.
modern.quality: Small single-centre study; same methodological limitations as the 2015 pilot. Included for completeness, not as support.

modern.title: A study on the method of Taila Bindu Pariksha (oil drop test).
modern.establishes: A methods paper that standardised the Taila Bindu Pariksha procedure in apparently healthy volunteers: shape and size of the testing container, volume of urine, size of the oil drop, height of the drop above the urine surface, and variety of sesame oil, each varied one at a time, with the whole procedure recorded on video. Its own stated premise is the reason it is cited here: 'Technique of this test is very crude and there are chances of variations in the observations', and the standardisation was undertaken 'so that the observations could be reproducible'.
modern.quality: A standardisation exercise, not a diagnostic accuracy or reliability study. No patients, no outcome, and no agreement statistic is reported, so it does not establish that the test is reproducible; it establishes that the problem was recognised in the literature and that a protocol was proposed. Added in this revision because the record's notKnown previously said the test's inter-observer reliability 'has never been reported' without noting that the reproducibility problem had been addressed at the protocol level.

modern.title: Prognosis of prameha on the basis of insulin level.
modern.establishes: The only study found in any of the searches run here that takes a classical sadhya/yapya/asadhya assignment and tries to test it against a measurement. Its stated premise, quoted from the abstract, is 'It has been mentioned in the text Kaphaj Prameha is sadhya, pittaj & vataj prameha is yapya & asadhya respectively', and its stated aim is 'to establish the prognostical aspect of prameha scientifically in relation to the insulin level of the body'.
modern.quality: Cannot be assessed from what is retrievable. The PubMed record carries only a three-sentence abstract that states the aim and reports no design, no sample size, no results and no statistics; the full text was not retrieved in this revision. It is cited for the existence and the shape of the attempt, not for any finding. It is enough, however, to require a correction: the record's notKnown previously said that whether a sadhya/yapya/asadhya assignment predicts anything had never been tested, and that is too strong. What can be said is that no study found here reports an adequate test.

modern.title: Comparative studies of Bhanumati and Nibandha Samgraha with special reference to Arista Vijnana (prognostic science).
modern.establishes: A comparative study of Dalhana's Nibandha Samgraha and Chakrapani's Bhanumati on arishta-vijnana as described in the Sutrasthana of the Sushruta Samhita. It states that the system 'has advised the physicians to strictly avoid treating the incurable diseases' and that the signs of incurability 'have been described in Brhattrayi of Ayurveda'; that Charaka placed them in a separate section while Chakrapani and Dalhana treated them at length in commentary; that Dalhana was greatly influenced by the Charaka Samhita on prognostic science; and that Chakrapani repeatedly recognised the superiority of Charaka's Indriya Sthana for the analysis of prognostic science.
modern.quality: A textual and commentarial study, not an empirical one. No patients, no data, no outcome. It is cited for two things only: that indexed scholarly work on arishta-vijnana exists, which this record previously denied by implication, and that the commentarial tradition on it is substantial and has not been consulted in the original here. Added in this revision as the direct counter-example to the record's unbounded negative.

modern.title: Importance of Ayu Pareeksha for the Management of Diseases.
modern.establishes: A short review of ayu-pariksha, the examination of life-span, whose stated purpose is 'to obtain knowledge regarding longevity, residual span of life in diseased person and rate of the mortality'. It locates the material across Charaka's Vimana, Chikitsa, Indriya and Sharira Sthanas, distinguishes ayu from vaya (age), and reports that Sushruta classifies ayu into dirghayu, madhyamayu and alpayu with characteristics given for each.
modern.quality: Narrative review in an indexed but general clinical journal. No data of any kind. Cited for scope rather than for evidence: it shows that the prognostic material is distributed across four of Charaka's sthanas rather than confined to Indriya Sthana, and it names the Sushruta three-fold life-span classification, which this record does not cite and has not retrieved. See notKnown.

modern.title: Reliability of Ayurvedic Diagnosis for Knee Osteoarthritis Patients: A Nested Diagnostic Study Within a Randomized Controlled Trial.
modern.establishes: Establishes only indirectly: it shows that Ayurvedic experts assessing the same patients agree poorly on the diagnostic components that would feed a prognostic judgement. No prognostic category was itself assessed for agreement.
modern.quality: Good methodology but not a prognosis study. Cited here because it bounds how reproducible a sadhya-asadhya assignment could be, given that its inputs are unreliable.

modern.title: Extent and determinants of error in doctors' prognoses in terminally ill patients: prospective cohort study.
modern.establishes: Prospective cohort in five outpatient hospice programmes in Chicago; 343 doctors gave survival estimates for 468 terminally ill patients at the time of hospice referral. Median survival was 24 days. Only 20 per cent (92/468) of predictions were accurate within 33 per cent of actual survival; 63 per cent were overoptimistic and 17 per cent overpessimistic, and overall the doctors overestimated survival by a factor of 5.3. Few patient or doctor characteristics predicted accuracy; doctors in the top quartile of practice experience were the most accurate, and accuracy fell as the duration of the doctor-patient relationship increased.
modern.quality: Strong for its question and the standard reference for it, which is why the audit named it. Limits: one city, hospice referrals only, year 2000, so the base rates are specific to that population and era. Its relevance here is as a benchmark and as a check on a framing error. It shows that the quantity Charaka's arishta chapters claim to deliver, a declaration that death is near, is one that conventional clinicians also attempt and are measurably bad at, and that the error is systematically in one direction. The honest comparison is therefore not between a tested method and an untested one but between a method whose error has been measured and one whose error has not.

modern.title: How accurate is the 'Surprise Question' at identifying patients at the end of life? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
modern.establishes: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the Surprise Question ('would I be surprised if this patient died in the next year?'), 26 papers included, 22 with complete data, 25,718 survival predictions. The c-statistic across studies ranged from 0.512 to 0.822 and the pooled accuracy was 74.8 per cent (95% CI 68.6 to 80.5). Doctors were more accurate than nurses at recognising people in the last year of life (c-statistic 0.735 against 0.688) and the tool was more accurate in oncology settings. The authors' own conclusion is that accuracy ranged 'from poor to reasonable'.
modern.quality: A well-conducted meta-analysis of a heterogeneous literature; the heterogeneity is the main limit and the authors say so. Its value here is methodological rather than substantive. It is the closest modern analogue to what the arishta material is: a single clinician-rated judgement intended to flag impending death. It shows what such a judgement has to be reported as in order to be assessable, namely a c-statistic or a sensitivity and specificity against a defined time horizon, and that is the exact form in which no arishta sign has ever been reported. It is cited to make the record's gap in notKnown specific rather than rhetorical.

modern.title: Prognostic utility of Palliative Prognostic Index in advanced cancer: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
modern.establishes: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the Palliative Prognostic Index in adults with advanced cancer; 23 studies, 11,235 patients. Higher PPI scores were associated with death in every meta-analysis performed: PPI greater than 6 against PPI 4 or less gave a pooled adjusted hazard ratio of 5.42 (95% CI 2.01 to 14.59), and PPI as a continuous variable gave a pooled unadjusted hazard ratio of 1.30 (95% CI 1.22 to 1.38). The authors caution that only 2 to 4 studies entered each analysis and that the original risk groups still need validation.
modern.quality: Reasonable evidence with the authors' own stated caution about the small number of studies per analysis. Cited as the comparator for a composite prognostic score rather than a single sign, because that is the form Sushruta's Su.Su.35 criteria and Charaka's Ca.Su.10/11-20 criteria take: a set of weighted features combined into a category. The PPI is built from performance status, oral intake, oedema, dyspnoea at rest and delirium, which is a shorter list than Charaka's. It is cited to show that a classical-style composite is the kind of instrument that can be validated, and to specify what validating one would require.

records.title: Samprapti (the Ayurvedic model of pathogenesis)
records.domain: Ayurvedic theory of health and disease: pathogenesis
records.summary:
Samprapti is the Ayurvedic term for the account of how a disease came about. This record keeps apart three objects that the word is used for, because the gathered version ran them together and that conflation was its central defect.

(1) Charaka's samprapti. Nidana Sthana 1 treats it as one of five things from which a disease is ascertained, alongside cause, premonitory signs, manifest signs and response to a trial of contrary measures (Ni. 1/6). It gives jati, birth, and agati, coming-on, as words of the same import (Ni. 1/11). It divides samprapti by five analytic heads (Ni. 1/12) and then defines each of the five in the lines that follow (Ni. 1/12.1 to 12.5): sankhya, number, as in eight kinds of fever; pradhanya, which dosha is the stronger or the strongest; vidhi, class, by two, three or four kinds; vikalpa, the measure in which doshas standing in combination have been excited; and balakala, strength-and-time, read off season, day, night and the hours of eating. That definitional run is the closest thing in the samhita to an operational definition of samprapti, and what it operationalises is how to subdivide a pathogenesis once stated, not how to establish one.

(2) The worked narrative. Charaka's fever chapter runs one such sequence end to end: excited vata enters the stomach, mingles with the heat of the digestive fire, overtakes the food-juice, obstructs the ducts bearing food-juice and sweat, displaces the digestive fire so that its heat spreads through the body, and fever is generated. Later samprapti narratives follow this shape.

(3) Samprapti ghataka and samprapti vighatana. Modern Ayurvedic teaching breaks samprapti into a checklist of ten to twelve 'components' (dosha, dushya, agni, ama, srotas, srotodushti-prakara, udbhava-sthana, sanchara-sthana, adhishthana, roga-marga, sadhya-asadhyata) and names the aim of treatment samprapti vighatana, breaking the chain. Object (3) is what contemporary clinicians and papers actually operate; the case reports at modern[5] and modern[6] are written in its vocabulary. It is not object (1). No classical verse enumerating the ghataka list was found by the searches this record names in gatheringNotes, sources do not agree on its membership, and it does not acquire Charaka's authority by sharing his word. Charaka gives five analytic heads; the ghataka list is a later teaching compilation.

Across all three, samprapti is reconstructed by the clinician from history and examination rather than measured. None of the sources retrieved for this record states an observation that would confirm or refute a proposed samprapti. That is a statement about a bounded search, not about the world; notKnown gives the bound.
records.evidenceState:
Samprapti rests on classical exegesis. This revision separates what is addressable in text from what is evidentially supported, because running those together was the gathered record's central defect.

WHAT IS ADDRESSABLE IN TEXT. Charaka's Nidana Sthana 1 defines samprapti by synonym (Ni. 1/11), divides it by five analytic heads (Ni. 1/12), and defines each of the five (Ni. 1/12.1 to 12.5). All of it is quotable from Kaviratna's public-domain translation and all of it is now numbered against the Trikamji Sanskrit rather than against a translator's own count or an unnamed 'modern edition'. The definitional run is the closest thing in the samhita to an operational definition, and it is worth being exact about what it operationalises: how to subdivide a pathogenesis once stated, not how to establish one, not how to choose between two, and not how to find one wrong. Charaka also gives a worked example in the fever chapter and the site-specificity principle at Su. 28/8 that the whole construct rests on.

WHAT THIS RECORD NO LONGER CLAIMS. The gathered evidenceState called samprapti 'a well-attested doctrinal construct with clear textual loci in Charaka's Nidana Sthana and a long commentarial and teaching tradition'. The second half is cut. A teaching tradition is the replication of a syllabus; it is transmission, not corroboration, and a construct taught for a thousand years is not thereby better evidenced than one taught for ten. The cut also removes a conflation that the gathered record's own contested[1] already refuted. Calling the loci 'clear' is true of Charaka's five analytic heads and false of samprapti ghataka, the ten-to-twelve-item checklist that modern clinical writing actually operates under the name samprapti; the searches named in gatheringNotes found no classical verse enumerating that list, and no retrieved source gives it an author or a date. Describing both as one well-attested construct let a twentieth-century teaching artefact inherit Charaka's authority. The two are now reported as two things, in summary, in components and in contested[1]. Nothing was deleted to make the old claim survivable: the contested entry that exposed it stands untouched and has been strengthened.

WHAT THE MODERN LITERATURE SUPPORTS. A PubMed search for 'samprapti' on 2026-10-06 returned 15 records. Those retrieved and read for this record are case reports, case series and narrative reviews that restate a classical pathogenesis for a modern disease label (psoriasis, blistering skin disease, uterine fibroid, infertility, migraine, hypertension, cancer), assert a correspondence, and stop; several close by proposing biomarker work as future research. Two studies bear empirically on the construct and both run against it. A 2024 emailed vignette survey of 141 experienced practitioners found a significant lack of consensus on diagnosis, on pathophysiology and on treatment across five scenarios, and concluded that these constructs do not uniformly determine prescriptions or individualisation (PMID 39183608). A 2019 reliability study nested in an RCT found chance-corrected agreement between four Ayurvedic experts of kappa 0 to 0.4 on core components including prakriti and agni, despite 95 percent agreement on the consented final diagnosis (PMID 30653338).

THE ATTEMPTS TO OPERATIONALISE IT, NAMED RATHER THAN DISMISSED. The gathered record's verdict of 'no validated operational definition' passed over the efforts that tried to build one, which is not an honest way to report a null. The named efforts, as far as these searches reach: AyuSoft, the C-DAC Pune decision-support software, whose prakriti module was measured against two independent physicians at ICC 0.72 for vata, 0.58 for pitta and 0.44 for kapha (PMID 33750638); the wider body of prakriti assessment tools, audited in a 2025 scoping review of 32 studies that found 3 of 16 questionnaires both reliable and valid, 3 of 5 algorithmic methods using validated machine-learning models, and 1 of 11 devices validated with reproducible data, and that names 'finding the ground truth in a robust manner' as the standing obstacle (PMID 40582042); and Ayurvedic health informatics generally, including 'development of Traditional Medicine databases for decision system support' (PMID 26160148). Two things must be said about this list, and the second is the more important. First, every one of these operationalises a samprapti INPUT, chiefly prakriti, and none of them encodes samprapti or samprapti ghataka; the searches run for this record, which are logged in gatheringNotes, returned no indexed study evaluating a computational encoding of samprapti itself, and 'AyuSoft' returns 7 records of which all 7 concern prakriti. Second, the audits of the inputs are themselves unfavourable, and the 2025 review's ground-truth problem is the one that bites hardest: a tool can only be validated against a reference standard, and for these constructs the reference standard is expert judgement of the kind measured at kappa 0 to 0.4.

WHAT FOLLOWS. A reader should treat samprapti as a structured clinical narrative and a teaching framework. Its reproducibility has been tested indirectly, through the components a samprapti is assembled from, and the results were poor; whether a samprapti statement itself is reproducible between two clinicians was not addressed by any study these searches found. It is not a validated pathophysiological model. This record does not assert that no validation exists anywhere, only that the searches it names did not find one, and notKnown states the bound on each of those searches.

contested.question: Does samprapti actually drive individualised Ayurvedic prescribing, as the curriculum claims?
positions: The standard Ayurvedic teaching position: diagnosis and treatment are individualised through samprapti, agni assessment and dosha analysis, and this is what distinguishes Ayurvedic from protocol-based practice.

The empirical finding of PMID 39183608: across 141 practitioners and five case scenarios the constructs did not determine prescriptions or individualisation uniformly, and the authors explicitly raise whether this reflects an inherently weak theoretical framework.

contested.question: Are the 'samprapti ghataka' a classical list or a modern teaching device?
positions: Common modern textbook and journal presentation treats the ghataka list (dosha, dushya, agni, ama, srotas, srotodushti prakara, udbhava sthana, sanchara sthana, adhishthana, roga marga, sadhya-asadhyata) as the standard anatomy of samprapti.

Charaka's own text gives only the five analytic heads (sankhya, pradhanya, vidhi, vikalpa, bala-kala), quoted at classical[2] and each defined at classical[3]. No classical verse enumerating the ghataka list was found by the searches named in gatheringNotes; it appears to be a later pedagogical compilation, sources do not agree on its exact membership, and no retrieved source names its author or its date. This position is unchanged from the gathered record. It is restated here because it is the entry that refuted the record's own evidenceState, and on this revision the evidenceState was rewritten to agree with it rather than this entry being softened to agree with the evidenceState.

contested.question: Verse numbering of the key Charaka passages.
positions: The Trikamji Sanskrit, verified at carakasamhitaonline on 2026-10-06, numbers the nidana-panchaka line Ni. 1/6, the jati/agati synonym line Ni. 1/11, the list of analytic heads Ni. 1/12, and the five definitions Ni. 1/12.1 to 12.5.

Kaviratna's public-domain translation numbers the same passages 3, 5, 6 and 7 to 10, and prints each number AFTER its aphorism. His partition is not Trikamji's: his aphorism 3 spans Trikamji 1/5 to 1/9, and he breaks pradhanya across his 7 and 8 where Trikamji has one sub-part. So his numbers do not stand at a fixed offset and must never be converted arithmetically to a Trikamji number. Any citation of these verses must state which system is meant.

The gathered record's own numbers were right but their source was vague: it said 'numbered 1.6 / 1.11 / 1.12 in modern editions' without naming an edition. On this revision every number is sourced to the named Trikamji Sanskrit instead, and no number anywhere in this record is taken on the authority of the in-copyright 1949 Gulabkunverba translation.

contested.question: Whether samprapti descriptions for modern disease entities are discoveries or restatements.
positions: Integrative reviews present mapped samprapti for conditions such as hypertension and cancer as clinically usable staging.
PMID 34566386, from 400 observed cancer patients, concludes that modern cancer cannot be equated with any single Ayurvedic disease entity, which undercuts one-to-one mapping claims.

contested.question: Are samprapti's analytic heads five or six?
positions: Six, which is the common count in modern Ayurvedic writing and is what Kaviratna's English at classical[2] reads as: 'number (or enumeration), predominance, kind (or order), solution of doubt, strength (or intensity), and Time'.

Five. The Sanskrit of Ni. 1/12 compounds strength and time into one member, 'sA sa~gkhyAprAdhAnyavidhivikalpabalakAlavisheShairbhidyate'; carakasamhitaonline divides the following definitions into five sub-parts and labels the fifth Bala Kala samprapti; and Kaviratna's own definitional sentence for that head runs strength and time together as dependent on one list, the season, day, night and the hours of eating. The six is an artefact of his English splitting one compound, and this record's components list has always had five. See classical[3] translatorVoice.

A third enumeration, which is in the critic's finding itself and is supported by neither of the above: 'sankhya, vikalpa, pradhanya, bala, kala', which splits balakala into two AND omits vidhi. Vidhi is defined at length by Charaka at Ni. 1/12.3. Recorded here because this project treats disagreement as data, including disagreement with the auditor.

notKnown: Whether two independent Ayurvedic clinicians examining the same patient produce the same samprapti. No study addressing this was found. The searches: PubMed 'samprapti' returns 15 records (2026-10-06), all of those retrieved being case reports, case series or narrative reviews; PubMed 'samprapti AND reliability' returns 0 records. The closest data, PMID 30653338, measures agreement on constituent judgements such as prakriti and agni between four experts and finds kappa 0 to 0.4, and PMID 33750638 measures a software tool against two physicians on prakriti alone at ICC 0.72 / 0.58 / 0.44. Both bound the question; neither answers it.

Whether any proposed samprapti has predictive validity. No study was found showing that a stated pathogenesis predicts course, complication or response to therapy better than chance, or better than the modern diagnosis alone. Bound: the samprapti searches above, plus the modern entries retrieved for this record, none of which reports a prediction tested against an outcome.

Whether treatment chosen by samprapti vighatana outperforms treatment chosen without it. No randomised comparison on this contrast was found. Bound: the same searches. The clinical reports that do invoke the principle, modern[5] and modern[6], are an uncontrolled case series of seven and a single case, so neither is a comparison at all.

What observation would falsify a proposed samprapti. No retrieved source gives a disconfirming criterion, and Charaka's definitional run at Ni. 1/12.1 to 12.5, newly added as classical[3], does not supply one either: it tells a physician how to subdivide a pathogenesis, not how to test one. This is the central epistemic gap in the record and retrieving the classical material the critic asked for made it sharper rather than closing it.

The textual locus of the universally quoted maxim that treatment is nothing but nidana-parivarjana and samprapti-vighatana. It is repeated in modern Ayurvedic journals, including in the abstract of modern[6], without a verifiable chapter and verse, and it was not confirmed as a verbatim verse in Charaka or Sushruta by the searches run here.

Whether any samprapti component (ama, agni, srotodushti) has a measurable biological correlate. Reviews retrieved for this record repeatedly propose biomarkers as future work; none of those retrieved reports a validated one.
How samprapti should be reconciled with, or distinguished from, biomedical pathophysiology when the two conflict for the same patient. The sources retrieved assert compatibility rather than test it.

THE COMMENTARIAL LAYER, scoped out explicitly rather than paraphrased. This record cites no commentary on samprapti and therefore says nothing about how the construct was read after Charaka. Specifically absent: Chakrapanidatta's Ayurveda Dipika on Charaka Nidana 1; Madhava Nidana chapter 1 with the Madhukosha of Vijayarakshita and Shrikanthadatta; and Vagbhata's variant at Ashtanga Hridaya Nidana 1. What was tried, so a later worker need not repeat it: GRETIL's Carakasamhita-with-Ayurvedadipika file (caraka_u.htm, retrieved 2026-10-06) does carry the commentary, but its Nidanasthana coverage is chapter 7 only, so Chakrapani on Nidana 1 is not in it. No public-domain English of the Ayurveda Dipika, the Madhukosha or the Ashtanga Hridaya was found; the standard English Madhava Nidana (Murthy, Motilal Banarsidass) is in copyright. By this project's rule of no quote, no citation, the gap is stated here rather than filled with paraphrase. The consequence for the record's claims should be stated too: because the commentarial layer is absent, this record cannot say where between Charaka and the modern manuals the ghataka checklist arose, and it does not try to.

THE ORIGIN OF SAMPRAPTI GHATAKA. No classical locus for the ten-to-twelve-item checklist was found, and beyond that, no retrieved source names its author, its date, or the text that first prints it, and retrieved sources do not agree on its membership or even its length. The record carries it in components because it is what modern clinical writing operates, labelled as a teaching construct. Who built it, when, and from what, is unknown to this record. Bound: the searches logged in gatheringNotes, which were run against PubMed and against the public-domain Charaka and Sushruta translations, and not against the MD(Ay) thesis literature or Indian-language teaching manuals where the critic suggests it originates and where it is most likely to be documented.

WHETHER SAMPRAPTI ITSELF HAS BEEN COMPUTATIONALLY ENCODED OR EVALUATED. The searches run for this record found no indexed study evaluating a decision-support encoding, ontology or knowledge graph of samprapti or of samprapti ghataka. What they did find is named in evidenceState and cited at modern[7] to modern[9], and in every case the construct operationalised is an input, chiefly prakriti, not samprapti. The bound, stated precisely because the critic is right that a null needs one: PubMed 'AyuSoft' returns 7 records (2026-10-06) and all 7 concern prakriti; 'Ayurveda knowledge graph' returns 3, none on samprapti; 'Ayurveda semantic web' returns 0; 'Ayurveda ontology' returns 38, of which the ones screened are dominated by gene-ontology and network-pharmacology work that uses 'ontology' in an unrelated sense. PubMed is the wrong index for this question: decision-support software of this kind is documented in IEEE and conference venues and in institutional reports, which were NOT searched. A reader should treat this as 'not found in the medical literature index searched', not as 'does not exist'.

WHETHER CHARAKA'S FIVE ANALYTIC HEADS WERE EVER USED AS THE MODERN GHATAKA ARE. classical[3] establishes that Charaka defines the five heads. Nothing retrieved here shows them being applied, in any period, to work up an individual patient, and the modern clinical reports retrieved use the ghataka vocabulary rather than the five heads. Whether the five heads are a live clinical instrument or a classificatory scheme that the teaching tradition replaced is not something this record can say.

components.gloss: The causative or exciting factors, dietary, behavioural, seasonal, psychological or traumatic, that begin the sequence.
Disturbance or aggravation of one or more of vata, pitta and kapha by those causes.
The tissue elements (dhatus and malas) that the disturbed dosha acts upon; literally 'that which is spoilt'.
The channel system and the anatomical site where the disturbed dosha settles and the disease takes form.
The resulting named disease, with its purvarupa (premonitory signs) and rupa (manifest signs).
Analytical head 1: the number of varieties of the disease. Charaka's own examples are eight kinds of fever, five kinds of tumour, seven kinds of leprosy.
Analytical head 2: which dosha predominates in the mixture. Charaka defines it as judging which fault is the stronger or the strongest, the comparative relating to two and the superlative to three.

Analytical head 3: the kind or order of classification. Charaka gives three cuts: two kinds, natural and accidental; three kinds, by which of wind, bile and phlegm has been excited; four kinds, by curability, incurability, mildness and violence.

Analytical head 4: the ascertainment of the measure in which the faults, existing in a state of union, have been excited. Kaviratna renders the term itself as 'solution of doubt', which is his English and not a second meaning; his following sentence gives the definition just quoted.

Analytical head 5: strength-and-time, ONE head and not two. Charaka defines the distinctions of strength and time together in a single sentence dependent on a single list, the season, day, night and the hours of eating, and the Sanskrit of Ni. 1/12 compounds them as balakala. Kaviratna's English splits them into 'strength (or intensity), and Time', which is where the widely repeated count of six analytic heads comes from. See classical[3] translatorVoice and contested[4].

The modern teaching-manual checklist of pathogenesis components (dosha, dushya, agni, ama, srotas, srotodushti prakara, udbhava sthana, sanchara sthana, adhishthana, roga marga, sadhya-asadhyata). LABEL, kept deliberately blunt: this is a twentieth-century pedagogical construct, not a classical enumeration. The searches named in gatheringNotes found no verse in Charaka or Sushruta listing it, sources disagree on its membership and even on its length, and no retrieved source gives it an author or a date. It is nonetheless the object modern clinical writing operates under the name samprapti, which is why it is in this list at all. See contested[1] and notKnown.

Breaking or dismantling the pathogenesis; the stated aim of treatment in modern Ayurvedic writing, and the only reason the concept carries clinical weight. Attested in use rather than in a located verse: the uterine-fibroid case series at modern[5] says its protocol was chosen 'befitting the Samprapti Vighatana of Granthi', and the migraine case report at modern[6] pairs it with nidana parivarjana in the same sentence. The textual locus of the maxim that treatment is nothing but nidana-parivarjana and samprapti-vighatana was not confirmed; see notKnown.

classical.verse: Ni. 1/6 in the Trikamji numbering; Kaviratna prints his aphorism number 3 AFTER the run that contains it
classical.establishes: That Charaka's Nidana Sthana 1 names samprapti as one of five things from which a disease is ascertained. It does NOT establish that Charaka groups the five under a collective name or calls them five: there is no collective noun in this line. Note on the Romanisation: Kaviratna's 'Upacaya' here renders upashaya, not upachaya, and his Romanisation of sha as c, g or s is inconsistent throughout the scan.
classical.quote: The ascertainment of disease is to be had from 'Nidana', 'Purva-rupa', 'Linga', 'Upacaya', and 'Samprapti.'
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna, Charaka-Samhita translated into English, Calcutta: Dass, issued in parts 1896-1913; public domain

classical.verse: Ni. 1/11 in the Trikamji numbering; Kaviratna's aphorism 5, printed after the aphorism
classical.establishes: The classical definition by synonym: samprapti, jati and agati are words of the same import. Kaviratna's own footnote to this aphorism glosses jati as janma, birth, and agati as 'coming in, as gati means going out'. That gloss is the translator's and is reported as his, not as Charaka's.
classical.quote: Samprapti, 'jati', and 'agati' of disease, are words of the same import
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna, Charaka-Samhita translated into English, Calcutta: Dass, issued in parts 1896-1913; public domain

classical.verse: Ni. 1/12 in the Trikamji numbering; Kaviratna's aphorism 6, printed after the aphorism
classical.establishes: That Charaka gives samprapti a list of analytic headings, and nothing more. The heads are sankhya, pradhanya, vidhi, vikalpa and balakala; each is defined at classical[3]. Kaviratna renders vikalpa as 'solution of doubt', and his following sentence glosses it as 'the ascertainment of the measure in which the faults, existing in a state of union, have been excited'. This citation establishes that the construct is subdivided. It establishes nothing about whether a samprapti can be reliably stated, and nothing about individualisation of treatment.
classical.quote: 'Samprapti' is distinguished by these considerations, viz., number (or enumeration), predominance, kind (or order), solution of doubt, strength (or intensity), and Time.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna, Charaka-Samhita translated into English, Calcutta: Dass, issued in parts 1896-1913; public domain

classical.verse: Ni. 1/12.1 to 1/12.5 in the Trikamji numbering as carakasamhitaonline divides it; Kaviratna's aphorisms 7 to 10, each printed after its aphorism
classical.establishes: Each of samprapti's five analytic heads defined in Charaka's own words. This is the material the critic's first 'missing' finding asked for, and it is the closest thing in the samhita to an operational definition of samprapti. What it operationalises should be stated precisely, because it is less than the finding implies: it tells a physician how to SUBDIVIDE a pathogenesis once he has one, by counting varieties, ranking doshas, assigning a class, estimating proportions and reading strength and timing off the calendar. It gives no procedure for arriving at a pathogenesis, no criterion for choosing between two rival ones, and no observation that would show one to be wrong. Retrieving it also settled the five-versus-six count against the translation; see translatorVoice.
classical.quote: By Number or (or enumeration) is meant such as these : Eight kinds of Fevers, Five kinds of tumours, Seven kinds of leprosy, and so on. Predominance, again, applies to faults, and consists in judging which is the stronger or the strongest. The comparative relates to two, the superlative to three. Kind (or Order) is as follows : — Diseases are of two kinds, as natural and accidental. They are of three kinds, according to the particular fault that has been excited among the three that exist (viz., wind, bile, and phlegm). They are of four kinds, considering curability, incurability, mildness, and violence. Solution of doubt (Vikalpa), in this connection, means the ascertainment of the measure in which the faults, existing in a state of union, have been excited. The distinctions of Strength and Time (in respect of disease) are dependant on the season (in which the disease has happened), day, night, the hours of eating, &c.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna, Charaka-Samhita translated into English, Calcutta: Dass, issued in parts 1896-1913; public domain

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorism 18; his aphorism 16-17, immediately preceding, is the list of causes that excite the wind. No Trikamji number is given: see numberingCheck
classical.establishes: A worked classical example of a samprapti, in Charaka's own sequence: the excited wind enters the amashaya, mingles with the heat of the digestive fire, overtakes the food-juice, obstructs the ducts bearing food-juice and sweat, then affects the digestive fire and expels its heat from the pakvashaya over the whole body, and fever is generated. The gathered record's claim that 'this is the template all later samprapti narratives follow' has been CUT: it is an unsourced generalisation over a literature this record has not surveyed, and the quote cannot carry it. What the passage establishes is that Charaka gives at least one pathogenesis as a staged narrative of this shape.
classical.quote: Overtaking in that state the food-juice which is the first product (or result) of food, it obstructs those ducts which bear the food-juice and the sweat.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna, Charaka-Samhita translated into English, Calcutta: Dass, issued in parts 1896-1913; public domain

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorism 15; the second sentence of the quote corresponds to Su. 28/8 in the Trikamji numbering. See numberingCheck before citing this as 28/8 whole
classical.establishes: The site-specificity principle that samprapti rests on: which disease appears depends on the place in which the disturbed dosha is excited, not on the dosha alone. Charaka says this and then undertakes to enumerate which diseases arise from which seat. The principle is stated; no criterion is given for determining, in a given patient, which seat is involved.
classical.quote: Through these causes, the wind, bile, and phlegm, being excited in particular parts of the body, produce different diseases. The faults becoming excited in particular places such as the food-fluids and others, produce particular diseases.
classical.translator: Avinash Chandra Kaviratna, Charaka-Samhita translated into English, Calcutta: Dass, issued in parts 1896-1913; public domain

classical.establishes: NARROWED. Two PubMed-indexed philological notes take the nidana-panchaka of Madhava Nidana chapter 1 as their subject and name samprapti among its five limbs: PMID 12572581 (1997) and PMID 12585278 (1999), the second explicitly a continuation of the first. Both were resolved by efetch on 2026-10-06 and both carry abstracts. That is the whole of what this entry now supports.

GUTTED, deliberately, and this entry should be read as a placeholder rather than as a citation. No verse of the Ashtanga Hridaya was retrieved for this record, in Sanskrit or in English. The gathered entry asserted that 'Vagbhata restates the five-limbed diagnostic scheme with samprapti as its final limb' and that the chapter is 'cited in secondary literature as a locus for sammurchana within the samprapti frame'. Neither claim is quoted and the second names no secondary source, so by this project's rule of no quote, no citation, both are withdrawn. See citationsRemoved[0]. The gap is now stated in notKnown rather than carried as a soft claim.

modern.title: Myth and reality of "theory-driven individualised practice" in Ayurveda: Mapping physicians' approaches using case-based scenarios.
modern.establishes: Directly tests whether samprapti and related constructs actually drive clinical decisions. 141 registered Ayurveda practitioners with five or more years' experience responded to five case vignettes, giving diagnosis, treatment plan and the principles behind the plan. The authors report a significant lack of consensus on clinical diagnoses, on interventions, and on the understanding of pathophysiology, with many conflicting opinions, and conclude that theoretical constructs do not uniformly determine prescriptions or individualisation.
modern.quality: Empirical cross-sectional vignette survey and the single most informative modern study for this concept, but with real limits: convenience sample, emailed self-report, hypothetical cases rather than observed consultations, and no measure of chance-corrected agreement. It is a negative finding and the authors state it as such.

modern.title: Reliability of Ayurvedic Diagnosis for Knee Osteoarthritis Patients: A Nested Diagnostic Study Within a Randomized Controlled Trial.
modern.establishes: Inter-rater reliability of Ayurvedic diagnosis, nested in a randomised controlled trial of knee osteoarthritis: 30 patients assessed sequentially by 4 Ayurvedic experts. Percentage agreement on the final consented diagnosis was high (95%), but chance-corrected kappa for central diagnostic components including prakriti and agni was fair to poor, with kappa values between 0 and 0.4. Agreement on disease-related entities was better than on constitutional entities.
modern.quality: Empirical diagnostic reliability study, small (30 patients, 4 raters), single condition, single centre. It measures the inputs a samprapti is built from, not the samprapti statement itself, so it bounds rather than directly tests the construct. Its result is unfavourable.

modern.title: Understanding hypertension in the light of Ayurveda.
modern.establishes: Proposes that hypertension be understood as the prasara stage of dosha spread involving vyana vata, prana vata, sadhaka pitta, avalambaka kapha and rakta, with avarana. Opens by stating that different theories have been proposed to explain hypertension from an Ayurvedic perspective and there is no consensus amongst the experts.
modern.quality: Narrative literature review. No patients, no data, no test of the proposal. Useful mainly as documentation that experts disagree about the samprapti of even a well-defined modern condition.

modern.title: Understanding the etiopathogenesis and diagnosis of malignancy in the framework of Ayurveda: A review based on experience of working in an institute of oncology.
modern.establishes: Proposes an Ayurvedic etiopathogenesis and diagnostic framework for malignancy based on observation of 400 cancer patients at an oncology institution, and concludes that modern cancer cannot be equated with any single disease entity in Ayurvedic literature.
modern.quality: Uncontrolled observational case-series-derived conceptual proposal. No comparator, no blinding, no reliability testing of the pathogenesis assignments. The honest conclusion (no one-to-one mapping exists) is more defensible than the proposed framework.

modern.title: Definition of Nidana Pancaka (first chapter of Madhavanidana).
modern.journal: Bull Indian Inst Hist Med Hyderabad
modern.establishes: Historical-textual account of the definition of nidana-panchaka in the first chapter of Madhava Nidana, covering nidana, purvarupa, rupa, upashaya and samprapti. With its companion PMID 12572581 (1997), of which it is explicitly a continuation, it attests that the five-limbed scheme is set out and defined in that chapter. It does NOT establish when or where the scheme was consolidated; the gathered record said it documented that, and the abstract does not.
modern.quality: Historical article in a history-of-medicine bulletin, not an empirical study. Cite for provenance only. CORRECTION to the gathered record, which said it is 'not indexed with an abstract of substance': an abstract IS indexed and was retrieved on 2026-10-06. It is short and is largely a continuation note pointing back to the 1997 article (PMID 12572581), stating that the present part deals with nidana, purvarupa, rupa, upashaya and samprapti. The accessibility complaint stands, the bulletin is not widely held, and no full text was obtained, so nothing beyond the abstract is claimed.

modern.title: Ayurvedic intervention in the management of uterine fibroids: A Case series.
modern.establishes: Seven cases of uterine fibroid treated with Ayurvedic formulations, with the abstract stating that the condition 'was critically reviewed in the context of Granthi Roga (disease) and treatment protocol befitting the Samprapti Vighatana of Granthi (encapsulated growth) was subjected in patients of uterine fibroids'. Cited for ONE narrow purpose: it is quoted evidence that samprapti vighatana is used as the operative treatment-selection principle in published clinical Ayurvedic writing, which is the only reason the concept carries clinical weight. It is not cited as evidence that the principle works.
modern.quality: Case series of seven, uncontrolled, no comparator, no blinding, outcome assessed by ultrasonography with no stated reader blinding, and no reliability check on the samprapti assignment itself. The reported outcome, absence of fibroid on USG at seven weeks in the reported cases, is not evidence of efficacy at this design and this record makes no efficacy claim from it. Its value here is terminological, not clinical.

modern.title: Ayurveda management of migraine - a case report.
modern.establishes: Single case report of migraine (Ardhavabhedaka) in a 35-year-old man, whose abstract reads 'For the proper Samprapti vighatana, Nidana parivarjana (abstinance from the eitiological factors), Deepana, Paachana, Siravyadha, Nasya and Dosha ShamanaChikitsa principles were adopted'. Cited for the same narrow terminological purpose as modern[5], and additionally because it pairs samprapti vighatana with nidana parivarjana in exactly the formula whose textual locus this record could not confirm; see notKnown. Spellings are the abstract's.
modern.quality: n = 1, uncontrolled, unblinded, self-reported outcome scales (MIDAS 19 to 4, NPR 8 to 2), no follow-up period stated for relapse in the abstract. No evidential weight for efficacy and none is claimed. It is quoted for its vocabulary.

modern.title: Correlation of prakriti diagnosis using AyuSoft prakriti diagnostic tool with clinician rating in patients with psychiatric disorders.
modern.establishes: The one measured evaluation of an AyuSoft module that these searches found. 112 stabilised psychiatric inpatients had prakriti determined by the AyuSoft tool '(developed by C-DAC, Pune, India)' and, independently, by two Ayurveda physicians on clinical examination. Agreement between tool and physicians, by intraclass correlation: vata ICC 0.72 (Cronbach alpha 0.83), pitta ICC 0.58 (0.62), kapha ICC 0.44 (0.51). The authors also state they 'could not find any literature regarding reliability of a prakriti diagnostic tool in patients with psychiatric conditions'. This is cited because the critic is right that a null cannot honestly be reported without naming the attempts: AyuSoft is the named attempt, this is its measurement, and the result is weakest on kapha. CRITICAL SCOPE LIMIT: AyuSoft is evaluated here on PRAKRITI, which is an input to a samprapti, not on samprapti or on samprapti ghataka. It bounds the construct; it does not test it.
modern.quality: Empirical, with chance-corrected and consistency statistics, which is rare in this literature. Limits are real: single centre, psychiatric inpatients only, two raters, agreement measured tool-against-clinician rather than clinician-against-clinician, and an ICC from a two-way mixed consistency model on mean ratings, which is the more forgiving choice. The authors' own conclusion is that the tool was 'feasible' and 'comparable'; an ICC of 0.44 on kapha is reported here as what it is rather than as comparability.

modern.title: Towards standardization of Prakriti Evaluation: A scoping review of modern assessment tools and their psychometric properties in Ayurvedic medicine.
modern.establishes: Scoping review (Arksey and O'Malley framework) of 32 studies of modern prakriti assessment tools and their psychometric properties. Of 16 questionnaire studies, 3 were validated, 6 had established reliability and 3 had both; 5 used algorithm-based methods, 3 of those validated machine-learning models; 11 used devices, with 'only one device validated and providing access to data for reproducibility'. The authors state that machine-learning models 'show potential but suffers challenges in accuracy, replicability and finding the ground truth in a robust manner'. This is the second half of naming the attempts: it documents that computational and instrumental operationalisation of an Ayurvedic diagnostic construct has been attempted at scale and audited, and reports the audit's result. Same scope limit as modern[7]: the construct operationalised is prakriti, not samprapti.
modern.quality: A scoping review, so it maps a literature rather than pooling effects; no meta-analysis, no risk-of-bias instrument reported in the abstract, and inclusion is limited to tools appearing in scientific literature, which will under-count unpublished clinical software. It is nonetheless a systematic, recent and adversarial-to-its-own-field audit, and its 'ground truth' point is the one that bears hardest on samprapti: a tool can only be validated against a reference standard, and for these constructs the reference standard is itself expert judgement of the kind PMID 30653338 measured at kappa 0 to 0.4.

modern.title: An analysis of application of health informatics in Traditional Medicine: A review of four Traditional Medicine Systems.
modern.establishes: Review of health informatics across four traditional medicine systems, including Ayurveda, in a mainstream medical informatics journal. The abstract states that 'amongst major advancements in TCM and Ayurveda are bioinformatics, development of Traditional Medicine databases for decision system support, data mining and image processing', and that 'informatics may not be able to address all the emerging areas of Traditional Medicine because the concepts in Traditional Medicine system of medicine are different from modern system'. Cited to name the decision-support and knowledge-representation effort at the level at which a retrieved source actually describes it, rather than leaving the critic's 'Ayurveda ontology / knowledge-graph literature' as an unaddressed gesture.
modern.quality: Narrative review with a stated but loose search (four databases plus Google, broad terms), no appraisal of the systems it describes, and now a decade old. It establishes that the effort exists and is described in the informatics literature. It reports no evaluation of any such system's accuracy or reliability, and names no encoding of samprapti.

records.title: Shodhana and Shamana (purification versus pacification)
records.summary: Shodhana and shamana name the two basic ways Ayurveda claims a disturbed dosha can be dealt with: expelled from the body by an eliminative procedure, or brought back to normal state in situ by diet, drug, fasting and regimen. The doctrine attaches a specific and falsifiable-sounding claim to the distinction: doshas subdued by fasting and digestive measures may be aggravated again, whereas doshas evacuated by purification do not recur. Sushruta adds diet and conduct as two further co-equal factors alongside the pair, and Vagbhata reorganises the whole scheme by making shodhana a subtype of langhana rather than its opposite. The choice between the two in any given case is said to turn on the strength of the patient, the strength and stage of the dosha, the season, and the presence or absence of ama. Quantified rules do exist in the passages retrieved for this record, and they sit at the level of dose and of adequacy rather than at the level of the choice itself: Charaka's Siddhi Sthana grades emesis and purgation by counted bouts and by measured volume, prescribes anuvasana basti in counts keyed to which dosha is dominant, and Sushruta grades basti pipe dimensions and asthapana volumes by the patient's age. What no retrieved passage supplies is a measurable definition of the terms the choice turns on, which is a narrower and different point from the one the 2026-09-19 version of this record made.
records.evidenceState:
The distinction rests on classical exegesis, and its single most testable claim has not been tested in anything found in the searches recorded in gatheringNotes. Charaka Su.16.20 asserts that doshas subdued by fasting and digestives may recur while those evacuated by shodhana do not, and Su.16.21 justifies it by a simile about tree roots rather than by any observation of relapse. That claim is a relapse-rate claim and would be straightforward to examine with a follow-up period, yet none of the comparative studies located includes one. The empirical literature located consists of very small unblinded comparisons, ten to twenty patients per arm, in which shodhana arms are additionally given shamana drugs so the two cannot be separated, with outcomes on symptom grades this record could not find validated. A 2026 registered protocol from an Ayurvedic university states plainly that the effect of seasonal purification on healthy individuals remains a gray area, which is a fair summary.

CORRECTED 2026-10-06, on criticFindings.overclaimed item 2. The 2026-09-19 version of this paragraph said there is no operational definition of when a patient is shodhana-eligible versus shamana-eligible. That conflated 'not validated' with 'not stated', and it was contradicted by this record's own citations. The criteria are stated, enumerated and operational. Charaka Siddhi Sthana 2 is built as a pravritti and nivritti list for each of the five procedures in turn, opening with avamyas tavat, 'those not to be given emesis are', and closing each pair with sesas tu vamyah, 'the rest are fit', so eligibility is defined by exclusion. Charaka Su.16.13-16, a passage this record already quoted but had mis-addressed, lists the signs of bahudosha and concludes that for such a patient purification is beneficial, upward or downward, yathadosam yathabalam. Ashtanga Hridaya Su.14.12-14 allocates patients between samshodhana, pachana-dipana and restraint of hunger and thirst by ordinal tiers of body bulk and strength. Sushruta's Sutrasthana gives contraindication lists for alkali, cautery and bloodletting, and at Chapter XII makes the physician's checklist explicit: the seat of the disease, the patient's strength, the marmas, the nature of the malady and the season. And the categories are not merely historical: a registered 2026 trial screens its participants for being vamanarha and virechanarha and for madhyama koshtha by questionnaire.

What is actually missing is narrower and worse. Not one term in any of those lists is given a measurable definition. Nothing in the retrieved passages says where atisthula begins, how durbala is distinguished from merely weak, or what instrument assesses koshtha; the 2026 protocol's koshtha questionnaire is unnamed and no validation of it is cited. No source located reports agreement between physicians applying these lists to the same patient. The lists also do not agree with each other: Siddhi Sthana 2.8 contraindicates emesis for the atisthula while Ashtanga Hridaya 14.12 directs samshodhana at those in whom sthaulya is in excess, and no retrieved source reconciles them.

CORRECTED 2026-10-06, on criticFindings.overclaimed item 1. The 2026-09-19 version said no classical text gives numeric thresholds for any of the variables the choice turns on. That was an unbounded negative about the whole corpus generalised from a reading that had never opened Siddhi Sthana, and it was false against a volume already on disk. Charaka Si.1.13-15 grades emesis and purgation by counted bouts, four, six and eight for emesis and ten, twenty and thirty for purgation, by prastha multiples, and by terminal product, excluding the first two or three faecal bouts from the count. Si.1.25 prescribes anuvasana basti in integers keyed to the dominant dosha, one or three for kapha, five or seven for pitta, nine or eleven for vata, in odd numbers. Sushruta Ci.XXXV grades basti pipe length and asthapana volume by the patient's age, two, four, eight and twelve prasritas, and its memorable verse ties the increase to age, strength and bodily capacity. These are real numbers. Two things keep them from being thresholds for the choice this record is about. They are dose and adequacy rules inside an already chosen course of treatment, not rules for choosing between shodhana and shamana. And the prasrita is defined in the main text as what the patient's own palms will hold, so even the measured unit is indexed to the individual body rather than being an absolute volume.

Beyond that, there is no biomarker of adequate purification reported in anything located, and no reliability data on either the clinical completion signs or the counted and measured ones. The doctrine is also not stable across the classical corpus: Charaka makes shodhana and shamana the primary fork, Sushruta makes them two of four, and Vagbhata subordinates both to langhana, this last now quoted in the Sanskrit at AH Su.14.4 rather than reported from a web summary. A reference work should record the distinction as a well-attested organising scheme of the tradition, with eligibility and dosing rules that are detailed, quantified in places, mutually inconsistent in places, and unvalidated throughout, whose central empirical claim is untested. Every negative in this paragraph is a statement about the searches recorded in gatheringNotes and not about the field.

contested.question: Is shamana genuinely less durable than shodhana?
positions: Charaka Su.16.20 asserts it directly and it is repeated throughout the later tradition and modern Ayurvedic writing as settled. Quoted and addressed in this record, standard numbering confirmed in the Sanskrit.

No study located in the searches recorded in gatheringNotes measures relapse after shodhana versus after shamana with a follow-up period, so the assertion is supported, within what this record has read, only by classical authority and analogy.

Practitioner-facing sources sometimes soften the claim to 'less likely to recur' rather than 'cannot recur', without flagging that this weakens the text. No such source is cited in this record, so this position is UNCITED and must not be promoted to a published claim.

ADDED 2026-10-06. Vagbhata's definition of shamana at AH Su.14.6, now quoted in the Sanskrit, cuts across the question rather than answering it: shamana is defined there as that which neither purifies the doshas nor stirs the settled ones but equalises the uneven (na sodhayati yad dosan saman nodirayaty api| samikaroti visaman). That is a statement about mechanism, not about durability, and no retrieved source joins it to the Charaka durability claim.

contested.question: Is shodhana the opposite of shamana, or a species of langhana that contains shamana measures as a sibling?
positions: Charaka's Sutrasthana 16 treats the two as the primary therapeutic fork. Quoted and addressed in this record.

Charaka's own Sutrasthana 22 lists the shodhana procedures and the shamana-type measures (pachana, fasting, exercise) together as the varieties of langhana, at Ca.Su.22.18, an address this record did not carry before 2026-10-06 and now does.

Vagbhata (Ashtanga Hridaya Su.14.4) resolves this in favour of the second reading, making shodhana and shamana the two subtypes of langhana and subordinating the entire pair to the brimhana/langhana division. STATUS CHANGED 2026-10-06. Until this revision this position rested on an unnamed web summary whose verse attributions the record itself called unconfirmed, which is what criticFindings.citationRisk item 2 objected to. The Sanskrit has now been retrieved from GRETIL and quoted: sodhanam samanam ceti dvi-dha tatrapi langhanam ||4||. The position is now citable on its own terms.

CAVEAT ADDED 2026-10-06, so the resolution is not over-read. AH Su.14.3 names snehana, rukshana, svedana and stambhana in the same breath, so Vagbhata is subsuming the six under the two rather than discarding them, and AH Su.14.7 ends by saying brimhana is itself the shamana of vayu and of pitta-with-vayu, which crosses the two branches. No retrieved source addresses whether that leaves his scheme internally consistent.

contested.question: What counts as shodhana?
positions: Charaka restricts internal shodhana to emesis, purgation, nasal cleansing and the two enemas. Ca.Su.22.18's catuhprakara samshuddhi is the fourfold form; the five-procedure enumeration is at Siddhi Sthana 2, whose chapter structure this record has retrieved.

Sushruta, as glossed in BHISHAGRATNA'S OWN FOOTNOTE at Vol I page 11 and not in Sushruta's text, includes bloodletting internally and counts surgery, cautery, alkali and plasters as external shodhana. Re-read 2026-10-06 and the attribution tightened: this is the translator's voice, flagged because absorbing it as doctrine is one of the three systematic defects established across this project's citations and this record had committed it in its components list.

Vagbhata's five explicitly include bloodletting. CONFIRMED FROM THE SANSKRIT 2026-10-06 at AH Su.14.5: nirtiho vamanam kaya-siro-reko 'sra-visrutih, that is niruha, vamana, purgation of the body, purgation of the head, and asra-visruti, the letting of blood. Until this revision this was reported from a web summary. There is no reconciliation of these three lists in anything retrieved for this record.

contested.question: Should shamana be given after shodhana as a matter of course?
positions: Several clinical studies combine them as standard sequence, implying the tradition treats shamana as consolidation. Both comparative trials in this record's modern array do so: PMID 23559794 Group B and PMID 24049408 in both arms.
Charaka Su.16.20 read strictly implies shodhana alone should suffice for durability, which would make routine follow-on shamana redundant.

No source located in the searches recorded in gatheringNotes addresses the tension. Note also that the strongest reported result in PMID 23559794 is the combined arm and the weakest is shamana alone, which is consistent with consolidation but equally consistent with two active treatments summing, and that trial cannot distinguish the two.

contested.question: Are the classical shodhana-eligibility lists mutually consistent?
positions: Charaka Siddhi Sthana 2.8 lists atisthula and atikrsa among the avamya, those not to be given emesis. Quoted in the Sanskrit in this record.

Ashtanga Hridaya Su.14.12 directs samshodhana at those in whom sthaulya, bala, pitta and kapha are in excess (tatra samsodhanaih sthaulya-bala-pitta-kaphadhikan). Quoted in the Sanskrit in this record.

The tension may be only apparent. Charaka's term is ati-sthula and Vagbhata's is sthaulya-adhika, and Charaka's exclusion is specific to vamana while Vagbhata's indication is for samshodhana generally, so a reading on which Charaka excludes only the extreme case from emesis while Vagbhata addresses the merely excessive case with purification in general would dissolve it. NO RETRIEVED SOURCE SAYS THIS. It is set out here as the obvious candidate reconciliation precisely so that it is not mistaken for one that has been found in a text.

No commentarial source was retrieved for this question. Chakrapani on Siddhi Sthana 2 and Arunadatta or Hemadri on Ashtanga Hridaya 14 were not consulted and no quotable public-domain English for any of them was sought.

notKnown: The relapse rate after shodhana versus after shamana for any condition. This is the doctrine's own central claim and no study located in the searches recorded in gatheringNotes measures it; none of the comparative trials retrieved includes a follow-up period at all. Stated as a fact about those searches, not about the field.

REWRITTEN 2026-10-06 on criticFindings.overclaimed item 2. The 2026-09-19 version said no criteria determine shodhana eligibility expressed as anything measurable, and that 'strength of the patient and strength of the dosha' has no instrument. The first half was wrong and has gone: the criteria exist and are enumerated at Ca.Si.2.8, 2.10 and 2.13, Ca.Su.16.13-16, AH.Su.14.12-14 and in Sushruta's Sutrasthana XI, XII and XIV, all now cited and quoted in this record. The second half survives and is the real gap. No retrieved passage gives a measurable definition of any term in those lists: not atisthula, not durbala, not bahudosha, not samvrtakostha, not the bala the Sushruta memorable verse at Ci.XXXV makes the dose depend on. The lists are categorical and the terms are left to the physician's judgment.

REWRITTEN 2026-10-06 on criticFindings.overclaimed item 1. The 2026-09-19 version asked whether any marker of adequate purification exists 'other than the clinical signs listed in Ch.Su.16.17-19', which was wrong because this record had never opened Siddhi Sthana. Charaka Si.1.13-15 gives three further completion criteria: counted bouts, a measured volume in prastha multiples, and a terminal product, pitta for emesis and kapha for purgation. What remains not known is whether any of the four criteria predicts any outcome, whether they agree with each other in a given patient, whether the clinical signs are reliably scored between observers, and whether any physiological or biochemical marker exists; PMID 42748372 proposes to measure three serum markers but has reported no results.

Whether the benefit seen in combined shodhana-plus-shamana arms comes from the shodhana, the shamana, the dietary regimen, the samsarjana krama, or the extended practitioner contact. Both comparative trials retrieved here give shamana to the shodhana arm, so neither can separate them.

Which of the three classical architectures (Charaka's fork, Sushruta's four factors, Vagbhata's subordination to langhana) modern practice actually follows, and whether practitioners are aware they differ. Nothing located addresses it.

Whether shodhana carries harms in specific populations that would offset its claimed durability advantage. The classical texts describe over- and under-administration symptoms in detail, including at Ca.Si.1.16-17 for emesis and in Sushruta's contraindication lists, but no modern comparative safety data for the choice was located in the searches recorded in gatheringNotes.

components.gloss: Eliminative or purificatory treatment: measures that expel aggravated doshas from the body rather than normalising them in place.

Charaka's division of eliminative treatment by direction of expulsion, upward (emesis) and downward (purgation and enema).

Division of purification into external (surgery, cautery, alkali, plasters) and internal (emesis, purgation, enema, bloodletting). CORRECTED 2026-10-06: this is Bhishagratna's own footnote at Vol I page 11, keyed to the four-factor sentence of Sushruta Sutrasthana 1, not a division printed in Sushruta's text. classical.quote: Anything that lightens or attenuates (the aggravated humours and altered constituents) in the body has been said to be a Langhana. That which promotes nutrition and bulk of the body is known as Vring-hana. That which brings about dryness, and roughness and paleness is said to be Rukshana. That which leads to secretions of oily matter, softness of the body, and increase of impurities, is said to be Snehana. Anything that produces perspiration and destroys stiffness and heaviness and sensation of cold is said to be Swedana. That which constipates or stops the motion of such constituents of the body as are liquid, restless, and endued with motion, is said to be Stambhana.

classical.establishes: Vagbhata's architecture, now quoted in the Sanskrit instead of reported from a secondary web summary. THE CRITIC'S FINDING HELD AND IS ANSWERED BY RETRIEVAL. The 2026-09-19 version carried this chapter from 'a retrieved chapter summary' whose verse attributions it admitted were 'reported rather than independently confirmed', while two contested items in this record leaned on those attributions to settle textual disputes. Every attribution it reported is now confirmed from the Sanskrit, so nothing had to be withdrawn, but it was being asserted on inadequate grounds until this revision. CHAPTER NUMBER confirmed independently of any summary: the GRETIL file is the Sutrasthana, whose own closing verse at 1.48 reads sutra-sthanam ime 'dhyayas trimsac charIram ucyate, thirty chapters; this is the fourteenth chapter marker in the file, and the variant-reading lines inside this block are tagged 14.14, 14.19, 14.23, 14.26, 14.29, 14.30, 14.31, 14.32, 14.34 and 14.35, which fixes the chapter number from inside the text. WHAT THE VERSES SAY, as this record reads the Sanskrit: 14.1, because the thing to be treated is two-fold the treatment is held to be two-fold, one santarpana and the second apatarpana; 14.2, brimhana and langhana are given as their synonyms, brimhana being for bulk and langhana for lightness; 14.3, snehana, rukshana, svedana and stambhana are also named here, so Vagbhata does not drop the six but subsumes them; 14.4, these too do not exceed the two-fold, and there too langhana is two-fold, shodhana and shamana (sodhanam samanam ceti dvi-dha tatrapi langhanam); 14.5, that which drives the doshas outward is shodhana and it is five-fold, niruha, vamana, kaya-reka, shiro-reka and asra-visruti, bloodletting named among the five; 14.6, that which neither purifies the doshas nor stirs the settled ones but equalises the uneven is shamana, and it is seven-fold; 14.7, pachana, dipana, kshut, trut, vyayama, atapa, maruta. This is a materially different architecture from Charaka's, in which shodhana and shamana are the primary fork. The verse 1 and verse 4 attributions the earlier version reported, the count of five with bloodletting among them, and the count of seven with exactly that membership, are all confirmed. classical.establishes: Vagbhata's allocation rule, which assigns patients to shodhana or to the milder shamana measures by graded tiers of body bulk and strength rather than by a binary test. As this record reads the Sanskrit: 14.12, with the purificatory measures treat those in whom sthaulya, bala, pitta and kapha are in excess, afflicted by ama-dosha, fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and heart disorders; 14.13, patients afflicted by obstruction, heaviness, eructation and nausea, and those of middling sthaulya and the like, generally first with pachana and dipana; 14.14, those afflicted by the same disorders but of lesser sthaulya and greater bala, by restraint of hunger and thirst, and those afflicted by the doshas who are of middling strength and firm. The tiers are ordinal (adhika, madhya, hina) and no quantity is attached to any of them, which is the precise shape of what this record can and cannot say about thresholds. This passage is relevant twice over: it is a stated, operational allocation rule, against the 2026-09-19 claim that no operational definition of shodhana eligibility exists; and it stands in tension with Charaka Siddhi Sthana 2.8, which lists atisthula among those for whom emesis is contraindicated. See contested item 5. LANGUAGE AND COPYRIGHT as in the preceding entry: Sanskrit only, English is this record's working gloss, GRETIL transcription CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

classical.establishes: Quantified grades of adequacy for emesis and purgation, which is the material that defeats the 2026-09-19 summary's claim that no classical text gives numeric thresholds, and which also narrows this record's own notKnown claim that the only completion criteria are the clinical signs at Ca.Su.16.17-19. As this record reads the Sanskrit: 1.13, for the lowest, middling and highest grades (jaghanya, madhya, pravara) the bouts desired in emesis are four, six and eight; 1.14, in purgation ten and twice and thrice that, and the prastha measure likewise two-, three- and four-fold, emesis being half of purgation, with pitta held to be the desired end of emesis and kapha of purgation; 1.15, in purgation the measure is counted after setting aside the first two or three bouts that contain faeces. So the chapter supplies a counted criterion, a measured-volume criterion and a terminal-product criterion. The commentarial names for these, vaigiki, maniki and antiki shuddhi, with laingiki for the clinical signs at 1.15-16, are NOT asserted here: they come from Chakrapani's Ayurvedadipika, which this revision did not retrieve, and no retrieved source prints them. WHAT THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH. The prastha is a volume unit whose modern equivalence is supplied only by the in-copyright 2020 editors and is not asserted here. Nothing in the passage states that any of these three criteria predicts outcome, and nothing links any of them to the shodhana-versus-shamana choice, which is where the record's summary made its claim. classical.establishes: A numeric rule keyed directly to which dosha is involved, and therefore the single sharpest refutation of the 2026-09-19 summary's claim that no classical text gives numeric thresholds for the strength and stage of the dosha. As this record reads the Sanskrit: one, likewise three, in a kapha-born disorder; in a pitta-constituted one five or seven; in vata nine or eleven; the skilled physician should administer the bastis in odd numbers. The number prescribed is a plain integer and the index is the dosha, not the patient. WHAT THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH. classical.establishes: Explicit, enumerated eligibility and contraindication lists for the shodhana procedures. This is the citation that answers criticFindings.overclaimed item 2 and it is the critic's point exactly: these criteria are stated and operational, and unvalidated, which is a different and more interesting finding than 'no definition exists'. The chapter's own structure is a pravritti and nivritti list for each of the five procedures in turn: its retrieved contents run contra-indications of vamana, adverse effects when given in contra-indicated conditions, indications of vamana, then the same three for virechana, asthapana basti, anuvasana basti and shirovirechana. As this record reads the quoted Sanskrit: 2.8 opens avamyas tavat, 'those not to be given emesis are', and enumerates them in a single long compound whose elementary members include ksata, ksina, atisthula, atikrsa, bala, vrddha, durbala, sranta, pipasita, ksudhita, garbhini and samvrtakostha; 2.10 opens sesas tu vamyah, 'the rest are fit for emesis', and then names conditions for which it is especially indicated; 2.13 opens sesas tu virecyah and does the same for purgation. The decision rule is therefore stated by exclusion: define who must not receive the procedure, and the remainder are eligible. WHAT THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH, and this is where the surviving gap sits. Not one term in the lists is given a measurable definition. Nothing says how durbala is distinguished from merely weak, where atisthula begins, or what instrument assesses samvrtakostha. No retrieved source reports agreement between physicians applying these lists to the same patient. ELISION DECLARED. The 2.10 and 2.13 quotes omit the enumerated disease-compound between the opening and closing clauses, marked by an ellipsis; the full strings were retrieved and read and the omitted material is a list of disease names, not reasoning. 2.8 is quoted whole.
