Whether the definition is stable within a person over time. No test-retest data for the composite were located; the agni and dosha instruments report internal consistency or single-occasion agreement, not stability.
Whether Ayurvedic and biomedical or WHO classifications of the same individuals agree, and by how much.

How swastha relates to the classical category of the person who is neither clearly healthy nor clearly diseased; the texts do not define an intermediate state and modern writers who assert one are extrapolating.
Whether the mental clause adds anything beyond existing subjective wellbeing instruments, since it has never been measured separately alongside one.

Whether the classical conduct chapters, Charaka Sutrasthana 5 (Matrashitiya, measure of food), 6 (Tasyashitiya, seasonal regimen) and 7 (Na vegan dharaniya, non-suppression of natural urges), supply any criterion for swasthya beyond prescribing the conduct that maintains it. Kaviratna's Lessons V, VI and VII are present in the retrieved OCR and were located by heading on 2026-10-06, but they were not read for this record; they are the subject of the ahara-vidhi, ritucharya-rationale and vega-dharana records, and this record does not claim to know what they say about assessment.

Whether Charaka's tenfold examination (Vi. 8.94) was ever used, classically or in modern practice, to classify a person as swastha rather than to gauge strength for dosing. The verse states the dosing purpose; no commentary or modern protocol that repurposes it for health classification was consulted here.

How many agni assessment instruments exist and how they compare. Two PubMed searches on 2026-10-06 (gatheringNotes) returned four instrument papers and one systematic-review protocol (42314162) whose authors say 'several' tools exist; the AYUSH research portal and DHARA, which that protocol will search, were not searched for this record, so the agni-instrument list here is a floor, not a count.

Whether any inter-rater reliability figure exists for the dhatu or mala clauses, or for current dosha state (vikriti) as distinct from constitution (prakriti). The three reliability studies cited rate prakriti, pulse, tongue and (in one) agni; none rates the other clauses, and no search specifically for vikriti reliability was run.

Whether the 15.41 / 15.48 numbering of the Sushruta definition reflects a difference in the division of the chapter's prose sutras or a difference in recension. This record documents that both numbers are in use and which editions carry them; it did not compare the editions themselves, and no philological reference (such as Meulenbeld's History of Indian Medical Literature) was consulted on the point.

Whether institutional operationalisations of swasthya exist in practice, for instance CCRAS Swasthya Rakshan programme proformas or AYUSH prakriti-assessment forms, and what criteria they apply. Not investigated for this record; the modern list is limited to PubMed-indexed instrument and reliability papers.

components.gloss: Equilibrium of the three doshas (vata, pitta, kapha) in quantity and function
Balanced agni, the digestive and metabolic fire; neither weak, irregular nor excessive
Normal formation and functioning of the seven dhatus (bodily tissues)
Normal formation and timely elimination of the malas (faeces, urine, sweat and other excreta)
Pleasant, clear or contented state of the self
Senses functioning clearly and agreeably
Mind in a pleasant, undisturbed state
Charaka's parallel formulation: equilibrium of the body's constituents, named as the purpose of the whole treatise

classical.verse: 41 (siva.sh and sa.wikisource numbering); printed as 48 in Ambikadatta Shastri's Chaukhambha edition
classical.establishes: The canonical definition of swastha as a conjunction of balanced agni, balanced doshas, normal dhatu state and quantity, and normal excretory, functional and mental processes. Bhishagratna prints no verse number here; his English is the second-to-last paragraph of Chapter XV, read in the archive.org OCR on 2026-10-06 immediately before 'Thus ends the fifteenth Chapter of the Sutrasthanam'. The verse number is an edition-dependent fact and is recorded as such: siva.sh gives 15.41 and has no page for 15.42; the 2026-09-20 verifier read it as 15.41 and as the chapter's closing verse on sa.wikisource; Desai et al. (World Journal of Pharmaceutical Research 10(8), 2021, reference 1) cite the same verse as Sutrasthana 15.48 in Kaviraj Ambikadatta Shastri's edition, Chowkambha Sanskrit Sansthan 1996, p. 64. The two numbers are two editions' counts of the same chapter, not a disagreement about which verse this is. This record cites 15.41 because that is the number on the Sanskrit it retrieved, and flags 15.48 so that a reader holding a Chaukhambha edition is not misled.
classical.quote: A person with an uniformly healthy digestion, and whose bodily humours are in a state of equilibrium, and in whom the fundamental vital fluids course in their normal state and quantity, accompanied by the normal processes of secretion, organic function, and intellection, is said to be a healthy person.
classical.sanskrit: समदोषः समाग्निश्च समधातुमलक्रियः । प्रसन्नात्मेन्द्रियमनाः स्वस्थ इत्यभिधीयते ॥४१॥

classical.establishes: That the chapter pairs the definition of health with a two-armed clinical duty, preservation in the well and correction of dosha, dhatu and mala in the sick. In the Sanskrit this verse PRECEDES the swastha definition (15.40 then 15.41); Bhishagratna prints the two in the opposite order, definition first, duty second, which is how the earlier draft came to infer a non-existent verse 42. The earlier framing that the definition is 'immediately operationalised' by this verse inverted the textual order and has been dropped.
classical.quote: An intelligent physician should preserve the state of health in a healthy individual, while he should increase or decrease the quantity of the bodily humours, vital fluids, or excrements in a sick patient according to the exigencies of the case until his health is perfectly restored.
classical.sanskrit: स्वस्थस्य रक्षणं कुर्यादस्वस्थस्य तु बुद्धिमान् । क्षपयेद्बृंहयेच्चापि दोषधातुमलान् भिषक् ॥४०॥

classical.verse: 14 (Sanskrit numbering; Bhishagratna prints no number in Sutrasthana 1)
classical.establishes: Sushruta's twofold statement of the aim of the science, parallel to Charaka's. The English is Dhanvantari's reply to Sushruta in Chapter I (Vedotpatti); the OCR has two damaged letters in 'may be grouped', normalised here.
classical.quote: The object or utility of the science which forms the subject of our present discussion, may be grouped under two distinct sub-heads such as (1) the cure of diseased persons, and (2) the preservation of health in those who are not afflicted with any sort of bodily distempers.
classical.sanskrit: वत्स सुश्रुत! इह खल्वायुर्वेदप्रयोजनं- व्याध्युपसृष्टानां व्याधिपरिमोक्षः, स्वस्थस्य रक्षणं च ॥१४॥

classical.establishes: The most-quoted statement of Ayurveda's purpose, swasthasya swasthya rakshanam aturasya vikara prashamanam cha. The quote was re-read on 2026-10-06 in the full /download/ OCR of BIUSante_47357 inside Lesson XXX, closing 'Thus ends the Thirtieth Lesson called Arthe Dapa Maha-muliya'. The verse number 26 is from a Sanskrit-numbered edition (carakasamhitaonline, read by the 2026-09-20 verifier: प्रयोजनं चास्य स्वस्थस्य स्वास्थ्यरक्षणमातुरस्य विकारप्रशमनं च ॥२६॥). Kaviratna's own number is not legible, so his numbering does not confirm 26 and 26 does not confirm his.
classical.quote: The purpose of the Science of Life is protection of the health of the hale and alleviation of disease of one that is ailing.

classical.establishes: Charaka's dhatusamya formulation: equilibrium of the body's constituents, not absence of symptoms, is the declared object of the treatise. Verse 53 was confirmed by the 2026-09-20 verifier against carakasamhitaonline's Sanskrit (धातुसाम्यक्रिया चोक्ता तन्त्रस्यास्य प्रयोजनम् ॥५३॥). Kaviratna prints 52 for this aphorism; in this stretch of Sutrasthana 1 he runs one behind the Sanskrit count. The offset is measured here and is not carried to any other chapter.
classical.quote: The modes of restoring the ingredient humours to their normal state have been said to be the object of this Science.

classical.establishes: That health and disease are predicated of body and mind jointly, which is the textual basis for treating the mental clause of the swastha definition as constitutive rather than decorative. Verse 55 confirmed by the 2026-09-20 verifier against carakasamhitaonline's Sanskrit (शरीरं सत्त्वसंज्ञं च व्याधीनामाश्रयो मतः। तथा सुखानां, योगस्तु सुखानां कारणं समः ॥५५॥). Kaviratna prints 54, one behind, consistent with the previous entry in this same chapter.
classical.quote: Body and mind are regarded as the subjects in which health and disease co-inhere; parity of correlation being the cause of health.

classical.establishes: Vagbhata compresses the definition to the formula rogastu doshavaishamyam, doshasamyam arogata: disease is dosha disequilibrium, health is dosha equilibrium. This drops the agni, dhatu, mala and mental clauses that Sushruta requires, and is the narrowest of the three classical definitions. The half-verse is numbered 20 on sa.wikisource, between 19 (kalartha-karmanam yogo hina-mithyati-matrakah) and 21 (nijagantu-vibhagena...). The earlier draft's 'near 20, located after verse 22 on one presentation' is superseded by this reading. No public-domain English translation of Ashtanga Hridaya is known to this project, so the Sanskrit is quoted and the English is a gloss, not a quotation.
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

classical.establishes: The dashavidha pariksha, Charaka's tenfold examination of the patient: prakriti, vikriti, sara, samhanana, pramana, satmya, sattva, aharashakti, vyayamashakti and vayas. This is the closest thing the Brihat Trayi has to an assessment protocol and it is relevant to swasthya because several of its heads (prakriti, vikriti, aharashakti, sattva) are the elements a clinician would use to judge the dosha, agni and mind clauses. But its own stated purpose is balapramana-vishesha-grahana, to gauge the patient's strength for dosing, not to classify a person as swastha or atura, and it names heads of examination without giving a scoring rule for any of them. It therefore shows WHERE the classical operational content sits and confirms that even there no threshold is given.
classical.quote: Hence, the patient should be examined in respect of his normal constitution in health, of the abnormal condition that has set in, of the predominance of some particular element in his constitution (such as blood, or flesh, &c.), of his compactness or otherwise, the make of his proportions such as stature, &c., of what things are suitable to his constitution, of his mental disposition, of his power of eating, of his power of exercise, and of his age.
classical.sanskrit: तस्मादातुरं परीक्षेत प्रकृतितश्च, विकृतितश्च, सारतश्च, संहननतश्च, प्रमाणतश्च, सात्म्यतश्च, सत्त्वतश्च, आहारशक्तितश्च, व्यायामशक्तितश्च, वयस्तश्चेति, बलप्रमाणविशेषग्रहणहेतोः ॥९४॥

classical.establishes: Charaka's fourfold classification of agni (tikshna, manda, sama, vishama) and the statement that sama agni belongs to persons whose three doshas are in their natural state. This is the classical content behind the samagni clause of the swastha definition: it defines sama agni behaviourally (not deranged by ordinary diet, deranged only by dietary abuse) rather than by any measurable quantity. Every modern agni questionnaire in this record's modern list builds its four-way classification on this aphorism. Quoted from Kaviratna's main text; his footnote on the same passage ('I have rendered Sama even...') is translator's commentary and is not cited as doctrine.
classical.quote: In the fires dwelling in the physical system, a fourfold distinction may be made agreeably to difference of strength. It is as follows: Keen, mild, even, and uneven. Amongst these that fire is said to be keen which can bear all kinds of dietary riotousness. That fire which is endued with characteristic of an opposite kind is called mild. That fire is said to be even which becomes vitiated by dietary riotousness, but which exists without being deranged when no dietary riotousness is indulged in. That fire which possesses characteristics that are the reverse of the above, is called uneven. These are the four different kinds of fire of four different kinds of persons. Amongst these, of those persons that are of equable wind, bile, and phlegm, and that are in their normal state, the (digestive) fires are even.
classical.sanskrit: अग्निषु तु शारीरेषु चतुर्विधो विशेषो बलभेदेन भवति। तद्यथा- तीक्ष्णो, मन्दः, समो, विषमश्चेति। तत्र तीक्ष्णोऽग्निः सर्वापचारसहः, तद्विपरीतलक्षणस्तु मन्दः, समस्तु खल्वपचारतो विकृतिमापद्यतेऽनपचारतस्तु प्रकृताववतिष्ठते, समलक्षणविपरीतलक्षणस्तु विषम इति। एते चतुर्विधा भवन्त्यग्नयश्चतुर्विधानामेव पुरुषाणाम्। तत्र समवातपित्तश्लेष्मणां प्रकृतिस्थानां समा भवन्त्यग्नयः ... ॥१२॥

modern.title: Swasthya Assessment Scale (SAS)-Ayurveda based health assessment tool-insights on its development and validation.
modern.establishes: Reports the development and validation of the Swasthya Assessment Scale, and states explicitly that before it no validated Ayurveda-principle-based health assessment scale existed. Content validity index was high and inter-observer agreement was tested in 183 individuals.
modern.quality: Single-centre instrument-development study. It establishes content validity and observer agreement only; there is no criterion validation against health outcomes, no external replication, and no demonstration that scale scores track anything clinically consequential. Its main value here is the authors' own admission that the field had no validated health measure until 2021, roughly two millennia after the definition was written.

modern.title: Reliability of Ayurvedic Diagnosis for Knee Osteoarthritis Patients: A Nested Diagnostic Study Within a Randomized Controlled Trial.
modern.establishes: Measured inter-rater reliability of Ayurvedic diagnosis among four experts assessing 30 knee osteoarthritis patients. Percentage agreement on the final consensus diagnosis was high (95%), but chance-corrected kappa for the central constitutional components, prakriti and agni, was fair to poor, in the range 0 to 0.4. Agreement on disease entities was better than on constitutional entities.
modern.quality: Small (30 patients, 4 raters) but genuinely empirical and nested in a randomised trial, which makes it one of the few chance-corrected reliability measurements in the field. It bears directly on the swastha definition because agni and dosha state are two of its required clauses, and it shows that trained experts do not reliably agree on them.

modern.title: Correlation of prakriti diagnosis using AyuSoft prakriti diagnostic tool with clinician rating in patients with psychiatric disorders.
modern.establishes: Compared prakriti determined by the AyuSoft software tool with two Ayurveda physicians' independent clinical assessments in 112 psychiatric inpatients. Intraclass correlation was 0.72 for vata, 0.58 for pitta and 0.44 for kapha.
modern.quality: Empirical reliability study with an adequate sample, but it measures tool-versus-clinician consistency in one specialised population, not test-retest stability or validity against any outcome. The kapha figure in particular is weak agreement. The authors frame the result positively; the numbers are more equivocal than the framing.

modern.title: Development of a reliable Dosha self-assessment questionnaire.
modern.establishes: Developed an open-source dosha self-assessment questionnaire, stating as its rationale that no existing open-source questionnaire had been shown to be reliable for self-assessment.
modern.quality: Instrument development with item analysis and repeat administration. Useful as documentation that, as of 2021, the field had no reliable open self-report measure of the dosha state that the swastha definition presupposes. It does not validate the construct, only the internal behaviour of items.

modern.title: Interrater reliability of diagnostic methods in traditional Indian ayurvedic medicine.
modern.establishes: Measured inter-rater reliability of Ayurvedic pulse (nadi), tongue (jivha) and constitution (prakriti) assessment: fifteen registered Ayurvedic doctors with 3 to 15 years' experience independently examined twenty healthy subjects. Average pairwise weighted kappa was 0.07 for pulse, 0.17 for tongue and 0.28 for prakriti; the null hypothesis of random rating was rejected for twelve of 105 doctor pairs on prakriti, one pair on pulse and none on tongue. Questionnaire and software prakriti assessment showed significant evidence against random rating.
modern.quality: Small (n=20, one centre, healthy volunteers only) but it is the largest rater panel in the field and the only study located here that measures pulse and tongue agreement. What it did NOT measure must be stated because an earlier draft of this cluster overreached from it: it rated prakriti, which is constitution, not current dosha state (vikriti), and it did not rate agni, dhatu or mala at all. It therefore bears on the swastha definition only indirectly, by showing that the clinical examination techniques Ayurvedic doctors use to reach constitutional judgements are poorly reproducible between examiners. It cannot support any statement about the reproducibility of the dosha, agni or dhatu-mala clauses themselves. Cross-record note: this paper is also cited in tridosha-theory and vyadhikshamatva; here it is one of three independent reliability studies (with PMIDs 30653338 and 33750638), not the sole empirical support.

modern.title: Formation and validation of questionnaire to assess Jāṭharāgni.
modern.establishes: Formation and validation of a 64-item questionnaire classifying jatharagni into the four classical states (manda, vishama, tikshna, sama) in 500 volunteers; Cronbach's alpha 0.916 overall, with subscale alphas of 0.909 (vishama), 0.873 (tikshna), 0.894 (manda) and 0.876 (sama).
modern.quality: Instrument development with internal-consistency statistics only. It operationalises the samagni clause as a questionnaire category and shows the items hang together; it does not validate the category against any physiological or clinical criterion, so it cannot say whether a person classified samagni differs in any measurable way from one classified otherwise. Its existence is what refutes the earlier draft's statement that no threshold had been proposed for any clause: a questionnaire cut-off is a proposed operationalisation, even though no biomarker threshold has been proposed or validated.

modern.title: Development, Validation, and Verification of a Self-Assessment Tool to Estimate Agnibala (Digestive Strength).
modern.journal: J Evid Based Complementary Altern Med
modern.establishes: Development, validation and verification of a self-assessment tool for agnibala (four functional states: regular, irregular, intense, weak) in 300 healthy volunteers aged 18 to 40; the authors report statistical reliability and validity and that serum lipid parameters varied significantly with agni status.
modern.quality: The one agni instrument located here that is checked against a laboratory measure, which makes it the nearest thing to criterion validation for any clause of the swastha definition. The abstract gives no coefficients, the lipid association is cross-sectional in healthy volunteers, and the authors frame it as a screening use rather than a validation of the construct. It supports 'an agni questionnaire has been related to a biomarker' and not 'samagni has a validated biomarker threshold'.

modern.title: Development and Preliminary Psychometric Evaluation of Agni Assessment Scale: A Measure of Functional Digestive Capacity Based on Ayurveda.
modern.establishes: Development and preliminary psychometric evaluation of a 26-item Agni Assessment Scale in 467 Indian participants (field study n=100, exploratory factor analysis n=367). Four subscales emerged (samagni, vishamagni, mandagni, tikshnagni) with alphas from 0.57 to 0.83; all subscales except samagni met conventional reliability thresholds.
modern.quality: The most recent agni instrument located and the one with the most explicit psychometrics. Its most relevant result for this record is a negative one: the samagni subscale, which is the clause the swastha definition actually requires, was the one subscale that did not reach acceptable internal consistency. The authors themselves call for further validation in clinical and cross-cultural settings.

modern.title: Evaluation of the Psychometric Properties and Applicability of Agni Assessment Tools in Ayurveda: Protocol for a Systematic Review.
modern.establishes: Protocol for a systematic review of agni assessment tools (self-report and clinician-administered), appraising content, construct and criterion validity, internal consistency and test-retest reliability with COSMIN and QUADAS-2, across PubMed, EBSCO, Cochrane, Google Scholar, the AYUSH research portal and DHARA; review initiated October 2025 with completion expected November 2026.
modern.quality: Protocol only; no results. It is cited for two facts it establishes by existing: that 'several' agni tools exist in the authors' view, which bounds this record's own agni-instrument list as incomplete, and that no synthesis of their psychometric quality had been published when the protocol was registered. When the review appears it should replace this record's own partial listing.

openQuestions: Citation 2 (Bhishagratna, 'An intelligent physician should preserve the state of health...') was refuted on location by the 2026-09-20 verifier: the verse is Sutrasthana 15.40, preceding the definition at 15.41, and no verse 42 exists in the Sanskrit presentations retrieved. The correction is applied in the entry and the full verifier text is preserved in its refutedBecause field.

records.title: Vriddhi and Kshaya: What the Body Has Too Much and Too Little Of
records.summary: Ayurveda holds that health is a state in which the doshas, the seven dhatus and the malas are each present in their proper measure, and that disease arises when any of them increases (vriddhi) or decreases (kshaya) from that measure. The governing rule is the principle of samanya and vishesha: like increases like, unlike decreases it, so a deficient constituent is replenished by substances resembling it and an excessive one is reduced by substances unlike it (Charaka Sutrasthana 1.44-45 in standard numbering; Kaviratna prints 43-44). Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 is the primary locus: it lists the signs of decrease and of increase for each dosha, each tissue and each excretion, prescribes replenishing or reducing treatment accordingly, and closes with the obesity and emaciation (sthaulya and karshya) that follow from rasa going wrong in either direction. On the question of measurement the chapter takes an explicit doctrinal position rather than leaving a gap: because bodies differ and change from moment to moment, the quantity of the doshas, dhatus and malas cannot be laid down (15.37); their equilibrium can be known only through the presence of health (15.38); their disparity is inferred from the state of the senses and the signs (15.39); and the physician reduces or builds until the patient is free of disease, which is itself the mark of balance (15.40). The system is therefore a sign-based and inference-based clinical method by its own account, and it defines the balanced state positively as well as negatively (15.41). Charaka's Ashtauninditiya chapter (Sutrasthana 21) supplies the companion material on the over-nourished and under-nourished body, and Sutrasthana 22 defines the two therapeutic directions, langhana and brimhana, that the diagnosis leads to.
records.evidenceState: This concept rests on classical exegesis, and the record's searches found no biological or psychometric study of any vriddhi or kshaya sign-set as such. What the searches were: PubMed via the NCBI eutils API on 2026-10-06, with these counts: raktakshaya 1 (the Panchakola trial, PMID 24250128); 'rakta kshaya' 0; 'dhatu kshaya' 6, none of them a study of the construct (a Shatavari eye-drop trial, an ojas biomarker essay, two case reports, a diabetic retinopathy concept paper and a geriatric anaemia trial); dhatukshaya 1 (an osteoarthritis trial); 'dhatu vriddhi' 0; 'kshaya ayurveda' 12; 'samanya vishesha' 5 (PMID 30401500 among them); 'ayurveda AND dhatu AND (reliability OR validation OR validity)' 3, of which the nearest is the dhatu sarata weighted-mean proposal (PMID 26834429); 'ayurveda AND (interrater OR inter-rater)' 15, none with a dhatu kshaya or vriddhi judgement in its title. Google Scholar, AYUSH Research Portal, DHARA and non-English literature were not searched, so these are counts for one database on one date and not claims about the world. Within that scope: no interrater reliability figure, no sensitivity or specificity against a reference standard, and no validated instrument for any dhatu kshaya or vriddhi judgement was located. On agreement in Ayurvedic assessment generally, the two measurements retrieved here point in different directions: Kurande et al. found average pairwise kappas of 0.07 (pulse), 0.17 (tongue) and 0.28 (prakriti) among fifteen doctors (PMID 24191170), while Rotti et al. found a kappa of 0.77 between physicians and a structured tool for prakriti in 3,416 subjects (PMID 25336848). Neither concerns kshaya or vriddhi, and they give no basis for predicting agreement on these sign-lists in either direction. On quantity, the record previously described the absence of a stated normal measure as a gap; Sushruta states it as doctrine (Su.Su.15.37: parimANaM na vidyate) and prescribes inference from health and from the signs in its place (15.38-40), so the model is non-quantitative by design, and the open question is whether any modern operationalisation has been attempted, not whether the texts omitted one. ICD-11 TM2 now assigns a code to every one of these patterns; in the project's enrichment data those codes carry names and index terms but no definitions, so they standardise the vocabulary without supplying criteria. The one trial that uses a dhatu kshaya as an enrolment category (PMID 24250128) reached its outcome measure by assuming rakta kshaya equals anaemia, which is the operationalisation that needed testing. The framework's standing on this record's evidence is as a structured clinical vocabulary with internal coherence, an explicit theory of why it cannot be quantified, and long use, not as a validated diagnostic system.

contested.question: Does rakta kshaya denote anaemia?
positions: The equation is standard in modern Ayurvedic clinical research and is assumed outright in the one trial on the subject (PMID 24250128), which uses haemoglobin, serum iron, ferritin and TIBC as outcomes.

Sushruta's own sign-list for rakta kshaya is rough skin, craving for acid food and drink, longing for cool places and flabby veins - pallor is not among them, and the chapter's separate signs for pitta kshaya include dullness of complexion. The mapping is therefore an interpretive choice, not a reading of the text.

A third position holds that rakta in Ayurveda is not blood as a measurable fluid compartment at all but a functional principle, in which case no haematological index could confirm or refute its deficiency.

contested.question: Does an increase in one dhatu necessarily increase the next?
positions: Sushruta Sutrasthana 15.18 states the cascade explicitly in its metrical text and uses it to justify treating any excess.

Charaka's samanya-vishesha principle (Sutrasthana 1.44-45 in standard numbering; Kaviratna prints 43-44) is about like substances increasing like, and does not by itself entail a forward cascade down the dhatu sequence; the two are often conflated in secondary writing.
Secondary literature also describes the opposite pattern, kshaya of a later dhatu following kshaya of an earlier one, without reconciling the two directions.

contested.question: Is the object of vriddhi and kshaya quantity or quality?
positions: A quantitative reading: the texts speak of a normal measure (Su.Su.15.40, 'until free of disease'), Bhishagratna's rendering of 15.17 warns against reducing a constituent below it, and ICD-11 TM2 codes each increase and decrease as a countable pattern, all of which imply a real amount.

A functional reading: Su.Su.15.37 says outright that no quantity exists to be stated, 15.38-39 make balance knowable only through health and imbalance only by inference, and the diagnosis is made entirely from function-related signs (cravings, sensations, capacity), so what varies is the tissue's functional adequacy, not its mass. Modern clinical writing slides between these without marking the shift.

contested.question: Are kshaya of a dhatu and vriddhi of a dosha the same event described twice?
positions: Treated as distinct in the texts, which list them in separate sections with separate signs.

But the sign-lists overlap heavily - dryness, emaciation and joint looseness appear under vata vriddhi, kapha kshaya, and several dhatu kshayas - and the tradition offers no decision rule for attributing an overlapping sign to one rather than another.

contested.question: Is sthaulya (obesity) medo-vriddhi?
positions: Charaka Sutrasthana 21.4: in the very obese 'fat alone accumulates, not so the other dhatus' (meda evopacIyate na tathetare dhAtavaH), a medas-centred account in which obesity is the increase of one tissue.

Sushruta Sutrasthana 15.32: 'obesity and emaciation are both caused by rasa' (rasanimittam eva sthaulyaM kArshyaM ca); immature, over-sweet rasa generates medas, so the primary disorder is of rasa and the fat is downstream. On this reading medo-vriddhi is a consequence of sthaulya's cause rather than its definition.

ICD-11 TM2 indexes the same Sanskrit term, medovRuddhi, under two codes: SR47 'Increase of adipose tissues pattern' and SP62 'High fat disorder'. The classification therefore encodes the ambiguity rather than resolving it.

contested.question: Does Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 state the causes of kshaya?
positions: Bhishagratna's translation carries a footnote to the kshaya section listing them (excessive cleansing and pacifying treatment, suppression of urges, violent exercise, sexual excess, unsuitable food, grief), and a reader of the English, including this record's critic, takes it as the text.

The root text of 15.7-12 in the Trikamji/NIIMH edition has no such sentence. Dalhana reports it as a reading that 'some read here' and that 'the teachers' reject as purposeless, because those causes mostly increase vata and deplete pitta and kapha, so the cause must be judged case by case. Bhishagratna rendered the disputed variant into a footnote.

Sushruta's in-text aetiology of depletion is elsewhere in the chapter: the causes of karshya at 15.33 and of ojas kshaya at 15.23. Charaka gives general kshaya causes at Sutrasthana 17.76-77 and karshya causes at 21.11-12. All four are quoted in this record.

contested.question: Does Su.Su.15.17 warn against reducing a constituent below normal?
positions: Bhishagratna's rendering: excesses 'should be checked or remedied ... so as not to reduce them to a smaller quantity than that in which they are found in the normal and healthy state of a body', an explicit overshoot warning.

The Sanskrit is three words, kShayAdaviruddhaiH kriyAvisheShaiH, and Dalhana records an alternative reading that omits kShayAt; the overshoot clause is therefore a translator's expansion of a phrase whose reading is disputed. The treat-to-target doctrine is better grounded in 15.40 (reduce or build 'until free of disease, that is the mark of balance').

notKnown: No normal quantity for any dhatu is stated in the classical passages this record retrieved, and Sushruta Sutrasthana 15.37 says one cannot be laid down; what is not known is whether any modern author has proposed and tested an operational quantity or threshold for any dhatu kshaya or vriddhi, since none was located by the searches logged in evidenceState.

No interrater reliability, sensitivity or specificity figure for any vriddhi or kshaya sign-set was located by the PubMed searches logged in evidenceState (2026-10-06); other databases and non-English literature were not searched.

No validated questionnaire, scale or examination protocol for dhatu kshaya or vriddhi was located in PubMed by the searches logged in evidenceState; the nearest retrieved item is a methods note on dhatu sarata, a different construct.
It is not known whether the classical sign-lists discriminate between tissues at all, given how much they overlap with each other and with dosha imbalance signs; no study testing this was located.

Whether brimhana (replenishing) therapy chosen by the samanya rule outperforms generic nutritional support for any defined deficiency state has not, in any study located here, been tested head to head.

No modern referent is established in the retrieved literature for medas, majja or shukra kshaya; the correspondences to adipose tissue, marrow and reproductive function are assumed by the papers that use them.
Whether the cascade rule holds (whether increase in one tissue is followed by increase in the next) has not, in any study located here, been observed or measured.

Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 11 and the Madhava Nidana are real loci for this material that the record does not cover: no public-domain English translation of either was located by this project and their Sanskrit was not retrieved in this pass, so their 'located' entries are not to be counted as quoted sources.

Charaka Sutrasthana 23 (Santarpaniya), on the diseases of over- and under-nourishment, was not retrieved in this pass and is not cited; it is the natural companion to the Sutrasthana 21 and 22 material added here.

Whether the ICD-11 TM2 entities for these patterns carry definitions or criteria on the WHO browser beyond the title and index terms held in the project's enrichment file is not known here; in that file every such entity has a null definition.

Whether the kshaya-cause sentence Dalhana reports as a disputed variant at Su.Su.15.7 appears as root text in any other edition of the Sushruta Samhita was not checked; only the Trikamji/NIIMH text and Bhishagratna's footnote were compared.
Kaviratna's printed verse number for the Sutrasthana 21.20 sentence (heavy-but-depleting regimen for the obese) could not be read from the OCR and is not asserted.

Whether physician-versus-instrument agreement of the kind Rotti et al. reported for prakriti has been attempted for any kshaya or vriddhi judgement is not known; none was located by the searches logged here.

components.gloss: Similarity. The principle that substances resembling a bodily constituent increase it. The operative rule for replenishment therapy.
Dissimilarity. The principle that substances unlike a bodily constituent decrease it. The operative rule for reduction therapy.
Pathological increase of a dosha, dhatu or mala above its proper measure, recognised by a set of signs specific to each.
Pathological decrease or wasting of a dosha, dhatu or mala below its proper measure, likewise recognised by specific signs.

The balanced state, the reference point. Sushruta defines it both negatively, as the absence of the signs of vriddhi and kshaya and as whatever state is present when the patient is free of disease (Su.Su.15.38, 15.40), and positively, as balanced doshas, balanced agni, balanced dhatus and malas in their functions, and a serene self, senses and mind (Su.Su.15.41). No quantity attaches to it, and the text says none can (15.37).

Three doshas (vata, pitta, kapha), seven dhatus (rasa, rakta, mamsa, medas, asthi, majja, shukra), the malas (faeces, urine, sweat), and in Sushruta's list also artava (menstrual blood), stanya (breast milk) and garbha (the foetus).

Examples from Sushruta (Su.Su.15.9): rasa kshaya gives cardiac pain, palpitation and thirst; rakta kshaya gives rough skin and craving for sour and cold; mamsa kshaya gives wasting of buttocks, cheeks, thighs; medas kshaya gives splenic enlargement and empty joints; asthi kshaya gives aching bones and wasting teeth; majja kshaya gives reduced semen and breaking joint pain; shukra kshaya gives genital pain and impotence.

Examples from Sushruta (Su.Su.15.14): rasa vriddhi gives nausea and salivation; rakta vriddhi gives reddened complexion and full veins; mamsa vriddhi gives fullness of buttocks, lips, arms and heaviness; medas vriddhi gives oily skin, bulk at the flanks, fetid odour, cough and dyspnoea; asthi vriddhi gives extra teeth and bony overgrowth; shukra vriddhi gives excessive emission and bladder concretions.

The two therapeutic directions that follow from the diagnosis: nourishing or building treatment for kshaya, lightening or reducing treatment for vriddhi. Charaka defines them in Sutrasthana 22.9-10 (whatever produces lightness in the body is langhana; whatever produces bulk is brimhana) and applies them to the obese and the emaciated in Sutrasthana 21.16 and 21.20.
Sushruta's metrical statement (Su.Su.15.18) that an over-increased constituent increases the one next in the sequence, which is why excess is to be reduced rather than left alone.

Obesity and emaciation, the whole-body expressions of over- and under-nourishment. Sushruta roots both in rasa (Su.Su.15.32-33); Charaka treats them as the two worst of the eight condemned body types (Su.21.3-4, 21.11-12) and holds that both are always diseased and always to be treated (21.16).

Sushruta's doctrine that no quantity (parimana) of the doshas, dhatus and malas can be laid down, because bodies differ and are not stable (Su.Su.15.37). This is a positive position in the text, not an omission, and it is the reason the model works through signs and inference rather than measurement.

classical.verse: Kaviratna prints 43 and 44 after the two sentences; standard (Trikamji) Sutrasthana 1.44-1.45
classical.establishes: The samanya-vishesha axiom from which the vriddhi/kshaya management scheme is derived, in a lawfully quotable public-domain translation, with the Sanskrit for both verses. Kaviratna's own footnote calls it 'almost the basis of the Science of Life'; that assessment is his, not the text's.
classical.quote: Of all things, at all times, similarity is the cause of increase; and dissimilarity is the cause of decrease. A tendency exists towards both. Similarity is that which produces oneness; and dissimilarity is that which produces diversity. Therefore, similarity is identity of substance, and dissimilarity is the reverse of this.
classical.sanskrit: sarvadA sarvabhAvAnAM sAmAnyaM vRuddhikAraNam| hrAsaheturvisheShashca, pravRuttirubhayasya tu||44|| sAmAnyamekatvakaraM, visheShastu pRuthaktvakRut| tulyArthatA hi sAmAnyaM, visheShastu viparyayaH||45||

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers; the content corresponds to standard (Trikamji) Su.Su.15.1-15.3
classical.establishes: That an entire dedicated chapter of Sushruta is given to the recognition of decrease and increase across doshas, dhatus and malas - this is the primary locus of the concept.
classical.quote: Now we shall describe the Chapter which treats of development and non-development of the humoral constituents of the body and excrements (Dosha-Dhatu-Mala-Kshaya-Vriddhi-Vijnaniya-madhyayam). Since the human body is constituted of humours, (Doshas), excretions (Mala), and the fundamental principles (Dhatus) of blood, marrow, etc., hear me discourse on the features which are peculiar to each of them.
classical.sanskrit: athAto doShadhAtumalakShayavRuddhivij~jAnIyamadhyAyaM vyAkhyAsyAmaH ||1|| yathovAca bhagavAn dhanvantariH ||2|| doShadhAtumalamUlaM hi sharIraM, tasmAdeteShAM lakShaNamucyamAnamupadhAraya ||3||

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers; the content corresponds to standard (Trikamji) Su.Su.15.9 (first part)
classical.establishes: The actual clinical sign-lists for rasa, rakta and mamsa kshaya. Note that rakta kshaya is characterised by rough skin and a craving for sour and cold, not by pallor - which matters for the modern equation of rakta kshaya with anaemia.
classical.quote: Similarly the loss of lymph chyle is marked by pain about the region of the heart, Angina Pectoris, with palpitation of the heart, a sensation of emptiness or gone-feeling in the viscus, and thirst. The loss of blood is attended with such symptoms as roughness of the skin, and a craving for acid food or drink. The patient longs to be in a cool place and asks for cool things, and the veins become loose and flabby. The loss of flesh is marked by emaciation of the buttocks, cheeks, lips, thighs, breasts, armpits, neck, and the calves of the legs.
classical.sanskrit: rasakShaye hRutpIDAkampashUnyatAstRuShNA ca, shoNitakShaye tvakpAruShyamamlashItaprArthanA sirAshaithilyaM ca, mAMsakShaye sphiggaNDauShThopasthoruvakShaHkakShApiNDikodaragrIvAshuShkatA raukShyatodau gAtrANAM sadanaM dhamanIshaithilyaM ca,

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers; the content corresponds to standard (Trikamji) Su.Su.15.9 (continued)
classical.establishes: The sign-lists for medas, asthi and majja kshaya, showing the pattern: each is diagnosed by subjective sensation, craving and gross appearance rather than by any measurement.
classical.quote: The loss of fat is followed by such symptoms as the enlargement of the spleen, a sense of emptiness in the joints, and a peculiar dryness of the skin and a craving for cold and emollient meat. The degeneration of the bones is marked by an aching pain in the bones and bone-joints, a wasting of teeth and gums, and a general dryness of the body. Similarly, the loss or waste of marrow is characterised by the formation of a lesser quantity of semen, aching pain in the bones and breaking pain in the bone-joints which have become marrowless.
classical.sanskrit: medaHkShaye plIhAbhivRuddhiH sandhishUnyatA raukShyaM meduramAMsaprArthanA ca, asthikShaye~asthishUlaM dantanakhabha~ggo raukShyaM ca, majjakShaye~alpashukratA parvabhedo~asthinistodo~asthishUnyatA ca,

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers; the content corresponds to standard (Trikamji) Su.Su.15.13 (opening sentence)
classical.establishes: The aetiological half of the samanya rule as applied to pathology: excess arises from over-use (atyupasevana) of what increases a constituent's own source (svayonivardhana). Together with the treatment rule 'svayonivardhanAnyeva pratIkAraH' for kshaya (15.8), this makes diet the primary lever.
classical.quote: The quantities of these humours, principles and secretion, are abnormally increased through the use of substances that primarily contribute to their formation in the organism.
classical.sanskrit: ata UrdhvamativRuddhAnAM doShadhAtumalAnAM lakShaNaM vakShyAmaH | vRuddhiH punareShAM svayonivardhanAtyupasevanAdbhavati |

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers; the content corresponds to standard (Trikamji) Su.Su.15.18
classical.establishes: The cascade rule linking vriddhi of one dhatu to vriddhi of the next, and the therapeutic imperative to correct excess. This is the clearest classical statement that the tissues are causally coupled in sequence.
classical.quote: An increased quantity of a bodily principle gives rise to a similar increase in the quantity of one immediately succeeding it in the order of enumeration as stated above ; aud hence an increase in any of the fundamental principles of the body should be checked and reduced to its normal quantity.
classical.sanskrit: pUrvaH pUrvo~ativRuddhatvAdvardhayeddhi paraM param | tasmAdatipravRuddhAnAM dhAtUnAM hrAsanaM hitam ||18||

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers; the content corresponds to standard (Trikamji) Su.Su.15.17
classical.establishes: That excess is to be reduced by cleansing (saMshodhana) and depleting (kShapaNa) measures appropriate to each constituent. The 'explicit warning against overshoot' that an earlier version of this record read into the sentence is Bhishagratna's rendering; the firmer classical locus for treating to a target is Su.Su.15.40, cited below.
classical.quote: These abnormal excesses of the aforesaid humours and principles, etc. of the body should be checked or remedied with corrective (cleansing) or pacifying measures as would be indicated by their respective natures, so as not to reduce them to a smaller quantity than that in which they are found in the normal and healthy state of a body.
classical.sanskrit: teShAM yathAsvaM saMshodhanaM kShapaNaM ca kShayAdaviruddhaiH kriyAvisheShaiH prakurvIta ||17||

classical.verse: Kaviratna prints 74-75 after the passage; standard (Trikamji) Sutrasthana 17.76-17.77
classical.establishes: Charaka's own list of the causes of kshaya (kShayahetavaH): exertion, fasting, worry, dry, scanty or measured food, wind and sun, fear, grief, dry drinks, sleeplessness, excessive loss of kapha, blood, semen and excreta, time, and bhUtopaghAta. The aetiology is predominantly behavioural and dietary. This is the record's primary classical source for why a dhatu is depleted; it was present in the version the critic reviewed.
classical.quote: The following are the causes of the attenuation, or loss of the constituent elements of the body, viz., excessive physical exercise, fasting, anxiety, taking food that is dry and insufficient, or food in excess, exposure to wind or the sun, circumstances creating fear, grief, drinking liquids whose properties are dry, night-keeping, the excessive emission of phlegm, blood, and semen (through disease), or expectorations and emissions of the same through other causes, phthisis, and afflictions caused by evil spirits or forces of nature.
classical.sanskrit: vyAyAmo~anashanaM cintA rUkShAlpapramitAshanam| vAtAtapau bhayaM shoko rUkShapAnaM prajAgaraH||76|| kaphashoNitashukrANAM malAnAM cAtivartanam| kAlo bhUtopaghAtashca j~jAtavyAH kShayahetavaH||77||

classical.verse: not asserted
classical.establishes: Vagbhata's condensed restatement of the increase and decrease of doshas, dhatus and malas, including the signs of ojas depletion. Located but not quoted: this project has not located a public-domain English translation of the Ashtanga Hridaya, and the Sanskrit was not retrieved in this pass. Not to be counted or published as a quoted classical reference; the gap is stated in notKnown.

The nidana tradition inherits the vriddhi/kshaya sign-lists as diagnostic criteria for individual diseases. Cited for location only; no public-domain English translation was located and no chapter is asserted. Not to be counted or published as a quoted classical reference; the gap is stated in notKnown.

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers; the content corresponds to standard (Trikamji) Su.Su.15.37-15.39
classical.establishes: Sushruta's doctrinal position on measurement, which an earlier version of this record misreported as a mere absence: the quantity (parimANa) of doshas, dhatus and malas does not exist to be stated (na vidyate), because bodies differ (vailakShaNya) and are not stable (asthAyitva); their balance can be asserted only from health (svAsthya) and from no other ground; and their imbalance is to be inferred (anumAnena) from a person whose senses are not serene. The model is inferential by design.
classical.quote: Since the temperament, constitution, size and the fundamental principles of) the body vary in different individuals ; and since the body, in its turn, undergoes such gradual transformations as infancy, youth and old age\ and changes its state each moment, it is absolutely impossible to lay down the exact quantity of the deranged humours, excrements and fundamental principles (of lymph chyle, blood, semen, albumen, etc.^ that may be found in the human organism. Hence it is necessary for a physician to ascertain their state of equilibrium (their continuance in normal state and quantity) at any particular time ; and which should be pronounced only in cases where signs of perfect health would be visible. An experienced physician would naturally draw a contrary inference from the improper functions of the organs in an individual.
classical.sanskrit: vailakShaNyAccharIrANAmasthAyitvAttathaiva ca | doShadhAtumalAnAM tu parimANaM na vidyate ||37|| eShAM samatvaM yaccApi bhiShagbhiravadhAryate | na tat svAsthyAdRute shakyaM vaktumanyena hetunA ||38|| doShAdInAM tvasamatAmanumAnena lakShayet | aprasannendriyaM vIkShya puruShaM kushalo bhiShak ||39||

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers; the content corresponds to standard (Trikamji) Su.Su.15.40-15.41
classical.establishes: The treat-to-target rule and the positive definition of balance. The physician depletes or builds (kShapayed bRuMhayec cApi) the doshas, dhatus and malas until the person is free of disease, and that state is the mark of sAmya; the healthy person is one of balanced doshas, balanced agni, balanced dhatu and mala function, and serene self, senses and mind. This is the textual footing for a target of therapy, and it is stated without any quantity. Note that Bhishagratna prints the definition before the treatment rule; the Sanskrit order is 40 then 41, and the two sentences are quoted here in the Sanskrit order with the omission marked.
classical.quote: An intelligent physician should preserve the state of health in a healthy individual, while he should increase or decrease the quantity of the bodily humours, vital fluids, or excrements in a sick patient according to the exigencies of the case until his health is perfectly restored. ... A person with an uniformly healthy digestion, and whose bodily humours are in a state of equilibrium, and in whom the fundamental vital fluids course in their normal state and quantity, accompanied by the normal processes of secretion, organic function, and intellection, is said to be a healthy person.
classical.sanskrit: (svasthasya rakShaNaM kuryAdasvasthasya tu buddhimAn) | kShapayedbRuMhayeccApi doShadhAtumalAn bhiShak | tAvadyAvadarogaH syAdetatsAmyasya lakShaNam ||40|| samadoShaH samAgnishca samadhAtumalakriyaH | prasannAtmendriyamanAH svastha ityabhidhIyate ||41||

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers; the content corresponds to standard (Trikamji) Su.Su.15.29-15.30
classical.establishes: That craving is treated as both a diagnostic sign of kshaya and a guide to its remedy: the depleted person desires what builds the depleted constituent (svayonivardhana), and obtaining it removes the kshaya. This is the classical basis for the cravings that appear throughout the sign-lists.
classical.quote: A person suffering from a wasting of any of the constituent humours or fundamental principles or excrements of the body, as well as one suffering from loss of Ojah (albumen) naturally craves for drink and food that tend to contribute directly to the formation of the matter (or bodily principle) so lost or wasted. Conversely, the particular food or drink longed for by a person suffering from a loss or waste of any of the abovesaid fluids or principles, should be looked upon as possessed of a curative virtue in that particular case.
classical.sanskrit: doShadhAtumalakShINo balakShINo~api vA naraH | svayonivardhanaM yattadannapAnaM prakA~gkShati ||29|| yadyadAhArajAtaM tu kShINaH prArthayate naraH | tasya tasya sa lAbhe tu taM taM kShayamapohati ||30||

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers; the content corresponds to standard (Trikamji) Su.Su.15.32 (opening and symptom list)
classical.establishes: Sushruta's own statement that obesity and emaciation are both rooted in rasa (rasanimittam eva sthaulyaM kArshyaM ca): immature (Ama), over-sweet rasa generates fat and so excessive stoutness. The symptom list for the obese follows. This is the primary text on whether sthaulya is a disorder of medas or of rasa, and it was unquoted in the version the critic reviewed.
classical.quote: Obesity or loss of flesh (Karsha) should be ascribed to changes in the condition of the lymph chyle. The lymph chyle derived from the assimilated food of a person, who is habituated to a course of diet which tends to promote the quantity of the bodily Kapham or is in the habit of pampering his belly even when a previous meal has not been thoroughly digested, or who is addicted to a habit of sleeping in the day, or leading a sedentary life, or is averse to taking any sort of physical exercise, continues in an immature state and is transformed into a serum of sweet taste which moves about within the body, engendering the formation of fat which produces excessive stoutness. A person afflicted with obesity develops such symptoms as shortness of breath, thirst, ravenous appetite, excessive sleepiness, perspiration, fetid odours in the body, wheezing sound in the throat during sleep or sudden suspension of breath, inert feeling in the limbs, dulness or heaviness of the body, and indistinctness of speech.
classical.sanskrit: rasanimittameva sthaulyaM kArshyaM ca | tatra shleShmalAhArasevino~adhyashanashIlasyAvyAyAmino divAsvapnaratasya cAma evAnnaraso madhuratarashca sharIramanukrAmannatisnehAnmedo janayati, tadatisthaulyamApAdayati ; tamatisthUlaM kShudrashvAsapipAsAkShutsvapnasvedagAtradaurgandhyakrathanagAtrasAdagadgadatvAni kShipramevAvishanti,

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers; the content corresponds to standard (Trikamji) Su.Su.15.33 (opening sentence)
classical.establishes: Sushruta's in-text aetiology of depletion: the causes of karshya, which the text roots in a dried-up (upashoShita) rasa-dhatu that fails to nourish the body. This is the chapter's own answer to why a dhatu is depleted, and it is in the root text (unlike the kshaya-cause sentence Bhishagratna prints as a footnote to 15.7; see the Dalhana entry).
classical.quote: Loss of flesh or a gradual emaciation of the body should be ascribed to the partaking of food in the composition of which, matter which aggravates the bodily Vayu largely or excessively enters, to over-fatiguing physical exercise, sexual excesses, over study, fright, grief or anxiety, to the keeping up of late hours, to unsatisfied hunger, insufficient food, and to astringent food which tends to dry up the lymph chyle.
classical.sanskrit: tatra punarvAtalAhArasevino~ativyAyAmavyavAyAdhyayanabhayashokadhyAnarAtrijAgaraNapipAsAkShu tkaShAyAlpAshanaprabhRutibhirupashoShito rasadhAtuH sharIramananukrAmannalpatvAnna prINAti, tasmAdatikArshyaM bhavati;

classical.verse: Bhishagratna prints no verse numbers; the content corresponds to standard (Trikamji) Su.Su.15.35
classical.establishes: The verse that pairs excess and deficiency as equally condemned states and ranks emaciation as the lesser evil, matching Charaka Sutrasthana 21.17. It is the clearest statement that vriddhi and kshaya at the level of the whole body are both pathology, not one of them a norm.
classical.quote: Excessively corpulent and excessively lean persons are alike condemnable. A body which is neither too stout nor too lean, but strikes the mean as regards plumpness, is the best. A lean frame should have the preference to a stout one.
classical.sanskrit: bhavanti cAtra- atyantagarhitAvetau sadA sthUlakRushau narau | shreShTho madhyasharIrastu kRushaH sthUlAttu pUjitaH ||35||

classical.verse: Su.Su.15.7 (commentary)
classical.establishes: That the kshaya-cause sentence (excessive saMshodhana and saMshamana, suppression of urges, unsuitable food, mental distress, exertion, fasting, sexual excess) is NOT in the root text of Su.Su.15 as transmitted in the Trikamji/NIIMH edition. Dalhana reports it as a reading that 'some read here' (kecid atra ... paThanti) and adds that 'the teachers say' these causes mostly increase vata and deplete pitta and kapha, so the cause must be judged case by case and 'there is no purpose in this reading' (nAsmin pAThe prayojanam). Bhishagratna translated the variant into a footnote. It is recorded here as a disputed variant, not as Sushruta's doctrine.
classical.withheld: no English translation of this passage has been cleared for reproduction, and the text held here is not the Sanskrit itself

classical.verse: Kaviratna prints 2 and 3 after these sentences; standard (Trikamji) Sutrasthana 21.3-21.4 (first part)
classical.establishes: Charaka's locus classicus for sthaulya and karshya: the eight condemned body types, with the over-nourished and the under-nourished singled out, and the eight faults of the obese. Charaka's mechanism in the same sutra is that in the obese 'fat alone accumulates, not so the other dhatus' (meda evopacIyate na tathetare dhAtavaH), which is a medas-centred account against Sushruta's rasa-centred one (Su.Su.15.32); see contested.
classical.quote: Referring to the body, there are eight persons that are regarded as worthy of condemnation. They are as follow: 1. one that is very tall in stature ; 2. one that is very short in stature ; 3. one that is very hairy ; 4. one that is not at all hairy ; 5. one that is very dark (or black) of complexion ; 6. one that is very white of complexion ; 7. one that is very corpulent or obese ; and 8. one that is very emaciated or lean. Amongst these, of him that is very corpulent and him that is very lean, there are certain incidents, wanting in the others, that are especially worthy of condemnation. Of him that is very corpulent are these eight faults, viz., 1. diminution of the period of life, 2. (untimely) attack of decrepitude, 3. excessive difficulty of sexual congress, 4. weakness, 5. foetid smell in every part of the body, 6. excessive perspiration, 7. abnormal appetite for food, and 8. abnormal thirst.
classical.sanskrit: iha khalu sharIramadhikRutyAShTau puruShA ninditA bhavanti; tadyathA- atidIrghashca, atihrasvashca, atilomA ca, alomA ca , atikRuShNashca, atigaurashca, atisthUlashca, atikRushashceti||3|| tatrAtisthUlakRushayorbhUya evApare ninditavisheShA bhavanti| atisthUlasya tAvadAyuSho hrAso javoparodhaH kRucchravyavAyatA daurbalyaM daurgandhyaM svedAbAdhaH kShudatimAtraM pipAsAtiyogashceti bhavantyaShTau doShAH|

classical.verse: Kaviratna prints 7-8 after the sentence; standard (Trikamji) Sutrasthana 21.11-21.12
classical.establishes: Charaka's in-text causes of karshya, the whole-body form of depletion: dry food, fasting (la~gghana), measured eating, over-treatment (kriyAtiyoga), grief, suppression of urges and of sleep, dry rubbing, habitual bathing, constitution, old age, the after-state of disease, and anger. With Su.17.76-77 and Su.Su.15.33 this gives the record three in-text aetiologies of depletion, which is the material the kshaya-nidana finding asked for, sourced from root text rather than from a translator's footnote.
classical.quote: The habitual use of dry food and drink, fasts, insufficiency of food, excessive administration of purgatives and emetics, grief, suppression of the urgings of nature and sleep, habitual use of dry unguents and indulgence in baths without rubbing oil on the body, natural waste, or the waste that follows disease and excessive wrath, these make a man lean or emaciated.
classical.sanskrit: sevA rUkShAnnapAnAnAM la~gghanaM pramitAshanam| kriyAtiyogaH shokashca veganidrAvinigrahaH||11|| rUkShasyodvartanaM snAnasyAbhyAsaH prakRutirjarA| vikArAnushayaH krodhaH kurvantyatikRushaM naram||12||

classical.verse: Kaviratna prints 12 and 13 after these sentences; standard (Trikamji) Sutrasthana 21.16-21.17
classical.establishes: That both extremes are permanently diseased (satataM vyAdhitau) and permanently under treatment, by karshana for the one and bRuMhaNa for the other, with emaciation the lesser evil. This is the therapeutic pairing that the record's brimhana/langhana component describes, stated in Charaka's root text, and it matches Su.Su.15.35.
classical.quote: He that is very corpulent, and he that is very emaciated, both these are to be regarded as always diseased. They should, therefore, be always subjected to treatment (by administration of medicines and diet) that is calculated to reduce bulk and promote nutrition and growth. Among the two, viz., excessive corpulency and excessive emaciation, the latter is rather tolerable ; for though the corpulent and the emaciated are equally situated, yet if disease assails both of them, it is sure to afflict the corpulent man more than the emaciated one.
classical.sanskrit: satataM vyAdhitAvetAvatisthUlakRushau narau| satataM copacaryau hi karshanairbRuMhaNairapi||16|| sthaulyakArshye varaM kArshyaM samopakaraNau hi tau| yadyubhau vyAdhirAgacchet sthUlamevAtipIDayet||17||

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed number after this sentence is OCR-damaged ('J1', most likely a footnote dagger plus 16); standard (Trikamji) Sutrasthana 21.20
classical.establishes: Charaka's paradoxical prescription: heavy but non-nourishing (guru, atarpaNa) regimen to reduce the obese, light but nourishing (laghu, santarpaNa) regimen to build the emaciated. It shows that brimhana and langhana are not simply 'more food' and 'less food' but qualities of regimen, which matters for how the samanya rule is applied in practice.
classical.quote: In reducing the bulk of persons that are very corpulent, food that is heavy and such dietary regulations and other practices as fall within Atarpana, are beneficial. For the nourishment, however, of persons that are very lean, food that is light and such dietary regulations and other practices as fall within Santarpana, are beneficial.
classical.sanskrit: guru cAtarpaNaM ceShTaM sthUlAnAM karshanaM prati| kRushAnAM bRuMhaNArthaM ca laghu santarpaNaM ca yat||20||

classical.verse: Kaviratna prints 7-9 after the block of six definitions; the two sentences quoted correspond to standard (Trikamji) Sutrasthana 22.9-22.10
classical.establishes: Charaka's definitions of the two therapeutic directions the vriddhi/kshaya diagnosis leads to: whatever produces lightness (lAghava) in the body is langhana; whatever generates bulk (bRuhattva) of the body is bRuMhaNa. Added because the record's component on brimhana and langhana previously carried no citation. The parenthesis '(the aggravated humours and altered constituents)' is Kaviratna's gloss; the Sanskrit says only 'in the body'.
classical.quote: Any thing that lightens or attenuates (the aggravated humours and altered constituents) in the body has been said to be a Langhana. That which promotes nutrition and bulk of the body is known as Vring-hana.

modern.title: Clinical efficacy of panchakola on raktakshaya.
modern.establishes: The one indexed clinical trial located by this record's searches that takes a named dhatu kshaya as its enrolment category. 46 patients with rakta kshaya, randomised to Panchakola tablet or rice-powder placebo for six weeks; the treatment arm showed a significant rise in haemoglobin and in classical symptom scores.
modern.quality: Small single-centre trial, and its central move is an assumption rather than a finding: the authors state at the outset that 'Raktakshaya can be correlated with anemia' and then use haemoglobin and iron studies as the outcome. That equivalence is never tested. So the trial is weak evidence that one formulation raises haemoglobin, and no evidence at all that the classical construct rakta kshaya picks out anaemia. Sushruta's own sign-list for rakta kshaya (rough skin, craving for sour and cold, flabby veins) does not mention pallor.

modern.title: Universal significance of the principle of Samanya and Vishesha beyond Ayurveda.
modern.establishes: A recent articulation of the samanya-vishesha principle, arguing for its applicability beyond medicine to ecology, economics and social policy.
modern.quality: Conceptual essay, explicitly argumentative rather than empirical, with worked illustrations drawn from family structure, climate governance and poverty reduction. It contains no clinical data and does not test the principle in its original therapeutic setting. Its presence in the indexed literature is a fair indicator of what that literature consists of for this concept.

modern.title: Explication on tissue nutrition in prenatal and postnatal life: An Ayurveda perspective.
modern.establishes: Supplies the mechanistic backdrop against which vriddhi and kshaya are supposed to occur, namely that tissues are nourished continuously at different rates governed by agni and are mutually dependent.
modern.quality: Narrative review, no data, no systematic method. Included here because the vriddhi/kshaya model presupposes the tissue-nutrition model, and this is the clearest indexed statement of the latter that this record located - not because it provides evidence for either.

modern.title: Interrater reliability of diagnostic methods in traditional Indian ayurvedic medicine.
modern.establishes: The interrater reliability study most often cited for Ayurvedic clinical assessment: fifteen registered Ayurvedic doctors examined twenty healthy subjects; average pairwise weighted kappa was 0.07 for pulse, 0.17 for tongue and 0.28 for prakriti, which the authors call a low level of reliability for all three.
modern.quality: Small (20 subjects, all healthy), single setting, three modalities only. It does not examine any dhatu kshaya or vriddhi judgement, so it is indirect evidence about the kind of sign-based assessment this record describes, not evidence about this construct. Cited so that the record's statement about poor agreement on other modalities has a source and a number.

modern.title: Reliability studies of diagnostic methods in Indian traditional Ayurveda medicine: An overview.
modern.establishes: The same group's overview of reliability studies in Ayurvedic diagnosis. Its abstract states that reliability studies in Ayurveda are 'in the preliminary stage' and offers study designs and statistics for future work.
modern.quality: Methodological overview, no new data. Only the abstract was retrieved for this record, so whether its body lists any study of a dhatu kshaya or vriddhi judgement is not known here; the abstract names prakriti classification and pulse diagnosis as its examples.

modern.title: Determinants of prakriti, the human constitution types of Indian traditional medicine and its correlation with contemporary science.
modern.establishes: A large multicentre prakriti study (3,416 healthy men aged 20-30) reporting 80 percent concordance and a kappa of 0.77 between Ayurvedic physician assessment and a computer-aided tool, with a significant association between dominant prakriti and BMI.
modern.quality: Cross-sectional; the agreement measured is physician versus software, not physician versus physician, and the construct is prakriti, not vriddhi or kshaya. It is included because it cuts against a blanket claim that agreement in Ayurvedic assessment is uniformly poor: with a structured instrument, agreement for one classical construct was substantial. No comparable instrument for any kshaya or vriddhi judgement was located by this record's searches.

modern.title: Weighted mean: A possible method to express overall Dhatu Sarata.
modern.establishes: The nearest thing to a dhatu-assessment methods paper that the record's PubMed search for 'ayurveda AND dhatu AND (reliability OR validation OR validity)' returned: a proposal to express overall dhatu sarata (tissue excellence grading) as a weighted mean rather than a single category.
modern.quality: A short methods communication with no data. Its abstract concedes that in dhatu sarata 'no substantial work has been carried out' on inter-rater variability, reliability or validation. Dhatu sarata grades the quality of a tissue in a healthy person and is a different construct from kshaya and vriddhi, so this is evidence about the state of the adjacent literature, not about this concept.

modern.establishes: That every vriddhi and kshaya pattern this record describes has an official ICD-11 TM2 code. From the project's own enrichment file (ayurveda-atlas/data/enrichment/icd-tm2.json, release 2026-01, fetched 2026-09-17), with the Sanskrit index terms the file carries: dosha patterns SR12 vAtavRuddhi, SR14 vAtakShaya, SR17 pittavRuddhi, SR19 pittakShaya, SR1C kaphavRuddhi, SR1E kaphakShaya; dhatu patterns SR41 rasavRuddhi, SR42 rasakShaya, SR43 raktavRuddhi, SR44 raktakShaya, SR45 mAMsavRuddhi, SR46 mAMsakShaya, SR47 medovRuddhi, SR48 medaHkShaya, SR49 asthivRuddhi, SR4A asthikShaya, SR4B majjAvRuddhi, SR4C majjAkShaya, SR4D shukravRuddhi, SR4E shukrakShaya; ojas SR4F ojaHkShaya, SR4G ojovyApat, SR4H ojovisraMsa; artava and stanya SR4J-SR4M; mala patterns SR80 purIShavRuddhi, SR81 purIShakShaya, SR82 mUtravRuddhi, SR83 reduced urine, SR84 svedavRuddhi, SR85 svedakShaya. The set mirrors Sushruta Sutrasthana 15 almost entity for entity, including the three ojas derangements of 15.24.
modern.quality: This is a nomenclature, not a measurement. In the enrichment file every one of these entities has a null definition and carries only a title and index terms, so what TM2 supplies is a standardised name and a code for each pattern, not diagnostic criteria, thresholds or a reference quantity. Whether coding counts as operationalisation is therefore answered narrowly here: it operationalises the vocabulary (each pattern can now be recorded and counted in health statistics) and leaves the record's central point untouched, that no criteria, instrument or reliability figure for assigning the code to a patient was located. Two further things the file shows and the record flags rather than resolves: the same Sanskrit term is indexed under a pattern code and a disorder code in several cases (medovRuddhi under SR47 and SP62 'High fat disorder'; shukrakShaya under SR4E and SN03 'Oligospermia disorder'; stanyakShaya under SR4M and SN10; svedavRuddhi under SR84 and SN45), and SR1T 'Blood deficiency pattern' is a Unani entity indexed by Arabic and Persian terms, not raktakShaya. The WHO browser's full entity pages were not read for this record, so any definitions published there and not carried in the enrichment file are not known here.

records.title: Tridosha: vata, pitta and kapha as the regulatory principles of the body
records.summary: Tridosha theory holds that three principles, vata (associated with movement and transport), pitta (with transformation, heat and digestion) and kapha (with cohesion, lubrication and structure), together constitute and regulate the body. In their normal state (prakrita) they sustain it; when deranged (vikrita) they produce disease. Each is assigned a set of physical qualities (guna) and anatomical seats, and each is said to be fivefold: Charaka names the five vatas (Ca. Su. 12.8), Sushruta names the five pittas as five agnis (Su. Su. 21/10) and locates five kaphas by seat without naming them (Su. Su. 21/14). Increase (vriddhi) and decrease (kshaya) of each dosha carry their own sign-lists (Su. Su. 15), and Sushruta's six-stage kriyakala (Su. Su. 21/18-37) is the classical account of how a deranged dosha moves from accumulation to manifest disease. The relative proportion of the three fixed at conception is prakriti, the individual constitution, which the texts hold to determine susceptibility, presentation and drug response. Sushruta calls the body tristhuna, three-pillared, and adds rakta (blood) as a fourth co-determinant; Charaka and Vagbhata keep the count at three. The theory functions in the classical texts as a general explanatory grammar covering physiology, pathogenesis, diagnosis, diet, season and therapeutics. It is not defined in the texts by reference to any observable substance, and the doshas are not the same as the humours of Greek medicine despite the standard English rendering of vata, pitta and kapha as wind, bile and phlegm.
records.evidenceState: Tridosha is the one concept in this cluster with a real, if thin, empirical research programme behind it, and it is important not to overstate what that programme has shown. There are genuine molecular studies: genome-wide expression differences between extreme prakriti types (Prasher 2008), a permutation-tested genome-wide SNP study in 262 men selected from 3,416 (Govindaraj 2015), DNA-methylation differences in 147 men from that same 3,416-subject screen (Rotti 2015), an immunophenotyping pilot (Rotti 2014), a 16S gut-microbiome study (Chauhan 2018) with two later microbiome studies on different protocols, and a 38-subject plasma metabolomics study (Shirolkar 2018). What these establish is that groups sorted by Ayurvedic constitutional criteria are not molecularly identical. Three things about them need saying plainly. First, their internal confirmations are often the selection restated: Govindaraj's principal-component separation is computed on the 52 SNPs chosen because they differed between groups, and Shirolkar's 97.87% model recognition is a supervised fit on 38 samples. Second, extreme-phenotype designs that keep one subject in thirteen say nothing about the people screened out. Third, the EGLN1 altitude result (Aggarwal 2010), usually presented as a discovery reached through Ayurvedic typing, recovered a signal that Simonson et al. and Bigham et al. had already established in Tibetan and Andean genomics earlier the same year with no Ayurvedic input; prakriti correlated with something real, but did not find it. None of these studies claims, and none shows, a correspondence between vata, pitta or kapha and an identified physiological system, pathway or measurable quantity. On biomarkers, this record now has a named search to stand on: Venkatesh et al. 2025 (PubMed, Scopus and Cochrane to November 2024, 94 included studies) found 32 categories of measurable correlates studied against prakriti, only five of them with validated assessment tools, and no tool fully meeting their scale-development criteria. The theory itself, as opposed to prakriti classification, has attracted mostly narrative and analogical work, of which Hankey's coenzyme A argument (an editorial, not a study) is representative. The more serious problem sits upstream of all of it. Assignment of dosha state is the measurement on which every downstream study depends, and it measures badly. Chance-corrected inter-rater agreement between four trained Ayurvedic experts for prakriti and agni was between 0 and 0.4; software-versus-clinician agreement for kapha was ICC 0.44; two 2025 reviews of the instrument literature (Gupta et al., 32 studies; Venkatesh et al., 64 tools) found that fewer than a third of the tools had any validation and that two met most of the standard criteria. High percentage agreement on a final consensus diagnosis coexisting with poor kappa on its components suggests convergence on a shared conclusion by routes that are not the stated ones. Until the classification is reproducible, molecular differences between prakriti groups cannot be cleanly attributed to the constructs they are labelled with, and the genomic, epigenomic, microbiome and metabolomic findings should be read as findings about a phenotyping heuristic rather than as validation of tridosha. On the classical side, the revision found one further translator intrusion of the kind this project tracks: Sushruta's mula names the five pittas (21/10) but no kapha subtype (15/4, 21/14); the kapha names in Bhishagratna are his headings and footnotes.

contested.question: Are there three doshas or four factors?
positions: Charaka and Vagbhata hold to three: vata, pitta and kapha

Sushruta explicitly adds rakta (blood) as a fourth co-determinant of the body's origin, maintenance and dissolution (Su. Su. 21/3, shonita-chaturthaih), and some later commentators treat rakta as a dosha in the full sense
A reconciling reading holds that Sushruta treats rakta as dushya (that which is vitiated) with dosha-like behaviour because of his surgical orientation, not as a fourth dosha proper

contested.question: Is agni a separate principle or a function of pitta?
positions: Sushruta answers directly that no fire other than pitta is found in the body and that the word 'internal fire' is applied to pitta by analogy with fire (Su. Su. 21/9), and he names the five pittas as five agnis (Su. Su. 21/10)

Much later and modern Ayurvedic writing treats agni as a distinct entity with thirteen subtypes, separable from pitta and separately assessable, which is what the swastha definition's samagni clause presupposes
Some commentators hold agni is pitta's action, so the distinction is functional rather than substantial

contested.question: Do the doshas denote substances, functions, or regulatory systems?
positions: Substance reading: the classical seats, quantities and increase/decrease language imply material entities, and the standard English rendering as wind, bile and phlegm follows this
Function reading: the texts define each dosha by an enumerated list of effects (Su. Su. 15/4, Ca. Su. 12.8), not by any observable substance, which makes them functional categories
Systems reading, advanced by modern authors such as Hankey: they are universal regulatory systems (transport, turnover, storage). This reading is speculative and has no empirical test behind it

contested.question: Do the prakriti genomics findings validate tridosha?
positions: Proponents read the expression, SNP, methylation and EGLN1 results as demonstrating a genetic basis for constitutional typing

A more conservative reading is that extreme-phenotype selection on any consistently applied criterion will surface group differences, that within-study confirmations such as PCA on selected SNPs are circular, and that without reproducible dosha assignment the findings cannot be attributed to the dosha constructs specifically

A third position treats prakriti as a useful stratification heuristic for gene discovery, while noting that in the one case usually cited (EGLN1) the gene had already been found by other means, and remaining agnostic about tridosha as physiology

contested.question: Is prakriti fixed for life?
positions: Classical position: prakriti is determined at conception and does not change; only vikriti changes

Practical position implied by repeat-assessment studies and questionnaire instability: measured prakriti varies between raters, between instruments and potentially over time, which is either a measurement problem or evidence against fixity, and no study distinguishes the two

contested.question: Are the fifteen subdosha names classical text or commentary?
positions: Charaka names the five vatas in the mula (Ca. Su. 12.8: prana, udana, samana, vyana, apana)
Sushruta names the five pittas in the mula, as agnis (Su. Su. 21/10: pachaka, ranjaka, sadhaka, alochaka, bhrajaka), but at 15/4 and 21/14 counts five vatas and five kaphas without naming them

The five kapha names (kledaka, avalambaka, bodhaka, tarpaka, shleshaka) appear in this record's sources only as Bhishagratna's section headings and footnotes. Their classical locus is conventionally given as Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 12, which this record did not gather, so the question of where they first appear is left open in notKnown rather than answered

notKnown: What physiological quantity, if any, corresponds to any single dosha. Many correlates have been proposed; Venkatesh et al. 2025 count 32 categories across 94 studies, only five studied with validated tools, and none validated as a biomarker for vata, pitta or kapha individually.

Whether the genome-wide prakriti findings replicate. Neither Prasher 2008 nor Govindaraj 2015 has an independent replication using the same phenotyping protocol in a different cohort.
