The Manipal work (Rotti 2014, 2015) was checked for this purpose and does not supply it: Rotti 2015 draws its 147 subjects from the same 3,416-subject screen as Govindaraj 2015, on which Rotti is a co-author, and it measures methylation rather than expression or SNPs. It is a further prakriti-stratified finding from the same cohort, not a replication.

Whether the microbiome and metabolomic differences replicate. Chauhan 2018, Shalin 2021 and Shirolkar 2018 are single-cohort studies on three different phenotyping protocols, two of them male-only, and no taxon or metabolite has been reported as differing in the same direction in two cohorts.
Whether prakriti is stable within an individual over time. No adequate longitudinal test-retest study was found; both 2025 reviews list test-retest reliability among the properties most tools lack.

Whether prakriti classification predicts anything prospectively: disease incidence, treatment response or prognosis. The claim is central to the theory and has not been tested in a prospective design.
Why percentage agreement on a final Ayurvedic diagnosis is high while chance-corrected agreement on its constitutional components is near zero.
Whether the seven-type (or eight-type) prakriti taxonomy is the right partition, or an artefact of enumerating combinations; no study has tested alternative clusterings against outcomes.
Whether the Sushruta four-factor and Charaka three-factor schemes make any different empirical prediction.
How the doshas relate to the dhatus and malas mechanistically. The texts assert relations of vitiation and nourishment without a stated mechanism, and no modern work operationalises the relation.

Whether findings from male-only, single-region Indian cohorts generalise to women or to other populations. Of the molecular studies in this record, Govindaraj 2015, Rotti 2014, Rotti 2015 and Shirolkar 2018 are male-only by design.

Whether the standard English renderings (wind, bile, phlegm) have distorted a century of interpretation, including Bhishagratna's own glosses of vayu as 'nerve force' and pitta's ojakrit function as acting on 'protoplasmic cells', and Kaviratna's 'cold ... bitter' for sasneha ... katu at Ca. Su. 1.60.

Where the five kapha names and the five vata names first occur in the mula texts. Sushruta's Sutrasthana names the pittas only. Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 12 (Doshabhediya), the chapter conventionally cited for all fifteen names, was not gathered, and no public-domain English translation of it exists, so this record does not state what it says.

Charaka's own account of the five vatas in Chikitsasthana 28 (Vatavyadhi), the address proposed by the critic. Kaviratna's public-domain translation in the archive.org scan ends with Chikitsasthana lesson 22 (Trishna), so Chikitsa 28 cannot be quoted from a public-domain English source, and the Sanskrit was not retrieved in this pass. The record uses Ca. Su. 12.8 for the names instead.

Charaka's dosha vriddhi and kshaya sign-lists (conventionally Su. 17 and 18). Not gathered; Kaviratna's numbering in Su. 18 is recorded elsewhere in this project as running five ahead of the standard, and the passages were not retrieved here. Only Sushruta's lists (Su. Su. 15) are carried.

Whether Sushruta's six-stage kriyakala has ever been tested as a sequence, that is, whether the stage signs occur in the stated order in observed illness. The doctrine is carried here from the text; no empirical study of the sequence was found in the searches made for this record, which were not designed to be exhaustive on that question.

components.gloss: Principle of movement: motor and sensory conduction, propulsion of food and wastes, retention and expulsion. Gunas at Ca. Su. 1.59: ruksha, shita, laghu, sukshma, chala, vishada, khara (dry, cold, light, subtle, mobile, clear, rough). Five subtypes named by Charaka at Ca. Su. 12.8: prana, udana, samana, vyana, apana

Principle of transformation: digestion and tissue metabolism, pigmentation, body heat, vision, and (per Sushruta) production of ojas and of intellect. Gunas at Ca. Su. 1.60, read from the Sanskrit: sasneha, ushna, tikshna, drava, amla, sara, katu (slightly unctuous, hot, sharp, liquid, sour, flowing, pungent). The gathered record's 'light' and the earlier 'cold' and 'bitter' were artefacts of Kaviratna's English and are withdrawn. Five subtypes named as agnis by Sushruta at Su. Su. 21/10: pachaka, ranjaka, sadhaka, alochaka, bhrajaka

Principle of cohesion and structure: joint lubrication, unctuousness, stability, healing of sores, bulk. Gunas at Ca. Su. 1.61: guru, shita, mridu, snigdha, madhura, sthira, picchila (heavy, cold, soft, unctuous, sweet, stable, slimy). Sushruta locates five kaphas by seat at Su. Su. 21/14 (amashaya, chest, tongue-root and throat, head, joints) but the Sanskrit of that aphorism names none of them; the names kledaka, avalambaka, bodhaka, tarpaka, shleshaka appear in this record only as Bhishagratna's headings and footnotes, and their first classical occurrence was not established here
The proportion of the three doshas fixed at conception; the individual constitutional type (seven combinations are conventionally enumerated). Covered in depth in the prakriti-determination record
The current deranged state of the doshas, distinguished from prakriti; what treatment addresses

Increase and decrease of a dosha beyond its normal measure. Sushruta gives a sign-list for the decrease and for the excess of each dosha at Su. Su. 15 (quoted below), and the rule that treatment of a decreased dosha is by agents that build it. Charaka's parallel lists (Su. 17 and 18) were not gathered; see notKnown

Sushruta's six stages of a deranged dosha: sanchaya, prakopa, prasara, sthanasamshraya, vyakti, bheda (Su. Su. 21/36, with the stage declarations at 21/18, 27, 32, 33, 34, 35). The summary verse is quoted below; the stage-by-stage text, Dalhana's commentary and the textual variants are carried in the shat-kriyakala record and are not duplicated here
Blood, counted by Sushruta as a fourth co-determinant of the body's origin, maintenance and dissolution alongside the three doshas
Rajas and tamas, the two doshas of the mind, held parallel to the three of the body

classical.verse: Su. Su. 21/3 (Sanskrit aphorism number; Bhishagratna prints no number)
classical.establishes: The core doctrine in one passage: the three doshas as the constitutive and regulatory principles, the tristhuna image, the normal-versus-deranged dichotomy, and Sushruta's distinctive addition of rakta as a fourth. The English was re-read against the archive.org OCR on 2026-10-06 (chapter XXI begins at the heading 'Now we shall discuss the Chapter which investigates the nature of bodily humours') and matches, with hyphenation normalised.
classical.quote: The Vayu, Pittam and Shleshma should be considered as the primary and the most essential factors in the constitution of human organism. These fundamental and vital humours, occupying respectively the lower, middle, and upper parts of the body, maintain its integrity. The human body is supported by the three fundamental humours in the same way as a dwelling house is propped up by three supporting poles or stays; from which fact, the body is called the three-supported one (Tristhunam) by certain authorities. A deranged condition of these three fundamental humours may bring about its dissolution or death, while on their continuance in a normal state depends the vitality of the organism. These three humours, in combination with a fourth, the principle of blood, determine the origin, preservation, and dissolution of animated organism and permeate it with their respective properties till the moment of death.
classical.sanskrit: वातपित्तश्लेष्माण एव देहसम्भवहेतवः । तैरेवाव्यापन्नैरधोमध्योर्ध्वसन्निविष्टैः शरीरमिदं धार्यतेऽगारमिव स्थूणाभिस्तिसृभिः अतश्च त्रिस्थूणमाहुरेके । त एव च व्यापन्नाः प्रलयहेतवः । तदेभिरेव शोणितचतुर्थैः सम्भवस्थितिप्रलयेष्वप्यविरहितं शरीरं भवति ॥३॥
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907), public domain

classical.verse: Su. Su. 15/4 (Sanskrit aphorism number, added in this revision; Bhishagratna prints no number)
classical.establishes: The functional definition of vata by its effects rather than by any substance, and the fivefold subdivision. Two translator intrusions to keep separate from the text. Bhishagratna's parenthetical gloss of Vayu as 'nerve force' is his own 1907 interpolation, not the Sanskrit, and is an early instance of the biomedical-correlate move that still dominates the literature. And the Sanskrit says only 'panchadha pravibhaktah', divided fivefold; the five names (Prana, Udana, Samana, Vyana, Apana) are in Bhishagratna's footnote, not in Sushruta's aphorism. Charaka's own naming of the five is at Ca. Su. 12.8, quoted below.
classical.quote: The imparting of motion to the body (Praspandanam), the carrying of the sensations of the respective sense organs (Udvahanam), the passing down of food to its proper receptacles (Puranam), the separation of excretions from the assimilated food matter (Viveka), and the retention and evacuation of urine and semen, etc. (Dharanam) should be ascribed to the functions of the five kinds of Vayu (nerve force) which support the body.
classical.sanskrit: तत्र प्रस्पन्दनोद्वहनपूरणविवेकधारणलक्षणो वायुः पञ्चधा प्रविभक्तः शरीरं धारयति ॥
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907), public domain

classical.verse: Su. Su. 15/4 (same aphorism as the preceding entry)
classical.establishes: That pitta is defined as a family of transformative functions including intellect, and is explicitly tied to agni (agni-karmana anugraham karoti), and that kapha is defined by the parallel list of cohesive functions and tied to water (udaka-karmana). 'Protoplasmic cells' is the translator's, not the text's. The footnote in which Bhishagratna names the five pittas and five kaphas is likewise his; Sushruta's own naming of the pittas is at 21/10, and his mula names no kapha subtypes at 15/4 or 21/14. OCR note: the archive.org text layer prints 'coloiu-ing' and 'Ushma- Krit' across line breaks; both are restored ('colouring', 'Ushma-Krit') and no other word differs from the OCR segment.
classical.quote: Pigmentations or colouring (Ragakrit), the digestion of food and metabolism of tissues (Paktikrit), the vitalisation and nutrition of the protaplasmic cells (Ojakrit), the origination and preservation of eye-sight (Teja-Krit), the germination of heat and maintenance of the temperature of the body (Ushma-Krit), and the origination of the faculty of intellection (Medha-Krit) should be regarded as the functions of the five kinds of Pittam, which contribute to the preservation of the body through its thermogenetic potency (Agni-Karma).
classical.sanskrit: रागपक्त्योजस्तेजोमेधोष्मकृत् पित्तं पञ्चधा प्रविभक्तमग्निकर्मणाऽनुग्रहं करोति; ॥ सन्धिसंश्लेषणस्नेहनरोपणपूरणबलस्थैर्यकृच्छ्लेष्मा पञ्चधा प्रविभक्त उदककर्मणाऽनुग्रहं करोति ॥४॥
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907), public domain

classical.verse: Su. Su. 21/9 (Sanskrit aphorism number, added in this revision; Bhishagratna prints no number)
classical.establishes: That the identification of pitta with agni was a live question inside the tradition and was answered by assimilation. This is the textual root of the persistent ambiguity about whether agni is a separate entity or a function of pitta. The three grounds the Sanskrit gives (a weakened fire-quality is treated with fire-like substances, an excessive one with cooling measures, and scripture) are all present in the English.
classical.quote: Now it may be asked whether the Pittam is identical with the elemental fire, or is it something other than that? The question may be answered by stating that the Pittam is the same as fire. Since such symptoms, as a burning sensation, digestion (boiling), and all other characteristics of fire can never exhibit themselves in the human body without the intervention of Pittam. Pittam therefore is called internal fire. Consequently, an enfeebled action of Pittam is remedied by the administration of drugs and substances which are akin to the elemental fire in their attributes, while an abnormal or excessive action (secretion) of Pittam is subdued by cooling measures as an over-kindled fire is subdued by moisture. There is no other fire (heat making factor) in the organism than Pittam.
classical.sanskrit: तत्र जिज्ञास्यं किं पित्तव्यतिरेकादन्योऽग्निः । अत्रोच्यते- न खलु पित्तव्यतिरेकादन्योऽग्निरुपलभ्यते, आग्नेयत्वात् पित्ते दहनपचनादिष्वभिप्रवर्तमानेऽग्निवदुपचारः क्रियतेऽन्तरग्निरिति; क्षीणे ह्यग्निगुणे तत्समानद्रव्योपयोगात् , अतिवृद्धे शीतक्रियोपयोगात् , आगमाच्च पश्यामो न खलु पित्तव्यतिरेकादन्योऽग्निरिति ॥९॥
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907), public domain

classical.verse: Su. Su. 21/10 (Sanskrit aphorism number; Bhishagratna prints no number)
classical.establishes: Sushruta's own naming of the five pittas, each as an agni with a seat and a function: pachaka (between pakvashaya and amashaya), ranjaka (liver and spleen), sadhaka (heart), alochaka (eye), bhrajaka (skin). This is the classical locus for the pitta subtypes and it confirms, from the mula, that Sushruta treats the subtypes of pitta as kinds of fire, which bears on the agni-versus-pitta question. The English paragraph headings are Bhishagratna's layout; 'lymph-chyle' for rasa and 'by the ordination of fate or necessity' for adrishta-hetukena are his renderings. Quoted from the archive.org OCR with hyphenation normalised and the OCR's broken diacritics ('Pd'Chakygni', 'Sa'dhaka'gni') restored to the plain spellings Bhishagratna uses elsewhere in the same passage. Three further OCR letter-defects corrected, each checked against the surrounding text and the Sanskrit: 'Am^shaya' to 'Amashaya', 'imguents' to 'unguents', and 'e5'es' to 'eyes'. A word-level comparison against the OCR segment on 2026-10-06 found no other difference.
classical.quote: The Pachakagni: By the ordination of fate or necessity (unfathomable natural cause) the Pittam, located in the region between the stomach (Amashaya) and the intestines (Pakvashaya), helps the digestion of the four kinds of food such as drink and edibles etc. partaken of by a living subject, and purges off the residue or impure morbiferous matter in the shape of urine and excreta after the completion of the process. Even thus located, it keeps up the temperature in its other distant locations (skin, etc.) in virtue of its native heat-giving attribute. Hence this Pittam is called the Pachakagni (digestive fire or heat) in an animated organism. The Ranjakagni: The function of the Pittam, which has its seats in the liver and the spleen, consists in imparting its characteristic pigment (Ragakrit) to the lymph-chyle and is hence known as Ranjakagni (lit: dyeing fire or pigment bile.) The Sadhakagni: The Pittam seated in the heart is denominated as the Sadhakagni (performing or operating heat or fire) inasmuch as its action is to bring about the fruition or realisation of one's desires. The Alochakagni: The Pittam, which is located in the pupils of the eyes, is called the Alochakagni (the Pittam or fire of sight) as its office is to catch the image of any external object presented to the eyes. The Bhrajakagni: The Pittam, which has its seat in the skin, is called the Bhrajakagni (illuminating or irradiating heat) inasmuch as it absorbs the substances used in the shape of unguents, lubrications, etc. and irradiates the glow of one's natural complexion.
classical.sanskrit: तच्चादृष्टहेतुकेन विशेषेण पक्वामाशयमध्यस्थं पित्तं चतुर्विधमन्नपानं पचति, विवेचयति च दोषरसमूत्रपुरीषाणि; तत्रस्थमेव चात्मशक्त्या शेषाणां पित्तस्थानानां शरीरस्य चाग्निकर्मणाऽनुग्रहं करोति, तस्मिन् पित्ते पाचकोऽग्निरिति सञ्ज्ञा; यत्तु यकृत्प्लीह्नोः पित्तं तस्मिन् रञ्जकोऽग्निरिति सञ्ज्ञा, स रसस्य रागकृदुक्तः; यत् पित्तं हृदयस्थं तस्मिन् साधकोऽग्निरिति सञ्ज्ञा, सोऽभिप्रार्थितमनोरथसाधनकृदुक्तः; यद्दृष्ट्यां पित्तं तस्मिन्नालोचकोऽग्निरिति सञ्ज्ञा, स रूपग्रहणाऽधिकृतः; यत्तु त्वचि पित्तं तस्मिन् भ्राजकोऽग्निरिति सञ्ज्ञा, सोऽभ्यङ्गपरिषेकावगाहालेपनादीनां क्रियाद्रव्याणां पक्ता छायानां च प्रकाशकः ॥१०॥
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907), public domain

classical.verse: Su. Su. 21/14 (Sanskrit aphorism number; Bhishagratna prints no number)
classical.establishes: The five seats and functions of kapha in Sushruta: the amashaya kapha serving the others by its watery action, the chest kapha supporting the heart (hridaya-avalambanam), the tongue-root and throat kapha serving taste, the head kapha nourishing the senses, the joint kapha binding the joints. It does NOT establish the five kapha names. The Sanskrit of ||14|| contains no name for any of the five; it has only the verbs from which the later names are formed (avalambanam, santarpana, samshlesha). The headings 'The Kledakam', 'The Avalamvaka', 'The Vodhakam', 'The Tarpakam', 'The Shleshakam' are Bhishagratna's, printed as paragraph heads, and whether he took them from Dalhana or from Vagbhata was not established in this pass. This is the translator-voice defect in the form this project has met three times before, caught here before the names were recorded as Sushruta's. The OCR prints 'The Shimcshakam' for the last heading; the spelling is restored from Bhishagratna's own footnote at chapter XV ('Shleshmaka').
classical.quote: The Kledakam: The Kapham, even though principally located in the stomach, permeates its four other distant localities with its peculiar watery or humid essence in virtue of its inherent attributes. The Avalamvaka: The Kapham, located in the region of the chest, protects the joints of the arms, the neck and the sternum, and enables the heart to perform its natural functions with the help of the lymph-chyle derived from the assimilated food and its own intrinsic potency. The Vodhakam: The Kapham, situated in the throat and at the root of the palate, lends its aid to the perception of tastes by maintaining the moist or humid character of the tongue. The Tarpakam: The Kapham, situated in the head, cools and bathes the different sense organs with its own humid essence, in virtue of its natural humid attributes. The Shimcshakam: The Kapham, situated in the joints, keeps them firmly united, protects their articulation and opposes their separation and disunion.
classical.sanskrit: स तत्रस्थ एव स्वशक्त्या शेषाणां श्लेष्मस्थानानां शरीरस्य चोदककर्मणाऽनुग्रहं करोति; उरःस्थस्त्रिकसन्धारणमात्मवीर्येणान्नरससहितेन हृदयावलम्बनं करोति; जिह्वामूलकण्ठस्थो जिह्वेन्द्रियस्य सौम्यत्वात् सम्यग्रसज्ञाने वर्तते; शिरःस्थः स्नेहसन्तर्पणाधिकृतत्वादिन्द्रियाणामात्मवीर्येणानुग्रहं करोत्; सन्धिस्थः श्लेष्मा सर्वसन्धिसंश्लेषात् सर्वसन्ध्यनुग्रहं करोति ॥१४॥
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907), public domain
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: aphorism number not retrieved for these two passages; chapter only is asserted. Bhishagratna prints no number, and the Sanskrit numbering for the kshaya and vriddhi sign-lists was not checked in this pass
classical.establishes: The classical content of 'dosha vriddhi and kshaya' that the gathered record named as a component without sourcing: Sushruta gives a sign-list for the decrease of each dosha and a separate sign-list for its excess, in the chapter whose title is the increase and decrease of doshas, dhatus and malas, and states the treatment rule for decrease (agents that build the lost principle). Both passages were retrieved from the archive.org OCR on 2026-10-06; the first follows the heading 'Now we shall describe the symptoms which attend the loss or waste of any of the foregoing principles', the second follows 'Now we shall describe the symptoms which mark the excess'. Bhishagratna's footnote to the vriddhi passage records that 'several editions read roughness of speech' for roughness of the skin, so the vata list is not textually settled at that item. 'Nerve-force' is again the translator's.
classical.quote: The loss of the bodily Vayu (nerve-force) is followed by a state of languor, shortness of speech, uneasiness or absence of hilarity, and loss of consciousness. The loss of (Pittam) is marked by a dulness of complexion, diminution of the bodily heat and an impaired state of internal fire (digestive heat). The loss of phlegm (Kapham) is marked by dryness, a sensation of internal burning, a feeling of emptiness in the stomach and other cavities or chambers of the body, looseness of the joints (a feeling as if the joints were all broken), thirst, weakness, and insomnia. In such cases the medical treatment should consist of remedial agents which are capable of directly contributing to the growth or formation of the humour so lost or deteriorated.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907), public domain

classical.verse: Su. Su. 21/36 (Sanskrit aphorism number; Bhishagratna prints no number)
classical.establishes: That the doshas are, in Sushruta's own text, dynamic quantities with a named sequence of states, and that knowing that sequence is the definition of a physician. This is the classical account of dosha dynamics that the gathered record referred to without carrying. Bhishagratna's English reorders the six: he puts Bheda fourth, before Sthana-samshrayam and Vyakti, because he has attached each term to an English relative clause. The order in this record is read from the Sanskrit: sanchaya, prakopa, prasara, sthanasamshraya, vyakti, bheda. The stage-by-stage declarations (21/18, 27, 32, 33, 34, 35), the therapeutic rationale at 21/37, Dalhana's commentary and the textual variants are carried in the shat-kriyakala record and are deliberately not duplicated here. Quoted from the archive.org OCR with the page-break hyphenation of 'accumula-tion' closed and the OCR's '(Prakopa}' corrected to '(Prakopa)'.
classical.quote: The physician, who fully knows about the accumulation (Sanchaya), disturbance or aggravation (Prakopa), expansion (Prasaram), and differentiating traits of the deranged humours (Bheda), and is well conversant with the specific localities in which they are respectively confined in the course of their expansion (Sthana-samshrayam), and with the symptoms which they respectively exhibit in connection with the incidental disease (Vyakti), is alone worthy of that epithet.
classical.sanskrit: भवन्ति चात्र- सञ्चयं च प्रकोपं च प्रसरं स्थानसंश्रयम् । व्यक्तिं भेदं च यो वेत्ति दोषाणां स भवेद्भिषक् ॥३६॥
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (1907), public domain

classical.verse: Ca. Su. 1.57 (standard Trikamji numbering). Kaviratna prints 56 after the paragraph
classical.establishes: The canonical enumeration of three bodily and two mental doshas in one verse, which is the basis for treating the mental and bodily systems as structurally parallel. Numbering: the standard number is 57 and Kaviratna's printed number is 56; they are recorded separately and neither is taken to verify the other. In the archive.org OCR the preceding paragraph (the atma verse, standard 56) also shows '56', so one of the two printed digits is an OCR misreading; the sequence 58, 59, 60 that follows fixes Kaviratna's number for this paragraph as 56.
classical.quote: Wind, bile, and phlegm have been said to be the causes of all bodily diseases. The qualities of Passion and Darkness have, again, been indicated to be the causes of mental diseases.
classical.sanskrit: वायुः पित्तं कफश्चोक्तः शारीरो दोषसङ्ग्रहः| मानसः पुनरुद्दिष्टो रजश्च तम एव च||५७||
classical.translator: Kaviraj Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (1896-1913), public domain

classical.verse: Ca. Su. 1.59-61 (standard Trikamji numbering). Kaviratna prints 58, 59 and 60 after the three paragraphs; the OCR renders the last two as '69' and '80'
classical.establishes: Two things, carried by two different parts of this entry. From the Sanskrit (confidence: quoted): that each dosha is specified by a list of gunas, that the lists are ruksha-shita-laghu-sukshma-chala-vishada-khara for vata, sasneha-ushna-tikshna-drava-amla-sara-katu for pitta, and guru-shita-mridu-snigdha-madhura-sthira-picchila for kapha, and that the therapeutic logic is treatment by opposite qualities (viparita-gunaih), which is what makes tridosha a closed inferential system rather than a descriptive taxonomy. From Kaviratna's English (confidence: located only): that the therapeutic rule is present in the public-domain translation. The English is NOT relied on for any guna.
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

classical.verse: Ca. Su. 12.8 (standard Trikamji numbering). Kaviratna splits the aphorism and prints 6 after the normal-function sentence and 7 after the excited-function sentence
classical.establishes: Charaka's own naming of the five vatas, in the mula and not in a footnote: 'pranodanasamanavyanapanatma'. This is the classical locus this record uses for the vata subtypes, in place of the Chikitsa 28 address proposed by the critic, because Kaviratna's public-domain translation ends at Chikitsa 22 (see notKnown). The passage is the speech of the royal sage Varyovida in the Vatakalakaliya debate, so it is one position in a staged discussion, not a bare doctrinal statement; the text then approves it. Numbering: standard 8, Kaviratna 6 and 7; recorded separately. The offset here (two behind, with a split) is not the offset at Su. 1 (one behind) and must not be carried between chapters. Quoted from the archive.org OCR with hyphenation normalised; the passage sits under Kaviratna's heading 'LESSON XII'.
classical.quote: The Wind upholds the constituents of the body (such as blood, flesh, marrow, fat, &c.) and their courses through the body. It exists in the fivefold form of Prana, Udana, Samana, Vyana, and Apana. It is the urging cause of movements of diverse kinds. It restrains the mind (from all undesirable objects) and concentrates it (on objects that are desirable). It causes all the (ten) senses (of knowledge and action) to perform their functions. It bears all the objects of the senses (after contact with the senses) to the mind. It holds together all the elements of the body. It assists the cohesion of the particles of the body. It causes speech. It is the prime cause of touch and sound, and the root of scent and touch. It is the origin of joy and cheerfulness. It excites the heat of fire. It dries up all faults. It throws out all impurities. It pierces through all the ducts of the body, gross and fine. It gives form to the embryo in womb. It furnishes the evidence of the existence of life. The Wind, when unexcited, achieves all these functions.
classical.sanskrit: वायुस्तन्त्रयन्त्रधरः, प्राणोदानसमानव्यानापानात्मा, प्रवर्तकश्चेष्टानामुच्चावचानां, नियन्ता प्रणेता च मनसः, सर्वेन्द्रियाणामुद्योजकः, सर्वेन्द्रियार्थानामभिवोढा, सर्वशरीरधातुव्यूहकरः, सन्धानकरः शरीरस्य, प्रवर्तको वाचः, प्रकृतिः स्पर्शशब्दयोः, श्रोत्रस्पर्शनयोर्मूलं, हर्षोत्साहयोर्योनिः, समीरणोऽग्नेः, दोषसंशोषणः, क्षेप्ता बहिर्मलानां, स्थूलाणुस्रोतसां भेत्ता, कर्तागर्भाकृतीनाम्, आयुषोऽनुवृत्तिप्रत्ययभूतो भवत्यकुपितः| ... ||८||
classical.translator: Kaviraj Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (1896-1913), public domain

classical.establishes: Vagbhata's compressed statement that vata, pitta and kapha are the three doshas, which vitiate the body when abnormal and sustain it when normal. Located on a verse-numbered presentation of the chapter. Ashtanga Hridaya has no public-domain English translation, so this is a paraphrase only and no quotation is given. Vagbhata's subdosha chapter (Sutrasthana 12) was not gathered; see notKnown.

modern.title: Whole genome expression and biochemical correlates of extreme constitutional types defined in Ayurveda.
modern.establishes: Prasher et al. phenotyped healthy individuals of the three extreme prakriti types in an Indo-European Indian population and reported differences in biochemical and haematological parameters and in genome-wide peripheral blood expression, with enrichment of differentially expressed genes in transport, cyclin-dependent kinase regulation, immune response and blood coagulation.
modern.quality: The most cited empirical work in the field and a genuine molecular study, but small, single-population, and not independently replicated with the same phenotyping protocol. The design cannot separate dosha assignment from correlated demographics, and gene-set enrichment on a small sample is fragile. It establishes that Ayurvedically-classified groups differ on some measures, not that vata, pitta and kapha correspond to identified biological systems.

modern.title: Genome-wide analysis correlates Ayurveda Prakriti.
modern.establishes: Govindaraj et al. performed genome-wide SNP analysis on 262 well-classified male individuals selected from 3,416 screened, found 52 SNPs differing between prakriti groups at p <= 1e-5 after 10^6 permutations without a stratification effect, reported that principal component analysis of those 52 SNPs separated the 262 into their groups, validated against 297 Indian samples of known ancestry, and reported that PGM1 correlates with the pitta phenotype.
modern.quality: Methodologically the strongest study in the area for its permutation testing and stratification control, but two features of the design limit what it shows and the gathered record did not draw them out. First, the PCA separation is not independent confirmation: it is computed on the 52 SNPs that were selected because they differed between the groups, so the separation restates the selection. Second, 262 of 3,416 is a roughly one-in-thirteen extreme-phenotype selection; discrimination between the tails of a distribution says nothing about the twelve in thirteen who were screened out, so the result carries no claim about ordinary people. It is also male-only, and the PGM1-to-Charaka link is interpretation rather than result. Affiliations are CSIR-CCMB Hyderabad, Manipal University and SDM College of Ayurveda, Udupi; Rotti H is a co-author. Independent replication in another cohort has not been published.

modern.title: EGLN1 involvement in high-altitude adaptation revealed through genetic analysis of extreme constitution types defined in Ayurveda.
modern.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
modern.establishes: Aggarwal et al. (IGIB, published 2 November 2010) report that EGLN1, one of 251 genes differentially expressed between prakriti types in their earlier work, carries variants rs479200 and rs480902 associated with high-altitude adaptation and with high-altitude pulmonary oedema, the TT genotype of rs479200 being more frequent in kapha types and nearly absent in high-altitude natives.
modern.quality: A real genetic finding about EGLN1 and altitude, but its relevance to tridosha is weaker than it is usually presented, and weaker than the gathered record stated. EGLN1 (PHD2) had already been identified as a high-altitude adaptation gene with no Ayurvedic input: Simonson et al. reported positively selected EGLN1 haplotypes in Tibetans in Science on 2 July 2010 (PMID 20466884), and Bigham et al. reported EGLN1 under positive selection in both Tibetans and Andeans in PLoS Genetics on 9 September 2010 (PMID 20838600), both before this paper. What the prakriti stratification did was recover, in Indian lowlanders, a signal already known from highland population genomics. That is consistent with the typing being correlated with something real; it is not a novel discovery produced by the typing, and the altitude result stands independently of whether tridosha is true.

modern.title: Genetic evidence for high-altitude adaptation in Tibet.
modern.establishes: Simonson et al. report genome-wide scans in Tibetans showing positive selection in several regions, with positively selected haplotypes of EGLN1 and PPARA significantly associated with the decreased-haemoglobin phenotype of that highland population.
modern.quality: Included as the independent prior for the EGLN1 altitude signal, not as a prakriti study; it has no Ayurvedic content. Published 2 July 2010, four months before Aggarwal et al. It is what makes the honest statement of the EGLN1 result 'recovered a known signal' rather than 'produced a discovery'.

modern.title: Identifying signatures of natural selection in Tibetan and Andean populations using dense genome scan data.
modern.establishes: Bigham et al. applied four population-genetic selection statistics to dense genome scans of Tibetans and Andeans and found EGLN1 (PHD2) under positive selection in both populations, with different patterns of variation in each.
modern.quality: Second independent prior for EGLN1 at altitude, from a second highland population and a second research group, published 9 September 2010. No Ayurvedic content. With Simonson 2010 it bounds the claim that can be made for Aggarwal 2010.

modern.title: Determinants of prakriti, the human constitution types of Indian traditional medicine and its correlation with contemporary science.
modern.establishes: Rotti et al. (Manipal University with SDM College of Ayurveda, Udupi) describe the cross-sectional, multicentre prakriti assessment of 3,416 healthy non-smoking, non-alcoholic male volunteers aged 20-30, assessed both by Ayurvedic physicians and by a computer-aided tool, with 80% concordance and kappa 0.77 between physician and software, and report association of dominant prakriti with BMI and place of birth.
modern.quality: This is the screening cohort behind both Govindaraj 2015 and Rotti 2015, which matters for the replication question: those two studies draw on the same 3,416 subjects and are not independent cohorts. The kappa of 0.77 is physician-versus-software on one protocol, not inter-physician agreement, and the BMI association is cross-sectional. Male-only by design.

modern.title: Immunophenotyping of normal individuals classified on the basis of human dosha prakriti.
modern.establishes: Rotti et al. ran flow-cytometry immunophenotyping (CD3, CD4, CD8, CD14, CD25, CD56, CD69, CD71, HLA-DR) on whole blood from 222 healthy subjects grouped as kapha (95), pitta (57) and vata (70), and report differences at p < 0.05 in CD14, CD25 and CD56, with CD25 and CD56 higher in kapha.
modern.quality: A pilot by the authors' own description. Nine markers, three groups, a p < 0.05 threshold with Bonferroni or Mann-Whitney corrections stated but not detailed in the abstract, and a closing sentence that reads a higher CD25/CD56 in kapha as 'in conformity with textual references', which is interpretation. It is a prakriti-stratified molecular measurement from a group other than IGIB, which is why it is here; it is not a replication of any earlier finding.

modern.title: DNA methylation analysis of phenotype specific stratified Indian population.
modern.establishes: Rotti et al. (Manipal) performed MeDIP microarray DNA-methylation analysis on whole-blood DNA of 147 healthy males aged 20-30 of defined prakriti, drawn from the 3,416-subject screen, and report prakriti-specific differentially methylated regions with bisulfite validation of promoter or 5'-UTR CpGs in LHX1 (vata), SOX11 (pitta) and CDH22 (kapha), the last also associated with BMI.
modern.quality: The study the critic named as possibly independent replication. Checked: it is from Manipal, not IGIB or TRISUTRA, but it is not an independent cohort, because its 147 subjects come from the same 3,416-subject screening as Govindaraj 2015, on which Rotti is a co-author. It also measures a different layer (methylation, not expression or SNPs), so it is a new prakriti-stratified molecular finding, not a replication of Prasher 2008 or Govindaraj 2015. Male-only, single age band, and the CDH22-BMI association raises the question whether some 'prakriti' signal is a BMI signal, which the design cannot separate.

modern.title: Ayurgenomics for stratified medicine: TRISUTRA consortium initiative across ethnically and geographically diverse Indian populations.
modern.establishes: The TRISUTRA consortium report describes the assembly of five genetically homogeneous cohorts across Indian populations, prakriti evaluation in more than 7,500 individuals, the identification of objective phenotyping parameters (anthropometry, skin biophysics, heart rate variability, spirometry, gustometry), and exome differences in 28 SNPs of 11 FDA-relevant pharmacogenomic genes between prakriti types.
modern.quality: A consortium description and interim report, classified as a review, not a hypothesis-testing study. It is the most serious attempt to standardise prakriti phenotyping and is valuable for that, but the SNP result is reported without multiple-comparison detail and the objective parameters were identified rather than validated against dosha assignment.

modern.title: Western Indian Rural Gut Microbial Diversity in Extreme Prakriti Endo-Phenotypes Reveals Signature Microbes.
modern.establishes: Chauhan et al. (TRISUTRA/IGIB with Maharshi Dayanand University) profiled gut microbiomes by 16S rRNA sequencing in three predominant prakriti groups from one genetically homogeneous western Indian rural cohort, found Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes dominant with a similar trend across groups, and report differential abundance of some core-microbiome species between prakriti types, with sex-specific signature taxa.
modern.quality: The first of the prakriti-microbiome studies and the one the critic named. Its own headline is that overall composition is uniform across prakriti and that the differences are in the abundance of particular taxa; a 16S study in a single rural cohort, with diet, which is the dominant known driver of gut microbiome composition and is itself prescribed by prakriti in Ayurvedic practice, not separable from the typing in this design. Neither of the two later Indian microbiome studies listed here used the same phenotyping protocol, so there is no replication of specific taxa across cohorts.

modern.title: Exploring the signature gut and oral microbiome in individuals of specific Ayurveda prakriti.
modern.establishes: Shalin et al. (Ramaiah Indic Specialty Ayurveda Restoration Hospital, Bangalore) analysed buccal and faecal bacterial metagenomes from 272 healthy individuals of predominant prakriti, found a shared core (Prevotella, Bacteroides, Dialister in gut), and report prakriti-specific signatures such as Paraprevotella and Christensenellaceae in vata individuals.
modern.quality: Larger than Chauhan 2018 and from an unconnected group, but the abstract's inference that microbes unique to each prakriti have 'functional roles similar to the physiological characteristics of various prakritis as described in Ayurveda' is a post hoc narrative match, not a tested prediction. No DOI is carried in the PubMed ArticleIdList for this record, so none is asserted. Included to document that the microbiome tranche exists and that its studies do not yet share a protocol or a replicated taxon.

modern.title: Plasma metabolomics reveal the correlation of metabolic pathways and Prakritis of humans.
modern.establishes: Shirolkar et al. (NRIBAS Pune, a CCRAS institute) ran untargeted plasma metabolomics (RRLC-ESI-QTOF-MS) on 38 healthy males of dominant prakriti, built a PLS-DA model with 97.87% recognition, and after FDR correction report 76 metabolites differing at p < 0.05 with fold-change > 2, with pathway analysis assigning catecholamine and arachidonic acid processes to vata, branched-chain amino acid and androgen processes to pitta, and aromatic amino acid, sphingolipid and pyrimidine processes to kapha.
modern.quality: Thirty-eight men, three groups, and a supervised discriminant model whose 97.87% recognition is a training-set figure: PLS-DA on high-dimensional metabolomic data with n = 38 will separate almost any labelling unless cross-validated, and the abstract reports no cross-validation or permutation test of the model. The pathway-to-dosha narrative (catecholamines to vata, and so on) is the Hankey-style correlate move at the metabolite level. Included as the representative of the prakriti-metabolomics literature the critic asked for, and as an example of why that literature does not yet move the evidence state.

modern.title: Reliability of Ayurvedic Diagnosis for Knee Osteoarthritis Patients: A Nested Diagnostic Study Within a Randomized Controlled Trial.
modern.establishes: Chance-corrected inter-rater agreement among four Ayurvedic experts for prakriti and agni fell between kappa 0 and 0.4 in 30 knee osteoarthritis patients, despite 95% consensus agreement on the final diagnosis.
modern.quality: Small but empirical and chance-corrected, and the most direct available test of whether the tridosha assignment is reproducible between trained clinicians. The answer it gives is that constitutional assignment is not reliably reproducible, which undercuts every downstream study that treats prakriti as a measured variable.

modern.title: Correlation of prakriti diagnosis using AyuSoft prakriti diagnostic tool with clinician rating in patients with psychiatric disorders.
modern.establishes: Agreement between the AyuSoft prakriti tool and two Ayurveda physicians in 112 psychiatric patients: ICC 0.72 for vata, 0.58 for pitta, 0.44 for kapha.
modern.quality: Adequate sample, straightforward analysis, but tests only tool-versus-clinician consistency within one setting. The kapha value is weak. The paper's conclusion that the tool is 'comparable to clinical diagnosis' is a more generous reading than the coefficients support.

modern.title: Development of a reliable Dosha self-assessment questionnaire.
modern.establishes: Developed a 39-item dosha self-assessment questionnaire, with the authors stating that no previously published open-source questionnaire had been shown reliable for self-assessment.
modern.quality: Item-analysis-driven instrument development on convenience samples. Establishes internal consistency and repeat-response behaviour, not validity. Chiefly useful as documentation of the authors' own assessment that the field's most basic measurement tool was still unsettled in 2022; that assessment is theirs and this record does not independently assert it.

modern.title: Towards standardization of Prakriti Evaluation: A scoping review of modern assessment tools and their psychometric properties in Ayurvedic medicine.
modern.establishes: Gupta et al. (IIT Delhi) scoping review of 32 studies of prakriti assessment tools: of 16 questionnaire studies three were validated, six had established reliability and three had both; of five algorithmic studies three used validated machine-learning models; of 11 device studies one device was validated with accessible data.
modern.quality: One of the two systematic-style reviews of prakriti assessment the critic asked for. Scoping method (Arksey and O'Malley), so no quality-weighted synthesis, but it is the named search that lets this record say something bounded about the instrument literature rather than nothing. Its own closing judgement is that questionnaires are the most validated tools 'despite their limited psychometric robustness' and that no device has been appropriately validated.

modern.title: Prakriti (constitutional typology) in Ayurveda: a critical review of Prakriti assessment tools and their scientific validity.
modern.establishes: Venkatesh et al. searched PubMed, Scopus and Cochrane in November 2024 for ('Prakriti') AND ('Ayurveda' OR 'Ayurvedic'), screened 635 plus 12 citation-found articles to 94 included studies, and identified 64 unique prakriti assessment tools published 1987-2024, of which 20 underwent any validation and two (CCRAS-PAS software and the ACPI scale) met seven of nine Boateng scale-development criteria; 32 categories of measurable correlates have been studied, only five of them with validated tools; most tools lacked dimensionality testing, test-retest reliability and testing across populations.
modern.quality: The most useful single paper for the measurement question, because it names its search and its criteria, which is what this record needs before it can make any bounded negative statement about validated instruments. Narrative review with systematic elements (SANRA), so inclusion judgements are the authors'. Its finding that only five of 32 correlate categories were studied with validated tools is the bound on the whole biomarker literature above: most of the molecular, microbiome and metabolomic work was done with unvalidated phenotyping.

modern.title: A test of the systems analysis underlying the scientific theory of Ayurveda's Tridosha.
modern.establishes: Hankey proposes that vata, pitta and kapha correspond to systems-analysis categories of input/output, turnover and storage, and argues from the universality of coenzyme A that these are evolutionary invariants, making the doshas universal properties of living organisms.
modern.quality: An editorial and theoretical argument, indexed as Editorial and Review, with no data of its own. It is speculation by analogy, and the coenzyme A argument does not test the dosha identification in any way that could have come out otherwise. Included here as a representative example of the theoretical-correlate literature, not as evidence.

modern.title: Ayurvedic genomics: establishing a genetic basis for mind-body typologies.
modern.establishes: Patwardhan and Bodeker's narrative review 'Ayurvedic genomics', the standard framing citation for the field, argues for a genetic basis to prakriti typologies, building on the earlier report of HLA allele correlations with prakriti type and drawing a parallel to Traditional Chinese Medicine typing.
modern.quality: Narrative review with no primary data; restates a small earlier HLA association as proof of concept. The HLA-prakriti finding it rests on has not been robustly replicated. Typical of the genre in which a preliminary correlation is repeated until it reads as established. This entry was present in the gathered record without the authors' names, which is why the critic listed it as missing; the names are now given.

records.title: Vega dharana: suppressible and non-suppressible urges
records.summary: Charaka devotes a whole Sutrasthana chapter to the proposition that certain bodily urges, once they have arisen, should not be voluntarily held back, and that a different class of urges should be held back. Thirteen physical urges are named as adharaniya (not to be suppressed): urine, faeces, semen, flatus, vomiting, sneezing, eructation, yawning, hunger, thirst, tears, sleep and laboured breathing after exertion. For each, the text names the disorders that suppression is said to produce and a treatment for those disorders. A second and opposite list, the dharaniya vegas, comprises mental and moral impulses (greed, grief, fear, anger, pride, shamelessness, envy, excessive attachment, and impulses of harsh, false or untimely speech, of harming others, of theft and of illicit sexual congress) which should be restrained. The chapter then continues into exercise in due measure and moderation generally, so the underlying principle is presented as one of non-obstruction of natural physiological flows combined with restraint of the mind. Sushruta treats the same thirteen urges in Uttaratantra 55 under the disease name udavarta, adding a fourteenth type arising from unwholesome food and drink, and also names suppression of urges as a cause and a thing to avoid in individual Chikitsasthana chapters. Vagbhata (Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 4) opens his chapter on the non-production of disease with the same instruction; his list verse names thirteen urges but includes cough and omits eructation, which he then treats separately, so he covers fourteen.
records.evidenceState: Scope first: the modern literature for this record was searched in PubMed only, through NCBI eutils queries, with Europe PMC used to verify each item and, on 2026-10-06, to locate the three additions below. DHARA (Digital Helpline for Ayurveda Research Articles), the AYUSH Research Portal and the Clinical Trials Registry of India were not searched, and several Indian Ayurvedic journals are incompletely indexed in PubMed, so every statement of absence here means absent from PubMed as searched, not absent from the world. Within that scope: the classical text is unusually specific and the PubMed-indexed Ayurvedic evaluation of it is close to nil, while two of its thirteen physical claims coincide with mainstream clinical knowledge arrived at independently. Charaka's chapter is the most operationally detailed preventive doctrine in the corpus: thirteen named urges, a named syndrome for each, and a named treatment for each, with a mirror list of mental and moral urges to be restrained; Sushruta (Uttaratantra 55) names the same thirteen as types of udavarta and Vagbhata (Su 4) covers fourteen. Of the thirteen physical claims, two have modern counterparts. For stool: one small randomised crossover experiment in healthy adults (Klauser 1990) shows voluntary withholding alone slows colonic transit, and the Rome IV paediatric literature treats withholding as central to functional constipation, though as a perpetuating response rather than an origin. For urine: the paediatric urology literature (Koff 1998) associates dysfunctional elimination, which includes infrequent voiding, with breakthrough infection in children with reflux, and one cross-sectional adult survey (Reynolds 2019) associates limiting restroom use with urgency and incontinence; neither isolates postponement as a cause in a healthy tract. Sneeze suppression has a documented mechanism of harm through case reports of barotrauma, which is not Charaka's named syndrome. For the remaining ten urges (semen, flatus, vomiting, eructation, yawning, hunger, thirst, tears, sleep, post-exertional breathing) the searches found no PubMed-indexed study testing whether suppression causes the named disorders, and several of the claimed consequences (giddiness or delirium from suppressed weeping, gulma from suppressed breathing) have no obvious modern reading. The Ayurveda-specific items found in PubMed are one 1981 paper whose methods cannot be assessed from the available record and one 2019 protocol without results. No PubMed-indexed study of the doctrine as a whole, no instrument for measuring vega suppression, and no test of the vata-obstruction mechanism were found. The honest position is that two of the thirteen physical claims have independent support of modest quality, one has case-report support for a different harm than the one named, and ten are untested classical assertions so far as PubMed shows; the coincidence on urine and stool does not transfer credibility to the rest of the list, and the unsearched Indian databases could change the Ayurveda-specific picture.

contested.question: Does suppressing urges cause disease, or does disease cause the suppression?
positions: Charaka treats suppression as the originating cause, with the disorders following from obstructed vata; Sushruta Uttaratantra 55 states the same mechanism explicitly.

The paediatric constipation literature reverses this: painful defaecation comes first and withholding is the learned response that perpetuates it. In the urological literature, dysfunctional voiding involves sphincter dyssynergia that is not simply voluntary postponement, and in Koff 1998 infrequent voiding is one part of a composite syndrome in children who already have reflux.

Klauser 1990 cuts across both: in twelve healthy adults with no antecedent pain or disease, one week of deliberate withholding slowed colonic transit, which is the direction Charaka asserts. It shows suppression can initiate constipation-like change in the short term; it does not show that this becomes disease, so neither direction excludes the other.

contested.question: Is shukra vega (semen) genuinely non-suppressible?
positions: Charaka lists it among the thirteen (Su 7.3, retas) and treats it as a physical urge like urination, with sexual congress among the remedies (7.11). Sushruta Ut 55 and Vagbhata AH Su 4.1 and 4.19-21 do the same; Vagbhata's remedies include 'priyah striyah', agreeable women.

Charaka's own mirror list in the same chapter requires suppression of the urge to stri-bhoga where it harms others (7.29), Vagbhata's mirror list (4.24) names raga (attachment) among urges to be held, and Charaka Sutrasthana 11 makes brahmacharya one of the three supports of the body. The passages retrieved qualify the suppressible urge as illicit or harmful rather than as sexual desire as such, which may dissolve the tension, but no retrieved passage states the reconciliation and the commentaries were not retrieved. Modern Ayurvedic writing generally sidesteps this.

contested.question: Is the list thirteen items long, and is it the same across Charaka, Sushruta and Vagbhata?
positions: Charaka names thirteen adharaniya vegas (Su 7.3-4), and Sushruta's enumeration, retrieved for this revision from Bhishagratna's Uttaratantra 55 sections 2-4, names the same thirteen in a different order and calls the resulting disorders thirteen types of udavarta. On the passages retrieved, the two lists match item for item.

Sushruta adds a fourteenth udavarta from unwholesome food (apathyaja), so his chapter has fourteen types though thirteen urges. Vagbhata's list verse (AH Su 4.1) also has thirteen items but a different thirteen: kasa (cough) is in and udgara (eructation) is out, and he then treats eructation anyway at 4.8, so his chapter covers fourteen urges. 'Thirteen' is therefore stable between Charaka and Sushruta and not a fixed feature of the tradition.

contested.question: Are the mental urges to be suppressed a medical doctrine or an ethical one?
positions: They appear in a medical chapter with the physical urges, use the same verb (dharayet) with the sign reversed, and Vagbhata keeps the pairing (AH Su 4.24). Charaka 7.52 later attributes mental disturbances of the same kind to prajnaparadha, which is a medical category.

The stated reward (7.30) is dharma, artha and kama, and the list (theft, untruth, adultery, violence) is a moral code. Reading it as psychosomatic medicine imports a modern frame the text does not use, but reading it as purely ethical ignores its placement.

contested.question: Is udavarta the classical umbrella name for all disorders of suppressed urges?
positions: In Sushruta Uttaratantra 55 it is exactly that: thirteen types of udavarta named from the thirteen urges, with a general treatment rule for all of them.

In Charaka Su 7 the word does not occur in the retrieved Sanskrit; the disorders are named urge by urge without an umbrella term. In Vagbhata AH Su 4.2 udavarta is one consequence of suppressing flatus only. Treating udavarta as the general classical name, as this record's earlier version did, follows Sushruta's usage and should be attributed to him.

notKnown: Whether suppressing the urge to ejaculate (shukra vega) causes any of the disorders Charaka Su 7.10 names (genital pain, languor, heart pain, urinary retention). No PubMed-indexed study found; DHARA, AYUSH Research Portal and CTRI not searched. The 2019 protocol in this record measures prevalence of the behaviour, not harm.
Whether suppressing flatus causes the obstruction, retention and abdominal vata disorders of Su 7.12. No PubMed-indexed study found.
Whether suppressing the urge to vomit causes the skin, fever and nausea syndrome of Su 7.14. No PubMed-indexed study found.
Whether suppressing eructation causes the hiccup, dyspnoea, tremor and chest-obstruction syndrome of Su 7.18. No PubMed-indexed study found.
Whether suppressing a yawn causes the convulsion, numbness and tremor syndrome of Su 7.19. No PubMed-indexed study found.

Whether deferring food when hungry produces the leanness, weakness, discolouration and giddiness of Su 7.20 in any dose short of starvation, which is a different question from the one the text asks. No PubMed-indexed study framed as urge suppression found.

Whether deferring drink when thirsty produces the deafness, exhaustion and heart pain of Su 7.21, as distinct from the dry mouth and throat, which are the definition of thirst. No PubMed-indexed study framed as urge suppression found.

Whether suppressing tears causes the catarrh, eye disease, heart disease and giddiness or delirium of Su 7.22. No PubMed-indexed study found; the psychology literature on emotional suppression was not searched and would be about a different construct.

Whether resisting sleep when sleepy causes the syndrome of Su 7.23 as distinct from sleep deprivation generally, which has a large literature that was not searched because it does not frame the exposure as suppression of an arisen urge.
Whether holding the breath after exertion causes gulma, heart disease or loss of consciousness (Su 7.24). No PubMed-indexed study found.

The incidence of mechanical injury from sneeze suppression, known only from scattered case reports, and whether the wry neck, headache and facial paralysis Charaka names (Su 7.16) ever follow it. No study found.

Whether voluntary postponement of urination in a healthy adult causes infection or retention. The paediatric evidence (Koff 1998) is in children with reflux and bundles infrequent voiding with other dysfunction; the adult evidence (Reynolds 2019) is cross-sectional and about symptoms. No prospective or experimental study of postponement alone was found.

Whether the one-week slowing of colonic transit produced by deliberate stool withholding (Klauser 1990) progresses to clinical constipation with continued withholding, and whether it reverses when withholding stops. Not studied in the retrieved literature.
How much suppression, and for how long, would be required to produce harm for any urge. The texts specify only that the urge must have arisen (jata; Kaviratna 'become pronounced').
Whether harm from suppression, where it exists, is reversible by the treatments Charaka names or by any treatment. No study found.
Whether there is any measurable marker of vega suppression or of udavarta. No instrument was found in PubMed.
Whether the vata-obstruction mechanism, stated explicitly in Sushruta Ut 55.19, corresponds to anything measurable. It has not been operationalised in any study found.
Whether suppressing the mental urges on the dharaniya list has any health effect, as opposed to a social or ethical one. Not studied as such.

Whether DHARA, the AYUSH Research Portal or CTRI hold Ayurvedic studies or registered trials on vega dharana. All three were reachable on 2026-10-06 but were not searched; the record's statements of absence are statements about PubMed.

The Sanskrit verse numbers of the Sushruta Uttaratantra 55 and Chikitsasthana 6 and 9 passages quoted. Bhishagratna prints only his own section numbers, and no Sanskrit edition of Sushruta was retrieved.

Whether Vagbhata's inclusion of cough and omission of eructation from his list verse (AH Su 4.1) reflects a textual tradition or his own arrangement, and whether any commentary (Arunadatta, Hemadri on Vagbhata; Chakrapani on Charaka) reconciles the shukra vega tension. No commentary was retrieved.

Whether Kaviratna's renderings of Su 7.14 as 'phlegmatic evacuations' and 7.18 as 'the tendency to vomit' rest on a variant reading in his base text. The retrieved e-text reads chhardi and udgara with no variant noted; Kaviratna's base edition was not identified.
Whether Charaka treats udavarta as a named disease elsewhere (secondary literature points to Chikitsasthana 26). Not retrieved; this record establishes only that the word is absent from Su 7.

components.gloss: Urine. Suppression is said to cause inflammation of the bladder and penis, painful micturition, headache, bending forward at micturition, inflammation of the pubic and iliac regions, and complete retention (Charaka Su 7.6 standard numbering; Kaviratna's 4)
Faeces. Suppression is said to cause abdominal pain, obstruction of vata, retention of stool, calf pain and flatulence (Su 7.8; Kaviratna's 6)
Semen. Suppression is said to cause pain in the penis and testes, bodily languor, pain in the heart and retention of urine (Su 7.10; Kaviratna's 8)
Flatus. Suppression is said to cause obstruction of wind, retention of urine and stool, flatulence, languor and other vata disorders of the abdomen (Su 7.12; Kaviratna's 10)

Vomiting. Suppression is said (Su 7.14, chhardi-nigraha) to cause itching, urticaria, loss of appetite, facial discolouration, swelling, pandu, fever, kushtha, nausea and visarpa. Kaviratna renders the urge in this verse (his 12) as 'phlegmatic evacuations', not vomiting; the retrieved Sanskrit reads chhardi
Sneezing. Suppression is said to cause wry neck, headache, facial paralysis, hemicrania and weakness of the senses (Su 7.16; Kaviratna's 14)

Eructation (belching). Suppression is said (Su 7.18, udgara-nigraha) to cause hiccup, dyspnoea, loss of appetite, tremor and obstruction of heart and chest. Kaviratna renders the urge in this verse (his 16) as 'the tendency to vomit' and shvasa as 'consumption'; the retrieved Sanskrit reads udgara and shvasa
Yawning. Suppression is said to cause bending, convulsion, contraction, numbness, tremor and shaking (Su 7.19; Kaviratna's 17)
Hunger. Suppression is said to cause leanness, weakness, loss of colour, bodily ache, loss of appetite and giddiness (Su 7.20; Kaviratna's 18)
Thirst. Suppression is said to dry the throat and mouth and to cause deafness, exhaustion, faintness and pain in the heart (Su 7.21; Kaviratna's 19)

Tears. Suppression is said to cause nasal catarrh, eye disease, heart disease, loss of appetite and giddiness (Kaviratna: delirium); the remedies given are sleep, wine and agreeable conversation (Su 7.22; Kaviratna's 20)
Sleep. Suppression is said to cause yawning, bodily languor, sleepiness, headache and heaviness of the eyes; the remedy is sleep and gentle rubbing of the limbs (Su 7.23; Kaviratna's 21)

Laboured breathing induced by exertion. Suppression is said to cause gulma (abdominal lumps), heart disease and loss of consciousness; the remedy is rest and anti-vata treatment (Su 7.24; Kaviratna's 22)

Ill-regulated courage or rashness; all fruitless impulses of thought, word and deed; greed, grief, fear, wrath, pride, shamelessness, envy, excessive attachment and covetousness; harshness, excessive, insinuating, untruthful or untimely speech; bodily acts that harm others, named as illicit sexual congress, theft and violence (Su 7.26-29; Kaviratna's 24-27). Vagbhata's parallel (AH Su 4.24) names greed, envy, hatred, malice and attachment

Sushruta's name (Uttaratantra 55) for the group of disorders produced by suppressed urges: thirteen types from the thirteen urges plus a fourteenth from unwholesome food and drink. The word does not occur in the retrieved Sanskrit of Charaka Su 7, which names the disorders urge by urge without an umbrella term. In Vagbhata (AH Su 4.2) udavarta appears only as one of the consequences of suppressing flatus

For each suppressed urge Charaka names a treatment, typically sudation, oleation, immersion, evacuative procedures and anti-vata measures. Sushruta (Ut 55.19 in Bhishagratna's sectioning) states the general rule explicitly: first restore the deranged vayu to its normal course, then treat each type specifically. Both texts conceive the disorders as obstructed vata reversed by restoring flow

Ashtanga Hridaya Su 4.1 includes cough among the urges not to be suppressed and 4.13 gives its syndrome (aggravation of the cough, dyspnoea, loss of appetite, heart disease, wasting, hiccup). Cough is not on Charaka's or Sushruta's list in the passages retrieved

classical.chapter: 7 (Navegandharaniya; Kaviratna's Lesson VII, 'the inadvisability of suppressing the urgings of nature')
classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed numbers 1 and 3 (a '2' is not legible in the scan; his 1 closes after the first six urges and his 3 after 'pronounced forms'). Standard (Trikamji) numbering 1-5, read separately from a retrieved Sanskrit e-text. The two numberings are recorded side by side and neither is claimed to verify the other.
classical.establishes: The canonical list of thirteen non-suppressible urges in a lawfully quotable translation, with the qualifier 'that have become pronounced' (Sanskrit jatan, 'arisen'). The doctrine is about urges that have actually arisen, not about scheduling.
classical.quote: We shall now expound the lesson on the inadvisability of suppressing the urgings of nature. Thus said the illustrious son of Atri. One endued with intelligence should not suppress urgings, that have become pronounced, in respect of urine and faeces; as also of the semen and the wind, and of vomitting and sneezing. The urgings also in respect of eructations, of yawns, of hunger and of thirst, of tears, of sleep, and of heavy breathing induced by toil (should not to be suppressed). Listen now to me as I discourse (to you) on the topic of treating the several diseases that are generated of the person who suppresses the urgings of these when they appear in pronounced forms.

classical.verse: Sanskrit verses 3-5 in the standard numbering, from the Charak Samhita Online e-text (the critic's own citation 'Su 7.3-4' uses the same numbering); not independently checked against a printed Trikamji edition
classical.establishes: The thirteen urges in their original terms (mutra, purisha, retas, vata, chhardi, kshavathu, udgara, jrimbha, kshut, pipasa, bashpa, nidra, nihshvasa with shrama) and the standard verse numbers against which Kaviratna's printed numbers are recorded. Confirms that the list verse reads chhardi (vomiting) and udgara (eructation), which matters for Kaviratna's renderings of 7.14 and 7.18.
classical.quote: न वेगान् धारयेद्धीमाञ्जातान् मूत्रपुरीषयोः| न रेतसो न वातस्य न छर्द्याः क्षवथोर्न च||३|| नोद्गारस्य न जृम्भाया न वेगान् क्षुत्पिपासयोः| न बाष्पस्य न निद्राया निःश्वासस्य श्रमेण च||४|| एतान् धारयतो जातान् वेगान् रोगा भवन्ति ये| पृथक्पृथक्चिकित्सार्थं तान्मे निगदतः शृणु||५||
classical.translator: none; Sanskrit original, out of copyright

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed numbers 4-6 (the quote ends at his 6; his 7, the stool treatment, is not quoted). Standard numbering 6-8.
classical.establishes: The structure of the chapter: for each urge, a named syndrome and a named treatment. The urinary syndrome described is clinically recognisable as the consequence of habitual voiding postponement.
classical.quote: By suppressing the call of urine, inflammation sets in of the bladder and the membrum virile. The other consequences are strangury or painful micturition, headache, bending forward at the time of micturition, inflammation of the pubic and iliac regions, and epistasis or suppression of urine. When retention of urine takes place, (the inducing of) perspiration, immersion (of the patient) in cool water, rubbing the body with oil, (the use of) clarified butter as snuff, and the three processes of evacuation, are the remedies that should be adopted. By suppressing (the call for) stools, pain in the abdomen, obstruction of the wind, suppression of stools, pain in the calf of the leg, and flatulence, are induced.

classical.verse: Sanskrit verses 14 and 18 in the standard numbering (Kaviratna's 12 and 16)
classical.establishes: That 7.14 is the vomiting (chhardi) syndrome and 7.18 the eructation (udgara) syndrome. Kaviratna labels 7.14 'suppressing phlegmatic evacuations' and 7.18 'suppressing the tendency to vomit', so a reader of his translation alone would attach the wrong syndromes to these two urges. Recorded so that the translator's rendering is not absorbed as doctrine.
classical.quote: कण्डूकोठारुचिव्यङ्गशोथपाण्ड्वामयज्वराः| कुष्ठहृल्लासवीसर्पाश्छर्दिनिग्रहजा गदाः||१४|| ... हिक्का श्वासोऽरुचिः कम्पो विबन्धो हृदयोरसोः| उद्गारनिग्रहात्तत्र हिक्कायास्तुल्यमौषधम्||१८||
classical.translator: none; Sanskrit original, out of copyright

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed numbers 20-23 (the scan shows '22' twice; the second is read as 23). Standard numbering 22-25.
classical.establishes: That the list is not confined to excretory functions: weeping, sleep and post-exertional breathing are treated as urges on the same footing, with the same reasoning. Kaviratna's 'delirium' for bhrama (7.22) is his rendering; the Sanskrit word more usually means giddiness. 'Faintness' in the breath verse has no counterpart in the retrieved Sanskrit of 7.24, which names gulma, hridroga and sammoha.
classical.quote: By suppressing tears, cattarrh in the nose, eye-diseases, heart-disease, loss of appetite, and delirium are induced. In these disorders, sleep, wines, and agreeable conversation are the remedies prescribed. Yawns, langour of body, sleepiness, headache, and heaviness of the eye-lids, are induced by suppression of sleep. In these disorders the remedy is sleep and gentle chafing of the limbs. Abdominal tumours, heart-disease, loss of consciousness, and faintness are born of suppression of breath. In these, rest, and all kinds of treatment that are destructive of disorders of the wind, are beneficial. If one desires that the disorders mentioned above, that are born of suppressing the calls of Nature, should not arise, one should not suppress those calls.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed numbers 24-28 (the scan prints '26' and '28-27' irregularly; read as 24, 25, 26-27, 28). Standard numbering 26-30.
classical.establishes: The mirror list. The doctrine is symmetrical and explicitly moral: physical flows must not be blocked, mental and moral impulses must be. The stated payoff is fame, merit, wealth and pleasure, not physical health, which shows the chapter is doing ethical as well as medical work.
classical.quote: One desirous of one's good both here and hereafter should suppress these impulses also, viz., those of (ill-regulated) courage and all fruitless impulses of thought, word, and deed. The man of intelligence should also suppress the impulses of cupidity, grief, fear, wrath, pride, shamelessness, envy, violent propensities of every kind, and covetousness. One should also suppress the rising impulses of harshness, of doing anything that is disagreeable to others, of untruthfulness of speech, of speech that is inopportune, of whatever tendencies that exist for giving pain to others, of sexual congress, of appropriating the property of others, and of all wrongful propensities. Through sinlessness of thought, word, and deed, a person earns righteous fame, and lives happily, acquiring and enjoying religious merit, wealth, and (sources of) pleasure.

classical.verse: Sanskrit verses 26-30 in the standard numbering (Kaviratna's 24-28)
classical.establishes: The dharaniya vegas in the original: the same verb (dharayet, 'should hold back') that 7.3 negates is here affirmed, so the two lists are formally one doctrine with opposite signs. The mental urges named are lobha, shoka, bhaya, krodha, mana, nairlajjya, irshya, atiraga, abhidhya; the speech urges are parusha, atimatra, suchaka, anrita and akalayukta; the bodily urges are stri-bhoga (sexual indulgence), steya and himsa, qualified by para-pida (harm to others). 7.30 names dharma, artha and kama as the payoff.
classical.quote: इमांस्तु धारयेद्वेगान् हितार्थी प्रेत्य चेह च| साहसानामशस्तानां मनोवाक्कायकर्मणाम्||२६|| लोभशोकभयक्रोधमानवेगान् विधारयेत्| नैर्लज्ज्येर्ष्यातिरागाणामभिध्यायाश्च बुद्धिमान्||२७|| परुषस्यातिमात्रस्य सूचकस्यानृतस्य च| वाक्यस्याकालयुक्तस्य धारयेद्वेगमुत्थितम्||२८|| देहप्रवृत्तिर्या काचिद्विद्यते परपीडया| स्त्रीभोगस्तेयहिंसाद्या तस्यावेगान्विधारयेत्||२९|| पुण्यशब्दो विपापत्वान्मनोवाक्कायकर्मणाम्| धर्मार्थकामान् पुरुषः सुखी भुङ्क्ते चिनोति च||३०||
classical.translator: none; Sanskrit original, out of copyright

classical.verse: Kaviratna's printed numbers 29-32. Standard numbering 31-34.
classical.establishes: That the vega chapter continues directly into a general doctrine of moderation, which is the unifying idea: neither obstruct what the body is doing nor drive it past measure.
classical.quote: That exertion of body which is productive of good consequences (to the body itself), which conduces to collectedness (of mind), and increases strength, is called physical exercise. One should have recourse to it in due measure. The consequences resulting from physical exercise are lightness of body, capacity for work, collectedness, power of enduring hardship, removal of all imperfections, and augmentation of the digestive fire. From excess of physical exercise result fatigue, faintness, loss of vigor, thirst, asthma, consumption, fever, and attacks of cold. An intelligent person should never indulge in physical exercise, laughter, talking, walking, sexual congress, and night-keeping, to excess even when these become necessary.

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section numbers 1 and 2-4. Bhishagratna prints his own section numbers only, not Sanskrit verse numbers; the Sanskrit verse numbers were not retrieved and are not claimed.
classical.establishes: Sushruta's own enumeration, which this record previously said had not been retrieved. The thirteen urges are the same thirteen as Charaka's (flatus, stool, urine, yawning, tears, sneezing, eructation, vomiting, semen, hunger, thirst, breathing, sleep), in a different order, and Sushruta adds a fourteenth udavarta from unwholesome food. Sushruta gives the material a dedicated chapter after all, in the Uttaratantra rather than the Sutrasthana, and frames it as a disease (udavarta) rather than as regimen.
classical.quote: Now we shall discourse on the chapter which deals with the (symptoms and) medical treatment of the disease due to the retention of any natural physical urging (Udavarta-Pratishedha). Causes: A wise man valuing his life shall never repress any natural urging of his body, whether upward or downward, e.g. that of Vayu, etc. Udavarta is so called from its origin from the repression of any natural urging such as Vata (flatus), evacuation of bowels, micturition, yawning, lacrimation, sneezing, eructation, vomiting and discharge of semen when it makes its appearance (Udita) and urges a person to answer its call. Udavarta is also brought on by the repression of hunger, thirst, respiration and sleep. I shall now fully describe its symptoms and the mode of medical treatment to be pursued therein. It is of thirteen different types and are brought about through the aforesaid causes, over and above the one incidental to the habitual use of unwholesome food and drink (Apathyaja).
classical.translator: Kunja Lal Bhishagratna, vol. 3 (1916), public domain

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section numbers 6, 7 and 14-17 (his numbering, not Sanskrit verse numbers)
classical.establishes: That Sushruta's per-urge syndromes largely coincide with Charaka's (compare Charaka Su 7.6, 7.8, 7.20-7.24): dry throat and deafness from thirst, gulma and heart disorder from suppressed breath after exertion, yawning and heaviness from suppressed sleep. The two texts agree on the list and broadly on the consequences; whether that is independent testimony or shared inheritance is not something the passages decide.
classical.quote: Purishaja Udavarta: A repressed urging for stool is followed by the exhibition of such symptoms, as rumbling in the intestines, severe pain (in the abdomen), cutting pain in the anus, upward coursing of the flatus, suppression of stool or even emission of feces through the mouth. Mutraja Udavarta: A repression of the desire of making water is followed by scanty emission of urine which is often given out by painful drops producing distension of the bladder and an excruciating pain in the urethra, anus, scrotum and the inguinal regions and about the umbilicus, and sometimes even in the head, accompanied with distortion of features in consequence. [...] Ungratified hunger brings on drowsiness, aching pain in the limbs, disrelish for food, sense of exhaustion, and weakness of eye-sight. An ungratified thirst brings on dryness of the throat and mouth, dulness of hearing and pain at the heart. A suppression of breath in an exhausted person brings on cardiac troubles, fainting fits and an attack of Gulma. An unindulged sleep produces yawning, aching pain in the limbs, and a sense of heaviness in the limbs as well as in the head and the eyes. It may also bring on drowsiness.
classical.translator: Kunja Lal Bhishagratna, vol. 3 (1916), public domain

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section numbers 18-19 (his numbering, not Sanskrit verse numbers)
classical.establishes: The explicit statement of the mechanism and the treatment principle: udavarta is obstructed, misdirected vayu and the first move in every case is to restore its normal course. This is the clearest classical statement of the vata-obstruction model that Charaka's chapter implies through its treatments without stating.
classical.quote: Prognosis: An Udavarta-patient afflicted with thirst and cramps (Sula), vomiting fecal matter and suffering from weakness and a distressing exhaustion should be given up by a wise physician. General Treatment: In all forms of Udavarta the preliminary treatment generally consists in restoring the deranged and incarcerated bodily Vayu to its normal course and direction. Now hear me again describe the specific medicinal remedies to be separately employed in each case.
classical.translator: Kunja Lal Bhishagratna, vol. 3 (1916), public domain

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section number 2 (his own numbering; he prints no Sanskrit verse numbers, and the Sanskrit verse number was not retrieved)
classical.establishes: Suppression of urges functioning as a routine aetiological item in Sushruta's Chikitsasthana, placed alongside dietary faults. Re-verified against the scan on 2026-10-06; the sentence that follows in the text, attributing skin disease also to sinful acts in this or a prior life, is not quoted here.
classical.quote: A cutaneous disease (Twag-dosha) originates through injudicious conduct of life such as, partaking of large quantities of unwholesome food, or taking it before the previously eaten one is digested (i.e., eating too often), indulgence in incompatible articles of fare, voluntary suppression of the natural urgings of the body, and improper application of medicated oil, clarified butter, or other lardacious articles.

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's section numbers 20-21 (his own numbering; he prints no Sanskrit verse numbers, and the Sanskrit verse numbers were not retrieved)
classical.establishes: Non-suppression appears as a standing item of therapeutic regimen, not only as prophylaxis. This is one of the places where the classical prescription (do not postpone defaecation if you have haemorrhoids) coincides with routine modern clinical advice. Re-verified against the scan on 2026-10-06.
classical.quote: Voluntary suppression of any natural urgings of the body, sexual intercourse, riding on horse-back, etc., sitting on the legs and such diets as would aggravate the Doshas, should be avoided in cases of haemorrhoids.

classical.chapter: 4 (roganutpadaniya-adhyaya, 'on the non-production of disease'; chapter title from the wisdomlib Sanskrit chapter index, chapter number and verses from the GRETIL e-text)
classical.verse: 1-2, 22, 24 (GRETIL e-text numbering, Das and Emmerick transcription)
classical.establishes: Vagbhata opens the chapter on the non-production of disease with the non-suppression rule, placed fourth in the Sutrasthana immediately after the daily (2) and seasonal (3) regimens, which is the clearest structural statement anywhere that vega dharana is preventive doctrine.
