His list verse names thirteen urges but the set differs from Charaka's: kasa (cough) is in and udgara (eructation) is not, though 4.8 then gives eructation its own syndrome, so the chapter treats fourteen urges. 4.22 generalises: diseases arise from both forcing (udirana) and suppressing (dharana) urges. 4.24 is the dharaniya mirror, naming lobha, irshya, dvesha, matsarya and raga. Udavarta appears at 4.2 as a consequence of suppressing flatus, not as the umbrella name.
classical.quote: vegān na dhārayed vāta-viṇ-mūtra-kṣava-tṛṭ-kṣudhām | nidrā-kāsa-śrama-śvāsa-jṛmbhāśru-cchardi-retasām || 1 || adho-vātasya rodhena gulmodāvarta-ruk-klamāḥ | vāta-mūtra-śakṛt-saṅga-dṛṣṭy-agni-vadha-hṛd-gadāḥ || 2 || ... rogāḥ sarve 'pi jāyante vegodīraṇa-dhāraṇaiḥ | nirdiṣṭaṃ sādhanaṃ tatra bhūyiṣṭhaṃ ye tu tān prati || 22 || ... dhārayet tu sadā vegān hitaiṣī pretya ceha ca | lobherṣyā-dveṣa-mātsarya-rāgādīnāṃ jitendriyaḥ || 24 ||
classical.translator: none; Sanskrit original, out of copyright. No public-domain English translation exists; none is quoted.

modern.title: Snap, crackle and pop: when sneezing leads to crackling in the neck.
modern.establishes: Yang, Sahota and Das, BMJ Case Reports. A 34-year-old man who suppressed a forceful sneeze by pinching his nose and holding his mouth closed sustained a pharyngeal perforation with cervical subcutaneous emphysema and pneumomediastinum, confirmed on CT.
modern.quality: A SINGLE CASE REPORT, the weakest study design there is. It establishes only that suppressing one specific urge by one specific mechanical method can cause a barotrauma injury. It does not establish the incidence of such injury, does not address any of the other twelve urges, does not support Charaka's named syndrome (wry neck, headache, facial paralysis), and has nothing to say about vata, udavarta or any Ayurvedic mechanism. It should be reported as a vivid illustration, not as support for the doctrine.

modern.title: Dysfunctional elimination behaviors and associated complications in school-age children.
modern.establishes: Kistner, Journal of School Nursing 25(2). Describes how school-environment factors (lack of privacy, bullying risk, limited access, dirty bathrooms) lead children to withhold urine and stool, and states that sustained withholding produces dysfunctional elimination syndrome, whose complications include urinary tract infection, vesicoureteral reflux and urinary or faecal incontinence.
modern.quality: A professional practice and advocacy article in a nursing journal, NOT primary research and not a systematic review. It reports an accepted clinical consensus rather than generating evidence. It is included because it is the closest modern statement of the same causal claim Charaka makes for mutra and purisha vega, and because that claim is clinically mainstream. But the pathophysiology given (learned voiding dysfunction, incomplete emptying, detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia) is not the Ayurvedic one.

modern.title: The relationship among dysfunctional elimination syndromes, primary vesicoureteral reflux and urinary tract infections in children.
modern.establishes: Koff, Wagner and Jayanthi, Journal of Urology 160(3 Pt 2):1019-1022. In 143 children with primary vesicoureteral reflux, dysfunctional elimination syndromes (bladder instability, constipation and infrequent voiding) were present in 43%; 82% of those children had a breakthrough urinary tract infection against 18% of children without the syndromes, reflux resolved more slowly, and surgical failures occurred only in the dysfunctional-elimination group.
modern.quality: A retrospective observational series, not a trial, and the exposure is a composite: infrequent voiding is bundled with bladder instability and constipation, so the contribution of voiding postponement on its own cannot be read off. The population is children who already have reflux, so it speaks to infection risk in an abnormal urinary tract, not to harm from postponement in a healthy one. It is the primary paediatric urology source behind the consensus that the Kistner article reports, and it is included for that reason. Verified against Europe PMC on 2026-10-06.

modern.title: Toileting Behaviors and Bladder Symptoms in Women Who Limit Restroom Use at Work: A Cross-Sectional Study.
modern.establishes: Reynolds and colleagues, Journal of Urology 202(5):1008-1014. Cross-sectional survey of 3,062 full-time working women in the United States; 11% limited restroom use at work most or all of the time, and this group reported a higher prevalence of unhealthy bladder habits, urgency, monthly urinary incontinence and infrequent voiding.
modern.quality: Cross-sectional and self-reported, so it cannot separate cause from effect, and the authors say so: they call for studies to determine whether limiting restroom use is a modifiable risk factor. It is the most direct modern item on deferred micturition in adults found by this record's searches, and it is about symptoms (urgency, incontinence), not about the infection or retention that Charaka names. Verified against Europe PMC on 2026-10-06.

modern.title: Behavioral modification of colonic function. Can constipation be learned?
modern.establishes: Klauser, Voderholzer, Heinrich, Schindlbeck and Muller-Lissner, Digestive Diseases and Sciences 35(10):1271-1275. Twelve healthy male volunteers spent one week with normal defaecation and one week voluntarily suppressing defaecation, in randomised order, under identical diet and activity. Suppression reduced bowel movements from 8.9 to 3.7 per week and stool weight from 1.30 to 0.98 kg per week, and lengthened total colonic transit from 28.8 to 53.1 hours, with increases in both rectosigmoid and right-colon segmental transit. The authors conclude that defaecation habits can induce changes in colonic function like those seen in constipation.
modern.quality: The closest thing in the retrieved literature to an experimental test of purisha vega dharana: a deliberate, randomised, within-subject suppression of a specific urge with objective outcome measures. It is small (12 men), short (one week), in healthy volunteers, and its outcomes are transit times and stool weights, not disease. It does not show that suppression leads to chronic constipation, nor whether the change reverses. What it does establish is that voluntary withholding alone, without antecedent pain or disease, slows colonic transit, which is the direction Charaka asserts and the paediatric account reverses. Verified against Europe PMC on 2026-10-06.

modern.title: The New Rome IV Criteria for Functional Gastrointestinal Disorders in Infants and Toddlers.
modern.establishes: Zeevenhooven, Koppen and Benninga, Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition 20(1):1-13. Review of Rome IV criteria stating that voluntary stool withholding, usually initiated by a painful defaecation, is considered to play an important role in the pathophysiology of functional constipation in young children, through a cycle of retention, increased water absorption, harder stool and more painful defaecation.
modern.quality: A review article, not primary research, but by authors central to the Rome criteria and reporting a mechanism that is well established in paediatric gastroenterology. It is, with Klauser 1990, the strongest modern parallel to the purisha-vega claim. Note the direction of the classical and paediatric accounts differs: Charaka treats suppression as the originating fault, while the paediatric account treats painful defaecation as the trigger and withholding as the perpetuating response.

modern.title: EVALUATION OF THE ROLE OF VEGA-VIDHARAN (SUPPRESSION OF NATURAL URGES) IN THE AETIOLOGY OF PSYCHOSOMATIC DISEASES (With special reference to voluntary retention of Urine and Neurohumoral Physiological and clinical changes in human volunteers).
modern.establishes: Tripathi, Shukla, Tiwari and Upadhya, Ancient Science of Life 1(2):83-93. The only experimental study of vega-vidharana found in PubMed by this record's searches, examining neurohumoral, biochemical and physiological changes on voluntary retention of urine in human volunteers, and concluding that the classical concept is validated.
modern.quality: This should be treated as essentially no evidence. It is a 1981 paper predating CONSORT and modern reporting standards; the PMC record retrievable gives an abstract asserting validation but no extractable methods, no stated sample size, no stated control group and no reported effect sizes. It has no DOI. No replication was found in PubMed. Its conclusion that the ancient concept is 'clearly validated' is not supportable from anything visible in the record.

modern.title: Prevalence of Shukra vega dharana in an Indian population: A cross sectional survey protocol.
modern.establishes: Tonde, Gandhi and Patil, Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine. A cross-sectional survey PROTOCOL to estimate the prevalence of shukra vega dharana (suppressed sexual urge) among married men aged 18 to 40 in three Maharashtra cities who are separated from their spouses.
modern.quality: A PROTOCOL, with no results. And even if completed it would measure prevalence of the behaviour, not harm from it. It is recorded because it is one of two vega-specific items found in PubMed by this record's searches, and because the fact that the PubMed-indexed recent output on this topic is a prevalence protocol is itself a fair summary of what PubMed holds. Whether the completed survey or other Ayurvedic work has been published in journals indexed only in DHARA or the AYUSH Research Portal was not checked.

records.title: Vikriti assessment (assessing the present deranged state)
records.summary: Vikriti is the assessment of a patient's current deranged state. Charaka defines it in one sentence, as deviation from what is normal, and sets it against prakriti as its reference point: where prakriti is what the person is by birth, vikriti is what has gone wrong now. In Charaka it is the second of the ten items of patient examination (dashavidha pariksha), and the text attaches to it a list of factors to be weighed, cause, dhatu, dosha, prakriti, place and time, together with the symptoms, by which the derangement is graded strong, middling or weak. That is the whole of what Charaka says about vikriti as such, and this record now says so plainly: the definition, the position in the list and the grading factors are quotable from a public-domain translation, but no examination procedure is attached to any of them. The procedure clinicians actually use for vikriti assessment, the eight-fold ashtavidha pariksha with pulse (nadi) and tongue (jihva) at its centre, is not in Charaka or Sushruta. The two public-domain translators of those texts both say so in their own voice, and the earliest text in which this record has located pulse examination is the Sharngadhara Samhita, Purva Khanda 3, quoted here in Sanskrit. So the quotable part of vikriti doctrine is not the operational part, and the operational part is not classical. Two adjacent doctrines give vikriti its content once a disturbed dosha is found: khavaigunya, the site defect that explains why disease lands where it does, and the sama / nirama distinction, the judgement that undigested matter (ama) is or is not bound up with the disturbed dosha, which Vagbhata makes the condition for whether the doshas may be expelled at all. Both are now cited from located verses and cross-referenced to their own records. Modern reliability measurement of pulse and tongue examination has produced chance-corrected agreement in the slight range (mean weighted kappa 0.07 and 0.17 in the one inter-rater study retrieved), which is among the lowest figures this record has encountered; no systematic comparison with other clinical assessments was made and none is claimed. Instrumented pulse acquisition and tongue-image classification exist and are cited; in the papers retrieved here the reference standard they are evaluated against is the practitioner's own judgement, which is the quantity whose reliability is in question.
records.evidenceState:
Vikriti assessment is where the gap between doctrine and measurement is widest, and this revision has had to narrow what it says about both sides.

THE CLASSICAL SIDE. What is quotable from a public-domain translation is small and definite: Charaka defines vikriti as deviation from normal, makes it the second item of the ten-fold examination whose stated purpose is 'ascertainment of the measure of strength (of the patient)', lists the factors by which the derangement's strength is graded, and gives the three grades. That is all. No procedure is attached to any of it, and the Sushruta parallel is a list of things to observe that does not use the prakriti/vikriti axis. The record previously called this basis 'clear and quotable', which was true of the definition and false of the method, and the phrase is withdrawn: the quotable part is not the operational part. The operational part, the eight-fold examination with pulse and tongue at its centre, is not in Charaka or Sushruta. Both public-domain translators say so in their own voice (Kaviratna's note at Indriya Sthana, p. 871; Bhishagratna's Introduction, p. lxvii), the project's own search of both scans finds no pulse procedure, and the earliest text in which this record has located pulse examination is Sharngadhara Samhita Purva Khanda 3, now quoted in Sanskrit from an archive.org scan. The attribution of the eight-fold list as a named set to Yogaratnakara rests on secondary literature; neither it nor Bhavaprakasha was retrieved. Two adjacent doctrines supply what Charaka's definition lacks and are now cited: khavaigunya, which explains why a disturbed dosha produces disease at one site (Su.Su. XXIV; Ca.Ci. XV; Ca.Ni. IV on the conjunction of cause, dosha and dushya), and the sama / nirama judgement, for which Vagbhata gives ten signs and a treatment rule, that sama doshas are not to be expelled until ripened (A.H.Su. 13/23-24, 27, 28-29, Sanskrit only).

THE MEASUREMENT SIDE. When pulse and tongue examination have been measured for inter-rater reliability, the one study located gives average weighted kappa 0.07 for pulse and 0.17 for tongue, with the null hypothesis of random rating not rejected for any of 105 doctor pairs on tongue (PMID 24191170); the companion pulse analysis ranges from poor to moderate (28664059); a single expert's self-consistency on pulse was 0.42 (27257530). These are among the lowest chance-corrected figures this record has encountered for a clinical assessment; the earlier version said 'some of the lowest ... recorded for any clinical assessment', which is a comparison across fields that no search behind this record supports, and it is withdrawn. In real patients, agreement on constitutional and functional entities such as agni sat between 0 and 0.4 while raw agreement on the final label reached 95% (30653338), which means the consensus label is not being produced by the component assessments in any traceable way. A 2024 vignette study (39183608) shows the disagreement persists when every clinician receives identical written case information, so it is not solely an artefact of hands-on technique.

INSTRUMENTATION. Pulse-acquisition hardware exists (Nadi Tarangini, 18002428, 2007) and a 2024 review counts 67 sensor papers (38815517). In the papers retrieved here the reference standard is the practitioner: the 2007 paper states the system 'is being evaluated by Ayurvedic practitioners', and the 2017 pilot (29103852) compares sensor positions, not diagnoses, and has no reference diagnosis at all. An instrument validated against practitioner judgement cannot be shown to exceed that judgement's reliability, which is the circularity a critic finding named; the record states it for the papers it has read and does not generalise it to the 67 it has not. The one Ayurveda-framed tongue-image classifier located (37702608) reports 99.17% accuracy with no statement of label provenance in its abstract.

CODING. ICD-11 Chapter 26 Module 2 (release 2026-01, held in a sibling repository snapshot) codes constitution patterns (SS50-SS56, prakriti by dosha) and per-dosha derangement stages (SR10-SR1E: prakopa, sanchaya, vriddhi, prasara, kshaya) and an ama state (SS15), but contains no entity for vikriti by name, no examination method and no grading of strength. The output of a vikriti assessment is thus internationally codeable; its method and warrant are not. The WHO's own Bulletin perspective (41180267) states that the chapter's inter-rater reliability requires dedicated study.

BOUNDED NEGATIVES. Within the searches named in modernCoverage: no operational definition of a vikriti state validated against an external criterion was located; no prospectively tested biomarker for dosha derangement, agni or ama was located; no study was located that tests whether a vikriti assessment predicts outcome or treatment response. These are statements about what was searched, not about the literature as a whole; DHARA, the AYUSH Research Portal, IEEE Xplore and Scopus were not searched. Beyond the reliability studies, the indexed literature retrieved on vikriti and its sub-concepts consists of narrative reviews that restate the classical categories in modern physiological vocabulary and propose candidate biomarkers as future work.

contested.question: Is nadi pariksha a legitimate part of classical Ayurvedic diagnosis?
positions: Traditional practice treats it as central and defends it by long historical use, and some Ayurvedic sources read scattered references to dhamani or sira in the samhitas as implicit pulse examination. Bhishagratna, himself a Kaviraj, concedes the absence from Sushruta and explains it as a division of labour with a separate pulse treatise (Introduction, p. lxvii).

Textual scholarship, and much Ayurvedic writing itself, accepts that Charaka and Sushruta contain no description of pulse examination and that the method appears later. Kaviratna states the absence flatly in his note at Indriya Sthana ('Suçruta also is silent, like Charaka, on the pulse'), and this record has located the method no earlier than Sharngadhara Purva Khanda 3. If so, the emblematic vikriti method has no samhita-period authority. Whether Sharngadhara is the EARLIEST text to carry it is a priority claim this record does not make; see notKnown.

contested.question: What is the relation between vikriti and the disease diagnosis?
positions: Vikriti is a separate axis: two patients with the same named disease can have different vikriti and therefore different treatment, which is the standard justification for individualisation. The classical ground for the separateness is khavaigunya and the conjunction requirement (Ca.Ni. IV): the same dosha produces different diseases by site and dushya.

The 2019 reliability data show agreement is better on disease entities than on constitutional and functional ones, which suggests the named disease is doing most of the work and the vikriti layer adds variance rather than information.

contested.question: Is high raw agreement on a final diagnosis evidence of a working method?
positions: Practitioners point to 95% agreement on the consensus final diagnosis as showing the method works in practice.

Methodologists point out that raw agreement is inflated by unequal prevalence of categories and that chance-corrected kappa for the same study's components was 0 to 0.4; the two figures cannot both describe a reproducible process.

contested.question: Can vikriti be assessed without first establishing prakriti, and is the pair circular?
positions: Charaka's definition makes vikriti deviation from the individual's own norm, so prakriti must be established first.

In practice many assessments grade current dosha states against a population norm rather than the individual's constitution, which is a different quantity. The literature retrieved here does not consistently distinguish the two, and no study comparing them was located.

The circularity, added on revision: in a sick patient prakriti is usually inferred from the same examination that produces the vikriti finding, so the reference and the deviation are read off one observation. The prakriti record carries the measurement side of this (prakriti inter-rater kappa 0.28 in PMID 24191170); if the reference is that unreliable, the deviation from it inherits the unreliability before any vikriti-specific error is added.

contested.question: Is ama a measurable state?
positions: It is treated clinically as assessable through tongue coating, appetite and other signs, and a validated ama instrument exists within the Ayurvedic literature. The classical sign list is now quoted (A.H.Su. 13/23-24), and ICD-11 TM2 carries an ama-state category (SS15).

No external biochemical or imaging correlate has been established in the literature retrieved here; the 2026 rheumatoid arthritis pilot is exploratory and the ama instrument's validation is internal to the same tradition, so the construct has no independent anchor.

contested.question: Does instrumenting the pulse escape the reliability problem?
positions: Device proponents hold that a sensor removes the subjectivity of finger palpation and that classifiers trained on recorded waveforms will be reproducible by construction.

Reproducibility of the signal is not validity of the label. In the papers retrieved here the labels come from practitioners (18002428) or there is no reference diagnosis at all (29103852), so a classifier can at best reproduce the practitioner's kappa-0.07 judgement more consistently. The field's own 2024 review concedes that 'procedure standardization is also required' (38815517). Added on revision after a critic finding; the circularity is stated for the retrieved papers, not asserted of the whole literature.

notKnown: What an operational definition of a vikriti state would be. No published definition specifying the observations, thresholds and combining rule required to assign a vikriti was located in the searches named in modernCoverage, so the assessment cannot be independently reproduced from any source this record has.
Whether any vikriti finding predicts treatment response or outcome. No prospective study testing this was located in the searches named in modernCoverage.
Whether the three-grade strength scale (strong / middling / weak) can be applied reproducibly. No reliability study of it was located, and none was specifically searched for.

Whether a vaidya's pulse finding carries information beyond rate and rhythm. The kappa of 0.07 is consistent with none. The instrumented work retrieved here (Nadi Tarangini, PMIDs 18002428 and 29103852) records the artery but either uses the practitioner as the reference or compares sensor positions without any diagnosis, so no study located here tests a practitioner's dosha reading against an instrumented measurement of the same artery as an independent criterion. Restated on revision; the earlier version said no study had tested pulse findings against instrumented measurement, which was too broad once the device literature was retrieved.
Whether tongue coating indexes anything beyond oral hygiene, smoking, hydration and medication; no study located here controlled for these while testing the ama association.
Whether agni has any measurable correlate. Candidate markers have been proposed in narrative reviews retrieved here but none was found to have been prospectively tested against an agni assessment.
Whether structured forms, training or image standardisation can raise agreement to usable levels. The one experience effect reported (p=0.04, small sample, unadjusted) is too weak to answer this.
How vikriti assessment should be documented for research. No agreed case record form was located, which is why the reliability studies retrieved here have each had to build their own item list.

What reference standard the sensor-based nadi pariksha literature uses. The 2024 review (38815517) counts 67 papers but its abstract does not say how their classification labels were obtained, and this record did not retrieve them individually. The circularity a critic finding asserted of the whole literature (that it validates against vaidya opinion) is confirmed here only for PMID 18002428 and cannot be asserted of the rest.

Where the disease labels in the tongue-image classification literature come from. The one Ayurveda-framed classifier located (37702608) reports 99.17% accuracy without stating label provenance, image-set size or evaluation protocol in its abstract; the full text was not read.

Whether Sharngadhara Samhita is the EARLIEST text to describe pulse examination, and what its date is. This record has located the method there and nowhere earlier among the texts it has retrieved, which is a statement about the retrieval; the 'c. 13th-14th century' date is from secondary literature and was not verified. Settling priority would need the Sanskrit of the other candidates named by the 2024 review (Ravana Samhita, Nadi Vijnana of Kanada) and a dating argument this record does not have.

What Yogaratnakara and Bhavaprakasha say in their own words about the eight-fold examination, and when they were composed. Neither was retrieved in any language; the attribution of the eight-fold list to Yogaratnakara is carried from secondary sources only. A critic's 'c. 17th c.' for Yogaratnakara was not adopted.

Which edition the archive.org Sharngadhara scan reproduces. The item carries no publisher, place or date metadata, and the verse text is quoted from a Tesseract OCR layer with regular conjunct errors. The normalised reading given in the record is this record's own and should be checked against the page images before publication.

Whether the classical texts stage ama in three steps (sama, pachyamana, nirama) or two. A critic finding named a three-stage sequence. What this record located is a two-state contrast, sama and nirama, in A.H.Su. 13/24 and a treatment rule keyed to it in 13/28-29. No verse naming pachyamana as a middle state was located in the Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana text searched, and the Charaka and Sushruta scans were not searched for it; the term may belong to the later fever literature. Scoped in rather than asserted.

Whether the sama / nirama judgement 'changes treatment immediately' in the general way a critic finding stated. A.H.Su. 13/28-29 supports one specific consequence (no expulsion of sama doshas until ripened); a survey of treatment rules keyed to the judgement across the texts was not made.

Whether khavaigunya and the sama / nirama judgement are in practice part of what clinicians record as vikriti, or are recorded separately. No case record form or practice survey retrieved here addresses this.

How clinicians select among the ICD-11 TM2 per-dosha stage codes (SR10-SR1E) and whether that selection is reproducible. The WHO's own Bulletin perspective (41180267) says the chapter's inter-rater reliability requires dedicated study; none was located.

Which standard-edition (Trikamji) verse numbers correspond to the Kaviratna aphorism numbers used throughout this record's Charaka citations (Vimana VIII 110 and the unnumbered vikriti passage; Nidana I 11; Nidana IV 3; Chikitsa XV 35-36 and 44-48). Kaviratna's offset is not constant across chapters and was not measured here except where the khavaigunya and dosha-dushya records had already done so by content. The earlier 'Vi. 8.94' mapping was never established by this project and has been withdrawn.

Whether the trividha pariksha (aptopadesha, pratyaksha, anumana) is correctly placed as the epistemic frame of vikriti assessment. The component is carried from general knowledge of Charaka Vimana IV and VIII and no passage was retrieved for it on this pass.

components.gloss: Charaka: 'an abnormal condition has been said to be a deviation from what is normal', assessed by explicit contrast with the patient's own prakriti. Kaviratna's footnote to aphorism 110 glosses the Sanskrit term: 'vikrititah has reference to the reverse of the above, i. e., to the abnormal condition that has set in', the 'above' being prakriti, 'the normal constitution in health'. The footnote is the translator's, but it fixes which Sanskrit word his English phrase renders.

Which of vata, pitta and kapha are disturbed, singly or in combination, and by how much (vriddhi, kshaya, or normal). Charaka's grading passage names 'faults (i. e., wind, bile, and phlegm)' among the things to be weighed; the vriddhi / kshaya vocabulary of degree is carried from the project's dosha records and is not quoted here.

Which of the seven tissues and which channels are affected. The dhatus are in Charaka's list of what must be weighed to grade the derangement ('constituent elements (of the body, such as juice, blood, flesh, fat, bones, marrow, and vital seed)'). The srotas item is NOT in that list; it enters through khavaigunya, the channel-site defect, which is now cited separately.

Seat or habitat of the disease, and time understood as both season of the year and the patient's age. Both are in Charaka's grading list, with Kaviratna's parenthetical glosses '(meaning seat or habitat of the disease)' and '(i. e., season of the year as also age of the patient)', which are the translator's and are marked as such.

The derangement is graded strong, middling or weak according to how far dhatu, dosha, prakriti, site and time agree with one another and how strong the cause and symptoms are. All three grades are now quoted: strong when the listed factors 'draw an agreement with one another' and cause and symptoms 'are possessed of strength'; of little strength 'when the reverse of this happens'; of middle strength when 'there is agreement between some only' and cause and symptoms are 'of middle strength'. Charaka also states the dependency outright: without weighing these particulars 'there can be no knowledge of the degree of strength of the disease'.

Vikriti is the second of Charaka's ten items for examining the patient: prakriti, vikriti, sara, samhanana, pramana, satmya, sattva, ahara-shakti, vyayama-shakti, vaya. Charaka frames the whole list as serving 'ascertainment of the measure of strength (of the patient)', which is the stated purpose of the examination, not diagnosis of a disease entity.

Nadi (pulse), mutra (urine), mala (stool), jihva (tongue), shabda (voice), sparsha (touch), drik (eyes), akriti (general appearance). This is the working method taught for vikriti assessment today, and it is post-classical. Pulse examination is absent from Charaka and Sushruta: both public-domain translators say so in their own notes, now quoted, and the earliest text in which this record has located it is the Sharngadhara Samhita, Purva Khanda chapter 3, whose colophon names the chapter after nadi pariksha, now quoted in Sanskrit. The eight-fold set as a named list is attributed by secondary literature to Yogaratnakara and is elaborated in Bhavaprakasha; neither has been retrieved for this record in any language, so that attribution is carried as located-and-paraphrased, not quoted. Dating: the 'c. 13th-14th century' commonly given for Sharngadhara is from secondary literature and is not verified here; no date is asserted for Yogaratnakara.

Charaka's three means of knowing: authoritative instruction (aptopadesha), direct perception (pratyaksha) and inference (anumana). The epistemic warrant under which vikriti findings are taken as knowledge. NOT sourced in this record: no passage stating the three pramanas was retrieved on this pass, so the component is carried from the project's general knowledge of Vimana IV and VIII and is flagged rather than left to look cited.

components.term: Khavaigunya as the locus of vikriti
components.gloss: The site defect that explains why a provoked dosha, circulating everywhere, produces disease in one place. Sushruta states it in one verse (Sutra XXIV, Bhishagratna pp. 235-236): the deranged humours 'give rise to a disease at the place in which they are incarcerated'. Charaka states it of circulating rasa (Chikitsa XV, Kaviratna's aphorism 36): 'in consequence of the fault of ether (i. e., the hollows of the ducts)' rasa becomes adherent and 'causes diverse diseases'. Charaka's Nidana IV adds the conjunction requirement, that manifestation of disease depends on the particular characteristics of cause, dosha and dushya together. This is the mechanism vikriti assessment is supposed to localise, which is why dosha vikriti alone does not determine the disease. The compound dosha-dushya-sammurchana used in modern teaching for this meeting is a modern term; see the project's record on it.

The judgement whether the disturbed dosha is bound up with undigested matter (sama) or free of it (nirama). Vagbhata gives the ten signs of sama doshas, 'srotorodha, balabhramsha, gaurava, anilamudhata, alasya, apakti, nishthiva, malasanga, aruchi, klama', with nirama as 'the reverse' (Ashtanga Hridaya Sutra 13/23-24), defines sama as doshas and dushyas 'conjoined with that ama' (13/27), and attaches the treatment consequence: sama doshas spread through the body are NOT to be expelled, 'like juice from an unripe fruit', but are first to be ripened with pachana, dipana, oleation and sudation and only then purified (13/28-29). Charaka's Chikitsa XV has the antecedent doctrine, that undigested food 'is a terrible poison' which, combining with excited bile, phlegm or wind, produces the diseases of each (Kaviratna's aphorisms 44-48). This is the vikriti judgement with the most direct treatment consequence in the located texts. A three-stage sama / pachyamana / nirama sequence was NOT located in any text retrieved here; see notKnown.

classical.verse: aphorism 110 in Kaviratna's numbering, printed after the aphorism
classical.establishes: The ten-fold examination of the patient, with vikriti ('the abnormal condition that has set in') as the second item and prakriti as the first. The sentence before it in the same run states the purpose: 'For ascertainment of the measure of strength (of the patient), these (ten) incidents beginning with (prakriti) the normal constitution in health, we shall explain here.'
classical.quote: Hence, the patient should be examined in respect of his normal constitution in health, of the abnormal condition that has set in, of the predominance of some particular element in his constitution (such as blood, or flesh, &c.), of his compactness or otherwise, the make of his proportions such as stature, &c., of what things are suitable to his constitution, of his mental disposition, of his power of eating, of his power of exercise, and of his age.

classical.verse: the prose immediately following Kaviratna's aphorism 115, which closes the prakriti section; no number is printed against this passage itself
classical.establishes: The definition of vikriti as deviation from normal, the list of factors to be weighed, and the explicit statement that grading disease strength depends on them. This is the whole of Charaka's statement about vikriti as such; no examination procedure is attached.
classical.quote: Next, as to abnormal conditions: an abnormal condition has been said to be a deviation from what is normal. In this connection, the physician should examine the abnormal condition, by observing the particulars, as regards strength, of cause, constituent elements (of the body, such as juice, blood, flesh, fat, bones, marrow, and vital seed) faults (i. e., wind, bile, and phlegm), nature or normal condition, and place (meaning seat or habitat of the disease), time (i. e., season of the year as also age of the patient). He should examine it by observing the symptoms of the patient as well. Without observing the particulars, as regards strength, of cause and the rest, there can be no knowledge of the degree of strength of the disease.

classical.chapter: Lesson VIII, continuation of the vikriti passage
classical.verse: the three grading sentences that follow the definition; the number printed after the last of them is OCR'd '*115' and is not asserted
classical.establishes: The three-grade strength scale (strong / middling / weak) is arrived at by whether the listed factors agree and by the strength of cause and symptoms. This is the nearest thing the classical text offers to an operational rule, and it is a rule about disease strength, not about which dosha is disturbed or how to find out. Extended on revision from the middle grade alone to all three grades.
classical.quote: That disease is strong (or violent) in which the constituent elements (of the body, the faults, nature or normal condition), place (or seat of disease), and time (that is, season or age), draw an agreement with one another, but whose cause or causes and symptoms are possessed of strength. When the reverse of this happens, the disease is regarded as of little strength. That disease is regarded as of middle strength in which among the constituent elements, faults, &c., there is agreement between some only, and whose cause or causes, and symptoms, are possessed of middle strength.

classical.verse: opening sentence of the block Kaviratna numbers 11; the number is printed two sentences later, after 'agreeably to truth'
classical.establishes: Links vikriti assessment back to the nidana-panchaka frame: the disease state is assessed through the five-limbed considerations. The sentences immediately before it in the same block define 'Solution of doubt (Vikalpa)' as 'the ascertainment of the measure in which the faults, existing in a state of union, have been excited', and state that 'the distinctions of Strength and Time (in respect of disease) are dependant on the season ... day, night, the hours of eating', which parallels the Vimana VIII grading factors.
classical.quote: Hence the physician, with unafflicted mind and intelligence, should duly examine diseases by the considerations of Cause and the rest.

classical.verse: the opening passage of the chapter. Bhishagratna prints NO number against it; the locator is the page.
classical.establishes: Sushruta's parallel examination list, which includes previous medication and endurance but does not use the prakriti/vikriti contrast as its organising axis. 'The nature of the disease' is the nearest item to vikriti.
classical.quote: A physician should first observe the vital condition (Ayu) of the patient before commencing the medical treatment. After that, the nature of the disease, the country and season of the year in which it has made its appearance, as well as the state of digestion, age, body, strength, disposition, habit, previous medicine, natural temperament and the power of endurance of the patient, etc. should be observed and carefully examined.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna, public domain

classical.verse: 1-4, with the chapter colophon
classical.establishes: Pulse examination as a diagnostic method, located in a text and quoted. The chapter opens with the site of examination (the artery at the root of the thumb), correlates pulse gait with provoked vata, pitta and kapha, and continues (verses 5-11, retrieved but not quoted) with sannipata, two-dosha, fatal, febrile, emotional, mandagni and sama pulses. Its colophon names the chapter after nadi pariksha. This is the earliest text in which this record has located pulse examination; whether it is the earliest text in which it occurs is a priority claim this record cannot make from one retrieved text and does not. The record previously carried this as located-and-paraphrased with no quote; upgraded on revision.
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

classical.chapter: Lesson I, Kaviratna's footnote to the opening of the Division
classical.verse: footnote; no aphorism
classical.establishes: A public-domain, attributed statement that Charaka and Sushruta contain no pulse examination, from someone who had translated the former in full. The record previously asserted this absence on the strength of the project's own search of the two texts; it now has an addressable witness as well. The same passage appears, almost word for word, in Kaviratna's prefatory synopsis of the Indriya Sthana in the unpaginated front matter of the same fascicule, which is not separately cited because its page cannot be given.
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

classical.chapter: Introduction, the paragraph on the Nidana Sthana
classical.verse: none
classical.establishes: A second public-domain translator, of the other samhita, stating that his text has no pulse instructions. Together with Kaviratna's note this gives the record two attributed witnesses for the absence it asserts, from opposite sides of the question (Kaviratna hostile to pulse diagnosis, Bhishagratna a defender of it).
classical.withheld: nobody has yet read this quotation against its printed source, and an unchecked quotation is not published here

classical.establishes: Secondary literature attributes the eight-fold examination (nadi, mutra, mala, jihva, shabda, sparsha, drik, akriti) as a named set to Yogaratnakara and its elaboration to Bhavaprakasha. NEITHER TEXT WAS RETRIEVED FOR THIS RECORD IN ANY LANGUAGE. No public-domain English translation is known to this record and no Sanskrit edition was located on this pass, so the attribution is carried as located-and-paraphrased from secondary sources, with no quote and no verse. No date is asserted for either text; a critic finding gave 'c. 17th c.' for Yogaratnakara and that figure is not adopted here because nothing retrieved supports it.

classical.verse: Bhishagratna's 'Authoritative verse on the Subject' at the close of the disease enumeration; the Sanskrit is Su.Su.24/10 per the project's khavaigunya record, which carries the verse
classical.establishes: The site-selection doctrine in one sentence: provoked doshas run everywhere, disease appears where they lodge. This is the mechanism a vikriti assessment is supposed to localise, and the reason a dosha finding alone does not identify a disease. Added on revision after a critic finding; cross-reference data/concepts/khavaigunya.json.
classical.quote: The deranged and aggravated humours, freely coursing through the body, give rise to a disease at the place in which they are incarcerated owing to an obstruction in their natural passage.
classical.translator: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna, public domain

classical.verse: Chikitsa Sthana, Lesson XV (Grahani-dosha Chikitsita), Kaviratna's aphorisms 35-37, pp. 1415-1416. Numbering quoted is Kaviratna's own printed numbering, not the Trikamji vulgate, and Kaviratna prints the number after the aphorism; the quote's final sentence falls inside his 37, whose marker stands after the following sentence ('...as also the food that is eaten.* 37'). Verified in the archive.org OCR of Kaviratna, item BIUSante_47357.
classical.establishes: Charaka's statement of the same site doctrine, with rasa rather than dosha as what lodges, followed by the sentence extending it to the doshas: where they 'become immovable (or adherent) in a particular place ... they become excited and cause diverse diseases'. Added on revision after a critic finding; cross-reference data/concepts/khavaigunya.json.
classical.quote: The 'dhatu' called 'Rasa' (that is, the juicy matter into which food is first converted) is continuously diffused through every part of the body simultaneously, by the life-breath called 'Vyana' whose function it is to diffuse. 35 If in consequence of the fault of ether (i. e., the hollows of the ducts), 'Rasa,' while it is being diffused (by the life-breath called 'Vyana'), becomes immovable (i. e., adherent), it causes diverse diseases, like clouds (when they mass together in the welkin owing to some obstruction) causing downpours below. 36 Even this is what happens in respect of faults when they become immovable (or adherent) in a particular place; that is, they become excited and cause diverse diseases.
classical.checked: checked, and the claim was narrowed

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorism 3, printed after the aphorism
classical.establishes: The conjunction requirement: whether a disease manifests, and how fully, depends on cause, dosha and dushya together. This is Charaka's own statement of the ground the modern compound dosha-dushya-sammurchana names, and it is the reason a vikriti assessment that stops at the dosha is incomplete by the text's own standard. Added on revision after a critic finding; cross-reference data/concepts/dosha-dushya-sammurchana.json, which establishes that the compound itself is modern.
classical.quote: Here (in the world), verily, from the particular characteristics of 'Nidana' or causes, 'doshas' or faults, and 'dushyas' or the ingredients or 'dhatus' composing the body, arise the manifestation, the non-manifestation, and the partial manifestation of diseases in general.

classical.verse: Kaviratna's aphorisms 44-45 (last sentence only) to 48, printed after the aphorisms
classical.establishes: The antecedent in Charaka of the sama-dosha doctrine: undigested matter combining with each excited dosha produces that dosha's diseases. This is what the later sama / nirama judgement sorts for. Added on revision after a critic finding; cross-reference data/concepts/ama-formation.json.
classical.quote: The food in the stomach that is not digested is a terrible poison. 44-45 Combining with excited bile, this undigested food, which becomes poison, produces burning of the skin, thirst, diseases of the mouth, sour bile, and other ailments born of (excited bile). 46 Combining with (excited) phlegm, it produces phthisis, inflammation of the Schneiderian membrane, gonorrhoea, and other diseases born of (excited phlegm). Combining with the (excited) wind, it produces diverse diseases that are born of the (excited) wind. 47 When it goes into the urine, that poison causes diseases of the urine. When it goes into the stools, it causes diseases of the abdomen. When combined with 'Rasa' and the rest, it produces diverse diseases born of 'Rasa' and the rest. 48

classical.establishes: The ten signs by which a disturbed dosha is judged sama (bound with ama) and the definition of nirama as their reverse. This is the located classical content of the sama / nirama judgement. The ama-formation record carried this locus as 'located' without text; the Sanskrit is now quoted. Added on revision after a critic finding.

classical.establishes: The definition of sama as a state of both doshas and dushyas, which makes the sama / nirama judgement a statement about the whole deranged state and not only about the dosha. Immediately preceding it, verses 25 and 26 give two rival accounts of ama's origin (weak agni leaving the first dhatu uncooked; or greatly vitiated doshas mixing with one another), which the ama-formation record treats. Added on revision.

classical.establishes: The treatment consequence that makes the sama / nirama judgement the vikriti decision with the most immediate practical effect in the located texts: sama doshas are not to be expelled until ripened. The record states this consequence only as far as this passage carries it; it does not generalise to 'the one judgement that changes treatment immediately', which is a critic's phrase and would need a survey of treatment rules this record has not made. Added on revision.
